00d3d57a5195.title: Wan 2.2 5B Fun Inpaint
00d3d57a5195.description: Efficient video inpainting from start and end frames. 5B model delivers quick iterations for testing workflows.
00d3d57a5195.metaDescription: Efficient video inpainting workflow using Wan2.2 model for creative video generation and quick iterations.
00d3d57a5195.extendedDescription:
The 'Wan 2.2 5B Fun Inpaint' workflow is designed for efficient video inpainting, leveraging the power of the Wan2.2 model. This workflow is particularly useful for generating video content by interpolating between start and end frames, allowing for creative exploration and testing of video generation techniques. The workflow employs a series of nodes, including KSampler for sampling, CLIPTextEncode for text prompt encoding, and VAEDecode for decoding latent variables into visual outputs. By using the Wan2.2 model, this workflow ensures high-quality video generation with quick iteration times, making it ideal for both experimentation and production scenarios.

Technically, the workflow is structured into several key steps. Initially, models are loaded using nodes like UNETLoader and VAELoader, setting the stage for video generation. The process continues with the creation of prompts using the CLIPTextEncode node, which guides the visual style and content of the video. The workflow then specifies the start image and video parameters, such as size and length, using nodes like LoadImage and CreateVideo. Finally, the video is generated and saved using the SaveVideo node, completing the inpainting process. This structured approach makes the workflow both efficient and flexible, catering to a wide range of video generation needs.
howToUse: Load the Wan 2.2 5B Fun Inpaint workflow in ComfyUI.
Use the UNETLoader and VAELoader nodes to load the necessary models.
Input your desired text prompt using the CLIPTextEncode node to guide the video content.
Set the start image and configure video parameters like size and length using the LoadImage and CreateVideo nodes.
Run the workflow to generate the video using the inpainting technique.
Save your generated video with the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating time-lapse videos with artistic inpainting effects.
Generating experimental video content for social media.
Producing video art installations with unique visual styles.
Testing and iterating video generation techniques quickly.
Developing educational content with dynamic visual elements.

0136284ecc19.title: cinematic_annotate_video
0136284ecc19.description: Cinematic Annotate turns one clean image into adirector-style camera-path markup, converts it into a Seedance 2.0 motion prompt, and generates a clean cinematic video from the original frame.
0136284ecc19.metaDescription: Turn one clean image into a cinematic video. Auto-annotate camera moves, convert to Seedance 2.0, and render smooth motion with ByteDance2ReferenceNode.
0136284ecc19.extendedDescription:
cinematic_annotate_video turns a single clean image into a short, smooth, cinematic shot by auto-writing a director-style camera path and translating it into a Seedance 2.0 motion prompt. The workflow starts with LoadImage and passes your frame into GeminiImage2Node, which analyzes the scene and generates camera-path markup using the "Nano Banana 2" annotation style. That markup is then refined/formatted by GeminiNode into a Seedance 2.0 motion specification.

The Seedance 2.0 prompt and your original image are fed into ByteDance2ReferenceNode to synthesize the motion while preserving the look of the source frame. PreviewImage and PreviewAny help you inspect the input frame and the auto-generated text prompts before you commit to a render. Finally, SaveVideo writes the result to disk. Groups are organized for clarity: Annotate Image (image analysis and camera notes), Prompt (LLM formatting to Seedance 2.0), and Seedance 2.0 (reference-driven video generation).
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the Annotate Image, Prompt, and Seedance 2.0 groups to review the node chain.
Configure GeminiImage2Node and GeminiNode (select your Gemini model and add credentials if required). These nodes create the director-style camera notes and convert them to Seedance 2.0.
Drop a clean, high-quality source frame into LoadImage. Use PreviewImage to confirm the frame is uncluttered and well-lit.
Run the Annotate Image group to generate the director-style camera-path markup (Nano Banana 2 style). Use PreviewAny to inspect the text output.
Run the Prompt group to convert the markup into a Seedance 2.0 motion prompt. Make any needed edits to timing or move intensity if the node exposes those fields.
Run the Seedance 2.0 group to synthesize the video with ByteDance2ReferenceNode and save it with SaveVideo. Use PreviewAny/PreviewImage to check frames and verify the motion before final export.
suggestedUseCases: Previsualization for film: Block out dolly/boom/zoom/arc moves on a single concept frame.
Product hero shots: Smooth parallax, gentle push-ins, or orbit moves from a studio product photo.
Travel and architecture: Cinematic pans and tilts across landmarks from a single postcard-like image.
UI/landing page motion: Subtle push/slide camera moves to bring static hero images to life.
Storyboarding: Rapid camera-move iterations on an illustrated keyframe.

faqItems.question: What exactly is Seedance 2.0 in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Seedance 2.0 is a motion-prompt format describing camera moves (e.g., path, timing, easing). GeminiNode formats the camera-path annotation into this schema, which ByteDance2ReferenceNode uses to drive the reference-based video generation.

faqItems.question: Do I need an internet connection or API key?
faqItems.answer: If your GeminiImage2Node/GeminiNode are configured to call a cloud Gemini API, you will need valid credentials and an internet connection. Check those nodes’ settings in ComfyUI and add your key or switch to a local provider if supported.

faqItems.question: How can I get cleaner, more stable motion?
faqItems.answer: Start with a clean, high-resolution image with clear subject/background separation. Keep camera moves moderate (avoid extreme zooms/rolls), and adjust duration/easing in the Seedance 2.0 prompt for smoother acceleration. Use PreviewAny to validate the generated motion text before rendering.

faqItems.question: Can I use multiple images or longer clips?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is designed for a single reference frame and a short cinematic move. For multi-shot sequences or longer durations, replicate the pipeline per shot or extend the Seedance 2.0 prompt and ByteDance2ReferenceNode settings if the node exposes longer frame counts.

02b3722db38c.title: Wan2.2-S2V Audio-Driven Video Generation
02b3722db38c.description: Transform static images and audio into dynamic videos with perfect synchronization and minute-level generation.
02b3722db38c.metaDescription: Audio-driven video in ComfyUI: turn a photo + audio into synced Wan 2.2 S2V videos with chunked extension, first-frame fix, and optional lightning LoRA.
02b3722db38c.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single reference image and an audio track into a synchronized video using the Wan 2.2 S2V (sound-to-video) model. It loads the Wan backbone with UNETLoader, CLIPLoader, and VAELoader, and sets the correct schedule via ModelSamplingSD3. Your text prompt is encoded by CLIPTextEncode, while the audio is processed by AudioEncoderLoader and AudioEncoderEncode. These signals, together with the image from LoadImage, drive WanSoundImageToVideo to synthesize motion that follows the rhythm and phrasing of the audio. The KSampler controls steps, CFG, and seed; VAEDecode converts latents to frames; and CreateVideo assembles the final clip.

Two engineering details make the workflow practical for production: a first-frame stabilization and scalable length. The Fix overbaked first frame group uses LatentCut and LatentConcat to duplicate the initial latent frame before decoding, then discards the first decoded frame to avoid the common VAE “overbaked” look on frame 0. For long clips, the Video S2V Extend subgraphs let you chain segments in chunks (77 frames by default) using LatentCut/LatentConcat, so you can build minute-level videos without blowing up VRAM. The workflow also supports a lightning path: with a Wan 2.2 lightning LoRA you can sample in 4 steps (recommended CFG ~1.0). If you prefer quality and stability, use the standard path at ~20 steps (CFG ~6.0).
howToUse: Step 1 – Load models: In the Step 1 - Load models group, point UNETLoader to a Wan 2.2 S2V checkpoint (e.g., wan2.2_s2v_14B_fp8_scaled.safetensors). Ensure CLIPLoader, VAELoader, and ModelSamplingSD3 are connected to the same model family. If your graph includes a lightning LoRA path, keep it disabled for a first baseline run.

Step 2 – Upload audio & reference image: Use LoadImage for your subject image (frontal or 3/4 portrait works best) and LoadAudio for the driving audio. AudioEncoderLoader and AudioEncoderEncode will extract conditioning from the audio to drive motion and lip-sync.

Step 3 – Prompt and negatives: Enter your description in CLIPTextEncode (e.g., “The man is playing the guitar. He looks down at his hands playing the guitar and sings affectionately and gently.”). Add a negative prompt to suppress artifacts (the provided Chinese negative list is a good starting point).

Step 4 – Sampler and batch settings: In Sampler settings and Step 3 - Batch settings, choose steps/CFG/seed and set resolution, FPS, and total frames. Recommended: with lightning LoRA use 4 steps, CFG ≈ 1.0; without lightning LoRA use ~20 steps, CFG ≈ 6.0. Keep seed fixed for repeatability.

Step 5 – Generate and export: Run the graph. WanSoundImageToVideo produces the video latents; the Fix overbaked first frame group duplicates the first latent and later trims the first decoded frame; VAEDecode turns latents into images; CreateVideo assembles the frames into a video. Note: CreateVideo typically outputs a silent MP4—mux your audio afterward if needed.

Step 6 – Extend to longer duration (optional): For longer clips, copy one Video S2V Extend subgraph (Ctrl+C, then Ctrl+Shift+V) per extra chunk you need. Each added subgraph extends the sequence by the chunk length (default 77 frames). Keep parameters (resolution, FPS, CFG, seed) consistent across chunks for smoother continuity, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Music covers and singing portraits with accurate lip-sync from a single photo.
Talking-head explainers driven by voiceover for tutorials or product demos.
Podcast or interview snippets that animate a static host image for social sharing.
Audio-reactive teaser clips (head nods, subtle expressions) from brand artwork.
Quick lyric or narration reels where the image animates in sync with TTS.

faqItems.question: How do I get longer videos without running out of VRAM?
faqItems.answer: Use the Video S2V Extend subgraphs. Each one adds a new chunk (77 frames by default) by slicing and appending latents with LatentCut and LatentConcat. Duplicate the subgraph per extra segment you need. Keep seed, resolution, FPS, and sampler settings consistent across chunks for smooth transitions.

faqItems.question: Why is the first frame washed out or overexposed?
faqItems.answer: Some VAEs overbake the very first decoded frame. The Fix overbaked first frame group duplicates the first latent before decoding and discards the first decoded frame afterward. Keep this enabled to avoid the issue; disable it only if your VAE doesn’t show the artifact.

faqItems.question: Should I use the lightning LoRA or the standard 20-step path?
faqItems.answer: Lightning LoRA is much faster (about 4 steps, CFG ≈ 1.0) but can reduce detail or stability. The standard path (≈20 steps, CFG ≈ 6.0) is slower but usually cleaner. If you see quality drops or mismatched LoRA keys, switch to the 20-step workflow. You can also A/B test both paths on a short clip before committing.

faqItems.question: Does the exported video include audio?
faqItems.answer: Typically CreateVideo outputs a silent MP4 and does not mux audio. The audio is used for motion conditioning via AudioEncoderEncode but isn’t embedded. To combine, mux your audio with the result in post (e.g., with ffmpeg: ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -i audio.wav -c copy -shortest out.mp4).

0309de53eb52.title: Interior Design - Add furniture into a Render
0309de53eb52.description: This workflow adds your input furniture into a render. It uses a manual mask to crop around the target area and generates your furniture into the scene at the highest pixel fidelity.
0309de53eb52.metaDescription: Tutorial: Add furniture into interior renders with manual masking, color transfer, high-fidelity inpainting, and seamless stitching in ComfyUI.
0309de53eb52.extendedDescription:
This workflow teaches you how to insert a furniture asset into an interior render with clean edges, correct lighting, and high pixel fidelity. It combines manual masking (Painter) with smart inpainting and patch-based upscaling to keep your room render sharp. The core flow crops the masked region with InpaintCropImproved, synthesizes and blends the furniture using ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2, then stitches the result back into the original image with InpaintStitchImproved so the full canvas remains unchanged outside your edit.

You’ll load your room render and the furniture reference via LoadImage, optionally sanitize transparency with ImageRemoveAlpha+ to avoid halo artifacts, and harmonize colors with ColorTransfer so the inserted piece matches the scene’s lighting. PrimitiveStringMultiline holds any guiding text (e.g., materials or style cues) for the generative step. PreviewImage and ImageCompare help you iterate quickly, and SaveImage captures the final composite. The result is a practical, repeatable edit pipeline for product visualization, staging, and design reviews.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then in the INPUTS group set your room render in a LoadImage node and your furniture asset (PNG/JPG) in another LoadImage. Enter optional guidance text (e.g., material, finish, shadow hints) in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node.
If either image has an alpha channel, route it through ImageRemoveAlpha+ to prevent transparency halos during color transfer and inpainting.
Use the Painter node to brush a mask roughly where the furniture should appear. Keep edges slightly outside the intended silhouette so the model can generate natural contact points and shadows.
Enable ColorTransfer to harmonize the furniture reference with the room’s color temperature. If the preview looks too warm/cool, toggle or adjust ColorTransfer settings before regenerating.

Run the inpaint pass: InpaintCropImproved extracts a high-res patch around your mask, ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 integrates the furniture guided by your reference and text hints, and InpaintStitchImproved merges the patch back into the original. Use PreviewImage and ImageCompare to review before/after.
Iterate by refining the mask, prompt text, or model parameters (steps/seed if exposed in ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2). When satisfied, export the result via SaveImage in the SAVE IMAGES group.
suggestedUseCases: Staging product shots: Drop catalog furniture into architect-provided room renders for quick sales visuals.
Design iterations: Test different sofas, tables, or lighting fixtures in the same scene without re-rendering the whole room.

faqItems.question: Do I need a perfectly cut-out furniture image?
faqItems.answer: A clean reference helps, but it doesn’t have to be perfect. Use Painter to define the placement mask, and let the inpainting step refine edges and contact areas. If your PNG has alpha, consider using ImageRemoveAlpha+ to avoid edge halos.

faqItems.question: How do I control size and placement of the furniture?
faqItems.answer: Placement and scale are primarily guided by the mask region and the reference image. Resize the furniture asset before loading if needed, and adjust the mask to set footprint and orientation. Include the floor/wall contact area in the mask for better grounding and shadows.

faqItems.question: Why do the colors look slightly off after insertion?
faqItems.answer: Lighting and white balance may differ between the reference and the room. Enable ColorTransfer to harmonize tones. If it still looks off, tweak your prompt with lighting cues (e.g., warm afternoon light) and ensure the mask includes nearby context for more accurate color adaptation.

faqItems.question: Will this reduce the quality of my original render?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow edits only within the mask. InpaintCropImproved processes a cropped, high-resolution patch, and InpaintStitchImproved composites it back so the rest of the image remains untouched and full-resolution.

04479f67187d.title: MiniMax Music 3: Text to Music
04479f67187d.description: Create full-length songs from text prompts with MiniMax Music 3, generating complete 5-minute tracks with stable structure and high-fidelity audio. Input a structured caption describing lyrics, style, mood, and arrangement, and receive a finished song as output. Ideal for music producers prototyping demos, and content creators needing original background tracks.
04479f67187d.metaDescription: Generate 5-minute songs from text captions and lyrics in ComfyUI using MiniMax Music 3. Includes structured prompts and SaveAudioAdvanced export.
04479f67187d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns structured text into full-length music using MiniMax Music 3. At its core is the MiniMax Music 3 generator node (UUID: ac99f841-a3de-4329-9564-953b81cf9e16), which accepts two key inputs: a Caption describing style, mood, tempo, instrumentation, and arrangement, and optional Lyrics formatted with section tags like [intro], [verse], [chorus], [bridge], and [outro]. The node renders a complete track—up to five minutes—with stable song structure and high-fidelity audio. A MarkdownNote block in the graph documents the prompt schema so you can quickly copy, tweak, and version your captions and lyrics inside the UI.

Under the hood, you can choose between two model weights: minimax_music3_dit_fp16.safetensors (recommended when VRAM allows) and minimax_music3_dit_int8_convrot.safetensors (optimized for lower VRAM). The generator node produces an audio tensor that is written to disk via SaveAudioAdvanced, where you control filename, format, and sample rate. The result is a finished, arranged song suitable for prototypes, background scores, and content production without leaving ComfyUI.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the MarkdownNote to review the prompt schema for Caption and Lyrics (section tags like [intro], [verse], [chorus]).

Download one model file and place it where the node expects (e.g., ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models): minimax_music3_dit_fp16.safetensors (higher fidelity, more VRAM) or minimax_music3_dit_int8_convrot.safetensors (low VRAM).

In the MiniMax Music 3 generator node (UUID: ac99f841-a3de-4329-9564-953b81cf9e16), paste a well-structured Caption describing genre, mood, tempo, key instruments, and arrangement. Optionally paste Lyrics with section tags.
Set generation controls on the node: song duration (up to 300 seconds), and any available seed/reproducibility options. Keep sections in your lyrics aligned with the requested duration.
Configure SaveAudioAdvanced: choose output path/filename, audio format (e.g., WAV/FLAC), and sample rate. This node will write the rendered track to disk.
Queue and run the workflow. If the structure or mix needs refinement, iterate: adjust the Caption (e.g., instrument balance, energy per section) or edit Lyrics, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid demo prototyping for producers and songwriters using structured captions and lyrics.
Original background music for video, podcasts, or livestreams with clear, stable sections.
Advertising and social clips that need on-brief genre, mood, and arrangement quickly.
Temp tracks for film/game previsualization before studio recording.
Instrumental stems for practice or rehearsal by omitting the Lyrics input.

faqItems.question: Which model variant should I use: fp16 or int8?
faqItems.answer: Use minimax_music3_dit_fp16.safetensors if you have enough GPU VRAM for best fidelity and stability. Choose minimax_music3_dit_int8_convrot.safetensors when VRAM is limited; it’s more memory-efficient with a potential slight quality trade-off.

faqItems.question: How should I structure the Caption and Lyrics for best results?
faqItems.answer: Keep the Caption explicit: genre, mood, tempo/BPM, key instruments, production style, and arrangement (e.g., intro–verse–chorus–bridge–outro). For Lyrics, include clear section tags like [intro], [verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]. Keep lines concise and align section lengths with your requested duration.

faqItems.question: Can it generate vocals or is it instrumental only?
faqItems.answer: If you provide Lyrics with section tags, the model will attempt to render vocal-like parts following your text and structure. If you leave Lyrics empty and supply only a Caption, it will generate instrumental music.

faqItems.question: What is the maximum song length and how do I set it?
faqItems.answer: The workflow supports up to about 5 minutes (300 seconds). Set the duration parameter on the MiniMax Music 3 generator node and keep your arrangement (in Caption/Lyrics) sized to fit that length.

04bae0edf048.title: ChronoEdit 14B: Image Edit
04bae0edf048.description: Image editing powered by video models' dynamic understanding, creating physically plausible results while preserving character and style consistency.
04bae0edf048.metaDescription: ChronoEdit 14B ComfyUI workflow for prompt-based single-image edits using Wan 2.1 video-model priors, preserving identity, style, and lighting consistency.
04bae0edf048.extendedDescription:
ChronoEdit 14B: Image Edit is a ComfyUI workflow that repurposes a video model’s dynamic understanding to make single-image edits that look physically plausible while preserving character and style consistency. The core path is simple—LoadImage feeds your source into a ChronoEdit subgraph (node id 2b61e18f-9327-49e6-98af-da8e557c2336), and the result is written out with SaveImage. The heavy lifting happens inside that subgraph: it loads the Wan 2.1/ChronoEdit weights, encodes your prompt with a large text encoder (UMT5 XXL), and runs an edit-oriented denoising pass designed to keep structure, lighting, and identity intact.

Technically, leveraging a video model for a single frame means the sampler benefits from priors that normally enforce temporal stability—here, they help maintain geometry and style during edits. Prompts are handled by a UMT5 XXL text encoder (for example, umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors), which gives strong language guidance for nuanced changes. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline guidance, while the Subgraph encapsulates typical controls like positive/negative prompt text, edit strength, steps, CFG guidance, seed, and resolution. The result is a practical, prompt-driven image editor that excels at gentle to moderate changes without breaking identity or composition.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and review the on-canvas MarkdownNote for tips and links (see the Subgraph guide).

Install required models: place ChronoEdit/Wan 2.1 weights per their instructions and download the UMT5 XXL text encoder (umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors) to ComfyUI/models/text_encoders (or the directory specified by the model pack).
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image. Keep the input resolution reasonable for your GPU (start around 512–1024 px on the long side).

Select the ChronoEdit subgraph (node id 2b61e18f-9327-49e6-98af-da8e557c2336) and set your positive prompt and (optionally) a negative prompt. Adjust edit strength, steps, CFG guidance, and seed. Lower strength for subtle edits; raise it for stronger changes.
Execute the workflow. If you encounter out-of-memory errors, reduce resolution, steps, or batch size. Keep seed fixed while iterating to compare parameter tweaks consistently.
Inspect the output from SaveImage. If details drift or identity shifts, lower edit strength, refine the prompt with concrete descriptors, and try a few nearby seeds.
suggestedUseCases: Character-preserving restyling (e.g., changing outfit color or material while keeping face and pose consistent).
Lighting and mood adjustments (warmer/cooler tone, time-of-day shifts) that remain physically plausible.
Brand or product look alignment across campaign images without breaking geometry.
Subtle environmental edits (weathering, patina, minor background harmonization) with minimal artifacts.
Key art refinements where composition must stay intact but details need to evolve.

faqItems.question: How is this different from a standard img2img or inpainting workflow?
faqItems.answer: ChronoEdit uses a video-model backbone (Wan 2.1) adapted for editing a single frame. Those temporal priors translate into stronger structural and style consistency during edits. You prompt for changes much like img2img, but results tend to preserve lighting, geometry, and identity more reliably. Masks aren’t required for global edits; for local changes, keep edit strength modest and use precise prompt phrasing.

faqItems.question: What hardware do I need?
faqItems.answer: This workflow targets NVIDIA GPUs in ComfyUI. A modern CUDA-capable GPU with 12–16 GB of VRAM is a practical starting point for 512–768 px edits. If you hit out-of-memory errors, reduce resolution, steps, or batch size. Larger images or heavier settings may require more VRAM.

faqItems.question: Where do I put the text encoder and model files?
faqItems.answer: Place the UMT5 XXL text encoder (e.g., umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors) into ComfyUI/models/text_encoders or the directory specified by the model pack you’re using. Install Wan 2.1/ChronoEdit weights per their documentation. The Subgraph will reference these paths when running.

faqItems.question: How do I keep identity and style consistent across edits?
faqItems.answer: Use clear, repeatable descriptors in your positive prompt, keep the seed fixed while iterating, and start with a lower edit strength. Increase strength only as needed. Negative prompts can help suppress unwanted style drift. Make small, incremental changes to steps and CFG to fine-tune fidelity versus creativity.

0553e57852fe.title: One Button Transformation
0553e57852fe.description:
Create transformation videos where a cube, sphere, capsule, or custom shape appears on a table with a button on top. A hand presses the button and the object transforms into a person, character, or item based on your reference images.

The workflow automatically uses the colors and theme of your subject to generate matching first and last frames while keeping the environment and style consistent throughout the transformation.

Simply provide your reference images, choose a shape, generate the frames, and feed them into Seedance to create the final animation effect.

Includes support for both Seedance 2.0 for higher-quality results and Seedance 1.5 as a more affordable alternative that still produces solid results.
0553e57852fe.metaDescription: Create a one-button transformation video in ComfyUI: shape-to-subject metamorphosis with matched first/last frames and Seedance 2.0/1.5 animation.
0553e57852fe.extendedDescription:
One Button Transformation is a guided ComfyUI pipeline that turns a simple tabletop prop into your subject with a single press, then animates the metamorphosis. You provide one or more reference images of a person, character, or product; the workflow builds a color-matched first frame where your chosen shape (cube, sphere, capsule, or a custom shape you describe) sits on a table with a button. It then creates a stylistically consistent last frame where your subject appears in the same scene, ready for a seamless transformation. Under the hood, the First Frame and Last Frame groups use the GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2V2 stack to render images based on your prompt and references, with SaveImage capturing each output and ImageConcanate available to quickly compare frames side-by-side. 

For motion, the Seedance 2.0 group uses ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode to synthesize in-between frames for higher-fidelity transitions, while the Seedance 1.5 Version group relies on ByteDanceFirstLastFrameNode for a faster, more affordable alternative. LoadImage brings in your references and previously generated frames, and SaveVideo exports the final clip. Because the workflow conditions both frames on your subject’s palette and scene description, the environment, lighting, and style are kept consistent from first to last frame—resulting in a convincing “button press” reveal animation with minimal setup.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the First Frame group. Use the LoadImage node(s) to add your subject/reference image(s). In the prompt section (GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2V2), specify the shape you want on the table (e.g., “a glossy red cube with a button on top”). Run only this group to generate the starting frame, then capture it with SaveImage.

Preview the result and, if included, use ImageConcanate to compare different tries. Tweak wording to control materials (wood/metal table), lighting, and color accents pulled from your subject until the first frame looks right.

Before generating the last frame, bypass/disable the First Frame group so only the Last Frame group is active. In the Last Frame group, set the first image input to the first frame you just made and the second image input to your original subject/reference image. You can click the image field next to the “image” label to select saved outputs. Run the Last Frame group and SaveImage the result.
Verify that the last frame matches the scene perspective and style of the first frame while clearly revealing the subject. If needed, adjust the prompt for pose, scale, or camera height and re-run.

Choose your animation path: for best quality, open the Seedance 2.0 group and feed the first frame and last frame into ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode. For a faster/cheaper run, use the Seedance 1.5 Version group with ByteDanceFirstLastFrameNode. Set duration/frame count (and any available motion settings) as desired, then execute.
Preview the clip and export it with SaveVideo. If you see flicker or drift, nudge the prompts for tighter scene description, keep both frames stylistically aligned, and re-run the Seedance step.
suggestedUseCases: Product reveal: a branded cube transforms into the actual product when the button is pressed.
Character introduction: a capsule morphs into a game or animated character in a consistent scene.
Logo-to-hero: a simple sphere in brand colors becomes a mascot or key visual for social teasers.
Prop-to-person montage: tabletop object turns into a portrait for creator or team intros.
Item evolution: basic shape morphs into a gadget or weapon for game asset previews.

faqItems.question: How do I choose the shape and make sure the button appears?
faqItems.answer: Describe the shape directly in the prompt within the First Frame group (e.g., “a matte white capsule with a small black button on top, on a wooden table”). The GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2V2 block uses this text to render the prop. Use terms like cube, sphere, capsule, or a custom shape description.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between Seedance 2.0 and 1.5 here?
faqItems.answer: Both take your first and last frames and synthesize in-betweens. The Seedance 2.0 group (ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode) generally produces higher-quality motion and detail, while the Seedance 1.5 Version (ByteDanceFirstLastFrameNode) is faster and more budget-friendly. Start with 2.0 for hero shots and 1.5 for quick iterations.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the style and environment consistent between frames?
faqItems.answer: Use the same subject reference(s) for both steps, avoid changing the scene description between the First Frame and Last Frame groups, and keep camera and lighting phrasing stable. If available, reuse the same seed. The workflow is designed to preserve palette and scene continuity from your inputs.

faqItems.question: Can I use a custom shape that isn’t a cube, sphere, or capsule?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Describe the custom shape clearly in your prompt (e.g., “low-profile hexagonal puck”) and include material and color cues. If you have a specific silhouette image, load it via LoadImage as a guiding reference where the workflow allows.

06caca08d30b.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, titled 'Inflation Lora Character Expansion Effect Video,' is designed to transform a static character image into an animated video with a unique inflation effect. By leveraging advanced AI models and custom nodes, this workflow allows users to input a character image and a descriptive prompt, which then guides the animation process. The workflow utilizes the 'wan2.2 Animate' model, known for its capability to produce dynamic and visually appealing animations. Key nodes such as 'ComfyUI-WanAnimatePreprocess' and 'ComfyUI-WanVideoWrapper' are employed to preprocess the input image and wrap it into a video format, respectively.

Technically, the workflow begins with the 'VHS_LoadVideo' node to handle video input, followed by 'GetImageRangeFromBatch' and 'ImageResizeKJv2' to prepare the image for processing. Pose and face detection are achieved using 'PoseAndFaceDetection' and 'OnnxDetectionModelLoader', ensuring that the character's features are accurately identified and animated. The 'WanVideoModelLoader' and 'WanVideoLoraSelectMulti' nodes are crucial for loading the animation models and selecting the appropriate Lora settings for the inflation effect. The workflow culminates in the 'WanVideoAnimateEmbeds' and 'WanVideoVAELoader' nodes, which generate the final animated video. This workflow is particularly useful for creating engaging content for social media, video games, or digital storytelling.
howToUse: Load the 'Inflation Lora Character Expansion Effect Video' workflow in ComfyUI.
Upload your character image and input a descriptive prompt to guide the animation.
The workflow preprocesses the image using nodes like 'ComfyUI-WanAnimatePreprocess'.
Select the appropriate Lora settings with 'WanVideoLoraSelectMulti' for the desired inflation effect.
Run the workflow to generate the animated video, utilizing nodes such as 'WanVideoAnimateEmbeds'.
Preview and download your animated video for use in various digital projects.
suggestedUseCases: Creating engaging animated content for social media platforms.
Developing dynamic character animations for video games.
Enhancing digital storytelling with unique visual effects.
Producing promotional videos with eye-catching animations.
Experimenting with creative visual effects for artistic projects.

faqItems.question: What type of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: High-resolution character images with clear features work best to ensure accurate pose and face detection.

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the intensity of the inflation effect?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the 'WanVideoLoraSelectMulti' node allows you to tweak the Lora settings to adjust the effect's intensity.

faqItems.question: Is this workflow suitable for real-time applications?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is designed for post-production and may not be suitable for real-time applications due to processing requirements.

faqItems.question: What output formats are supported?
faqItems.answer: The workflow outputs standard video formats, compatible with most media players and editing software.

0740bf78b7b6.title: Video Upscale
0740bf78b7b6.description: A simple upscaling app for your videos. Uses the open source model SeedVR2 to sharpen your clips.
0740bf78b7b6.metaDescription: ComfyUI Video Upscale workflow: load a clip, enhance with SeedVR2, and export a sharper, higher-resolution video using VHS and Create/SaveVideo nodes.
0740bf78b7b6.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial walks you through a lean, reliable pipeline to upscale and sharpen existing videos using the open-source SeedVR2 model. The workflow loads your source clip with VHS_LoadVideo, reads technical details like frame rate and resolution via VHS_VideoInfo, and breaks the clip into frames with GetVideoComponents. You can quickly iterate on a small section using Video Slice, then set your target output size with ResizeImageMaskNode.

Each frame is enhanced by the SeedVR2 inference node (3531d186-daf3-492a-bb11-94a4c791a3f3) to recover detail and improve perceived sharpness. Finally, CreateVideo reassembles the processed frames at the original FPS from VHS_VideoInfo, and SaveVideo writes the result to disk. The result is a pragmatic, easy-to-tune upscaler you can use for everything from legacy phone footage to screen recordings without extra complexity or proprietary dependencies.
howToUse: Load the Video Upscale workflow in ComfyUI. Ensure the Video Helper Suite (VHS_LoadVideo, VHS_VideoInfo) is installed and that the SeedVR2 model node (3531d186-daf3-492a-bb11-94a4c791a3f3) is available with its weights in the correct models folder.
In VHS_LoadVideo, set the path to your source video. Execute up to VHS_VideoInfo to confirm the clip’s FPS and dimensions are detected correctly.
Optionally, use Video Slice to select a short frame range for fast testing. This lets you preview quality and timing without processing the entire clip.
Set your target upscale size in ResizeImageMaskNode (e.g., 2× the original width and height). Keep the aspect ratio consistent using the dimensions reported by VHS_VideoInfo.
Run the graph to process your test slice. Inspect the preliminary output from SaveVideo and adjust the ResizeImageMaskNode size if you see over-sharpening or artifacts.
Disable slicing (or set the full frame range) when satisfied. Ensure CreateVideo is using the FPS from VHS_VideoInfo, set your final output path in SaveVideo, and run the full export.
suggestedUseCases: Upscale older smartphone or camcorder footage to HD/4K while improving clarity.
Sharpen low-resolution screen recordings so UI text and icons remain legible.
Prepare archival or social media clips for re-publication with a cleaner look.
Enhance gameplay captures for YouTube uploads while keeping the original FPS.
Create higher-res b-roll from small proxy files for editorial workflows.

faqItems.question: What formats are supported for input and output?
faqItems.answer: VHS_LoadVideo relies on ffmpeg, so common formats like MP4, MOV, MKV, and WEBM typically work. SaveVideo outputs a standard encoded video file. If you encounter format issues, transcode your source to H.264 MP4 and try again.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow keep audio?
faqItems.answer: This minimal pipeline focuses on video frames; CreateVideo/SaveVideo outputs are usually silent by default. If you need audio, extract and remux it externally or extend the workflow with audio-capable nodes before final export.

faqItems.question: How much should I upscale?
faqItems.answer: You can set any width/height in ResizeImageMaskNode, but quality and VRAM usage scale with resolution. A 2× upscale is a safe starting point; pushing beyond 4× can increase artifacts and processing time.

faqItems.question: How can I iterate faster or reduce VRAM usage?
faqItems.answer: Use Video Slice to test short segments, lower the target output resolution in ResizeImageMaskNode, and process long videos in multiple passes. Close background apps to free GPU memory if you’re near your VRAM limit.

Load the workflow in ComfyUI and configure the OpenAIChatConfig node with your API credentials.

faqItems.question: How do I configure the OpenAI API in this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for image-based inputs?

faqItems.question: What network requirements are needed to use the API?

Use the GetImageSize node to verify the output dimensions.

Preparing illustrations for large format printing.

faqItems.question: What types of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is best suited for digital illustrations, particularly those needing enhanced resolution and color accuracy.

faqItems.question: Will the workflow introduce artifacts into my image?

faqItems.question: How can I access the Image Compare feature?

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the level of enhancement applied to the image?

085a4bba12f8.title: Depth Motion Capture with Seedance 2.0
085a4bba12f8.description:
Feed a reference video through depth extraction to strip away everything but structure — pure spatial motion, no pixels, no color, no identity. That depth sequence becomes the skeleton.

Hand the skeleton to Seedance 2.0 as your motion reference, then drop in a reference image to define the look. The depth map dictates how things move; the image dictates what they are. Camera moves, body motion, and scene geometry carry over intact while the visual identity is fully swapped.

Dial in duration, resolution, and aspect ratio to match your target format. Route the original audio straight through to the final output so the new footage stays locked to the source timing.
085a4bba12f8.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: drive a new look from a single image using depth-guided motion from a reference video. Keep camera moves, swap identity, and pass through audio.
085a4bba12f8.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Depth Dancer turns any source clip into a motion “skeleton” by extracting a depth map sequence, then rebuilds the visuals from a single reference image. In this workflow, VHS_LoadVideo ingests your reference video (and audio), the custom Seedance 2.0 node (4871bd59-7f4e-475a-a872-bf5457365402) converts each frame to depth to capture camera moves, body motion, and scene geometry, and then synthesizes new frames guided by a look you define with LoadImage. Finally, SaveVideo assembles the generated frames and can pass through the original soundtrack to keep everything in sync.

Technically, the depth pass strips away color and identity, leaving only spatial structure over time. Seedance 2.0 uses that per-frame depth as the motion driver while the reference image sets the subject’s appearance and style. You control duration (frame range), resolution, and aspect ratio in the Seedance 2.0 node to match your target format, and you connect the audio from VHS_LoadVideo to SaveVideo so timing remains locked to the source. A MarkdownNote is included in-graph to document settings and the recommended routing.
howToUse: Load the workflow, then open VHS_LoadVideo and choose your reference video. If needed, set the frame range and confirm FPS so the clip length is exactly what you want to re-create.
In the Seedance 2.0 node (4871bd59-7f4e-475a-a872-bf5457365402), point its video/depth input to the output of VHS_LoadVideo. The node will extract a depth map per frame and use it as motion guidance.
Use LoadImage to bring in a single reference image that defines the subject’s look. Connect it to the Seedance 2.0 image/style input.

In Seedance 2.0, set output width, height, and aspect ratio. Match or intentionally change from the source, but keep proportions consistent for stable results. If available, set a fixed seed for repeatability.
Open SaveVideo and connect the Seedance 2.0 frame output. Route the audio output from VHS_LoadVideo to SaveVideo’s audio input to preserve the original soundtrack. Match FPS to your source.
Click Run. Preview a short segment first to validate motion and framing, then render the full range. The result is a new video with the source motion and your reference image’s visual identity.
suggestedUseCases: Music videos: keep choreography and camera moves from rehearsal footage while swapping in final character or wardrobe from a single key image.
Previs and animatics: block camera and action with rough footage, then restyle quickly into a specific character or art direction.
Social content remixes: retain a trending motion or dance while replacing identity and look for brand-safe outputs.
Cinematic tests: explore how different characters or costumes behave in the same shot motion without re-shooting.
Product hero shots: reuse a smooth turntable or dolly move while changing the product’s finish or design via a single reference image.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between this and pose transfer?
faqItems.answer: Pose transfer uses 2D keypoints; this workflow uses per-frame depth maps. Depth preserves camera motion and scene geometry (parallax, relative distances), so movement feels more 3D and faithful to the original shot.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original background or subject identity?
faqItems.answer: By design, no. The depth pass removes pixel identity and color, and the Seedance 2.0 synthesis rebuilds visuals from the reference image. If you need the original background, composite later in your editor using the new render and the source plate.

faqItems.question: Why does the output flicker or distort on fast motion?
faqItems.answer: Depth quality drops with motion blur or low light. Use cleaner source footage (higher shutter speed, more light), keep aspect ratio consistent between source and output, and avoid aggressive cropping. Matching FPS between VHS_LoadVideo and SaveVideo also helps stability.

faqItems.question: How do I keep timing and audio perfectly in sync?
faqItems.answer: Keep the frame range and FPS consistent from VHS_LoadVideo through SaveVideo, and connect VHS_LoadVideo’s audio output to SaveVideo’s audio input. This preserves the original timing and soundtrack in the final render.

085ff06f65f2.metaDescription: Learn to generate and edit 2K images in seconds using Seedream 4.0's multi-modal AI model with natural language control.
085ff06f65f2.extendedDescription: The Seedream 4.0: Image Edit workflow is a powerful tool for both generating new images from text prompts and editing existing images using natural language commands. At its core, this workflow leverages the ByteDanceSeedreamNode, which integrates the Seedream 4.0 model, known for its rapid image processing capabilities. With the ability to generate high-resolution 2K images in under two seconds, this workflow is particularly useful for users needing quick iterations and high-quality outputs. The BatchImagesNode is particularly noteworthy as it allows for processing multiple images simultaneously, enhancing productivity and efficiency. Use the LoadImage node to import an image you wish to edit, or skip this step to generate a new image from text.
Configure the ByteDanceSeedreamNode with your desired text prompt or image editing instructions.

Run the workflow to generate or edit images, which will be processed in under two seconds.

suggestedUseCases: Creating high-resolution concept art quickly for design projects.
Editing existing marketing images with specific text-based modifications.
Generating multiple variations of a product image for e-commerce platforms.
Rapidly prototyping visual ideas for creative brainstorming sessions.
Enhancing photos with AI-driven adjustments for social media content.

faqItems.question: What is the Seedream 4.0 model used for?
faqItems.answer: Seedream 4.0 is a multi-modal AI model designed for both text-to-image generation and image editing, capable of producing 2K images rapidly.

faqItems.question: How do I enable batch processing?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for both creating new images and editing existing ones?

faqItems.question: What file formats are supported for image import and export?

08d91c5f3020.title: OmniGen2: Text to Image
08d91c5f3020.description: Generate high-quality images from text prompts using OmniGen2's unified 7B multimodal model with dual-path architecture.
08d91c5f3020.metaDescription: Generate high-quality images from text in ComfyUI with OmniGen2’s unified 7B model. Simple node setup, reproducible seeds, and easy saving with SaveImage.
08d91c5f3020.extendedDescription:
This workflow demonstrates a minimal, fast path from text prompt to finished image using OmniGen2’s unified 7B multimodal model. A single OmniGen2 node (custom node id 4b17d220-4312-4981-9eae-9a76bf3b6ec9) ingests your prompt, encodes it with the Qwen2.5-VL text encoder, and produces a high-quality image without the complexity of diffusion samplers or long node chains. The output is then passed to SaveImage for consistent file naming and export, while a MarkdownNote provides in-canvas guidance and links to the official docs.

Technically, the prompt is embedded via the qwen_2.5_vl_fp16.safetensors text encoder and routed through OmniGen2’s dual-path architecture, which unifies language understanding with image generation in a single model. The node exposes practical controls—such as resolution, seed, and batch/count—so you can tune aspect ratio and reproducibility. The entire setup can be wrapped as a Subgraph for a clean UI: expand it any time to reveal advanced parameters and adjust defaults. This makes the workflow ideal for quick iteration, predictable outputs, and easy handoff to teammates.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. If it’s provided as a Subgraph, click to expand it and reveal the OmniGen2 node and SaveImage node.
Install model files if needed: place qwen_2.5_vl_fp16.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/text_encoders (see the linked OmniGen2 repack on Hugging Face).
Open the OmniGen2 node (id 4b17d220-4312-4981-9eae-9a76bf3b6ec9) and enter your text prompt. Set image width/height to define aspect ratio and choose a seed for repeatable results.
Optionally adjust batch/count to generate multiple variations in one run. Keep resolution and batch size within your available VRAM.
Configure the SaveImage node (filename prefix, output format, and directory) so results are organized as you iterate.
Queue and run the workflow. Review outputs in ComfyUI’s gallery or your configured output folder, then refine the prompt or settings and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Concept art and mood boards for early visual exploration
Product mockups and packaging ideation from concise briefs
Social media banners and thumbnails tailored to platform aspect ratios
Storyboards and shot ideation for video or animation projects
Style exploration (lighting, materials, composition) with fast iteration

faqItems.question: Where do I put the Qwen2.5-VL text encoder file?
faqItems.answer: Place qwen_2.5_vl_fp16.safetensors in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders. If you’re using the repackaged OmniGen2 weights from Hugging Face, follow their folder structure and naming exactly.

faqItems.question: How do I control image size and aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Set width and height in the OmniGen2 node. Common pairs are 1024x1024 (square), 1344x768 (16:9), or 832x1216 (2:3). Higher resolutions require more VRAM, so increase gradually.

faqItems.question: How can I get repeatable results?
faqItems.answer: Use a fixed seed value in the OmniGen2 node. To explore variations, either change the seed slightly or enable batch/count to generate multiple outputs in one pass.

faqItems.question: Does OmniGen2 support negative prompts?
faqItems.answer: If your OmniGen2 node exposes a negative_prompt input, use it to steer away from undesired elements. If not, phrase constraints directly in your prompt (e.g., “no text, minimal background, without watermark”).

094c40ffb14f.title: Seedance2.0 Real Human: FLF2V
094c40ffb14f.description: Upload a reference image of a real person for identity verification and generate a personalized video with first and last frame control using Seedance2.0 FLF2V.
094c40ffb14f.metaDescription: Verify a real person once, then generate Seedance 2.0 FLF2V videos with controlled first and last frames using Access IDs or images in ComfyUI.
094c40ffb14f.extendedDescription: Seedance2.0 Real Human: FLF2V is a ComfyUI workflow that verifies a real person’s identity once and then generates a personalized video where both the first and last frames are constrained by your chosen references. It uses ByteDanceCreateImageAsset to upload and verify a reference photo, returning an Asset or Access ID and a Group ID to keep all assets for the same person linked. Video generation is handled by the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, which calls the Seedance 2.0 FLF2V model to condition the opening and closing frames while smoothly interpolating motion in between. PreviewAny lets you inspect results in-graph, and SaveVideo writes the final clip to disk.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure your ByteDance or Seedance credentials are configured according to the plugin documentation.
First-time verification: connect a clear portrait to LoadImage, feed it into ByteDanceCreateImageAsset, and run. Copy the returned Access or Asset ID and the Group ID. Store these IDs for reuse.

Configure frame controls in ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode. For each frame, choose either an Access ID or an image input (do not use both for the same frame). You may provide only a first or only a last frame if desired. If you have a Group ID for the same person, enter it.
Set generation parameters exposed by ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, such as duration, frame rate, resolution, and seed. Use PreviewAny to check a quick result and adjust inputs or settings if needed.
When satisfied, connect the node’s video output to SaveVideo and run to export the final clip. Name the file and confirm the output path.
For future runs with the same person, reuse the Group ID and either reference an existing Access ID or upload new assets under that Group ID for fast, consistent identity recognition.
suggestedUseCases: Personalized creator intros where the opening pose matches a verified headshot and the final frame lands on a branded end-card look.
Marketing cutdowns that A or B test different endings by swapping the last-frame Access ID while keeping the same subject.
Storyboarding or previz that locks the start and end compositions, with Seedance 2.0 filling in a smooth transition between them.
Corporate announcements where a spokesperson’s identity is verified once and reused across multiple clips with consistent framing.
UGC-style shoutouts that start on a known profile image and conclude on a specific facial expression or pose.

faqItems.question: What are Access or Asset IDs and the Group ID, and when should I use them?
faqItems.answer: ByteDanceCreateImageAsset returns an Access or Asset ID that represents a verified reference you can reuse instead of reuploading the same image. It also creates a Group ID after the first successful verification. Save the Group ID and use it when uploading additional assets of the same person so the backend recognizes them as one identity.

faqItems.question: Can I mix Access ID and image inputs for the first and last frames?
faqItems.answer: Not for the same frame. For the first frame, use either an Access ID or an image input, but not both at once. The same rule applies to the last frame. You can, however, use an Access ID for one frame and an image for the other.

faqItems.question: Do I need to verify the person every time I generate a video?
faqItems.answer: No. Verify once to get a Group ID. For future assets of the same person, supply that Group ID in ByteDanceCreateImageAsset. You can then reference existing Access IDs or create new ones under the same Group ID as needed.

faqItems.question: How do I get the best visual results from FLF2V?
faqItems.answer: Use high-quality, front-facing images with good lighting and minimal occlusions for your first and last frames. Keep resolution and aspect ratio consistent with your target output, tune duration and FPS in ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, and iterate using PreviewAny before exporting with SaveVideo.

0a6672ca248d.title: SAM3 - Video Masking via Text Prompts
0a6672ca248d.description: SAM 3 lets you mask objects in a video just by typing a short phrase like "red car" or "person" — no frame-by-frame rotoscoping. It finds every matching instance, tracks them across frames with stable IDs, and outputs per-frame masks ready for compositing, blurring, or replacement.
0a6672ca248d.metaDescription: Mask and track objects in video from a text prompt using SAM3 in ComfyUI. Load a clip, type a prompt, and export overlay, masks, or cut-outs.
0a6672ca248d.extendedDescription:
This workflow demonstrates text-driven video masking with the SAM3 Video Masking node (ID: 9cea40bb-b0cf-4b40-a758-8935cfe8d52f). You load a clip with VHS_LoadVideo, describe the target in plain language (for example, "red car", "person", "coffee cup"), and the node finds every matching instance and tracks them across frames with stable IDs. It produces three parallel outputs: a preview overlay (colored masks drawn over the original frames), a raw binary/gray mask stream, and a cut-out stream where only the masked pixels are kept.

Technically, the node performs text-conditional object detection and segmentation per frame, then links detections across time to keep IDs stable. VHS_LoadVideo supplies the frame sequence and fps; SaveVideo writes each output stream to disk. For quick iteration, the frame_load_cap parameter on VHS_LoadVideo lets you limit how many frames are processed; set it back to 0 for a full run. A MarkdownNote node in the graph provides inline reminders for prompt writing and testing.
howToUse: Open the workflow and load your source clip in VHS_LoadVideo. During testing, set frame_load_cap to a small number (e.g., 60–120) so you can iterate quickly.

In the SAM3 Video Masking node (ID: 9cea40bb-b0cf-4b40-a758-8935cfe8d52f), enter a clear mask_prompt such as "red car", "person", or "blue backpack". Use distinctive attributes (color, clothing, size) to narrow matches.
Run the workflow to generate a short preview. Inspect the overlay output to confirm the right objects are being found and that IDs remain consistent across frames.
Refine results as needed: adjust your prompt for specificity, and if available in the node, raise confidence/score thresholds to reduce false positives or lower them to catch missed frames.

When satisfied, set VHS_LoadVideo frame_load_cap to 0 for a full sequence. Connect the overlay, raw mask, and/or cut-out outputs from SAM3 to separate SaveVideo nodes. Feed the fps from VHS_LoadVideo into SaveVideo or set a value manually.

Choose output paths and formats in each SaveVideo node (e.g., MP4), then run the full render. You’ll get three videos ready for compositing: overlay preview, binary/gray masks, and the cut-out subject against a transparent/black background depending on your viewer.
suggestedUseCases: Privacy and compliance: Automatically blur faces or license plates by masking and applying post-blur.
Product focus reels: Isolate a product in handheld footage for clean background swaps or spotlight effects.
Cinematic color isolation: Create masks for subjects to grade actors separately from the scene.
VFX prep: Generate per-frame mattes to replace skies, signage, or screens without manual rotoscoping.
Sports analysis: Track players or equipment to overlay metrics and highlights.

faqItems.question: How do I export each output (overlay, mask, cut-out)?
faqItems.answer: Connect each SAM3 output to its own SaveVideo node. Use VHS_LoadVideo’s fps output to drive the SaveVideo fps input (or set it manually), pick a file path and format, and render. You can export any or all of the streams independently.

faqItems.question: Can I target multiple objects at once?
faqItems.answer: Yes. If the prompt matches multiple instances (e.g., "person"), the node will segment and track each with stable IDs. To limit results, make the prompt more specific (e.g., "person in red jacket") or crop the input to the region of interest.

faqItems.question: Why do masks flicker or miss frames during fast motion?
faqItems.answer: Rapid motion, motion blur, or heavy occlusion can reduce per-frame confidence and disrupt tracking. Improve results by using a more specific prompt, increasing the node’s confidence/score thresholds, and processing the original-resolution video (or less downscaling) if VRAM allows.

faqItems.question: What hardware do I need for reasonable speed?

0bb057fd76e3.title: SD3.5 Large Canny ControlNet
0bb057fd76e3.description: Generate images guided by edge detection using SD 3.5 Canny ControlNet.
0bb057fd76e3.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate images with SD 3.5 Large guided by Canny edges using ControlNet for precise composition with flexible style control.
0bb057fd76e3.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow uses Stability AI’s SD 3.5 Large model with a Canny ControlNet to generate images that follow the structure of an input image’s edges. The pipeline loads the SD 3.5 checkpoint (CheckpointLoaderSimple) and the Canny ControlNet (ControlNetLoader), encodes your text prompt (CLIPTextEncode), and extracts a high-contrast edge map from your guide image (Canny). The edge map is applied as a structural constraint via ControlNetApplyAdvanced so the KSampler can synthesize new content that respects the outlines while still following your prompt.

Technically, the workflow creates a latent canvas at your target resolution (EmptySD3LatentImage), conditions the model with your positive prompt plus the ControlNet edge guidance, and optionally zeroes the negative prompt (ConditioningZeroOut) for simplicity. After sampling (KSampler), the result is decoded to RGB (VAEDecode), previewed (PreviewImage), and saved (SaveImage). ImageScale is included to match the Canny edge map to the chosen output size for consistent alignment. This setup is ideal when you want strong compositional control—like sticking to silhouettes or product contours—while letting SD 3.5 handle detail, texture, and style.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then in Step 1 - Load models: set CheckpointLoaderSimple to sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors and ControlNetLoader to sd3.5_large_controlnet_canny.safetensors.
In Step 2 - Load image: connect your guide image with LoadImage. Use PreviewImage to quickly inspect it.
In Canny preprocessing: adjust the Canny node thresholds (e.g., lower threshold for more edges, higher to simplify). Use PreviewImage on the Canny output to verify clean outlines.
In Image size: set your target resolution with EmptySD3LatentImage. Use ImageScale to resize the Canny edge map to exactly match the latent width/height.

In Step 3 - Prompt: enter your text in CLIPTextEncode (e.g., "crystal pink dragon on a blue mystery sky, hyperdetailed"). The workflow uses ConditioningZeroOut for the negative by default; if you want a negative prompt, add another CLIPTextEncode and wire it to KSampler’s negative input.
Tune ControlNetApplyAdvanced (e.g., weight 0.6–1.0, start 0.0, end 1.0) and KSampler settings (seed, steps, sampler, CFG). Run the workflow, review the VAEDecode/PreviewImage output, then SaveImage.
suggestedUseCases: Stylizing line art or sketches into fully rendered illustrations while preserving composition.
Turning product photos into consistent, on-brand renders that keep the original contours.
Architectural massing or elevation references converted into detailed concept art.
Storyboards or thumbnails refined into polished frames with controlled layout.
Converting simple silhouettes into diverse styles (e.g., fantasy, sci‑fi, painterly) while keeping shape fidelity.

faqItems.question: How do I make the result follow the edges more or less strictly?
faqItems.answer: Increase ControlNetApplyAdvanced weight (e.g., 0.8–1.0) for strong adherence to edges; decrease it (e.g., 0.3–0.6) for looser, more creative outputs. You can also shorten the guidance window (raise start or lower end) to reduce influence during part of the sampling.

faqItems.question: What Canny thresholds should I use?
faqItems.answer: Start with a moderate range (e.g., low 80–120, high 160–220). Lower values capture more fine detail but can introduce noise; higher values simplify to bold outlines. Always preview the Canny output and aim for clean, unbroken primary contours.

faqItems.question: Do I have to match the edge map size to the output size?
faqItems.answer: Yes—consistent results come from matching resolutions. Use ImageScale to resize the Canny edge map to the same width/height as EmptySD3LatentImage so ControlNet conditioning aligns with the sampling canvas.

faqItems.question: How do I use a negative prompt with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: By default, ConditioningZeroOut supplies an empty negative. To add one, create another CLIPTextEncode with your negative text (e.g., "blurry, low quality"), and connect its output to KSampler’s negative conditioning input.

These images are processed to extract latent features, which are then conditioned using the Hunyuan3Dv2ConditioningMultiView node. 1043317e75c9.title: 1 input multiple styles from prompt

1043317e75c9.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows you how to turn a single image into a gallery of 12 distinct styles using prompt-driven editing. The workflow is simple and fast: LoadImage imports your source, the image fans out to twelve GrokImageEditNodeV2 instances (each driven by a different style prompt and the Grok Imagine Quality engine), and each result is written to disk by a SaveImage node. The result is a quick style board that’s ideal for exploration, A/B testing, or presenting options to a client.

Technically, the graph duplicates the same input image across parallel branches. Each GrokImageEditNodeV2 applies the style instructions you provide (e.g., “watercolor sketch,” “cyberpunk neon,” “studio portrait retouch”) while preserving the core content and composition of the original. SaveImage nodes handle file naming and output paths so every variant is saved separately. Because each branch is independent, ComfyUI can schedule work efficiently, and the Grok Imagine Quality model is optimized for rapid, consistent edits—making it practical to generate a dozen variations in a single run.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the three key components: LoadImage (input), twelve GrokImageEditNodeV2 nodes (style edits), and SaveImage nodes (outputs).
Click LoadImage and select your source image. Use a clean, well-lit image for best results; portraits and product shots work especially well.

For each GrokImageEditNodeV2, set or adjust the style prompt text to match the look you want (e.g., "oil painting," "minimalist flat design," "film noir"). The node is configured to use Grok Imagine Quality.
Optionally fine-tune any available controls in GrokImageEditNodeV2 (such as prompt wording or seed) to steer consistency across runs or to increase variety.
Open each SaveImage node and confirm the output directory and filename prefix to avoid overwriting. Use distinct prefixes if you want style groups to be easy to sort.
Queue the workflow (Execute/Queue Prompt). When it finishes, review the 12 saved images in your output folder and iterate on any prompts you want to refine.
suggestedUseCases: Creative moodboards: Generate a quick wall of different art directions for the same subject.
Brand/style exploration: Test how a product or logo reads across multiple visual treatments.
Social media variants: Produce multiple looks from one photo to schedule diverse posts.
Client presentations: Offer style options side-by-side without rebuilding a scene.

faqItems.question: How do I change the number of styles from 12 to more or fewer?

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key or special setup for GrokImageEditNodeV2?
faqItems.answer: If your GrokImageEditNodeV2 relies on an external Grok service, you may need to configure credentials in the node or its settings. Check the node’s documentation or the node UI for any required keys or endpoints.

faqItems.question: How can I control how strongly the style changes the image?

faqItems.question: Why do some outputs look similar even with different prompts?

113c9ab2c6d7.title: Wan2.7: Reference to Video
113c9ab2c6d7.description: Upload a reference video and character image to generate a video with consistent character features.
113c9ab2c6d7.metaDescription: Generate motion-consistent videos with a target character using Wan2.7 in ComfyUI. Load an image, feed a reference video, and export with SaveVideo.
113c9ab2c6d7.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a reference video into a new video featuring your chosen character while preserving the motion, framing, and timing of the original. It uses the Wan2.7 model via the Wan2ReferenceVideoApi node to track the reference video’s movement and composition, then conditions generation on a single character image you load with the LoadImage node. The output is a sequence of frames that maintain the target character’s facial features and overall look across time, which the SaveVideo node encodes into a final video file.

Technically, Wan2ReferenceVideoApi ingests the reference video and extracts per-frame motion cues and scene layout. It then conditions Wan2.7 with the identity information from your character image so the model synthesizes each frame with consistent facial features and styling, while following the original camera and body movement. The node outputs generated frames for SaveVideo to assemble at your chosen frame rate and filename. This approach is useful when you want character consistency without manual keying or heavy rotoscoping, and it works well for short clips, social content, and previz.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three core nodes are present: LoadImage, Wan2ReferenceVideoApi, and SaveVideo.
In LoadImage, select a high-quality character image (well-lit, facing the camera, head-and-shoulders if possible). Its output should feed the character/image input of Wan2ReferenceVideoApi.
In Wan2ReferenceVideoApi, set the path to your reference video. Ensure the model selection is Wan2.7 and review any exposed settings (e.g., resolution or frame range) to match the source clip.
Verify the node connections: the character image from LoadImage should go into Wan2ReferenceVideoApi, and the generated frame output from Wan2ReferenceVideoApi should connect to SaveVideo.
Configure SaveVideo with your desired filename and frame rate (matching the reference video typically yields the most natural timing).

Queue and run the workflow. After it finishes, review the saved video. If identity drifts or details blur, try a sharper character image, adjust the image crop, or shorten the reference clip and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Character swap for short social clips while preserving original motion and timing.
Previz for film or animation to test how a character reads in a scene without manual compositing.
Marketing demos that place a brand mascot or spokesperson into existing motion footage.
Cosplay and VTuber intros where a static avatar image is animated via reference motion.

faqItems.question: What inputs do I need?
faqItems.answer: You need a single character image (loaded with LoadImage) and a reference video (set inside Wan2ReferenceVideoApi). The node will output generated frames that SaveVideo encodes into a final video.

faqItems.question: How do I get the best identity consistency?
faqItems.answer: Use a high-resolution, front-facing, well-lit character image with minimal occlusions. Match the aspect ratio of the character crop to the reference video subject, and avoid reference clips with extreme motion blur, rapid cuts, or heavy occlusions.

faqItems.question: What frame rate and resolution should I use?
faqItems.answer: For natural motion, set SaveVideo’s frame rate to match the reference video. Keep resolution moderate for stability and speed (matching the reference or the API node’s default). If results look unstable, try slightly lower resolution or a shorter clip.

faqItems.question: Can I reproduce the same result reliably?
faqItems.answer: Results depend on the exact inputs and settings. Keep the same character image, reference video, and node options to get consistent outputs. If the node exposes a seed parameter, reusing the same seed further improves reproducibility.

11657ed32877.title: Krea-2: Text to Image
11657ed32877.description: Generate images from text prompts using Krea 2, a foundation model built for aesthetic quality and creative control. It focuses on rendering expressive and artistic styles. Ideal for concept art exploration, visual brainstorming, and creating stylized imagery for design projects.
11657ed32877.metaDescription: Krea-2 Turbo text-to-image in ComfyUI with resolution presets, style LoRAs, and one-click saving—fast, expressive renders for concept art and design.
11657ed32877.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns text prompts into images using Krea-2 Turbo, a distilled text-to-image model designed for speed and expressive, stylized results. It includes a ResolutionSelector so you can switch aspect ratios without touching width/height by hand, optional style LoRAs for creative control, and a SaveImage node that writes finished renders to your ComfyUI/output folder. A MarkdownNote in the graph links to the official Krea-2 model and LoRA resources so you can install the exact files the graph expects.

Technically, your prompt flows into the Krea‑2 Turbo inference node (b0e5ca93-2731-42b9-8e0a-d28ea851ff81), which loads a diffusion checkpoint such as krea2_turbo_fp8_scaled.safetensors. If you select one or more LoRAs from ComfyUI/models/loras, those adapters are applied during sampling to steer style. The ResolutionSelector subgraph outputs a matched width/height pair to the Krea‑2 node so you can generate at common sizes reliably. The image tensor then routes to SaveImage, which saves numbered files and embeds metadata for reproducibility. The graph is grouped into a compact subgraph so you can work from a single control surface instead of hunting through nodes.

It’s especially useful for concept art and visual brainstorming: start with a general idea, toggle a style LoRA to explore different looks, iterate seeds, and lock a resolution preset for downstream design work. For best control, include any LoRA trigger words in your prompt and start with a moderate LoRA weight (around 0.6), then fine‑tune from there. See the linked Krea‑2 and LoRA docs for model variants and style lists.
howToUse: Load the Krea-2: Text to Image workflow in ComfyUI. Read the MarkdownNote for quick links and tips.
Download a Krea-2 Turbo checkpoint (e.g., krea2_turbo_fp8_scaled.safetensors) from Comfy-Org/Krea-2 and place it in ComfyUI/models/checkpoints. Restart ComfyUI so it appears in node dropdowns.
Optional: Download style LoRAs from Comfy-Org/Krea-2/loras and place the .safetensors files in ComfyUI/models/loras. Note any trigger words listed in the repo.

In the Krea-2 Turbo node (UUID b0e5ca93-2731-42b9-8e0a-d28ea851ff81), enter your prompt. If the node exposes a negative prompt input, add things to avoid (e.g., "no watermark, no text"). Select the Krea-2 Turbo model from its model dropdown.
Pick an output size using the ResolutionSelector. Choose an aspect ratio preset that matches your target use (e.g., square for thumbnails, 16:9 for slides).

Optionally add one or more style LoRAs in the node’s LoRA controls, include their trigger words in your prompt, and start with a weight around 0.6. Set a Seed for reproducibility (if exposed), then click Queue Prompt. Your images will appear in the preview and be saved by SaveImage to ComfyUI/output.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept art exploration for characters, environments, or props with stylized looks
Visual brainstorming and moodboards for branding, editorial, or pitch decks
Style studies using LoRAs to compare different art directions from the same prompt
Thumbnail and social asset ideation at preset aspect ratios
Sketch replacements and paint-over bases for design iterations

faqItems.question: Where do I put the model and LoRAs?
faqItems.answer: Place the Krea-2 Turbo checkpoint (e.g., krea2_turbo_fp8_scaled.safetensors) in ComfyUI/models/checkpoints and style LoRAs in ComfyUI/models/loras. Restart ComfyUI so the files are detected.

faqItems.question: How do I control or mix styles with LoRAs?
faqItems.answer: Select one or more LoRAs in the Krea-2 node, include each LoRA’s trigger words in your prompt, and adjust their weights. A good starting point is ~0.6 per LoRA, then fine-tune up or down to balance multiple styles. Refer to the LoRA table in the Hugging Face repo for trigger words and recommended ranges.

faqItems.question: How do I change resolution or aspect ratio safely?
faqItems.answer: Use the ResolutionSelector. It outputs matched width/height presets so you don’t have to calculate sizes manually. Choose a preset that matches your target use case and regenerate. For crisp results, generate at the target aspect rather than upscaling a mismatched crop.

faqItems.question: My results vary each run. How can I make them repeatable or improve consistency?
faqItems.answer: Set a fixed Seed on the Krea-2 node (if exposed) before queuing the prompt. Keep the same prompt, model, LoRA set, and resolution. If the node provides guidance or step controls, small adjustments there can improve adherence to the prompt (higher guidance) or smoothness (tuning steps).
