2652985596d8.extendedDescription:
Wan2.1 VACE Control Video is a guided video-to-video workflow that preserves the motion and timing of a source video while restyling or re-characterizing it with a text prompt and a reference image. It loads Wan2.1 VACE checkpoints (1.3B or 14B) via UNETLoader and VAELoader, encodes your text with CLIPTextEncode, and conditions generation with control signals derived from simple image preprocessing (Canny by default). GetVideoComponents reads frames and FPS from the input clip, and TrimVideoLatent keeps the latent sequence aligned with your chosen frame range and resolution before sampling.

Under the hood, ModelSamplingSD3 configures the expected sampler schedule for Wan2.1 VACE, and KSampler performs denoising on a sequence of video latents assembled by WanVaceToVideo using your control video, prompt, and reference image. VAEDecode converts the final latents back to frames, CreateVideo assembles them at the desired FPS, and you can export either MP4 (SaveVideo) or animated WebP (SaveAnimatedWEBP). An optional CausVid LoRA (LoraLoader) can accelerate or stabilize motion with very low steps, though you may need to tune its strength. The 14B model yields higher fidelity (and supports 720p) but runs slower and uses more VRAM; the 1.3B variant is faster and suited to 480p outputs.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and point the UNETLoader, VAELoader, and CLIPLoader nodes to the Wan2.1 VACE model you want to use (1.3B for speed at 480p, 14B for higher quality up to 720p). If you plan to swap the preprocessor, install comfyui_controlnet_aux.

In the Load control video group, connect your source clip with LoadVideo. GetVideoComponents will extract frames, FPS, and dimensions. If needed, use TrimVideoLatent to crop the frame range and ensure the target resolution matches the chosen model’s capability.

In the Load reference image group, add your style/identity image with LoadImage. In Image preprocessing, the Canny node generates edge guidance (you can replace it with another preprocessor such as Lineart or Depth). Adjust Canny thresholds to control how strictly edges are followed.

Open the Prompt group and enter your main prompt (and, if provided in the template, a negative prompt). Set the sampling parameters in Sampling & Decoding: for default generation use steps=20 and cfg=6.0; if using the CausVid LoRA, start with steps=2–4 and cfg≈1.0. Load the LoRA in LoraLoader and set its strength between 0.3 and 0.7, or bypass it to disable.

Run the graph. WanVaceToVideo assembles the conditioning, KSampler performs denoising using ModelSamplingSD3, and VAEDecode turns latents into frames. Use PreviewImage to sanity-check frames, then CreateVideo to compile them at the detected or chosen FPS.

Export your result from Save Video(Mp4) with the SaveVideo node, or from Save Video(WebP) with SaveAnimatedWEBP. If you see shake or blur, try lowering LoRA strength, slightly increasing steps, reducing CFG to 5–6, or relaxing the Canny thresholds.
suggestedUseCases: Character restyling: Keep a performer’s motion from a source clip while swapping to a new character look defined by a reference image.
Cinematic re-grading: Apply a prompt-driven aesthetic to B‑roll footage while using Canny to preserve scene structure and composition.
Product visualization: Retain camera moves from a control video and change materials or colors according to a prompt and reference swatch.
Animated concept previews: Quickly explore variations of a scene at 480p with the 1.3B model, then upscale fidelity with the 14B model for selects.
Consistent series outputs: Use the same reference image and prompt across multiple control clips to maintain a unified style.

faqItems.question: Should I choose the 1.3B or 14B Wan2.1 VACE model?
faqItems.answer: Use 1.3B for faster iteration and 480p outputs. Choose 14B if you need higher fidelity or 720p. The 14B model is slower and requires more VRAM but typically yields cleaner detail and temporal stability.

faqItems.question: My video looks shaky or blurry when using the CausVid LoRA. How can I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Lower the LoRA strength toward 0.3–0.5, slightly increase steps (e.g., from 2 to 3–4), and keep CFG near 1.0 for the LoRA preset. If artifacts persist, bypass the LoRA entirely or relax the Canny thresholds so edges are less constraining.

faqItems.question: How do I change duration or FPS?
faqItems.answer: TrimVideoLatent lets you limit or align the frame range. GetVideoComponents reads FPS from the source; you can keep it or override during CreateVideo. Shorter clips and moderate FPS will reduce VRAM and speed up sampling.

faqItems.question: Can I use a different preprocessor instead of Canny?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Replace the Canny node with another comfyui_controlnet_aux preprocessor (e.g., Lineart or Depth) and route its output to the same control input used by WanVaceToVideo. Different preprocessors change how strictly structure is preserved.

268307c5793e.title: GIMM Frame Interpolation
268307c5793e.description: Generate intermediate frames between existing video frames to create smoother motion. Input a video and receive a fluid, higher-frame-rate output without changing the total duration.
268307c5793e.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: GIMM VFI frame interpolation to boost FPS without changing video length using VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine.
268307c5793e.extendedDescription:
This workflow performs video frame interpolation in ComfyUI to make motion look smoother without changing the total playback time. It uses the comfyui-videohelpersuite for I/O and the comfyui-gimm-vfi custom node to synthesize in-between frames. VHS_LoadVideo ingests your source clip and exposes its frames and native FPS. Those frames are passed to the GIMM VFI interpolator node (UUID: 8d69124f-cc0e-4891-b9ca-9c1b04432c40), which inserts synthetic frames between each pair of originals according to an interpolation factor you set (for example, 2x or 3x). Finally, VHS_VideoCombine assembles the expanded frame sequence back into a video file.

Technically, the GIMM VFI node estimates motion between consecutive frames and generates temporally consistent intermediate frames. The MarkdownNote in the graph spells out the key timing rule: output_fps = input_fps × interpolation_factor. By multiplying the output FPS in VHS_VideoCombine to match the factor, the clip’s duration remains identical while motion appears more fluid. No diffusion or checkpoint models are required; everything hinges on the VFI node and reliable video read/write via the Video Helper Suite.
howToUse: Install the required custom nodes: comfyui-gimm-vfi and comfyui-videohelpersuite. Restart ComfyUI, then load the "GIMM Frame Interpolation" workflow JSON.
Open the VHS_LoadVideo node and select your input video. Confirm it loads correctly and note the displayed input FPS.

Select the GIMM VFI interpolator node (UUID: 8d69124f-cc0e-4891-b9ca-9c1b04432c40) and choose an interpolation factor (commonly 2x or 3x). Higher factors increase smoothness but also computation time and potential artifacts.
In VHS_VideoCombine, set the output FPS to input_fps × interpolation_factor (for example, 30 × 3 = 90). Choose your container/codec and quality settings (CRF/bitrate) as desired.
Set the output file path in VHS_VideoCombine. Optionally, if your Video Helper Suite build supports it, configure audio passthrough or plan to remux audio afterward.
Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the output video for smoothness and artifacts. If needed, adjust the interpolation factor or encode settings and rerun.
suggestedUseCases: Smoothing handheld footage or gimbal shots to reduce micro-judder without altering runtime.
Upgrading screen captures or UI pans/scrolls to higher FPS for clearer motion.
Converting cinematic 24/30 fps material to 48/60+ fps for fluid playback on high-refresh displays.
Increasing temporal density before further processing (e.g., stabilization or denoising) that benefits from more frames.
Enhancing animation or game recordings where consistent frame pacing improves perceived quality.

faqItems.question: Will my video get longer after interpolation?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow multiplies the output FPS to match the interpolation factor (output_fps = input_fps × factor), so total duration remains the same. This rule is highlighted in the MarkdownNote.

faqItems.question: What interpolation factor should I use?
faqItems.answer: Start with 2x for most footage. Use 3x if you need extra smoothness and the motion is not too complex. Very high factors increase compute time and can introduce ghosting or artifacts on fast action and occlusions.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: If your VHS_VideoCombine node supports audio passthrough, point it to the original audio or enable the appropriate option to mux it into the output. If not, export the video and remux the audio with a tool like ffmpeg using the original track.

faqItems.question: How do I make slow motion instead of keeping the same duration?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is set up to preserve duration by raising the FPS. For slow motion, keep the output FPS equal to the original (or another lower value) while using a >1x interpolation factor so the added frames extend playback.

26e1f4eddd7e.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a text prompt into four high-quality, stylistically varied images using the Krea v2 image generation service. At its core is the Krea2ImageNode, which sends your prompt (and any optional parameters the node exposes) to the Krea API, returning a batch of images in one run. The SaveImage node then writes those images to your ComfyUI output directory with your chosen filename prefix.

Technically, ComfyUI orchestrates the request/response cycle while compute happens remotely on Krea. You supply the prompt in Krea2ImageNode and, if available in your installation, can set options like seed (for reproducibility), aspect/size, and the number of images. The workflow is preconfigured to produce four outputs for creative variety. The SaveImage node receives the image batch directly from Krea2ImageNode and saves each item as a separate file, which makes iterating and curating results straightforward.

Because generation runs in the cloud, this setup is fast to iterate on without a local GPU. It’s ideal for quickly exploring multiple visual directions from a single prompt, then narrowing in by locking a seed (if exposed) or refining the prompt. The minimal node graph—Krea2ImageNode plus SaveImage—keeps the process simple while still letting you manage output naming and batching inside ComfyUI.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and ensure the Krea2ImageNode is installed and visible in the graph.
Open Krea2ImageNode and add your Krea API key (either in the node’s API key field or via the method documented for your install).
Enter your text prompt. If the node exposes options like negative prompt, aspect/size, seed, or batch size/num_images, set them (use 4 for four outputs or leave as preconfigured).
Configure SaveImage (set a clear filename_prefix so results are grouped; leave other defaults unless you have a custom output path).
Queue the prompt and run. Watch the images appear in the ComfyUI preview; the batch will also be written to your output directory.
Iterate: refine the prompt for style/subject accuracy; if available, lock a seed for reproducible tweaks or leave it blank for more variety.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept exploration for characters, environments, or products from a single prompt.
Moodboards and look-dev: generate four stylistic variations to compare tone and composition.
Thumbnail and social post ideation where multiple layout/style options are useful.
Client review sheets: produce a small set of distinct takes to discuss direction before refining.

faqItems.question: Do I need a local GPU to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No. Krea2ImageNode sends your prompt to the Krea API and generation runs in the cloud. ComfyUI orchestrates the request and saves the returned images.

faqItems.question: Why am I not getting four images?
faqItems.answer: Check the Krea2ImageNode settings. If your version exposes a batch size or num_images parameter, set it to 4. If not, the node may be preconfigured; update the node or refer to its docs.

faqItems.question: How can I reproduce a specific result?
faqItems.answer: If the node exposes a seed parameter, record and reuse that seed with the same prompt and settings. Without a fixed seed, each run may produce different images.

faqItems.question: Where are my images saved?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage writes files to your ComfyUI output folder (by default, ./output). Set a filename_prefix in SaveImage to keep runs organized or change the path if your setup allows.

The user can guide these motions using trajectory guidance, ensuring precise and controlled animation of image elements. The CreateVideo and SaveVideo nodes then compile these movements into a cohesive video file. This workflow is particularly useful for creators looking to animate still images with detailed motion paths, offering a high level of customization and control over the final video output.
howToUse: Load the workflow into ComfyUI and ensure all required models, such as Wan2.1 and Wan, are installed.
Use the LoadImage node to import the image you wish to animate.
Utilize the GenerateTracks node to define motion paths for specific points in the image. Visualize these paths with the WanMoveVisualizeTracks node.
Adjust the motion paths using the WanMoveTracksFromCoords node for precise control over the animation.
Compile the animated frames into a video using the CreateVideo node, then save the output with the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating animated marketing materials from static images.
Developing educational content with dynamic visual aids.
Enhancing social media posts with engaging video content.
Producing artistic video projects from photographic stills.
Animating architectural or design visualizations for presentations.

faqItems.question: What models do I need for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You need the Wan2.1 and Wan models to effectively use this workflow.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for any image?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can use any image, but results may vary based on the complexity and detail of the motion paths you create.

faqItems.question: How do I create motion paths?
faqItems.answer: You can create motion paths using the GenerateTracks node and visualize them with the WanMoveVisualizeTracks node. For more control, use the WanMoveTracksFromCoords node.

faqItems.question: Is there a way to preview the motion before finalizing the video?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can use the PreviewImage node to see how your motion paths will affect the image before creating the final video.

2a95da601676.title: Video Aspect Ratio Extension
2a95da601676.description: Extend any video to a custom aspect ratio. Convert vertical videos to horizontal format and vice versa. Includes an application mode for easy use.
2a95da601676.metaDescription: Extend videos from vertical to horizontal (and vice versa) with Kling O3 outpainting in ComfyUI. App mode UI, slicing, and audio passthrough included.
2a95da601676.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow converts vertical videos to horizontal (and vice versa) by outpainting new canvas areas while keeping the original content intact. It uses LoadVideo and GetVideoComponents to pull frames, FPS, and audio, then normalizes frame size with JWImageResizeByShorterSide so the shorter side matches your target resolution. A masking stage—powered by masquerade-nodes-comfyui and a custom utility node (UUID: 7594b5c0-2b90-4aeb-846b-e3eb8fa89f33)—defines where to synthesize new content versus where to preserve the source. The core transformation happens in KlingOmniProEditVideoNode running the Kling O3 model, which content-aware outpaints the added side bands to reach your target aspect. Video Slice lets you process in manageable chunks for stability and VRAM efficiency, and CreateVideo + SaveVideo assemble and write the final file, with optional audio passthrough from GetVideoComponents.

What makes this useful is that you don’t have to crop away important action. Instead, you reframe with horizontal/vertical offsets and extend the scene, maintaining motion continuity and subject integrity. The workflow is organized into groups—Input Video, Video Resize and Extend, and Video Outpaint—and includes an application mode for a simplified UI: set the target aspect, tweak offsets, and run. Note: this pipeline is optimized for 9:16 ↔ 16:9 conversions. For minor aspect changes or square (1:1), the Kling video edit node isn’t recommended; consider basic crop/pad instead.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the Input Video group. In LoadVideo, select your source clip. GetVideoComponents will expose frames, FPS, and audio.
In Video Resize and Extend, set JWImageResizeByShorterSide to your base resolution (e.g., 1080). This resizes frames by the shorter edge while preserving content for outpainting.

Choose your target orientation (16:9 or 9:16) and adjust the horizontal/vertical offsets as noted in the Note node. Reframe the subject before extension so the new canvas grows in the desired direction.

In the Video Outpaint group, verify the mask settings (masquerade-nodes-comfyui and the custom UUID node) so protected regions cover the subject and the outpaint area lies in the added borders. If exposed, widen the mask or increase feather.

Open the KlingOmniProEditVideoNode and select the Kling O3 model. Review strength/consistency parameters (if present) and ensure Video Slice is set to a chunk size your GPU can handle. For 1080p, start with moderate slices.

CreateVideo should receive frames and FPS (and audio if desired) from GetVideoComponents. Connect to SaveVideo, pick an output path, then run. Review results; if artifacts appear, reduce the outpaint width or refine offsets/mask and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Reformat TikTok/Reels (9:16) footage for YouTube 16:9 without cropping out key action.
Convert landscape webinars or demos into vertical stories while preserving presenters and slides.
Extend gameplay or B‑roll to fill 9:16 for Shorts without letterboxing.
Reframe talking‑head interviews and outpaint background edges for platform‑specific aspect ratios.
Prepare ad creatives once and repurpose across vertical and horizontal placements.

faqItems.question: Does this preserve audio?
faqItems.answer: Yes—if you wire audio from GetVideoComponents into CreateVideo, the audio track is passed through. If you omit it, the output will be silent.

faqItems.question: What if I only need a slight aspect ratio change or a 1:1 square?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is optimized for 9:16 ↔ 16:9 conversions. For small tweaks or 1:1, use a basic crop/pad/resize pipeline instead of KlingOmniProEditVideoNode.

faqItems.question: How do I avoid artifacts or stretching in the outpainted borders?
faqItems.answer: Reduce the extension amount, improve your subject mask (wider and slightly feathered), and keep the subject centered with the offset controls. If available, increase temporal consistency in the Kling node and process with moderate Video Slice sizes.

faqItems.question: What are the hardware and performance tips?
faqItems.answer: For 1080p, a 12–16 GB GPU is recommended. If you hit VRAM limits, lower JWImageResizeByShorterSide, reduce outpaint width, and shorten Video Slice lengths. Passing original FPS from GetVideoComponents helps maintain smooth motion.

2a9b4417b44f.title: Z-Image: Text to Image
2a9b4417b44f.description: Foundation for creative freedom. Diverse aesthetics with exceptional photorealistic quality; ideal for fine-tuning; responsive to negative prompts; high generation diversity.
2a9b4417b44f.metaDescription: Transform text into stunning images with Z-Image: Text to Image workflow, offering photorealistic quality and diverse aesthetics.
2a9b4417b44f.extendedDescription:
The Z-Image: Text to Image workflow is designed to transform textual descriptions into high-quality images with a focus on photorealism and aesthetic diversity. Utilizing the Z-Image model, this workflow is particularly adept at producing images that are not only visually stunning but also highly responsive to both positive and negative prompts, allowing for fine-tuning and creative exploration. The workflow employs specific nodes such as SaveImage for output management and MarkdownNote for documentation, alongside a unique node type identified by the ID 9b9009e4-2d3d-445f-9be5-6063f465757e, which plays a crucial role in the image generation process.

Technically, this workflow leverages the qwen_3_4b.safetensors text encoder and the z_image_bf16.safetensors diffusion model to interpret and render textual inputs into images. The process involves running the diffusion model for 30 to 50 steps with a classifier-free guidance (cfg) scale of 3 to 5, ensuring a balance between adhering to the prompt and introducing creative variability. This setup makes the workflow particularly useful for artists and designers seeking to generate diverse image outputs from textual descriptions, providing a foundation for creative freedom and exploration.
howToUse: Load the Z-Image: Text to Image workflow in ComfyUI.
Input your desired text description into the text prompt field.
Adjust the diffusion steps between 30 to 50 for desired detail.
Set the cfg scale between 3 to 5 to control adherence to the prompt.
Run the workflow to generate the image.
Save the output using the SaveImage node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating concept art for visual storytelling.
Generating photorealistic images for marketing materials.
Exploring diverse aesthetic styles for design projects.
Producing fine-tuned images for digital art portfolios.
Developing responsive visual content for social media campaigns.

faqItems.question: What type of images can I generate with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You can generate a wide range of images, from photorealistic scenes to diverse aesthetic styles, depending on your text prompts.

faqItems.question: How do negative prompts affect the image generation?
faqItems.answer: Negative prompts help steer the model away from undesired elements, allowing for more refined and targeted image outputs.

faqItems.question: What are the optimal settings for diffusion steps and cfg scale?
faqItems.answer: For most cases, 30 to 50 diffusion steps with a cfg scale of 3 to 5 provide a good balance between detail and creative variability.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for commercial projects?
faqItems.answer: Yes, as long as you comply with the licensing terms of the models and assets used within the workflow.

2b3403ae14e9.title: Switch Node
2b3403ae14e9.description: Guide on how Switch Nodes work, simple Text Switch and LoRA Switch
2b3403ae14e9.metaDescription: Learn ComfyUI Switch Nodes: toggle between prompts and enable/disable a LoRA on Z-Image-Turbo for fast A/B testing and reproducible image comparisons.
2b3403ae14e9.extendedDescription:
This tutorial workflow demonstrates how to use ComfyUI's ComfySwitchNode to route between two inputs with a simple boolean toggle. It includes two focused examples: Example 1 - String Selection shows how to switch between two prompt strings using PrimitiveString and PrimitiveStringMultiline, previewing the active choice with PreviewAny. Example 2 - LoRA Switch shows how to toggle a LoRA on and off around a base model: UNETLoader loads Z-Image-Turbo, LoraLoaderModelOnly applies a selected LoRA, and a ComfySwitchNode chooses either the plain UNet (on_false) or the LoRA-modified UNet (on_true) to feed the generation node.

Under the hood, ComfySwitchNode exposes four pins: on_false, on_true, switch (boolean), and output. When the switch is OFF (false), the output forwards whatever is connected to on_false; when ON (true), it forwards on_true. The workflow wires these switches to real tasks. The text switch selects a single prompt string used downstream, and the LoRA switch controls whether a LoRA weight is applied to the Z-Image-Turbo UNet before image generation. A SaveImage node captures results for easy A/B comparison, and MarkdownNote blocks explain the routing inline. The generation path uses Z-Image-Turbo via UNETLoader and a generation node (ID 0f79b7f9-d214-4587-b475-bc429519b976) that consumes the chosen model and prompt to render images.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and install the required models: place z_image_turbo_bf16.safetensors in diffusion_models and your LoRA (e.g., zimage-90_s_anime_melancholy.safetensors) in loras. Confirm UNETLoader points to Z-Image-Turbo and LoraLoaderModelOnly points to your LoRA.

Explore Example 1 - String Selection: edit the two text sources (PrimitiveString and PrimitiveStringMultiline). Use the PrimitiveBoolean to toggle the ComfySwitchNode. PreviewAny shows which string is currently selected.

Explore Example 2 - LoRA Switch: set LoRA strength in LoraLoaderModelOnly (e.g., 0.6–1.0). The switch OFF path (on_false) routes the plain UNet from UNETLoader; the ON path (on_true) routes the LoRA-modified UNet. Flip the PrimitiveBoolean to enable/disable the LoRA.

Set your main prompt input (from the selected string in Example 1) for the generation node (ID 0f79b7f9-d214-4587-b475-bc429519b976). If you want fair A/B tests, set a fixed seed in your generation/sampler node.
Click Queue Prompt to render. Use SaveImage to write outputs and compare results side-by-side. Flip the switch(es) and re-queue to perform A/B comparisons (text variant vs LoRA on/off).
Tip: You can connect the same PrimitiveBoolean to multiple ComfySwitchNode switch pins to synchronize changes (e.g., switch prompt and LoRA together) for fast style presets.
suggestedUseCases: A/B testing prompts: quickly compare short vs detailed prompts or different style descriptors.
Style toggling with LoRA: enable or disable a style LoRA on top of Z-Image-Turbo without rewiring your graph.
Batch runs with optional stylization: run the same prompt twice, with and without LoRA, for client or team reviews.
Teaching and debugging: visualize how data types flow through a graph and validate switch behavior with PreviewAny.
Reusable templates: build workflows with safe defaults and switches to expose just the key choices to end users.

faqItems.question: How does ComfySwitchNode decide which input to use?
faqItems.answer: The boolean switch pin controls routing: OFF (false) forwards on_false; ON (true) forwards on_true. Both inputs must be compatible types (e.g., both strings or both UNet models).

faqItems.question: Does switching the LoRA reload the base model each time?
faqItems.answer: No. UNETLoader holds the base Z-Image-Turbo model. LoraLoaderModelOnly applies the LoRA when that path is active. Toggle the switch and re-queue to recompute with or without the LoRA.

faqItems.question: Can I switch between more than two options?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Chain multiple ComfySwitchNodes (e.g., first selects A vs B, second selects that result vs C). Keep data types consistent across all switch branches.

faqItems.question: How do I get fair comparisons when switching?
faqItems.answer: Use the same prompt and a fixed seed in your generation node, change only one variable at a time (prompt OR LoRA), and save outputs with SaveImage for side-by-side review.

2c4b652466d9.title: SDXL Simple
2c4b652466d9.metaDescription: Generate high-quality images with the SDXL model using ComfyUI's SDXL Simple workflow. Perfect for artists and designers.
2c4b652466d9.extendedDescription:
The 'SDXL Simple' workflow is designed to generate high-quality images by leveraging the capabilities of the SDXL model. This workflow utilizes a series of nodes to transform text prompts into stunning visual representations. The process begins with the 'CheckpointLoaderSimple' node, which loads the SDXL model with optimal settings. The 'CLIPTextEncode' node encodes the input text prompts, which are then processed by the 'KSamplerAdvanced' node to generate latent images with added noise. This noise is crucial as it allows the model to effectively denoise and refine the image. The 'VAEDecode' node plays a critical role by converting the latent data into visible images, which are subsequently saved using the 'SaveImage' node.

This workflow is particularly useful for artists and designers looking to create detailed and high-resolution images with minimal effort. By using the SDXL model, users can ensure that their images are generated with state-of-the-art techniques in AI image synthesis. The workflow's flexibility allows for the use of different SD model versions, making it adaptable to various creative needs. The inclusion of nodes like 'PrimitiveNode' and 'MarkdownNote' provides additional customization and documentation options, enhancing the user experience.
howToUse: Load the SDXL Simple workflow in ComfyUI.
Select your local SDXL model using the 'CheckpointLoaderSimple' node.
Input your desired text prompt in the 'CLIPTextEncode' node.
Run the workflow to generate a latent image with the 'KSamplerAdvanced' node.
Decode the latent image using the 'VAEDecode' node to view the final result.
Save the generated image using the 'SaveImage' node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating high-resolution concept art for digital media projects.
Generating unique backgrounds for graphic design work.
Producing detailed illustrations for storytelling or comics.
Developing custom visuals for marketing and advertising campaigns.
Exploring creative ideas and visual brainstorming.

faqItems.question: What models can I use with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You can use the Base SDXL model, as well as SD1.5 and SD2.x models, by selecting them in the 'CheckpointLoaderSimple' node.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow handle text prompts?
faqItems.answer: The 'CLIPTextEncode' node encodes text prompts using optimal CLIP settings, allowing the model to accurately interpret and generate images based on the input text.

faqItems.question: Why is noise added to the latent image?
faqItems.answer: Noise is added to help the model denoise and refine the image, which is a crucial step in generating high-quality visuals.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the workflow settings?
faqItems.answer: Yes, while the workflow is set up with optimal settings, you can adjust nodes like 'PrimitiveNode' and 'MarkdownNote' for additional customization and documentation.

2cf9f9f6d205.title: Character & Outfit to Fashion Video
2cf9f9f6d205.description: Upload your character and clothing items or accessories. Generate a fashion photograph base and use as a reference to 8x grid images, together with multi-KeyFrame Video Stitching
2cf9f9f6d205.metaDescription: Transform character and outfit images into dynamic fashion videos using ComfyUI's Character & Outfit to Fashion Video workflow.
2cf9f9f6d205.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, titled 'Character & Outfit to Fashion Video,' is designed to transform static images of characters and their clothing into dynamic fashion videos. The process begins by uploading images of characters and clothing items, which are then used to generate a fashion photograph base. This base image serves as a reference to create an 8x grid of images. The workflow utilizes a variety of models, including Google Gemini Image and Nano Banana Pro, to enhance the image-to-video conversion process. Key nodes like GeminiImage2Node and ImageBatch play a crucial role in processing and managing image data, while custom nodes such as comfyui-kjnodes and comfyui_essentials facilitate specific functionalities tailored to fashion video generation.

The technical backbone of this workflow involves a series of node operations that stitch together multiple keyframes into a seamless video. Nodes like SaveImage and LoadImage handle the initial image input and output, while RegexReplace and PrimitiveStringMultiline manage text and metadata processing. The workflow also employs advanced techniques such as multi-KeyFrame Video Stitching, enabled by nodes like SaveVideo and GetImagesFromBatchIndexed, to ensure smooth transitions and high-quality video output. This workflow is particularly useful for fashion designers, marketers, and content creators who wish to showcase clothing designs in a visually engaging format, leveraging AI to automate and enhance the creative process.
howToUse: Load the ComfyUI 'Character & Outfit to Fashion Video' workflow.
Upload your character and clothing images using the LoadImage node.
Generate a fashion photograph base with the GeminiImage2Node.
Create an 8x grid of images using the ImageBatch node for reference.
Utilize multi-KeyFrame Video Stitching to compile images into a video.
Save the final video output using the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Fashion designers can create promotional videos for new clothing lines.
Content creators can generate dynamic video content for social media platforms.
Marketers can produce engaging advertisements showcasing fashion collections.
E-commerce platforms can enhance product listings with animated fashion videos.
Virtual fashion shows can be created for online audiences using this workflow.

faqItems.question: What types of images should I upload to this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Upload high-quality images of characters and clothing items for the best results.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the grid size for the image references?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is set to create an 8x grid by default, but you can adjust this by modifying the ImageBatch node settings.

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate a video using this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The processing time depends on the complexity of the images and the performance of your hardware, but it typically takes a few minutes.

faqItems.question: Is it possible to add audio to the generated fashion video?
faqItems.answer: This workflow focuses on video generation; you can add audio using video editing software after exporting the video.

2da831d21d09.title: Batch Process Text Prompts From List
2da831d21d09.description: Loads and executes a workflow sequentially using prompts from a text list. Iterates through each entry to generate multiple outputs from a single batch operation.
2da831d21d09.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow that batch-processes a list of text prompts with Z-Image-Turbo, selecting one line per step via FL_PromptSelectorBasic and saving each image.
2da831d21d09.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow automates running a list of text prompts one-by-one and saving an image for each entry. It uses the custom FL_PromptSelectorBasic node to read a multiline prompt list and select a single line based on an index provided by a PrimitiveInt node. That selected prompt is then fed into the generation chain powered by the Z-Image-Turbo model, and the resulting image is written to disk by SaveImage. A MarkdownNote in the graph documents the intent and wiring so you can quickly see how the pieces fit together.

Under the hood, FL_PromptSelectorBasic exposes a text field where you paste prompts (one per line). The PrimitiveInt node supplies an index that determines which line is currently active. In a batch run, the index advances one step per batch iteration (when driven by your generation/driver node; listed here as ca7506c4-0f1a-4a77-9d2e-b9077eaf58d5), so each iteration consumes the next prompt from the list. This pattern is ideal for prompt A/B testing, producing sets of assets, or iterating through a campaign brief without manually editing the graph between runs.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and wait for all nodes to appear. Confirm Z-Image-Turbo is available in your models and that SaveImage is connected at the end of the chain.
Open FL_PromptSelectorBasic and paste your prompts into its prompts field, one prompt per line. Avoid quotes or commas; just one clean prompt per line.
Set the PrimitiveInt node to the line index you want to test (e.g., 0 for the first line) and run a single inference to verify the prompt flows into Z-Image-Turbo and produces an image.

For a full batch run, configure your generation/driver node (ca7506c4-0f1a-4a77-9d2e-b9077eaf58d5 in this workflow) to iterate once per prompt line. The FL_PromptSelectorBasic will advance one prompt per batch step via the connected index.
Optionally adjust SaveImage (e.g., filename prefix) so outputs are easy to identify. Then queue the batch. Each step will use the next prompt and save its result.
Review the outputs in your ComfyUI/output directory. If any prompt needs refinement, edit that line in FL_PromptSelectorBasic and re-run just that index with PrimitiveInt.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid prompt A/B testing to compare phrasing and subject variations side by side.
Producing cohesive social or marketing asset sets from a pre-approved prompt list.
Generating small datasets for prototyping or fine-tuning workflows that need varied prompts.
Creative exploration: iterate style or camera directions across the same subject list.
Content QA pipelines where each prompt maps to a checklist item or acceptance test.

faqItems.question: How does the index map to lines in FL_PromptSelectorBasic?
faqItems.answer: The PrimitiveInt provides the selected line’s index. Use 0 for the first line, 1 for the second, and so on. In batch mode, the connected driver advances the index one step per iteration.

faqItems.question: What happens if there are more batch steps than prompt lines?
faqItems.answer: When the index exceeds the number of lines, the selector returns an empty prompt. This can yield generic or unintended images. Match your batch iterations to the number of lines, or trim trailing blank lines.

faqItems.question: Can I keep my negative prompt and other generation settings fixed?
faqItems.answer: Yes. FL_PromptSelectorBasic only swaps the main text prompt. Keep your negative prompt, seed, and other generation parameters set in the Z-Image-Turbo chain and they will apply to every iteration.

faqItems.question: Where are images saved and how do I keep them organized?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage writes to the ComfyUI/output directory using its configured filename prefix. Set a clear prefix (e.g., zturbo_list_run_01) before batching so files are easy to track against your prompt list.

2da9ee24ad74.title: Seedance 2.0 + LLM Prompt Helper
2da9ee24ad74.description: This workflow uses two reference images and a simple text description to automatically generate a detailed Seedance 2.0-style prompt using an LLM. Instead of spending time figuring out complex prompting structure, the workflow analyzes your references and builds the prompt for you, making it much faster and easier to create high-quality results. The included LLM helper is designed to match the style and formatting that works well with Seedance 2.0, helping streamline the entire process while still giving you full control over the final output. Just drop in your references, describe the scene or motion you want, and the workflow handles the prompt generation automatically.
2da9ee24ad74.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use two reference images and Gemini to auto-build Seedance 2.0 prompts, then generate consistent, high-quality videos fast.
2da9ee24ad74.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 + LLM Prompt Helper is a ComfyUI workflow that turns two reference images and a short scene description into a detailed, Seedance-optimized prompt—then renders your video. It uses GeminiNode to analyze your references and expand your brief into the style and structure Seedance 2.0 expects, so you spend less time wrestling with prompt formatting and more time iterating on look, motion, and composition. The Seedance 2.0 generation runs through ByteDance2ReferenceNode, giving you reference-driven consistency from first frame to last.

Technically, the Reference Images group uses LoadImage to bring in two guides and ImageConcanate to combine them for quick visual context, previewed with PreviewImage. Your short description and the two images feed the LLM group, where GeminiNode produces a refined Seedance-style prompt that’s displayed via MarkdownNote for easy review and edits. That text flows to the Seedance 2.0 group: ByteDance2ReferenceNode conditions on the two references plus the generated prompt to synthesize frames, which you can inspect in PreviewAny and export with SaveVideo. The result is a streamlined loop: drop images, describe the motion, let the LLM draft the prompt, tweak if needed, and render.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm required nodes are available: GeminiNode and ByteDance2ReferenceNode (plus built-ins like LoadImage, PreviewImage/PreviewAny, ImageConcanate, SaveVideo). Ensure GeminiNode is configured with a valid API key.
Add your two reference images in the Reference Images group using the LoadImage nodes. The ImageConcanate node will combine them for a side-by-side preview (check it with PreviewImage).
Type a short description of the scene or motion you want in the LLM input. Temporarily bypass the Seedance generation (select ByteDance2ReferenceNode and press Ctrl+B) so only the LLM runs.
Queue the graph to run the LLM. Review the generated Seedance-style prompt in the MarkdownNote. Edit or refine the text there if you want more specificity (subjects, camera moves, lighting, pacing).

Re-enable ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Ctrl+B again). Optionally adjust its key settings (e.g., reference weighting, steps, guidance, resolution, and frame count if exposed). Queue the graph to generate frames and preview them in PreviewAny.
When satisfied, use SaveVideo to export the result. Set filename and basic video options (e.g., fps) as needed, then queue to write the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Style-locked character or product motion: keep design consistent across shots by anchoring on two reference angles.
Fast concept iterations: explore multiple motion directions by quickly re-running the LLM with small prompt edits.
Shot continuity for short-form content: maintain look and feel across a sequence of clips using the same reference pair.
Previs and storyboarding: generate motion studies from rough references before committing to full production.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use the LLM, or can I write the Seedance prompt myself?
faqItems.answer: You can do either. The LLM (GeminiNode) is optional—use it to draft a Seedance 2.0–style prompt, then edit it in MarkdownNote. If you already have a strong prompt, skip the LLM and feed your text directly to ByteDance2ReferenceNode.

faqItems.question: Why two reference images?
faqItems.answer: Using two references gives Seedance 2.0 a clearer target for subject, style, and context (e.g., front and three-quarter views, or subject plus environment). This typically improves consistency and reduces drift compared to a single reference.

faqItems.question: The LLM isn’t running—what should I check?
faqItems.answer: Make sure GeminiNode is configured with a valid API key and internet access, and that you’re only running the LLM at first (bypass ByteDance2ReferenceNode with Ctrl+B). If the request exceeds model limits, shorten your description or resize references before retrying.

faqItems.question: How do I improve quality or stabilize motion?
faqItems.answer: Start with better references (clear subject, lighting, and style). In ByteDance2ReferenceNode, increase steps or guidance for sharper detail, and adjust reference weighting to keep the look locked in. If available, reduce resolution or frame count during exploration and scale up once you like the motion.

2e37304a2fbd.title: Outpaint to Any Aspect Ratio - Nano Banana Pro
2e37304a2fbd.description: Upload your image, input your desired aspect ratio and the images position (as a percentage) in the new aspect ratio composite. Uses Nano Banana Pro to generate an outpainted version of your image to fit the new dimensions.
2e37304a2fbd.metaDescription: Outpaint any image to a new aspect ratio without cropping. Anchor the original by percentage and let Nano Banana Pro fill the rest seamlessly in ComfyUI.
2e37304a2fbd.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow outpaints a single image to any target aspect ratio without cropping or distorting your original. You load an image with LoadImage, then the custom Image Extender node (b26cc822-68bf-4fd0-b66f-bb3f99cd1443) builds a new canvas based on your chosen aspect ratio and anchors the original at a user-defined position (in percent). Only the newly added canvas area is generated—your original pixels remain intact. Under the hood, the Image Extender wraps the diffusion process using the Nano Banana Pro model to synthesize surrounding content that blends naturally with the source.

Supporting nodes make the process clear and repeatable: GetImageSize reads the source dimensions, ImageResizeKJv2 optionally scales inputs or outputs for cleaner detail, and PreviewImage/ImageCompare help you evaluate before/after results. If you prefer guided generation, GeminiImage2Node can provide an image-aware prompt that feeds into the Image Extender. When you’re satisfied, SaveImage writes the final outpainted result. The combination of precise placement controls, aspect ratio targeting, and a capable outpainting model makes this a practical tool for repurposing images for social, web, and print formats without losing key content.
howToUse: Load the workflow and drop your source image into the LoadImage node. Use GetImageSize and PreviewImage to confirm the input looks correct.

Open the Image Extender node (b26cc822-68bf-4fd0-b66f-bb3f99cd1443) and set your target aspect ratio (e.g., 16:9 or 9:16). Set the image position as percentages (X% and Y%), where 0%/0% is top-left and 100%/100% is bottom-right.

Optional: If you want prompt guidance, connect GeminiImage2Node to analyze the input image and feed a descriptive prompt to the Image Extender, or enter your own prompt/style text directly in the node if it exposes a prompt field.
Optional: Use ImageResizeKJv2 to scale the input (or target output) so dimensions are reasonable for your GPU and are multiples of 8 for diffusion stability.
Run the graph. Inspect the outpainted result with PreviewImage and compare it to the original using ImageCompare. Adjust aspect ratio, position, or prompt as needed and re-run.
When satisfied, save the final image with SaveImage.
suggestedUseCases: Convert landscape photos to vertical 9:16 for Reels/Stories without cropping the subject.
Extend product photos into banner-ready 16:9 or 21:9 hero images while preserving the original packshot.
Reformat film stills or key art to multiple storefront aspect ratios from a single master image.
Add safe margins around UI mockups or screenshots for device frames and captions.
Turn a portrait into a desktop wallpaper by outpainting cohesive background scenery.

faqItems.question: How does the aspect ratio and position control work?
faqItems.answer: The Image Extender creates a new canvas sized to your target aspect ratio, then places the original image at the specified X/Y percentages. Percentages map to the canvas: 0% is left/top, 50% is centered, and 100% is right/bottom. The empty regions are filled by Nano Banana Pro, while the original pixels are preserved.

faqItems.question: Will my original image be altered or blurred?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow composites the untouched original over the generated content. Only the newly added canvas area is synthesized; the source pixels remain exactly as loaded.

faqItems.question: Do I need a prompt for good results?
faqItems.answer: Not strictly. Nano Banana Pro can infer context from the source image, but a short prompt often improves style consistency (e.g., "soft natural light, cohesive background"). You can type a prompt directly in the Image Extender (if available) or use GeminiImage2Node to auto-suggest one from the image.

faqItems.question: Any tips to reduce artifacts or seams?
faqItems.answer: Keep expansions moderate for the first pass and ensure output dimensions are multiples of 8. If the Image Extender exposes settings like steps or denoise, increase them slightly and re-run. Repositioning the subject (position percentages) to give the model more room on the outpaint side can also help. If VRAM is limited, downscale with ImageResizeKJv2, outpaint, then upscale later.

2f10814fd823.title: Cinematic Bridge Video
2f10814fd823.description: Generate or use a final frame, then create a cinematic transition from the input frame to the end frame.
2f10814fd823.metaDescription: Create a cinematic video that bridges a starting frame to a generated or supplied final frame using Gemini and Seedance 2.0 in ComfyUI.
2f10814fd823.extendedDescription:
Cinematic Bridge Video is a first-to-last frame translator that turns a single starting image into a short, cinematic clip that arrives at a chosen destination image. You can either supply your own end frame or let the workflow generate one for you. The flow begins with LoadImage for the opening frame. If you don’t have a final frame, a Prompt group uses GeminiNode to expand or refine your idea, then GeminiImage2Node synthesizes a dramatic endpoint image in the same story world and resolution. Both frames are previewed with PreviewAny, and SaveImage can archive the generated endpoint for reuse.

The actual motion is created by Seedance 2.0 via ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, which interpolates between the first and last frames to produce a smooth, cinematic transition. You control duration and pacing by adjusting frame count and FPS, and you can nudge motion strength and consistency to balance creativity with subject fidelity. Finally, SaveVideo writes the bridge clip to disk, while SaveImage can optionally save key frames or the generated endpoint. MarkdownNote blocks in the canvas document recommended settings and usage tips.

This setup is ideal when you want story-consistent reveals or scene transitions without animating a full sequence from scratch. Keeping both frames aligned in subject, lighting, and aspect ratio helps Seedance 2.0 generate stable, believable in-betweens with minimal flicker.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the three groups: Prompt, First to Last Frame Translator, and Seedance 2.0.

In the Prompt group: Load your first frame with LoadImage. If you already have a final frame, load it with another LoadImage node. Otherwise, enter a concise description in GeminiNode and feed it to GeminiImage2Node to generate the end frame. Match the end frame’s resolution to the first frame.

Open the Seedance 2.0 group and set ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode to use your first and last frames. Adjust key parameters such as total frame count (or duration) and FPS to control clip length and pacing. Tune motion/consistency controls as needed to keep subjects stable.

Use PreviewAny to inspect the generated endpoint image and quick test runs from the translator. If the look isn’t right, refine the Gemini prompt, adjust seeds (for reproducibility and variation), or regenerate the end frame.
When satisfied, run the full graph. SaveImage will export the generated final frame (if you created one), and SaveVideo will write the finished bridge clip to disk.

Review the output. If you see jitter or mismatched composition, bring the first and last frames closer in framing/lighting, lower motion strength, or slightly increase duration for a smoother blend, then rerun.
suggestedUseCases: Product or character reveal: start from a neutral shot and transition into a hero pose or branded key art.
Storyboard polishing: bridge a rough opening frame to a refined concept frame for pitch-ready motion previews.
Before-and-after demos: smoothly morph from an original scene to a retouched or redesigned endpoint.
Title or scene transitions: move from a live-action still into a styled title card or environment matte.
Social teasers: create short cinematic bridges for platform-friendly reveals and announcements.

faqItems.question: Do I need to provide the final frame, or can the workflow generate it?
faqItems.answer: Either works. If you already have a destination image, load it with LoadImage. If not, enter a description in GeminiNode and use GeminiImage2Node to synthesize a cinematic endpoint that matches your story and resolution.

faqItems.question: How do I change the clip length and pacing?
faqItems.answer: In ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode (Seedance 2.0), set the total frame count (or duration) and FPS. More frames or a higher FPS lengthens the clip and smooths motion. For punchier pacing, reduce frames or use a slightly lower FPS.

faqItems.question: My video flickers or warps. How can I stabilize it?
faqItems.answer: Keep both frames the same size and aspect ratio, and ensure similar composition and lighting. Make the endpoint semantically close to the start (same subject, pose, wardrobe). In Seedance 2.0, reduce motion strength or increase duration. If available, set a fixed seed for reproducibility and regenerate.

faqItems.question: What resolution should I use?
faqItems.answer: Use matching dimensions for the first and last frames. If generating the endpoint with GeminiImage2Node, set its output size to match the loaded first frame. If you import your own end frame, crop/resize externally so both inputs have identical width and height.

3427fd6e0fa8.title: Wan2.1 VACE Outpainting
3427fd6e0fa8.description: Generate extended videos by expanding video size using Wan VACE outpainting.
3427fd6e0fa8.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Outpaint and enlarge videos with Wan 2.1 VACE. Learn setup, masks, prompts, and constraints to create extended, coherent video frames.
3427fd6e0fa8.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow teaches you how to outpaint a video—expanding its canvas while keeping the original content intact—using Wan 2.1 VACE. It loads your source clip with LoadVideo and extracts dimensions and frame count via GetVideoComponents and PreviewImage. You then define where to expand using ImagePadForOutpaint and a mask built from ImageToMask/MaskToImage, replicated across time with RepeatImageBatch. Prompts are encoded with CLIPTextEncode, and generation runs through KSampler with ModelSamplingSD3 scheduling on a Wan 2.1 VACE UNet/Decoder stack (UNETLoader, VAELoader), with VAEDecode converting latents to frames. WanVaceToVideo handles video-specific conditioning, and TrimVideoLatent ensures temporal shapes align. The result is assembled with CreateVideo and saved via SaveVideo.

Technically, two alignment rules matter for stable inference: the spatial size you set for outpainting must be divisible by 16 (a constraint of WanVaceToVideo and the VAE), and the sequence length must satisfy the temporal constraint (Length - 1 divisible by 4), which TrimVideoLatent addresses. Because core Comfy nodes don’t yet expose video size/frame-count utilities, this template uses PreviewImage as a practical workaround; you can swap in custom utility nodes if available. The workflow includes model groups for Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B (lighter, recommended for 480p) and Wan2.1-VACE-14B (higher quality, suitable for higher resolutions like 720p if resources allow). Default generation settings are steps: 20 and cfg: 6.0, with optional CausVid LoRA tuning at steps: 2–4 and cfg: 1.0.
howToUse: Load the workflow and select your model: in the "Load models here" group, choose either the 1.3B or 14B path. Point UNETLoader and VAELoader to the Wan2.1 VACE checkpoints that match your choice.

Import your source clip with LoadVideo. Use GetVideoComponents and PreviewImage to read the current width/height and total frames. In the "Video size - Must be divisible by 16" group, set your target outpainted width/height to multiples of 16.

Define the outpaint region: configure ImagePadForOutpaint to add pixels on the sides you want to expand. Build a binary mask with ImageToMask/MaskToImage to protect the original content area, then RepeatImageBatch so the mask length matches all frames.

Write prompts in the "Prompt" group using CLIPTextEncode (positive) and a negative like "bad quality, blurry, messy, chaotic" if desired. In KSampler, start with steps=20 and cfg=6.0 (or for CausVid LoRA: steps=2–4, cfg=1.0). Choose your sampler/scheduler via ModelSamplingSD3 and set a seed.

Ensure temporal alignment: use the "Length - 1 should be divisible by 4" group and TrimVideoLatent so the sequence length conforms to VAE/VACE expectations. Then run WanVaceToVideo -> VAEDecode to generate the outpainted frames.
Assemble and save: feed frames into CreateVideo, set fps from GetVideoComponents, and export with SaveVideo (MP4). If edges look off, adjust the mask or padding, tweak CFG/steps, and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Reformatting horizontal videos to vertical (or vice versa) by outpainting additional background for social platforms.
Adding safe headroom or side-space for titles, lower thirds, and UI overlays without cropping the subject.
Extending establishing shots by widening the scene for a more cinematic composition.
Repairing tight framing: add background context around the subject to avoid cutoffs.
Creating gentle push-in/pull-back storytelling space while preserving the original action area.

faqItems.question: Why must width/height be divisible by 16 and length-1 be divisible by 4?
faqItems.answer: WanVaceToVideo and the VAE downsample spatially by powers of two, so dimensions must align to 16 for clean latent shapes. The temporal pathway expects sequence lengths that satisfy (frames - 1) % 4 == 0. TrimVideoLatent enforces the temporal rule; set your target resolution to multiples of 16 for the spatial rule.

faqItems.question: Which model should I use: Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B or 14B?
faqItems.answer: Use 1.3B for faster runs and 480p outputs on modest GPUs. Choose 14B for higher quality and, if your VRAM allows, higher resolutions such as 720p. The 14B model produces better detail but is slower and more memory-intensive.

faqItems.question: How do I control where outpainting happens?
faqItems.answer: Use ImagePadForOutpaint to add canvas on chosen sides (top/bottom/left/right). Then create a mask that protects the original video region (ImageToMask/MaskToImage) and replicate it across frames with RepeatImageBatch. The model synthesizes only in the unmasked, newly padded areas.

faqItems.question: My output is black/misaligned. What should I check?
faqItems.answer: Verify three points: 1) Output width/height are divisible by 16, 2) TrimVideoLatent is applied so (frames - 1) is divisible by 4, 3) VAEDecode is connected before CreateVideo/SaveVideo. Also confirm fps and frame count from GetVideoComponents, and that your mask batch length matches the video length.

3515c5083027.title: Image to Video
3515c5083027.description: This app generates a high quality video with sound. All you need is to upload an input image and write prompt.
3515c5083027.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a video with prompt-guided motion in ComfyUI. LoadImage + Image-to-Video node + SaveVideo for fast, controllable results.
3515c5083027.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short video guided by a text prompt. It uses LoadImage to bring in your source frame, passes it to a dedicated Image-to-Video generator node (ID: 770dde0e-f342-49aa-ad1e-184724671c5d), and then encodes the resulting frame sequence with SaveVideo. The generator node conditions on both the input image (as a visual anchor) and your prompt (to suggest motion, style, or scene changes), producing a coherent set of frames that evolve over time.

Technically, the generator node synthesizes a batch of images (frames) from the static input by sampling with a controllable seed and typical parameters such as number of frames, motion/denoise strength, guidance, and resolution. SaveVideo then assembles those frames into a playable clip at your chosen FPS and output format (e.g., MP4 or WebM). You control duration via frame count and playback feel via FPS, while the seed lets you repeat or iterate on results consistently. This makes the workflow useful for quick motion studies, cinemagraph-like clips, and social-ready animations without needing full video capture.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three key nodes are present: LoadImage, the Image-to-Video generator (ID: 770dde0e-f342-49aa-ad1e-184724671c5d), and SaveVideo.
Open LoadImage and select your source image. Use a reasonably sized input (e.g., 512–1024 on the long side) to balance quality and VRAM usage.
In the Image-to-Video generator node, enter a clear prompt describing desired motion and mood (e.g., “gentle camera push-in, soft breeze moving hair, golden-hour lighting”).

Adjust core parameters in the generator node: set number of frames (clip length), FPS (playback speed), resolution, motion/denoise strength (how much it departs from the source), guidance scale, and seed for reproducibility.
Configure SaveVideo: choose FPS to match the generator output and your preferred output format/quality. Set an output file name/path.

Click Queue Prompt to run. When finished, open the saved video to review. If you see artifacts or over-strong motion, lower motion/denoise strength, reduce resolution or frame count, and re-run with the same or a new seed.
suggestedUseCases: Cinemagraph-style loops from product or portrait photos (subtle motion like hair, fabric, or light shifts).
Quick animated previews for concept art or storyboards to explore camera moves and atmosphere.
Social media posts that add motion to key visuals for higher engagement without full video shoots.
Product hero animations for e-commerce banners and landing pages.
Ambient motion backgrounds derived from brand imagery for intros or titles.

faqItems.question: How long can the generated video be?
faqItems.answer: Length is determined by the number of frames and FPS. For example, 48 frames at 12 FPS ≈ 4 seconds. Longer clips require more VRAM and time; increase frames gradually and consider lowering resolution or FPS if you hit memory limits.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the video faithful to the original image?
faqItems.answer: Use a conservative prompt and reduce the node’s motion/denoise strength so it deviates less from the source. Also try increasing guidance strength and using a fixed seed. If available, choose a sampler or setting that favors stronger conditioning.

faqItems.question: My output has jitter or artifacts. What should I change?
faqItems.answer: Lower motion/denoise strength, reduce resolution, and try a different seed. You can also decrease the number of frames or use a slightly higher guidance value. Subtle, specific prompts often produce more stable motion than broad or conflicting ones.

faqItems.question: Which formats can I save to?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo can assemble the frames into a video container like MP4 or WebM (options depend on your node’s settings and installed encoders). Match FPS between the generator and SaveVideo to avoid timing issues.

36794f399aa0.title: Z-Image-Turbo_Oldschool-Hud-Graphics
36794f399aa0.description: Create Oldschool Hud Graphics with a LoRA and Z-Image Turbo. Use a LoRA to create unique styles, characters or looks.
36794f399aa0.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate old-school HUD graphics fast with a style LoRA and Z-Image Turbo. Batch variants, then export images or animated clips.
36794f399aa0.extendedDescription:
This workflow generates retro, old‑school HUD graphics from text prompts by combining a style LoRA with a turbo sampler for rapid iteration. The "Oldschool Hud Graphics" LoRA steers the base checkpoint toward geometric UI motifs—reticles, gridlines, rings, readouts—while the Z‑Image Turbo node accelerates sampling for fast previews and quick style exploration. BatchImagesNode lets you spin up variations in one pass, and SaveImage captures your chosen frames. When you’re ready to animate, CreateVideo and SaveVideo assemble your batch into a short motion clip.

Under the hood, your prompt is encoded and fed to the base model with the LoRA applied at a user‑set weight, biasing attention layers toward the HUD aesthetic. Z‑Image Turbo then samples with low step counts for speed, which you can tune for crisper lines or more detail. Keep the LoRA weight moderate to strong to emphasize the graphic look, and pair it with concise prompts (e.g., "retro heads‑up display, concentric circles, grid overlay, monochrome green") plus a negative prompt to suppress photoreal clutter. The included MarkdownNote contains in‑graph tips, while the custom nodes (listed by UUID) handle the LoRA/Turbo plumbing so you can focus on prompts, batch size (BatchImagesNode), and output (SaveImage/SaveVideo).
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. Place your base checkpoint in models/checkpoints and the "Oldschool Hud Graphics" LoRA in models/loras, then select them in the corresponding model/LoRA nodes in the graph.

Open the prompt nodes feeding Z-Image Turbo and write a concise positive prompt (e.g., "old-school HUD, reticle, wireframe circles, grid overlay, monochrome green"). Add a negative prompt to suppress unwanted elements (e.g., "photoreal, face, background scene, text artifacts").
Set the LoRA weight to control style intensity (start around 0.7–1.0). Use BatchImagesNode to choose how many variants to generate per run (e.g., 4–8) for quick exploration.

Configure Z-Image Turbo for speed and clarity: begin with low steps for previews (e.g., 4–8), moderate guidance (CFG) to avoid clutter, and a layout-friendly resolution/aspect ratio suited to your design (e.g., square for icons, portrait for posters).
Run the graph. Review the batch outputs, then fine-tune the prompt, LoRA weight, steps, and CFG until the HUD elements are crisp and legible. Use SaveImage to export final stills.
Optional: To create an animated clip from your batch, connect the images to CreateVideo, set frame rate and order, then finalize with SaveVideo.
suggestedUseCases: Editorial and poster layouts needing retro HUD accents, frames, and readouts.
Branding moodboards and styleframes exploring techy, wireframe visual language.
Game UI concepts and overlays for prototypes or pitch decks.
YouTube/TikTok bumpers and lower‑thirds using animated HUD elements.
Icon sets and badges with minimal, high‑contrast instrumentation motifs.

faqItems.question: Which base model should I use with the Oldschool Hud Graphics LoRA?
faqItems.answer: Use a checkpoint that matches the LoRA’s architecture (e.g., SD 1.5 LoRA with an SD 1.5 checkpoint, SDXL LoRA with an SDXL checkpoint). Check the LoRA’s model card or filename for its target version. Mixing versions will reduce quality or fail to load.

faqItems.question: How do I control how strong the HUD style appears?
faqItems.answer: Adjust the LoRA weight (lower for subtle, higher for strong). Refine prompts to emphasize geometry (reticle, grid, ring, UI readouts) and use a negative prompt to suppress photoreal features. If outputs feel busy, slightly lower CFG or reduce steps to simplify shapes.

faqItems.question: My lines look soft or messy—how can I sharpen them?
faqItems.answer: Increase sampling steps modestly in Z‑Image Turbo, keep CFG moderate, and try a resolution that matches your final layout (avoid extreme upscales in one pass). Tighten the prompt to fewer, clearer elements (e.g., one reticle + one grid) and avoid conflicting style terms.

faqItems.question: How do I turn a batch of images into a video?
faqItems.answer: After generating a batch with BatchImagesNode, connect the sequence to CreateVideo, set your frame rate and ordering, then export with SaveVideo. This compiles your HUD variants into a short motion clip for previews or social posts.

38a5302d2c2d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds a guided style and scene transition on top of the LTX-2.3 text-to-video model by applying the ltx2.3-transition LoRA. The core generation happens inside a custom LTX-2.3 pipeline node (beb19732-5803-4af6-b2d2-289692ce780b), which takes your prompt, applies the LoRA at a user-defined weight, and renders a sequence of frames that smoothly evolve from one style or scene description to another. MarkdownNote is embedded to keep prompting tips visible as you iterate, and SaveVideo encodes the final frames into a video file at your chosen frame rate and quality. The result is a reliable, loop-friendly way to blend visual elements—style, lighting, subject emphasis, or even scene composition—without hand-animating or post-processing crossfades.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the embedded MarkdownNote for LTX-2.3 prompting tips and the trigger word guidance.
Open the custom LTX-2.3 pipeline node (beb19732-5803-4af6-b2d2-289692ce780b) and confirm LTX-2.3 is selected as the base model and the ltx2.3-transition LoRA is enabled.

Write your prompt to describe the transition over time (e.g., "A city street at dusk slowly becomes a neon cyberpunk alley, camera dolly forward, soft fog"), then add the trigger word "zhuanchang" near the end. Keep subject, scene, camera movement, and transformation behavior clearly stated.

Optionally use LoadImage to bring in a style or subject reference and connect it to the pipeline’s reference input. Start with a moderate LoRA strength (e.g., 0.6–0.8) and keep other defaults as-is for a first pass.
Set frame count and FPS to control transition duration (more frames = slower, smoother change). Fix a seed for reproducibility if you plan to iterate. Then run the graph.

Preview the output and, if needed, adjust LoRA strength (lower for subtler transitions, higher for stronger shifts), refine the prompt timing language, and re-run. Use SaveVideo to export at your chosen FPS and quality.
suggestedUseCases: Scene-to-scene bridges in short films: evolve from one location or time-of-day to another without a hard cut.
Style morphs for product reels: smoothly change materials, finishes, or lighting styles around a single subject.
Title and logo reveals: transition from abstract textures to clean branding assets.
Mood shifts in music videos: gradually shift color grade and atmosphere to match track sections.
Concept art explorations: iterate across art styles while maintaining core composition and subject.

faqItems.question: What does the "zhuanchang" trigger word do, and where should I put it?
faqItems.answer: It activates the ltx2.3-transition behavior in the model+LoRA combo. Place it near the end of your prompt so your core subject, scene, camera, and transformation details remain dominant. This helps the base description stay clear while the transition logic is applied.

faqItems.question: How do I control how fast the transition happens?
faqItems.answer: Use frame count and FPS. More frames at the same FPS produce a longer, slower transition; fewer frames produce a faster one. You can also phrase timing cues in your prompt (e.g., "first half… then…"), but duration is primarily governed by total frames and playback speed.

faqItems.question: When should I use a reference image with LoadImage?
faqItems.answer: Use a reference if you want to anchor color palette, texture, or a specific subject look. Connect it to the pipeline’s reference input. If you aim for a purely text-driven transition, skip the reference and rely on descriptive prompts.

faqItems.question: The transition feels too strong or inconsistent. How can I improve stability?
faqItems.answer: Lower the LoRA strength to 0.4–0.6 for subtler shifts, fix the seed for repeatability, and simplify the prompt to fewer, clearer visual goals. Avoid conflicting descriptors; keep subject and camera consistent while describing how the scene or style evolves.

3cb47a67b81a.title: LTX 2.3 - Cozy Felt
3cb47a67b81a.description: Stylized text-to-video generation using VRGameDevGirl84's LTX 2.3 LoRAs + Workflow, adapted to run on Comfy Cloud. Creates adorable felt worlds and characters.
3cb47a67b81a.metaDescription: Create adorable felt-style text-to-video clips with LTX 2.3 LoRAs in ComfyUI. Pick a LoRA, add its trigger word, and export with VHS_VideoCombine.
3cb47a67b81a.extendedDescription:
LTX 2.3 - Cozy Felt is a stylized text-to-video workflow that wraps VRGameDevGirl84’s LTX 2.3 LoRAs around the LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1 model to generate short, adorable "felt" animations from a prompt. The core generation is driven by a custom LTX node (ID 45d6b185-beee-4467-b4c2-debdf835cb35) configured to load the LTX2 video VAE (LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors) for latent-space video sampling. You pick a LoRA from a dropdown, include its trigger word in your prompt (for example, F3ltCut0u7 for the cozy felt look), and the node produces a sequence of stylized frames. The MarkdownNote node embedded in the canvas provides quick instructions and lists the LoRA trigger words so you don’t have to leave the workspace.

After diffusion, frames are assembled into a playable clip with VHS_VideoCombine, where you set the frame rate and output format. This separation (generate frames first, then encode) makes iteration fast and predictable: you can tweak prompts, LoRA strength, seed, frame count, or resolution on the generation node, then re-run only the combine step to change FPS or container. The result is a reliable, beginner-friendly pipeline for creating soft, craft-like animations—great for cozy title cards, character snippets, or looping social posts. Note: the audio VAE (LTX2_audio_vae_bf16.safetensors) is listed in the assets but is not wired into this canvas by default.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI (or Comfy Cloud) and confirm the required files are available: LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1-GGUF and LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors. If a node reports a missing model, update the file path in the core LTX node.

Open the core LTX generation node (ID 45d6b185-beee-4467-b4c2-debdf835cb35). Choose a LoRA from the lora_name dropdown and include its trigger word in your positive prompt (e.g., “F3ltCut0u7” for the cozy felt style). Add a concise subject and simple motion cues.

Set key parameters on the generation node: seed (fixed for repeatability), steps (increase for cleaner detail), guidance/CFG (moderate values for style adherence), resolution (keep the short side ~512–768 for speed), frames and FPS (e.g., 24–48 frames at 8–12 FPS). Adjust LoRA strength if exposed.

Optionally add a negative prompt to reduce unwanted textures or artifacts (e.g., “text, watermark, logo, blurry, noisy”). Keep camera motion and scene complexity simple for the most consistent felt look.
Run the generation to produce frames. Inspect a few frames to confirm the style and subject match your intent; if needed, refine the prompt, LoRA strength, or steps and re-run.
Open VHS_VideoCombine, set the desired FPS and container (e.g., MP4), then execute it to assemble the frames into a video. Download the result from the file browser or Comfy Cloud output panel.
suggestedUseCases: Cozy title cards or intros for craft, DIY, or children’s content
Short character loops for social posts or stickers with a handmade aesthetic
Whimsical product stingers for toy or stationery brands
Educational snippets for kids’ apps with soft, friendly visuals
Seasonal greeting animations with felt cutout themes

faqItems.question: Do I have to use the LoRA trigger word?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Each LTX 2.3 LoRA has a trigger keyword (e.g., F3ltCut0u7) that activates its style. Include it in the positive prompt along with your subject for consistent results.

faqItems.question: What controls improve temporal consistency?
faqItems.answer: Keep prompts simple, use a fixed seed, avoid rapid camera moves, and limit clip length (e.g., 24–48 frames). Increasing steps can help detail, while moderate guidance/CFG avoids jittery overcorrection.

faqItems.question: Where do I put the models and VAE files?
faqItems.answer: Place the base model (LTX-2.3-22B-DISTILLED-1.1-GGUF) and LTX2_video_vae_bf16.safetensors in the paths expected by the core LTX node. If the node reports a missing file, update its model and VAE fields to your actual paths. The audio VAE is not used by default.

faqItems.question: How do I change the playback speed without re-generating frames?
faqItems.answer: Use VHS_VideoCombine. Re-run only that node and change the FPS or format; it will re-encode the existing frames into a new video without redoing diffusion.
