3ddb7afa1aa4.title: Seedance 2.5: FLF2V
3ddb7afa1aa4.description: Generate a smooth video transition between a user-provided start frame and end frame with Seedance 2.5, which automatically interpolates the motion, camera movement, and visual evolution while locking both endpoints. Ideal for shot transitions, storyboard previz, and before-and-after scene showcases like empty-to-packed or day-to-night shifts.
3ddb7afa1aa4.metaDescription: Create smooth, locked-endpoint video transitions from two images using Seedance 2.5. Load start/end frames, auto-interpolate motion, and export with SaveVideo.
3ddb7afa1aa4.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.5: FLF2V is a first–last frame to video workflow that generates a smooth, locked-endpoint transition between two user-provided images. It uses two LoadImage nodes to bring in your start and end frames, then passes them to ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, which calls the Seedance 2.5 model to synthesize the in-between motion and appearance changes while preserving both endpoints. Finally, SaveVideo encodes the returned frame sequence into a playable video file.

Technically, the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode estimates a coherent motion path and visual evolution between the first and last frames so the video “lands” exactly on your inputs. This makes it ideal for creating believable camera moves, time-of-day shifts, or scene population changes without re-shooting. Because endpoints are locked, the output is especially stable for shot bridges, storyboard previz, and before–after showcases. SaveVideo then packages the generated frames at your chosen playback rate for quick review or handoff.
howToUse: Load the Seedance 2.5: FLF2V workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the three nodes are present: two LoadImage nodes, ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, and SaveVideo.
Import your start and end images with the LoadImage nodes. For best results, use matching resolution and aspect ratio; crop or pad so both images are the same size.
Connect the start image output to the First/Start input on ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and the end image output to the Last/End input. Verify the node shows both images are received.

Open ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode and set its available generation controls (e.g., number of in-between frames or duration if exposed, any seed/reproducibility options, and interpolation quality settings). If the node uses an API, make sure your credentials are configured.
Configure SaveVideo (e.g., filename/prefix and playback FPS) so the final timing matches your target duration. Higher FPS yields smoother playback at the same frame count.
Queue and run the workflow. Review the saved video output; if you see warping or pacing issues, adjust the input alignment or interpolation settings, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Shot transitions: bridge two adjacent storyboards or plates with a believable move that lands precisely on the next shot.
Before–after reveals: transform empty-to-crowded spaces, clean-to-stylized looks, or day-to-night progressions while keeping endpoints fixed.
Previsualization: quickly iterate camera paths and scene evolution between two keyframes for pitch decks or animatics.
Product makeovers: show refurbish or colorway changes from baseline to final without retraining a model.
Environmental changes: simulate seasonal or lighting shifts between two photographic keyframes.

faqItems.question: Do my start and end images need the same size?
faqItems.answer: Yes—use matching resolution and aspect ratio for stable interpolation. Crop or pad one image to match the other before sending both into ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode.

faqItems.question: How do I control the speed of the transition?
faqItems.answer: Adjust the total frames generated (if exposed by ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode) and/or the FPS in SaveVideo. More frames or lower FPS lengthens the clip; fewer frames or higher FPS shortens it.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or warping in the middle frames?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, minimally compressed inputs with consistent framing. Align subjects similarly across both images, avoid drastic composition jumps, and, if available, tweak the node’s interpolation/quality settings or try a different seed.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow export audio?
faqItems.answer: No. SaveVideo writes a silent video. Add music or sound effects later in a video editor.

3ddf4a6144a7.title: Runway: Gen4 Turbo Image to Video
3ddf4a6144a7.description: Generate dynamic videos from images using Runway Gen4 Turbo.
3ddf4a6144a7.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: convert a still image into a short video using Runway Gen4 Turbo with LoadImage, RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4, and SaveVideo.
3ddf4a6144a7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, dynamic video using Runway’s Gen4 Turbo image-to-video model. It wires together four nodes: LoadImage to bring your source image into the graph, RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4 to call the hosted Gen4 Turbo API and synthesize motion over time, SaveVideo to encode the result to a standard video file, and a MarkdownNote with links and setup guidance. Because the heavy lifting runs through the Runway partner node, the workflow stays lightweight and fast on your local machine.

Technically, the LoadImage node supplies the pixel data to RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4, which sends the image (and your chosen settings like duration and frame rate) to the Runway API. The API returns a generated video stream compatible with ComfyUI’s SaveVideo node, which encodes the final clip (e.g., MP4) at your selected FPS. The partner node uses HTTPS and requires a secure network setup as noted in the Author Notes (see "About API Node"): run from localhost/127.0.0.1 and ensure outbound HTTPS is allowed. The result is a clean, reproducible image-to-video pipeline that’s easy to iterate: swap the input image, adjust motion/duration parameters, and re-run to explore different looks.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and review the MarkdownNote for the partner-node setup link and network requirements (localhost/127.0.0.1 and HTTPS).
In the RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4 node, add your Runway API credentials (token/key) if prompted, and verify your machine can reach the API over HTTPS.
Use the LoadImage node to select your source image. For best results, choose a clean, high-resolution image and crop to the aspect ratio you want in the final video.
Configure the RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4 settings: set duration (seconds), target frame rate (fps), and any motion/style controls exposed by the node. Start with moderate motion for fewer artifacts.
Set SaveVideo parameters (output path and fps). Match fps to the Runway node’s output to avoid timing mismatches.
Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the saved clip; iterate by adjusting duration, motion intensity, or trying alternative source images.
suggestedUseCases: Give static product shots subtle camera motion for social posts or landing pages.
Animate concept art or key visuals to create quick motion studies and mood pieces.
Add gentle parallax and subject movement to portraits or editorial images.
Create short teaser loops and background motion for slides, reels, or hero banners.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use Runway Gen4 Turbo in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The RunwayImageToVideoNodeGen4 node is a partner/API node and requires valid Runway credentials. Enter your token/key in the node’s settings and ensure outbound HTTPS access.

faqItems.question: What image sizes and aspect ratios work best?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, high-quality images cropped to your target aspect ratio. Avoid extreme aspect ratios and cluttered backgrounds. If your output looks stretched or cropped, resize/crop the input image to match the intended video aspect.

faqItems.question: How do I reduce flicker or artifacts in the generated video?
faqItems.answer: Try lowering motion intensity or complexity in the Runway node settings, shorten the duration, and use higher-quality, well-lit source images. Subtle motion generally produces cleaner results. Re-run with small tweaks until the motion stabilizes.

faqItems.question: I get connection errors—how do I fix them?
faqItems.answer: Follow the partner-node requirements: run ComfyUI locally (localhost/127.0.0.1), ensure your environment allows HTTPS, and that your firewall/proxy is not blocking the Runway API. See the "About API Node" link in the workflow’s MarkdownNote for setup details.

3eb92c1b2380.metaDescription: End-to-end ComfyUI text-to-video workflow using Qwen-VL prompt enhancement, keyframe synthesis, and video assembly with preview and export.
3eb92c1b2380.extendedDescription:
AI on the Lot 2026 - Final WF - t2v is a complete text-to-video pipeline that stitches together prompt design, image synthesis, and video assembly inside ComfyUI. It uses AILab_QwenVL and AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer to turn a simple idea into a rich, structured prompt. From there, the workflow generates high-quality keyframes with the image synthesis stage (node ID e9d2dda8-2509-4d8d-9702-a9bf00c26650), previews results with PreviewAny, and then builds a cohesive video clip in the video stage (node ID 99c27236-513e-427c-9ed4-49406365f0d3). SaveImage and SaveVideo provide clean, reproducible exports at each stage.

Technically, the flow is: your base text prompt (and optionally a reference image) goes into AILab_QwenVL to extract and enrich scene details. AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer refines the text into a model-friendly prompt with clearer subjects, styles, and shot descriptors. That prompt feeds the image generator node (e9d2dda8-2509-4d8d-9702-a9bf00c26650) to produce one or more seed-controlled keyframes at your chosen resolution. Those frames are then passed to the video node (99c27236-513e-427c-9ed4-49406365f0d3), which synthesizes a clip based on duration and motion/consistency settings. PreviewAny helps you iterate quickly, while SaveImage and SaveVideo lock in stills or a final video once you’re happy. Because the stages are modular, you can use it for text-to-image only, image-to-video only, or end-to-end text-to-video with the same graph.
howToUse: Load the "AI on the Lot 2026 - Final WF - t2v" JSON in ComfyUI and confirm all custom nodes load without errors. Look for AILab_QwenVL, AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer, PreviewAny, SaveImage, and SaveVideo in the graph.

Enter your base prompt in the AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer input. Optionally provide a reference image to AILab_QwenVL if the workflow exposes that input—this grounds the enhanced prompt in your visual reference.

Configure the image generation stage (node ID e9d2dda8-2509-4d8d-9702-a9bf00c26650): set width/height (aspect ratio), steps, guidance/CFG, and seed. Use PreviewAny to check a quick keyframe and SaveImage to export promising stills.

Adjust the video stage (node ID 99c27236-513e-427c-9ed4-49406365f0d3): set clip length (frames or seconds), frames per second, and motion/consistency parameters. Keep resolution modest while iterating for faster previews.

Run a short test render. If you see flicker or drift, try increasing consistency, reducing noise strength, or fixing the seed in the image stage. Iterate on the prompt with AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer for clearer subjects and style.
When satisfied, raise quality settings (steps/resolution if supported), then render the final and export with SaveVideo. Use SaveImage to archive keyframes and thumbnails for future reference.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard and previsualization: generate keyframes from a script prompt, then assemble short motion tests.
Product and logo stingers: produce a single stylized keyframe and animate it into a short looping reveal.
Social micro‑videos: craft a compact prompt, iterate quickly at low resolution, then export a final 5–10s clip.

faqItems.question: Do I need specific models installed for this to work?
faqItems.answer: You need the custom AILab_QwenVL nodes to load successfully; they will rely on Qwen‑VL assets for prompt enhancement. The image and video synthesis nodes (e9d2dda8‑… and 99c27236‑…) use whatever model/checkpoint configuration the workflow provides or you connect. If ComfyUI reports missing models, follow the node warnings to download or point to the correct files.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or subject drift between frames?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing motion/consistency strength in the video node, lowering noise strength, and keeping a fixed seed in the image stage. Clear, specific prompts from AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer (subjects, camera, style) also help. Shorter clips and moderate resolutions are easier to stabilize during iteration.

faqItems.question: What settings should I change for faster previews?
faqItems.answer: Lower resolution, reduce steps in the image node (e9d2dda8‑…), use a smaller clip length or fps in the video node (99c27236‑…), and keep a fixed seed. Use PreviewAny to validate direction before committing to a full‑quality render.

faqItems.question: Can this workflow do image‑to‑video or just text‑to‑video?
faqItems.answer: Both. You can stop after the image stage and export stills (SaveImage), or feed existing/reference imagery through the prompt and video stages to produce motion. The end‑to‑end path is text‑to‑video, but the stages are modular so you can mix and match.

3ef4de40106b.title: Song Generator
3ef4de40106b.description: This app uses Ace-Step 1.5XL to generate a full song and allows you to choose the genre and write the lyrics, either automatically or manually.
3ef4de40106b.metaDescription: ComfyUI Song Generator: use Ace-Step 1.5XL to auto-write BPM/duration-aware lyrics or use your own, then generate and export a complete song.
3ef4de40106b.extendedDescription:
Song Generator is a ComfyUI workflow that synthesizes complete songs with the Ace-Step 1.5XL audio model. It supports two lyric paths: automatic, where a short topic is expanded into BPM- and duration-aware lyrics, and manual, where you paste your own text. A ComfySwitchNode routes between these paths before the lyrics are encoded by TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 and used to guide the audio model. You can preview the result with PreviewAny and export with SaveAudioAdvanced.

Under the hood, UNETLoader and VAELoader load the Ace-Step 1.5XL checkpoints. EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio allocates a latent audio canvas sized to your target duration. ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the sampler for the model, and KSampler performs the iterative denoising on that latent using the conditioning produced by TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5. ConditioningZeroOut is included to safely zero optional negative conditioning when not used. After sampling, VAEDecodeAudio converts the latent to a waveform for monitoring and export.

The BPM/duration-aware lyric module uses PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveFloat to capture BPM and target length, StringReplace to inject those values into a songwriter instruction, and TextGenerate to create structured verses/choruses sized for the track. StringCompare helps detect empty input, and the ComfySwitchNode cleanly selects between the auto-lyrics and a PrimitiveStringMultiline node for manual lyrics. DualCLIPLoader/CLIPLoader are available for workflows that optionally mix in CLIP-style text conditioning, though the primary path uses TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 for Ace-Step.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then point UNETLoader and VAELoader to your Ace-Step 1.5XL UNet and VAE checkpoints.
Pick your lyric mode: set the ComfySwitchNode to Auto (use Topic + BPM + Duration) or Manual (paste lyrics in PrimitiveStringMultiline).
For Auto lyrics: enter a short Topic, set BPM (PrimitiveInt) and Duration (PrimitiveFloat). The StringReplace/TextGenerate nodes will produce structured lyrics sized to your track.
For Manual lyrics: paste your lyrics and, if desired, add style or mood descriptors in the Prompt group strings that feed TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5.

Configure generation basics: set seed/steps/CFG in KSampler, confirm duration in EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio, and leave ModelSamplingAuraFlow at its default unless you know you need a different sampler.
Queue the workflow to generate. Use PreviewAny to audition, then adjust prompts or sampler settings as needed. When satisfied, set filename/format in SaveAudioAdvanced and run to export.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid song ideation from a topic and target BPM/duration for demos or writer’s rooms.
Creating tight-length jingles, intros, or outros that must hit a specific runtime.
Generating alternative lyric drafts over a consistent musical style for songwriting exploration.
Producing quick temp tracks for video editors or game prototyping with approximate timing.

faqItems.question: Do I need specific model files for this to work?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Point UNETLoader and VAELoader to the Ace-Step 1.5XL UNet and VAE checkpoints. The workflow relies on TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 for conditioning, so ensure the corresponding text encoder resources are available as packaged with Ace-Step.

faqItems.question: How accurate are the BPM and duration settings?
faqItems.answer: Duration is enforced by the latent length from EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio, so the output length will match closely. BPM guides the lyric density via TextGenerate and prompt injection but does not force strict metronomic alignment; treat it as a strong narrative/timing hint rather than a beat-locked constraint.

faqItems.question: Can I use my own lyrics?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Switch to the Manual path and paste lyrics into PrimitiveStringMultiline. The ComfySwitchNode routes your text directly to TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 for conditioning before generation.

faqItems.question: How do I improve audio quality or reduce artifacts?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing KSampler steps moderately, lowering CFG if the sound is harsh, and keeping prompts concise and specific. Ensure the correct Ace-Step VAE is loaded, and avoid overly long durations on a single pass if you encounter instability.

3efed399a12d.extendedDescription:
The Flux.1 Dev fp8: Text to Image workflow is designed to generate images from text prompts using a quantized version of the Flux.1 model. This workflow is particularly useful for devices with limited VRAM, as it requires only one model file and operates efficiently with reduced memory demands. The trade-off for this efficiency is a slight reduction in image quality compared to the full version of the model. Technically, the workflow leverages the Flux.1 model, which has been optimized for lower resource consumption by employing an fp8 quantization technique. This reduces the precision of the model's weights, allowing it to run on less powerful hardware without significant performance loss.

The workflow includes several key nodes: the SaveImage node, which handles the output of generated images, and the MarkdownNote node, which provides documentation and notes within the workflow for easier understanding and modification. The ddd1571b-c923-4645-9eba-e238fb45ee9e node is a custom node that facilitates the integration of these components, ensuring smooth operation and efficient processing. This setup makes the workflow not only accessible to users with limited hardware capabilities but also provides a streamlined process for generating images from text prompts, making it highly practical for quick prototyping and experimentation.
howToUse: Load the Flux.1 Dev fp8: Text to Image workflow into ComfyUI.
Prepare your text prompt that describes the image you want to generate.
Ensure the Flux.1 model file is available and properly configured in your environment.
Run the workflow, which will process the text prompt and generate an image.
Use the SaveImage node to save the generated image to your desired location.
Review the MarkdownNote node for additional documentation and tips.
suggestedUseCases: Generating concept art for projects with limited hardware resources.
Creating quick visual prototypes for design brainstorming sessions.
Developing educational materials where high-end graphic quality is not critical.
Producing images for social media content where speed is prioritized over quality.

faqItems.question: What is fp8 quantization and why is it used?
faqItems.answer: Fp8 quantization reduces the precision of the model's weights, allowing it to run on devices with limited VRAM by decreasing memory usage at the cost of slight image quality reduction.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow on any device?
faqItems.answer: Yes, this workflow is designed to work on devices with limited VRAM, making it suitable for a wide range of hardware, including less powerful devices.

faqItems.question: How does the image quality compare to the full version of the model?
faqItems.answer: The image quality is slightly lower than the full version due to the fp8 quantization, but it remains effective for many practical applications.

faqItems.question: Do I need any special setup to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Ensure you have the Flux.1 model file and that your ComfyUI is updated. No additional special setup is required.

40a427168ef7.title: 1 image input Split Stack - Nano Banana 2 + Kling 3.0
40a427168ef7.description: Upload 1 input image and generate 5 alternate angles to be used as start frames with Kling 3.0. Each video is stacked horizontally in a final 9x16 video.
40a427168ef7.metaDescription: Turn one image into five Kling 3.0 videos from alternate angles and auto-stack them into a single 9:16 comparison clip in ComfyUI.
40a427168ef7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow takes a single reference image and generates five alternate camera angles to use as starting frames for Kling 3.0 image-to-video. A set of utility nodes (including Reroute and PrimitiveNode) fans out your input from LoadImage into five branches, where a preconfigured "Nano Banana 2" angle-synthesis group produces varied viewpoints of the same subject. Each start frame is saved via SaveImage so you can verify framing and subject integrity before video generation.

Each of the five frames is then sent to KlingVideoNode to create short motion clips guided by your prompt (e.g., orbit, pan, dolly). Finally, the clips are tiled into a single portrait output using CreateVideo and saved with SaveVideo. The stacker uses a horizontal strip layout inside a 9:16 canvas, so you can compare all five angles in one shareable video. Optional GeminiImage2Node can auto-caption the input image to augment your motion prompt; if not used, the workflow falls back to manual text from a PrimitiveNode. This setup is practical when you need consistent, multi-angle starters for Kling 3.0 without hand-authoring separate variations.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the LoadImage node. Import a single, high-quality image with a clear subject and minimal motion blur.

If you use GeminiImage2Node, add your API key (if required) and enable it to generate a descriptive caption/tags. Otherwise, set your manual motion prompt (e.g., subtle orbit) in the provided PrimitiveNode connected to KlingVideoNode.

Adjust parameters exposed via PrimitiveNode/Reroute controls: duration and fps for KlingVideoNode, and the output resolution/aspect for CreateVideo (author presets include options like 720p, 2K, 16:9; final is arranged on a 9:16 canvas).

Run the first stage to generate the five alternate angles. Check the SaveImage outputs to confirm each start frame looks correct (subject centered, no cropping issues). If needed, tweak angle spacing or framing controls provided in the Nano Banana 2 group.
Run the KlingVideoNode stage to create five motion clips from the generated start frames. Keep motion prompts modest for realism (small orbit, gentle pan/dolly).
Run the final CreateVideo/SaveVideo stage to tile the five Kling clips into a single 9:16 stacked video. Review the composite and export the final file for sharing.
suggestedUseCases: Product spins and turnarounds: Generate multi-angle starters and compare motion variants in one vertical clip.
Character or portrait motion tests: Subtle head/torso or camera orbits from a single hero image.
Environment reveals: Pan/dolly variants across a scene to choose the most cinematic motion.
Social media A/B testing: One 9:16 stacked video showing five angles to quickly gather feedback.
Previsualization: Rapidly explore angle and motion direction before committing to longer renders.

faqItems.question: Do I need a Kling 3.0 account or API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The KlingVideoNode requires valid credentials. Enter your API key or session token in the node’s settings (or environment, if supported by your install) before running the video stage.

faqItems.question: What does the Nano Banana 2 step do?
faqItems.answer: It’s a preconfigured angle-synthesis group that takes your single input image and produces five alternate viewpoints to use as start frames for Kling 3.0. This helps you preview different angles without manually crafting separate inputs.

faqItems.question: Can I change the number of angles or their spacing?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The workflow is set up for five branches by default. You can duplicate or remove a branch after the Reroute fan-out, then update the tiling/stacking inputs going into CreateVideo so the composite matches the new count. Angle spacing controls (if exposed) live inside the Nano Banana 2 group.

faqItems.question: Why is the final video 9:16 if my source clips are 16:9?
faqItems.answer: The compositor tiles the five Kling outputs into a portrait canvas for mobile/social viewing. If you prefer landscape, change the aspect/size in the CreateVideo node (author presets include 720p/2K/16:9). Ensure all branches feed the compositor at the same resolution.

41f029c74cd4.title: Stylize Video - Frame by Frame - Flux.2 Klein 4b
41f029c74cd4.description: Create a stylized frame by frame effect on your input video by using Flux.2 Klein 4b Distilled image editing model.
41f029c74cd4.metaDescription: Stylize any video frame-by-frame with Flux.2 Klein 4b Distilled. Load, prompt-cycle, and reassemble frames for consistent, artistic video-to-video results.
41f029c74cd4.extendedDescription:
This workflow applies a consistent, frame-by-frame style transfer to any input video using the Flux.2 Klein 4b Distilled image editing model. It decodes your video with LoadVideo and reads resolution/FPS via GetVideoComponents, then uses VHS_SelectEveryNthImage to choose how densely to process frames (every frame, or every Nth for speed). Frames are organized with ImpactImageBatchToImageList so each image can be paired with a per-frame prompt.

Style prompts are generated and aligned with frames using a small prompt pipeline: GeminiNode can draft style-transfer lines following the Author Notes, RegexReplace cleans and normalizes the text (for example, removing numbering and enforcing "the source frame" phrasing), and FL_PromptMulti distributes one prompt per frame in a repeating cycle. Each frame and its corresponding prompt are fed into the Flux.2 Klein 4b editing node (the Flux.2 Klein 4b Distilled image editing model) to produce a stylized image while preserving the source frame’s structure. The processed images are repacked with ImageListToImageBatch, converted to a video using CreateVideo (matching the original FPS from GetVideoComponents), previewed via PreviewAny as needed, and written to disk with SaveVideo.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and drag in your source video to the LoadVideo node. GetVideoComponents will auto-read the video’s width/height/FPS.
Set the frame stride in VHS_SelectEveryNthImage. Use 1 to stylize every frame (best quality), or 2–4 to speed up tests with fewer frames.

Prepare prompts: either paste a multiline list into PrimitiveStringMultiline following the Author Notes format, or let GeminiNode draft them (ensure your Gemini API key is configured). RegexReplace will clean numbering and enforce the phrase “the source frame.”
Use FL_PromptMulti to map exactly one prompt per frame in a repeating cycle. Confirm prompt–frame pairing by sampling a few results in PreviewAny.
Run the Flux.2 Klein 4b Distilled image editing node to stylize frames. If results are too strong or inconsistent, simplify prompt wording and emphasize “the source frame.”
Rebuild the video: ImageListToImageBatch -> CreateVideo (feed FPS from GetVideoComponents) -> SaveVideo. Inspect the output and iterate on prompts or stride as needed.
suggestedUseCases: Music videos and reels that alternate visual treatments in a rhythmic, repeating cycle.
Editorial B-roll stylization for documentaries or YouTube segments without changing scene composition.
Motion tests for concept art: rapidly try multiple looks on the same footage by cycling prompts.
Brand experiments: apply a house style to diverse clips using the same prompt template.
Social clips with bold, consistent style transfer while preserving motion and layout.

faqItems.question: How does the prompt cycling work?
faqItems.answer: Provide a multiline list of style prompts or let GeminiNode generate them using the Author Notes’ pattern. FL_PromptMulti assigns one prompt per frame and repeats the list after the final line, ensuring a predictable style cycle across the video.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use GeminiNode for prompts?
faqItems.answer: No. You can paste hand-written prompts into PrimitiveStringMultiline. GeminiNode is optional and helps draft prompts; RegexReplace then normalizes them (e.g., removes numbering and enforces using “the source frame”).

faqItems.question: Will the output have audio?
faqItems.answer: This setup focuses on frame-to-frame visual stylization. If your CreateVideo/SaveVideo configuration doesn’t pass through audio, you can remux the original audio onto the stylized video using a video editor or ffmpeg.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker between frames?
faqItems.answer: Keep prompts concise and consistent, always referencing “the source frame.” Avoid subject re-descriptions, keep style terms stable across frames, and process every frame (Nth=1) for best temporal consistency. Larger N values speed tests but increase perceptual jumps.

44d156cf2723.title: Beeble SwitchX: Video Edit
44d156cf2723.description: Upload a source video and a reference image, then provide a prompt describing the desired environment and lighting. Generate an edited video where masked regions follow your prompt and reference, while unmasked regions preserve the original pixels and motion, plus an alpha matte for compositing.
44d156cf2723.metaDescription: ComfyUI video edit workflow using Beeble SwitchX to relight and replace regions by prompt and reference, preserving motion and outputting an alpha matte.
44d156cf2723.extendedDescription:
Beeble SwitchX: Video Edit is a targeted video editing workflow that lets you change only what you describe, while keeping everything else intact. You load a source video and (optionally) a reference image, then enter a prompt describing the new environment and lighting. The BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit node applies the Beeble SwitchX video-edit model to generate an edited clip where masked regions follow your prompt and reference, while unmasked regions preserve the original pixels and motion. The workflow also produces an alpha matte so you can composite the edited regions over the untouched source in any NLE.

Technically, the graph decodes your clip with LoadVideo, extracts dimensions and frame count via GetVideoComponents, and uses the "Get frame counts (need < 240)" group to help you stay under the model’s recommended frame limit. If your clip is too long, Video Slice trims it to a workable range. LoadImage brings in an optional look reference, and GetImageSize ensures the pipeline accounts for dimension matching. BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit then processes frames with temporal consistency, outputting both the edited video and a per-frame alpha matte. Use PreviewAny to inspect intermediate results, and SaveVideo to render the final edit. The result is a practical, non-destructive way to relight scenes, replace environments, or stylize specific objects without breaking the original motion.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and locate the main nodes: LoadVideo, LoadImage (optional reference), BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit, GetVideoComponents, Video Slice, PreviewAny, and SaveVideo.
In LoadVideo, select your source clip. Check the "Get frame counts (need < 240)" group to see total frames; if it’s over 240, set the in/out range in Video Slice to trim the clip.

Optionally set a reference look with LoadImage (e.g., a lighting or environment photo). Use GetImageSize to confirm dimensions; matching the video’s aspect ratio typically yields more coherent results.

Open BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit and enter a concise prompt describing the desired environment and lighting (e.g., "golden-hour sunset, warm directional light, soft shadows"). Ensure the reference is connected if you want the look to be enforced.

Queue the workflow. Use PreviewAny to check both the edited frames and the generated alpha matte. If the effect bleeds into areas you want untouched, refine your prompt to focus on the intended subject or provide a clearer reference image.
When satisfied, use SaveVideo to export the edited clip. To export the alpha matte as well, connect or duplicate SaveVideo on the matte output branch of BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit.
suggestedUseCases: Relighting a scene to match a specific time of day without re-shooting.
Environment or sky replacement while keeping original actors and camera motion.
Product shots: changing background and mood lighting while preserving the product’s true pixels.
Brand or art-direction alignment using a reference image to lock style and color tone.
Selective cleanup or stylization of a single object while leaving the rest of the frame untouched.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use a reference image?
faqItems.answer: No. The reference is optional. Without it, the edit follows your prompt. With a reference connected via LoadImage, the BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit node can better match style, color, and lighting to that image.

faqItems.question: Why is there a < 240 frame limit and how do I handle longer clips?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is tuned for clips under ~240 frames for memory and consistency. Use GetVideoComponents to inspect frame count and Video Slice to trim your clip to a shorter segment or process in batches.

faqItems.question: How do I keep specific areas unchanged?
faqItems.answer: The node preserves unmasked regions by design. If edits spill into unwanted areas, make your prompt more specific to the target subject or provide a clearer reference image so the internal matte focuses on the correct regions.

faqItems.question: How can I export the alpha matte?
faqItems.answer: Preview the matte with PreviewAny. To save it, route or duplicate SaveVideo on the matte output from BeebleSwitchXVideoEdit so you can export a separate grayscale or RGBA matte video for compositing.

45a8be9c1124.title: SD3.5 Large Depth
45a8be9c1124.description: Generate images guided by depth information using SD 3.5.
45a8be9c1124.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use SD 3.5 Large with ControlNet Depth to generate images that keep scene structure from a reference photo while changing style and details.
45a8be9c1124.extendedDescription:
This workflow teaches you how to guide Stable Diffusion 3.5 with a depth map so your generations respect the structure and perspective of a reference image. It loads the SD 3.5 Large checkpoint (sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors) with CheckpointLoaderSimple and a high‑quality VAE (vae-ft-mse-840000-ema-pruned.safetensors). Your text prompt is encoded by CLIPTextEncode, and KSampler handles diffusion using a latent canvas defined by EmptySD3LatentImage, so you can set an exact output size. VAEDecode, PreviewImage, and SaveImage complete the loop so you can inspect and export results.

Depth guidance is provided through ControlNet. ControlNetLoader loads sd3.5_large_controlnet_depth.safetensors and ControlNetApplyAdvanced attaches the depth conditioning to your prompt with adjustable strength and start/end percentage. The reference image comes in via LoadImage, is optionally resized with ImageScaleToTotalPixels, and then converted to a depth map by the included depth preprocessor node (the custom node identified by 6b0ed7ac-f476-44c9-9dad-b3f23ef985f8) using the lotus-depth-d-v1-1.safetensors model. For image-to-image variants, VAEEncode can seed KSampler with the reference image latents; for pure text-to-image with depth guidance, use EmptySD3LatentImage. ConditioningZeroOut is available if you want an empty negative prompt. This combination makes it easy to preserve scene layout while freely changing style, lighting, and details with your prompt.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then load models: set CheckpointLoaderSimple to sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors and load the VAE vae-ft-mse-840000-ema-pruned.safetensors. In ControlNetLoader, choose sd3.5_large_controlnet_depth.safetensors.
Upload a reference image with LoadImage. Optionally use ImageScaleToTotalPixels to bring it near your target pixel count so the depth map aligns well with your output size.
Run the depth preprocessor: the custom depth node (using lotus-depth-d-v1-1.safetensors) converts your uploaded image to a depth map. Verify the depth output with PreviewImage if provided.

Set output size with EmptySD3LatentImage (width/height or total pixels). Connect its LATENT output to KSampler so the sampler uses your chosen size. Enter your text prompt with CLIPTextEncode; use ConditioningZeroOut if you want a blank negative prompt.

Wire ControlNet: feed the depth map into ControlNetApplyAdvanced, set control strength (e.g., 0.6–0.9) and start/end percentages (e.g., start 0.0, end 0.8), then connect its conditioning to KSampler along with the prompt conditioning.

Adjust KSampler parameters (steps, cfg scale, sampler/scheduler). For image-to-image, connect VAEEncode from the same input image to KSampler and use a denoise strength below 1.0 (e.g., 0.4–0.7). Generate, review with PreviewImage, and export with SaveImage.
suggestedUseCases: Restyle a photographed room while preserving layout and perspective (e.g., modern to rustic).
Maintain character pose or subject silhouette while changing clothing, lighting, or background.
Product mockups that keep camera angle and proportions consistent across design variations.
Previsualization for scenes where composition must remain fixed but look and feel can change.
Concept art iterations that keep geometry intact while exploring different atmospheres.

faqItems.question: Do I need to provide an input image for this to work?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the depth guidance comes from a reference image. Load it with LoadImage so the depth preprocessor can produce a depth map. You can still run SD 3.5 without ControlNet by disconnecting the control or setting strength to 0, but then you lose depth guidance.

faqItems.question: How do ControlNet strength and KSampler denoise strength differ?
faqItems.answer: ControlNet strength in ControlNetApplyAdvanced determines how strictly the model follows the depth map. Denoise strength (when using VAEEncode for img2img) controls how much the output changes from the init image overall. High ControlNet strength keeps structure; lower denoise preserves more original detail and texture.

faqItems.question: What’s the correct way to set output resolution?
faqItems.answer: Use EmptySD3LatentImage to define width/height (or total pixels) and connect its LATENT to KSampler. If you’re using a reference image, consider resizing it with ImageScaleToTotalPixels so the depth map scale is compatible with your chosen output size.

faqItems.question: My results ignore the depth or look distorted. What should I adjust?
faqItems.answer: Increase ControlNet strength and ensure ControlNetApplyAdvanced start is near 0.0 so depth applies early. Try more steps or a slightly higher cfg. If using img2img, lower denoise strength to keep structure from the init latents. Also verify that the depth preprocessor output is connected to ControlNetApplyAdvanced.

45c0ce6bcf2e.title: Wan2.1 VACE First-Last Frame
45c0ce6bcf2e.description: Generate smooth video transitions by defining start and end frames. Supports custom keyframe sequences.
45c0ce6bcf2e.metaDescription: Breakthrough: Wan2.1 VACE first–last frame synthesis for smooth, prompt-guided transitions. 480p/720p, keyframes, and LoRA-accelerated low-step video.
45c0ce6bcf2e.extendedDescription:
Wan2.1 VACE First–Last Frame introduces endpoint-anchored video synthesis: you provide a starting frame and an ending frame, and the model plans a temporally coherent path between them. Instead of naive optical-flow interpolation, the workflow synthesizes intermediate content in latent space using Wan2.1’s VACE prior, guided by your prompt and optional LoRA. This delivers stable identity, style continuity, and believable motion planning across the entire sequence.

In ComfyUI, the pipeline pairs WanVaceToVideo with a ModelSamplingSD3 profile, KSampler, and a strict frame/layout regimen: spatial dimensions must be divisible by 16, and the total frame count follows a 4n+1 rule (Length − 1 divisible by 4). This structure, plus TrimVideoLatent for exact clip length, produces transitions that are both smooth and controllable. The 14B model supports clean 480p and 720p outputs, while the lighter 1.3B is optimized for 480p. With optional LoRA (e.g., CausVid), you can cut sampling steps dramatically while maintaining temporal coherence.
howToUse: Step 1 – Load models: Use UNETLoader, VAELoader, and CLIPLoader to load Wan2.1 VACE. Choose the 1.3B model for 480p or the 14B model for 480p/720p (wan2.1_vace_14B_fp16.safetensors). Keep ModelSamplingSD3 connected to the UNet to apply the correct sampling profile.

Step 2 – Provide endpoints: With LoadImage, upload the first and last frame (match aspect ratio and resolution). In the video size group, set width/height divisible by 16. In the length group, set Length so that (Length − 1) is divisible by 4 (e.g., 5, 9, 13…).

Step 3 – Prompts and LoRA: Enter your positive/negative text using CLIPTextEncode (the negative prompt can include quality filters). Optionally enable LoraLoader; start with strength 0.3–0.7. If using a CausVid-style LoRA, reduce KSampler steps to 2–4 and cfg to ~1.0.

Step 4 – Sampling config: Set KSampler steps to ~20 and cfg to ~6.0 by default. Set Batch Size = Length − 2 as indicated by the workflow group. Fix a seed for repeatability or randomize for variations.

Step 5 – Generate latents: WanVaceToVideo synthesizes the transition between your first and last frame (and any defined keyframes). Use TrimVideoLatent to conform the latent sequence exactly to your Length.

Step 6 – Decode and export: Decode with VAEDecode, assemble with CreateVideo, and finalize with SaveVideo (MP4). Review the clip; iterate on prompt, Length, or LoRA strength to refine motion and style.
suggestedUseCases: Editorial transitions: Seamless scene bridges where the opening and closing frames are fixed by design.
Product reveals and hero shots: Move from a pristine packshot to a styled endpoint with consistent branding.
Character motion beats: Define a pose-to-pose action while preserving identity and wardrobe continuity.
Cinematic bumpers and title sequences: First–last control for on-brand, repeatable motion motifs.
Concept art to shot planning: Lock key frames and explore plausible motion paths before full production.

faqItems.question: How is this different from optical-flow interpolation?
faqItems.answer: Rather than warping pixels between frames, WanVaceToVideo synthesizes intermediate content in latent space using the Wan2.1 VACE prior. This yields more stable identity, fewer artifacts on large disocclusions, and better adherence to your text prompt or LoRA style.

faqItems.question: Why must (Length − 1) be divisible by 4 and the size be divisible by 16?
faqItems.answer: The VACE transition and UNet operate on stride-aligned temporal and spatial blocks. Using a 4n+1 frame count (e.g., 5, 9, 13…) and dimensions divisible by 16 ensures the sampler and decoder align correctly, preventing artifacts and dropped frames.

faqItems.question: When should I use 1.3B vs 14B, and what resolutions are supported?
faqItems.answer: VACE-1.3B is optimized for 480p and is lighter to run. VACE-14B supports both 480p and 720p and typically delivers stronger detail and motion coherence. Choose 14B for higher fidelity or 720p; use 1.3B when resources are limited or for fast previews.

faqItems.question: How do LoRAs affect quality and speed in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: With LoraLoader enabled, you can guide style or motion while reducing steps. For a CausVid-style LoRA, set steps to 2–4 and cfg ≈ 1.0; otherwise, defaults like 20 steps and cfg ≈ 6.0 work well. Start LoRA strength at 0.3–0.7 to balance guidance and temporal stability.

4600a60d661b.title: Gemini Omni - Outfit Swap
4600a60d661b.description: Upload a video of a person and a reference image of the outfit you want them to wear. Gemini Omni maps the clothing onto the moving subject while preserving their appearance, movement, camera framing, and original environment—ideal for virtual try-ons, fashion concepts, and styling previews.
4600a60d661b.metaDescription: ComfyUI outfit swap tutorial: map a reference outfit onto a person in your video with GeminiVideoOmni while keeping motion and background intact.
4600a60d661b.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial walks you through a focused outfit-swap workflow powered by the GeminiVideoOmni node. You load a person video with LoadVideo (Your Footage) and a single outfit photo with LoadImage (Outfit Reference). The GeminiVideoOmni node takes these inputs plus a plain-language instruction (provided via a PrimitiveNode) to map the outfit from the reference image onto the moving subject in your clip, while preserving identity, motion, camera framing, and the original background. The generated result is written out with SaveVideo.

Technically, the workflow conditions a video-aware generative model on both the source frames and the reference outfit image. The source video guides structure and motion so faces, hands, and environment remain stable, while the reference guides the appearance of clothing across frames for temporal consistency. The MarkdownNote nodes in the graph provide inline guidance; they don’t affect processing. With just a few nodes and no manual masking or rotoscoping, this setup is ideal for fast virtual try-ons, fashion concepting, and styling previews.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the key nodes: LoadVideo (Your Footage), LoadImage (Outfit Reference), PrimitiveNode (instruction text), GeminiVideoOmni, and SaveVideo.
In LoadVideo (Your Footage), browse to your source clip. For best first results, choose a short 3–10s segment with a clear view of the person and minimal fast occlusions.
In LoadImage (Outfit Reference), select a single, high-quality outfit photo. Aim for a clear, front-facing view of the clothing; crop out distractions and keep the garment well-lit.

Open the PrimitiveNode connected to GeminiVideoOmni and set the instruction. Start with the author’s prompt: "change my outfit to the outfit in image_1. Keep everything else exactly the same." Adjust wording if needed (e.g., "keep face and hair unchanged").
Set the SaveVideo node’s output path and filename. Confirm the nodes are connected: LoadVideo and LoadImage into GeminiVideoOmni, then GeminiVideoOmni into SaveVideo.

Click Queue/Run. Review the output. If you see artifacts, try a cleaner outfit reference, a shorter clip, or refine the instruction to emphasize preservation (e.g., "preserve background, hands, and skin tones").
suggestedUseCases: Virtual try-on previews for fashion e-commerce and wardrobe planning.
Rapid styling iterations for lookbooks, mood boards, and concept pitches.
Social content and reels demonstrating outfit variations without reshoots.
Previsualizing wardrobe continuity fixes for indie film or commercial edits.
Client-facing styling mockups for personal shoppers and stylists.

faqItems.question: Do I need to mask the person or use a green screen?
faqItems.answer: No. The GeminiVideoOmni node uses the source video as structure guidance and aims to preserve the original scene. A clean subject and fewer occlusions will improve results, but no masking is required.

faqItems.question: What kind of outfit reference works best?
faqItems.answer: Use a single, sharp image with the garment clearly visible, minimal wrinkles or motion blur, and a view that matches the pose and angle in your video. Crop away faces and busy backgrounds if possible to reduce ambiguity.

faqItems.question: How long and how large can my video be?
faqItems.answer: Shorter clips (e.g., under 10–15 seconds) are recommended for faster iteration. Longer or high-resolution videos increase compute and time. If you hit memory or time limits, downscale the video or process in segments.

faqItems.question: Will it handle loose fabrics, patterns, or accessories?
faqItems.answer: It can, but complex elements (flowing skirts, transparent fabrics, shiny materials, intricate logos) are harder to track and may flicker. Choosing a clear reference and moderate motion helps improve temporal consistency.

460daa6b205d.title: LTX 2.3 Cameraman IC-LoRA
460daa6b205d.description: Create camera-motion-driven videos with LTX 2.3 and the IC-LoRA Cameraman model.
460daa6b205d.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a video by transferring camera motion from a reference clip using LTX 2.3 with IC-LoRA Cameraman in ComfyUI.
460daa6b205d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a video by transferring camera motion from a reference clip using the LTX 2.3 video model with the IC-LoRA Cameraman motion controller. The core generation happens in the LTX 2.3 node (custom generator node: 067cf66f-afc2-4672-8d26-481249ad5485) configured to preserve the visual content of your source image while applying the camera path extracted from the reference video. LoadImage provides the source frame, LoadVideo imports the motion reference, and GetVideoComponents reads the reference clip’s fps, duration, and dimensions so the render can match timing and playback characteristics. The resulting frames are assembled with CreateVideo and written out via SaveVideo, with PreviewAny available for quick checks.

To streamline setup, the workflow is organized into groups: Load Image, Load Reference Video, Reference Video, LTX 2.3 IC-LoRA Cameraman, and Create IC-LoRA Cameraman Prompt. The optional GeminiNode in the prompt group helps you draft or document simple camera directions (e.g., "slow dolly-in, slight pan left") for reproducibility, while the actual motion is driven by the reference clip. ImageFromBatch ensures a single starting frame is passed into generation, and MarkdownNote provides in-canvas guidance. The net result is cinematic camera motion—pan, tilt, orbit, dolly, or zoom—applied to your still without manually animating layers or keyframes.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and review the grouped sections: Load Image, Load Reference Video, Create IC-LoRA Cameraman Prompt, and LTX 2.3 IC-LoRA Cameraman.
In the Load Image group, use LoadImage to select your source still. If you import a batch, use ImageFromBatch to route just the desired frame.
In the Load Reference Video group, use LoadVideo to add a short clip that has the camera move you want (e.g., pan, dolly, orbit). GetVideoComponents will extract fps, frame count, and resolution.

Optionally open the Create IC-LoRA Cameraman Prompt group and use the GeminiNode to jot a brief camera-direction note (helps document intent). This note is ancillary; the reference video drives the motion.

Run the workflow. The LTX 2.3 generator node (067cf66f-afc2-4672-8d26-481249ad5485) applies IC-LoRA Cameraman motion to your still, matching timing to the reference. Use PreviewAny to inspect intermediate outputs.
CreateVideo assembles the frames, and SaveVideo writes the final file. If the aspect ratio differs between image and reference, adjust one or the other to avoid unwanted crop/padding, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Product hero shots: orbit or slow dolly around a single product image for polished promos.
Portrait motion: add subtle push-ins, tilts, or parallax to still portraits for reels and social posts.
Architecture and interiors: simulate handheld walkthroughs or slider moves from a single render.
Concept and key art: prototype cinematic shots from static concept images without 3D or compositing.
UI/brand visuals: add tasteful camera motion to static layouts for dynamic presentation clips.

faqItems.question: What does IC-LoRA Cameraman do in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: IC-LoRA Cameraman is a motion-control LoRA used with the LTX 2.3 video model. It guides the model to apply camera-style motion (pan, tilt, dolly, orbit, zoom) to your still while preserving the source image’s content.

faqItems.question: How does the reference video affect the output?
faqItems.answer: LoadVideo plus GetVideoComponents set the timing (fps, duration) and provide the camera motion path. Your final video length and motion pacing follow the reference clip, so choose a clip with the exact move and speed you want.

faqItems.question: How do I avoid jitter or unwanted warping?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, stable reference with a single, smooth camera move; avoid excessive shake or abrupt cuts. Keep the source image’s aspect ratio close to the reference. If you see warping, try a shorter, steadier reference and moderate the move intensity.

faqItems.question: Can I use any aspect ratio or resolution?
faqItems.answer: Yes, but for best results, match your still image’s aspect to the reference video. GetVideoComponents passes fps and dimensions downstream; mismatches may cause cropping or padding depending on node settings. Align sizes to minimize artifacts.

4638e59ae7d2.title: AI on the Lot 2026 - QwenVL - Prompt Enhancer
4638e59ae7d2.description: The fourth workflow released for AI on the Lot 2026, made available for ComfyUI 101 workshop attendees to open and follow along if they choose. A prompt enhancer powered by the Qwen VL LLM node: enter a simple prompt and get back a richer, more detailed version ready to use.
4638e59ae7d2.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow using Qwen-VL to expand short prompts into rich, ready-to-use image prompts with instant preview. Fast, consistent prompt crafting.
4638e59ae7d2.extendedDescription:
AI on the Lot 2026 - QwenVL - Prompt Enhancer is a lightweight ComfyUI workflow that turns a short idea into a rich, production-ready prompt. It uses the AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer node to pass your input through a Qwen-VL language model, which expands key details like subject attributes, mood, composition, and technical cues. The output is displayed with PreviewAny so you can quickly copy it into any downstream image or video generation pipeline.

Technically, the workflow is a simple but effective chain: your text input is formatted into an instruction for Qwen-VL, the model generates a polished prompt that preserves intent while adding concrete visual language, and PreviewAny renders the final string for inspection. Because the output is plain text, it works with common ComfyUI text fields (e.g., positive prompts for Stable Diffusion or other T2I nodes). This makes it especially useful for teams and beginners who want consistent, detailed prompts without hand-writing long templates.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI (drag-and-drop the file into the canvas or use Load). You should see AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer connected to PreviewAny.

Open AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer and enter a short, clear prompt (e.g., “portrait of a golden retriever in a park at sunset”). Add any constraints you care about (e.g., “no text, natural colors, cinematic lighting”). If your setup requires selecting a Qwen-VL model or backend, choose it and ensure it’s available.
Click Queue Prompt to run. The node will send your instruction to the Qwen-VL model and generate an enhanced version with richer visual details.
Select the PreviewAny node to view the enhanced prompt. Right-click the text to copy it to your clipboard.

Paste the enhanced prompt into your image/video generation workflow’s positive prompt field in ComfyUI. If your downstream pipeline supports negative prompts, you can add exclusions directly to your input or trim any unwanted parts from the enhanced text.
Iterate: refine your original input with clearer goals (style, composition, camera, mood) and re-run. For variety, try rephrasing the input or running multiple times to collect alternates.
suggestedUseCases: Rapidly turning rough creative briefs into detailed, consistent prompts for Stable Diffusion image generation.
Previsualization and shot ideation for on-set or pre-production teams needing cinematic, camera-aware prompt language.
Standardizing prompt quality across a team by using a shared enhancement step before final renders.
Teaching newcomers how to structure effective prompts by comparing their input with the model’s enriched output.
Generating multiple prompt variants for A/B testing style directions before committing GPU time to high-res renders.

faqItems.question: What is Qwen-VL and why use it for prompt enhancement?
faqItems.answer: Qwen-VL is a vision-language large language model. In this workflow it’s used in text-only mode via the AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer node to expand concise ideas into concrete visual descriptions (subjects, style, lighting, composition) that are ready for image/video generation.

faqItems.question: Do I need internet access or an API key?
faqItems.answer: It depends on how your Qwen-VL backend is set up. Some installations run locally (no internet required), while others call a remote service (API key required). Open the AILab_QwenVL_PromptEnhancer node and follow its configuration notes for your environment.

faqItems.question: How can I steer the style or keep the model from adding unwanted elements?
faqItems.answer: State constraints in your input (e.g., “no text on image, no watermark, natural colors, documentary style”). If the node exposes creativity/temperature settings in your build, lower values make results more literal, higher values more creative. You can also iterate by rephrasing your request with explicit dos and don’ts.

faqItems.question: Will the enhanced prompt work with any ComfyUI image pipeline?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The output is plain text, so you can paste it into the positive prompt field of Stable Diffusion or other text-to-image/video nodes. If your pipeline uses a separate negative prompt, include exclusions in that field or in your initial instruction to the enhancer.

46a303cbccf9.title: MiniMax H3: Reference to Video
46a303cbccf9.description: Generate a new video by feeding MiniMax H3 a reference image, up to nine images, three videos, and three audio clips alongside a text prompt, letting the model match character identity, motion, camera, voice, or style from those sources while producing native stereo audio in a single pass. Output is a single MP4 video at up to 2K resolution and 24fps for roughly 15 seconds. Ideal for character-consistent animation, style-transfer video generation, and audio-synced content creation.
46a303cbccf9.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate a 15s MP4 with stereo audio from MiniMax H3 using prompt + image/video/audio references at up to 2K and 24fps.
46a303cbccf9.extendedDescription:
This workflow demonstrates MiniMax H3’s reference-to-video generation in ComfyUI: you provide a text prompt plus up to nine reference images, three short reference videos, and three audio clips, and the model produces a single MP4 with native stereo audio in one pass. The MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo node is the core, fusing multi-modal context (identity, motion, camera, style, and voice) with your prompt to synthesize a ~15s clip at up to 2K resolution and 24fps.

Under the hood, the Switch Model and Settings group loads the MiniMax H3 model stack via UNETLoader and CLIPLoader, while KSamplerSelect, BasicScheduler, SamplerCustomAdvanced, and BasicGuider manage sampling behavior (seeded by RandomNoise for reproducibility). ResolutionSelector sets a 16:9 size aligned to multiples of 32, and ComfyMathExpression with PrimitiveFloat handles derived values like frame count from duration and fps. After generation, VAELoader provides both video and audio VAEs; VAEDecode reconstructs frames from video latents and VAEDecodeAudio reconstructs stereo waveforms. CreateVideo multiplexes frames and audio, and SaveVideo writes the final MP4. This makes the workflow practical for character-consistent animation, style-guided motion, and audio-synced content without separate TTS or sound design steps.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. Install the MiniMax H3 weights from Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3 and place the VAEs (minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors, minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors) into your models/vae folder. Ensure the UNet/CLIP weights are in the appropriate models directories, then restart ComfyUI.

Open the User Inputs group: enter your text prompt in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node. Add reference media: use the MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo node’s inputs to attach up to nine images, three short videos, and three audio clips (voice, music, or SFX). If the workflow exposes LoadImage nodes, use them for image references; supply video/audio via the MiniMax node’s file inputs.

Pick your resolution with ResolutionSelector. For 16:9, choose a target megapixel level that maps to multiples of 32 (e.g., 0.7 MP → 1152x640, 0.9 MP → 1280x736). Keep within 2K for best VRAM stability. Set fps to 24 and duration near 15s unless you know your hardware headroom.

In the Sampling group, choose your sampler and scheduler via KSamplerSelect and BasicScheduler. Set guidance scale in BasicGuider (a moderate value like 4–7 often balances prompt adherence with reference fidelity). Set a seed in RandomNoise for repeatability, or -1 for fresh variations.

Review any switches in the Switch Model and Settings group (e.g., toggling audio on/off via a ComfySwitchNode, or selecting model variants if provided). Confirm the VAELoader is set to minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16 for video and minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32 for audio.
Run the graph. After sampling completes, VAEDecode and VAEDecodeAudio reconstruct video and stereo audio. CreateVideo muxes frames with the decoded audio, and SaveVideo outputs a single MP4 file.
suggestedUseCases: Character-consistent animation: feed a face or full-body photo and guide motion/camera with a short reference video.
Style-transfer video: provide style frames (illustrations, film stills) to steer look and grading while following your prompt.
Voice- or music-synced content: condition with a voice clip or beat and let H3 co-generate visuals and stereo audio.
Product teasers: combine product photos with a motion reference for smooth hero shots and matching sound design.
Social clips and memes: rapidly iterate prompt+reference combos for 10–15s edits with coherent audio.

faqItems.question: What models and files do I need, and where do they go?
faqItems.answer: Download MiniMax H3 from Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3. Place minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors and minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors in models/vae. Ensure the H3 UNet and CLIP/text encoder weights are in the correct ComfyUI model folders (e.g., models/unet, models/clip). Restart ComfyUI so UNETLoader, CLIPLoader, and VAELoader can find them.

faqItems.question: How long and how big can the output be?
faqItems.answer: This workflow targets about 15 seconds at up to 24fps and up to 2K resolution. Use ResolutionSelector’s 16:9 presets (multiples of 32) like 1152x640 or 1280x736. Higher resolutions, frame rates, or longer durations increase VRAM and time costs and may be unstable.

faqItems.question: How do I improve identity/style matching from references?
faqItems.answer: Use a small set of high-quality references (start with 1–3). Make your primary identity image the first input. Keep reference videos short and representative of the motion/camera you want. Tight, explicit prompts plus moderate guidance (CFG ~4–7) often preserve references better.

faqItems.question: Can I disable or replace audio?
faqItems.answer: Yes. If the workflow exposes a ComfySwitchNode on the audio path, set it to bypass VAEDecodeAudio. Alternatively, leave the audio inputs empty to generate minimal audio, then replace or mute in the CreateVideo stage or in post.

faqItems.question: Is the result deterministic?
faqItems.answer: Set a fixed seed in RandomNoise to reproduce the same sampling trajectory with the same inputs and settings. Changing seed, references, resolution, or sampler parameters will change the output.

46a80518c9c6.title: NetaYume Lumina Text to Image
46a80518c9c6.description: High-quality anime-style image generation with enhanced character understanding and detailed textures. Fine-tuned from Neta Lumina on Danbooru dataset.
46a80518c9c6.metaDescription: Generate high-quality anime images using NetaYume Lumina with enhanced character details and textures. Perfect for artists and creators.
46a80518c9c6.extendedDescription:
The NetaYume Lumina Text to Image workflow is designed to generate high-quality anime-style images with a keen understanding of character details and textures. This workflow utilizes the OmniGen model, which is fine-tuned from the Neta Lumina model on the Danbooru dataset, known for its rich collection of anime imagery. The workflow incorporates several key nodes such as KSampler for sampling, CheckpointLoaderSimple for model loading, and VAEDecode for decoding the latent space into images. This setup allows users to create detailed and vibrant anime images by inputting descriptive text prompts.

Technically, the workflow is structured into three main steps: loading the model, setting the image size, and crafting the prompt. The CheckpointLoaderSimple node is responsible for loading the OmniGen model, while the KSampler node handles the sampling process to ensure high-quality output. The VAEDecode node then translates the latent image data into a final visual output, which is saved using the SaveImage node. This workflow is particularly useful for artists and creators looking to produce anime-style illustrations with precise control over character features and scene composition.
howToUse: Load the NetaYume Lumina Text to Image workflow into ComfyUI.
Use the CheckpointLoaderSimple node to load the OmniGen model.
Set your desired image size, ideally 1024x1024, using the appropriate node.
Craft your text prompt, keeping the prefix fixed until the 'Prompt Start' tag.
Run the workflow to generate the image.
Find the output image saved in the ComfyUI/outputs folder.
suggestedUseCases: Creating custom anime character illustrations for personal projects.
Generating high-quality anime-style artwork for digital media.
Designing unique visual content for anime-themed merchandise.
Developing concept art for anime-inspired video games.
Producing detailed scene compositions for anime storyboards.

faqItems.question: What is the best image size for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The recommended image size is 1024x1024, but you can experiment with higher resolutions like 1024x1536.

faqItems.question: Can I use artist tags in the prompt?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can include artist tags using the @ symbol in the prompt to influence the style of the generated image.

faqItems.question: Where can I find more information about crafting prompts?
faqItems.answer: You can refer to the Neta Lumina prompt book available on the Neta.art blog for guidance on creating effective prompts.

faqItems.question: Where are the generated images saved?
faqItems.answer: The output images are saved in the 'ComfyUI/outputs' folder on your system.

46fc617ad144.title: Seedance1.0 Pro: Start End to Video

46fc617ad144.metaDescription: Create cinematic video transitions with Seedance1.0 Pro using ByteDance's model for smooth, professional results.

howToUse: Load the workflow into ComfyUI.
Use the LoadImage node to upload your first frame.
Upload your last frame using the LoadImage node designated for the end frame.
Configure the ByteDanceFirstLastFrameNode to set transition parameters.
Run the workflow to process the frames and generate the video.

suggestedUseCases: Creating smooth transitions for video intros and outros.
Enhancing slideshow presentations with cinematic effects.
Producing professional-quality video content for marketing.
Adding dynamic transitions in film editing projects.
Developing engaging social media video posts.

faqItems.question: What is the Seedance1.0 Pro model?
faqItems.answer: Seedance1.0 Pro is a model developed by ByteDance for generating smooth video transitions between two static frames.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for high-resolution videos?

faqItems.question: Do I need any prior video editing experience to use this workflow?

faqItems.question: How can I adjust the transition speed?

471717404074.title: Grok: Video Extend
471717404074.description: Upload a short video and a text prompt describing the next scene. Generate a seamless video extension using Grok extend.
471717404074.metaDescription: Extend videos seamlessly with Grok: Video Extend. Upload a clip, add a text prompt, and generate new scenes effortlessly.
471717404074.extendedDescription: The 'Grok: Video Extend' workflow is designed to seamlessly extend a short video by generating additional scenes based on a user-provided text prompt. This innovative process leverages the Grok model, which is specifically trained for video extension tasks. The workflow begins with the 'LoadVideo' node, where users upload their initial video clip. This is followed by the 'GrokVideoExtendNode', which takes the uploaded video and the text prompt to generate a new scene that smoothly transitions from the existing content. 473606b441c6.title: Wan3.0: Image to Video

Produces authentic, realistic footage with unique facial details and believable motion in one pass. Ideal for cinematic storytelling, product visualization, and documentary-style scene recreation.
473606b441c6.metaDescription: Create up to 30s of realistic video from a single image in ComfyUI using the Wan 3.0 Image-to-Video API with LoadImage and SaveVideo nodes.
473606b441c6.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a high-fidelity video clip using the Wan 3.0 Image-to-Video API. It’s built around four nodes: LoadImage to bring your source frame into the graph, Wan3ImageToVideoApi to generate the animated sequence on a remote service, SaveVideo to encode the frames to a standard video file, and MarkdownNote for inline instructions. The pipeline is simple and reliable: your input image is loaded, sent to Wan 3.0 for temporal synthesis, and the returned frames are packaged into a playable video.

Technically, Wan 3.0 performs motion synthesis conditioned on the content of the single image, producing realistic camera/lens movement and subject dynamics in one pass. While the Wan 3.0 family supports multimodal inputs, this specific workflow is image-only and focuses on up to 30 seconds of output. You control the key generation settings in the Wan3ImageToVideoApi node (e.g., clip duration and any parameters exposed by your API endpoint), and finalize playback characteristics like FPS and file path in SaveVideo. This makes it well-suited for cinematic b-roll, product hero shots, and documentary-style scene recreation directly from a still.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure ComfyUI is up to date. The template references input/beetle_rider.png as the default image.
Open the LoadImage node and either keep input/beetle_rider.png or point it to your own high-resolution source image. Use a clean, well-lit image for best results.

Open the Wan3ImageToVideoApi node and enter your API credentials/endpoint as required. Configure the available parameters (e.g., target duration up to 30s and any size/aspect settings the node exposes).
Open the SaveVideo node and set your output path and FPS. FPS controls perceived motion smoothness when encoding the returned frames.
Queue the workflow. The input image will be sent to the Wan 3.0 service, which returns frames that SaveVideo encodes into a single video file.
Review the output. If you see artifacts or motion that’s too strong or too subtle, adjust the Wan3ImageToVideoApi parameters (and FPS in SaveVideo) and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Cinematic b-roll and establishing shots generated from a single still for film, trailers, or YouTube intros.
Product hero shots or lightweight turntable-style motion to showcase design and materials without a full 3D setup.
Documentary-style scene recreation from archival photos to visualize environments with subtle, believable motion.
Storyboard and previz beats from concept art or keyframes to explore pacing and camera movement quickly.
Social media loops and reels that bring static imagery to life with minimal setup.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key for the Wan3ImageToVideoApi node?
faqItems.answer: Yes. This node calls an external Wan 3.0 service and typically requires an API key and/or endpoint. Enter your credentials in the node’s fields before running.

faqItems.question: What is the maximum video length this workflow can generate?
faqItems.answer: Up to 30 seconds, as supported by the Wan 3.0 Image-to-Video API. Set the desired duration in the Wan3ImageToVideoApi node if that parameter is exposed.

faqItems.question: Which settings control smoothness and playback speed?

49a2f3a0811f.title: Seedance 2.0 + LLM Prompt Helper
49a2f3a0811f.description:
This workflow uses two reference images and a simple text description to automatically generate a detailed Seedance 2.0-style prompt using an LLM. Instead of spending time figuring out complex prompting structure, the workflow analyzes your references and builds the prompt for you, making it much faster and easier to create high-quality results.

The included LLM helper is designed to match the style and formatting that works well with Seedance 2.0, helping streamline the entire process while still giving you full control over the final output. Just drop in your references, describe the scene or motion you want, and the workflow handles the prompt generation automatically.
49a2f3a0811f.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow that uses two reference images and an LLM to auto-generate Seedance 2.0 prompts, then renders and saves video with ByteDance2ReferenceNode.
49a2f3a0811f.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 + LLM Prompt Helper streamlines prompt creation for ByteDance/Seedance-style video generation by pairing two reference images with a short scene description. The workflow routes your images through LoadImage and ImageConcanate to form a clear, side-by-side visual context, which the GeminiNode then analyzes along with your text to draft a Seedance 2.0–formatted prompt. PreviewAny lets you inspect and copy the LLM’s output before it’s sent on, while PreviewImage helps you sanity-check your references.

Once you’re happy with the generated prompt, it feeds into ByteDance2ReferenceNode (the Seedance 2.0 runner) to produce the motion result. You can review frames with PreviewAny/PreviewImage (as applicable) and export the final animation via SaveVideo. A MarkdownNote in the canvas documents tips and conventions the LLM uses so the prompt it produces aligns with Seedance 2.0’s expected structure and tags. The result: you spend less time reverse-engineering prompt syntax and more time iterating on visuals and motion.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the Reference Images group. Use the two LoadImage nodes to import your subject and style/location references. Use PreviewImage to confirm they’re clean, well-lit, and correctly oriented.
Optionally concatenate the references for context: ensure both LoadImage outputs feed into ImageConcanate. This combined image helps the GeminiNode see both references side-by-side.

Open the LLM group. In the GeminiNode, enter a concise scene or motion description (e.g., “slow dolly-in on a dancer under neon lights, subtle hair movement”). Queue the LLM subgraph with the Seedance node bypassed: select ByteDance2ReferenceNode and press Ctrl+B to bypass so only the prompt helper runs.

Inspect the generated prompt: connect GeminiNode’s text output to PreviewAny (already wired in the template). Review tags, camera cues, and style notes. Edit the text (either in the GeminiNode prompt, re-run, or paste and refine directly into the ByteDance2ReferenceNode’s prompt field).

Un-bypass the ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Ctrl+B again) when the prompt looks right. Queue the full workflow. The Seedance 2.0 node will use the two references and the LLM-refined prompt to render the motion sequence.

Use SaveVideo to export your result. Adjust SaveVideo settings (e.g., fps/quality if exposed) and save to your desired location. Iterate: tweak the text prompt, swap references, or re-run for variations.
suggestedUseCases: Style transfer for motion: use a subject reference plus a separate aesthetic reference to guide the look while generating Seedance 2.0 motion.
Product motion previews: pair a clean product shot with an environment/style reference to draft quick marketing loops.
Character motion studies: combine a character render with a lighting/mood reference to test subtle motion and camera moves.
Location scouting mockups: mix a subject with a venue reference to preview how motion and framing might play together.
Social-ready loops: rapidly iterate on short, on-brand motion clips using repeatable prompt patterns.

faqItems.question: Do I need the LLM to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No. The LLM (GeminiNode) is optional. You can bypass it and write your own Seedance 2.0–style prompt directly in ByteDance2ReferenceNode. The LLM simply drafts a well-structured prompt from your references and description.

faqItems.question: How are the two reference images used?
faqItems.answer: They ground the content and style the LLM describes and guide Seedance 2.0’s final render. Use one image for the subject and one for style or environment. The ImageConcanate node provides a side-by-side composite to give the LLM clearer context.

faqItems.question: Does GeminiNode require an internet connection or API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes, GeminiNode typically relies on the Google Gemini API. You’ll need a valid API key configured in your ComfyUI environment and a working internet connection. If that isn’t available, bypass the LLM and input prompts manually.

faqItems.question: How can I improve consistency and quality?
faqItems.answer: Use high-resolution, clean references without heavy text/watermarks. Keep the subject well-centered, match lighting between references, and be explicit in your description about camera motion (e.g., “slow pan left”), timing, and mood. Iterate by refining the LLM prompt and re-running.
