4a6697085e75.title: Graphic Design Recomposer
4a6697085e75.description: Upload a graphic design and select your desired aspect ratio. This workflow generates and recomposes the graphic to fit the new aspect ratio.
4a6697085e75.metaDescription: Recompose any design to a new aspect ratio in ComfyUI using smart crop, letterbox, or outpainting. Load, set ratio, and save clean, ready-to-use variants.
4a6697085e75.extendedDescription:
Graphic Design Recomposer takes any existing graphic (logos, posters, social tiles, UI mockups) and reformats it to a new aspect ratio without manual layout work. The workflow is intentionally lean: LoadImage ingests your source file, a custom recomposition node (UUID 172f1008-9337-4d2f-9212-ee081cb4faf5) analyzes the target aspect and adapts the layout, and SaveImage writes the final result. Depending on your settings, it can scale-to-fit with letterboxing, crop-to-fill, or extend the canvas and synthesize new surrounding content for a seamless look.

Technically, the recomposer node computes the optimal scale and offset for the source image relative to the requested aspect ratio, then applies one of three strategies: smart crop, letterbox padding, or canvas expansion with outpainting. For outpainting, the node builds a border mask around the newly created areas and fills them using context from adjacent pixels to minimize visible seams—no prompt required. Feathering around mask edges and adaptive blending reduce halos or sharp transitions. The result is saved via SaveImage, making it quick to generate multiple aspect variants ready for web, print, or social placements.

This is especially useful when you need consistent assets across 1:1, 4:5, 16:9, or 9:16 formats without redrawing layouts. By keeping the pipeline simple and node-local (LoadImage → 172f1008-9337-4d2f-9212-ee081cb4faf5 → SaveImage), you get predictable results with minimal setup, and you can iterate fast by adjusting aspect, crop/fit/extend behavior, and seam smoothing.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the LoadImage node. Select your source graphic (PNG/JPG).
Open the recomposer node (UUID 172f1008-9337-4d2f-9212-ee081cb4faf5). Set your target aspect ratio (e.g., 1:1, 4:5, 16:9, 9:16) or enter explicit width/height.
Choose the recomposition mode: Fit (letterbox with no cropping), Fill (smart crop to fully occupy the frame), or Extend (outpaint to expand canvas).
If using Extend/outpainting, adjust border size, edge feathering, and synthesis strength to control how much new content is generated and how softly it blends with the original.
Confirm the recomposer’s output is connected to SaveImage. In SaveImage, set filename prefix, output folder, and format (e.g., PNG).
Click Queue Prompt to run. Review the output, then fine-tune aspect, mode, or feathering and re-run until you’re satisfied.
suggestedUseCases: Repurpose a square social post into vertical story and horizontal banner variants without redesigning.
Adapt print posters to web hero images while preserving key focal elements.
Create platform-optimized ad sets (1:1, 4:5, 16:9) from a single master graphic.
Generate clean video thumbnails by smart-cropping or extending backgrounds to avoid awkward letterboxing.
Localize or reformat UI mockups to different device aspect ratios while maintaining composition.

faqItems.question: Do I need a text prompt or extra models for outpainting?
faqItems.answer: No. This workflow uses the custom recomposer node (UUID 172f1008-9337-4d2f-9212-ee081cb4faf5) to handle cropping, fitting, and outpainting directly—no prompt required. Just load your image, choose the aspect and mode, and run.

faqItems.question: How can I avoid stretching or distorting logos and text?
faqItems.answer: Use Fit (letterbox) to preserve geometry or Extend (outpaint) to add surrounding context. Avoid Fill when critical text sits near edges; if you must fill, adjust the anchor/focus so important elements remain inside the safe area.

faqItems.question: I see seams or halos at the extended edges. How do I fix that?
faqItems.answer: Increase edge feathering, reduce the outpaint/border size, or try Fit instead of Extend for minimal synthesis. Running a smaller extend in multiple passes can also reduce artifacts.

faqItems.question: What resolution can I export?
faqItems.answer: Set your desired aspect and, if available, explicit width/height in the recomposer node. SaveImage will write exactly that resolution. For lossless results, export PNG; for lighter files, use JPG with appropriate quality.

4ab928487496.title: SYSTMS ACTION: QWEN IMAGE EDIT 2511
4ab928487496.description: Turn just about anything into a toy with the ACTION Qwen Image Edit 2511 LoRA! Simply upload an image and prompt it by writing "action the [subject]"!
4ab928487496.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Edit any photo into a toy-like version using Qwen Image Edit 2511, ACTION LoRA, and Qwen VL text encoder with instruction prompts.
4ab928487496.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates instruction-based image editing with Qwen Image Edit 2511 and a targeted "ACTION" LoRA that turns subjects into toy-like versions. It loads the Qwen Image Edit 2511 diffusion model with UNETLoader and applies the ACTION LoRA via LoraLoaderModelOnly to bias the aesthetic toward playful, miniature, or collectible-toy looks. The QwenEditTextEncode_EditUtils node pairs a dedicated Qwen 2.5 VL text encoder with your input image and instruction (for example, "action the cat") to create edit-aware conditioning, while RandomNoise initializes the latent. SamplerCustomAdvanced runs the diffusion process using your chosen sampler from KSamplerSelect and the schedule from BasicScheduler, with CFGGuider controlling classifier-free guidance strength.

The input image is prepared for the model using ResizeImagesByLongerEdge and ImageCrop+ to standardize dimensions, with GetImageSize and PrimitiveInt passing size info to the sampler. After sampling, VAELoader and VAEDecode convert latents back to an RGB image, and SaveImage writes the result. Because this is an instruction-following edit model, you don’t need an init-latent path—your original photo is consumed by the Qwen encoder as a visual reference while the LoRA steers the result toward a consistent toy style. The included Note node documents the prompt pattern ("action the [subject]") so you can quickly produce consistent outputs.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. In UNETLoader, select the Qwen Image Edit 2511 model (qwen_image_edit_2511_fp8mixed.safetensors). In LoraLoaderModelOnly, choose the ACTION LoRA. In QwenEditTextEncode_EditUtils, point to the Qwen 2.5 VL text encoder.

Install the model files from the author’s links: place the diffusion model in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models and the Qwen text encoder in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders. Load or confirm a compatible VAE in VAELoader.
Use LoadImage to import your photo. The ResizeImagesByLongerEdge and ImageCrop+ nodes will adapt it to a model-friendly size; you can adjust the long edge or crop settings to control framing.
In QwenEditTextEncode_EditUtils, write an instruction like: "action the dog" or "action the vintage camera". Keep it concise and literal; the LoRA is tuned to "action the [subject]" phrasing.

Set your sampling options: choose a sampler in KSamplerSelect (e.g., DPM++ or Euler), set steps (e.g., 20–30), and guidance in CFGGuider (start low-to-moderate, e.g., 3–6, to preserve identity). Fix a seed in RandomNoise for repeatable results.
Run the workflow. Inspect the output from SaveImage. If the toy style is too strong or too weak, adjust the LoRA strength in LoraLoaderModelOnly and guidance in CFGGuider, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Turn product shots into collectible toy mockups for playful campaign variations.
Create toy-style character portraits or avatars from selfies or studio photos.
Generate concept art for toy packaging or merchandising pitches.
Produce kid-friendly, miniature versions of everyday objects for educational visuals.
Make a series of consistent toy-themed social media posts from existing images.

faqItems.question: Which models do I need, and where do they go?
faqItems.answer: Download the Qwen Image Edit 2511 diffusion model (UNET) and the Qwen 2.5 VL text encoder from the links provided. Place the diffusion model in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models and the text encoder in ComfyUI/models/text_encoders. Load a compatible VAE in VAELoader. The ACTION LoRA is loaded via LoraLoaderModelOnly.

faqItems.question: How do I control how "toy-like" the result is?
faqItems.answer: Increase or decrease the ACTION LoRA strength in LoraLoaderModelOnly and tune CFG in CFGGuider. Higher LoRA strength and higher CFG generally intensify the toy effect; lowering them preserves more of the original look. You can also adjust steps for detail (more) vs. speed (fewer).

faqItems.question: Do I need an init image strength or img2img denoise setting?
faqItems.answer: No. This workflow uses instruction-based editing: the input image and text instruction are encoded together by QwenEditTextEncode_EditUtils, and the diffusion starts from noise. Control intensity via LoRA strength, guidance (CFGGuider), sampler choice, and steps.

faqItems.question: What sampler and resolution should I use?
faqItems.answer: Start with a balanced sampler like DPM++ 2M Karras or Euler and 20–30 steps. The ResizeImagesByLongerEdge and ImageCrop+ nodes set a consistent canvas—use a size appropriate for your GPU. Higher resolutions need more VRAM and time; if you see OOM errors, lower the long edge size or steps.

The Florence2Run node uses the Florence-2 multimodal model to extract detailed information from the image, such as object attributes, spatial relationships, and scene context, which are then used to create a comprehensive prompt. This dual approach not only improves the visual quality of the image but also enriches the metadata associated with it, making it particularly useful for applications that require both high-quality visuals and detailed descriptive data.

The upscaling process is achieved through diffusion techniques that increase the image's resolution by adding denoised pixels, thereby preserving the original content and structure while enhancing clarity. The workflow uses a low denoise value in the Z Image Turbo model to ensure that the upscaled image retains its original details. This makes it an excellent tool for applications where image quality is paramount, such as digital art, photography, and media production. By combining image upscaling with automatic image analysis, this workflow offers a comprehensive solution for enhancing and understanding visual content.

Use the LoadImage node to import the image you wish to upscale and analyze.
Configure the Florence2Run node to enable detailed image analysis and prompt generation.
Adjust the Z Image Turbo settings, ensuring a low denoise value for optimal upscaling results.

4ca799182440.title: Refocus LTX 2.3 IC LoRA
4ca799182440.description:
The Refocus IC LoRA for LTX 2.3 makes it possible to bring slightly out-of-focus footage back into clarity.

Even in more extreme cases, it can recover detail that would typically be lost, opening up new possibilities for salvaging footage that would otherwise go unused.
4ca799182440.metaDescription: Recover soft or out-of-focus footage using LTX 2.3 with the Refocus IC LoRA in ComfyUI. Load video, enhance per-frame, and recombine to a sharp final clip.
4ca799182440.extendedDescription:
This workflow restores soft or slightly out‑of‑focus footage using the Refocus IC LoRA on top of the LTX 2.3 model. It ingests your clip with VHS_LoadVideo, processes each frame through a custom LTX 2.3 + LoRA processor (node UUID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3), and then reassembles the enhanced frames back into a video with VHS_VideoCombine. The Refocus IC LoRA biases the LTX 2.3 backbone toward reconstructing fine edges and mid‑frequency detail that typical sharpening filters can’t recover, helping pull subjects back into clarity while minimizing halos and ringing.

Technically, the pipeline works frame‑wise: VHS_LoadVideo decodes your source and outputs frame tensors; the custom node loads the LTX 2.3 base and applies the Refocus IC LoRA weights to guide inference toward crisp, natural detail; and VHS_VideoCombine stitches the processed frames into a finished clip at your chosen frame rate and quality. Because this is model‑driven enhancement rather than a simple unsharp mask, it can plausibly restore subtle textures and edge definition in footage that would otherwise be unusable. Keep LoRA strength conservative for realism, and iterate to balance sharpness against potential artifacts.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. Ensure VideoHelperSuite is installed (for VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine) and that the LTX 2.3 model and the Refocus IC LoRA are available in your models/loras directories.
Open VHS_LoadVideo and set your input file path. Optionally define a frame range or downscale factor for testing. Confirm the FPS and color space settings match your source.

In the custom LTX 2.3 + Refocus IC node (UUID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3), select the LTX 2.3 base model and the Refocus IC LoRA file. Start with a moderate LoRA weight/intensity so edges look crisp without halos.
If the clip is very soft, gradually increase the LoRA weight. Preview a short frame range first to judge detail recovery versus artifacts before committing to the full timeline.

Open VHS_VideoCombine and set output parameters: destination path, FPS (usually match source), codec/quality, and container. Note: audio isn’t processed—plan to reattach your original audio in an editor if needed.
Queue and run the workflow. Review the output for oversharpening or texture hallucination; adjust the LoRA strength and rerun until you get a natural, consistent look.
suggestedUseCases: Rescuing slightly out-of-focus interviews or talking-head clips where facial features need gentle restoration.
Stabilizing detail in handheld b‑roll with minor focus breathing or soft focus pulls.
Improving smartphone or action camera footage that missed focus in low light.
Polishing archival or event footage that’s a touch soft from older lenses or adapters.
Prepping social content where quick, natural clarity gains matter more than heavy denoising or upscaling.

faqItems.question: How is this different from a standard sharpen filter?
faqItems.answer: Instead of boosting existing edges, LTX 2.3 with the Refocus IC LoRA uses a learned prior to reconstruct plausible detail. This can recover mid‑frequency structure that simple unsharp masks miss, but overly strong settings can introduce artifacts—keep the LoRA weight moderate.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow handle audio?
faqItems.answer: No. VHS_VideoCombine outputs a video from processed frames only. Export your enhanced clip and reattach the original audio in your NLE or a separate muxing step.

faqItems.question: What footage benefits most?
faqItems.answer: Clips that are slightly soft or marginally out of focus. Extreme defocus or heavy motion blur won’t fully recover—try small increases in LoRA strength and evaluate on a short segment before processing the full video.

faqItems.question: What performance should I expect?
faqItems.answer: Speed depends on resolution, clip length, and GPU VRAM. Processing per-frame with a generative model is compute-heavy; test on a short frame range first and consider batching or downscaling for faster previews.

4d10908bd0bc.title: Wan 2.1 Inpainting
4d10908bd0bc.description: Generate videos from start and end frames using Wan 2.1 inpainting.
4d10908bd0bc.metaDescription: Generate coherent videos from start and end frames using Wan 2.1 inpainting in ComfyUI. Prompt-guided motion, temporal attention, and easy export.
4d10908bd0bc.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a pair of images into a short, coherent video by leveraging Wan 2.1’s inpainting-based video diffusion. You provide a start frame and an end frame; the WanFunInpaintToVideo node then guides the model to synthesize the in‑between motion while preserving subject and scene details anchored in your images. Text prompts (via CLIPTextEncode) steer style and content, while negative prompts help suppress artifacts.

Under the hood, Step1 loads the core components: UNETLoader (Wan2.1 / Wan), VAELoader/VAEDecode for latent <-> pixel space conversion, and CLIPLoader for text conditioning. Your start/end frames are brought in with LoadImage and encoded using CLIPVisionLoader + CLIPVisionEncode to produce image conditioning for the UNet. KSampler drives the diffusion process using ModelSamplingSD3 for the correct sigma schedule, with CFGZeroStar and SkipLayerGuidanceDiT stabilizing guidance. The Attention Booster group applies UNetTemporalAttentionMultiply to strengthen temporal consistency across frames. Finally, CreateVideo assembles frames and SaveVideo writes the finished clip.
howToUse: Step 1 – Load models: In the "Step1 - Load Models" group, set UNETLoader to Wan2.1 (or Wan), pick the matching VAE in VAELoader, and load the text encoder in CLIPLoader. Keep ModelSamplingSD3 connected to KSampler.

Step 2 – Add start and end frames: In "Step2 - Start & End Images", use LoadImage to select your start and end images. The frames are encoded with CLIPVisionLoader + CLIPVisionEncode and routed to WanFunInpaintToVideo.

Step 3 – Prompting: Enter your positive and negative prompts in CLIPTextEncode. Start with a concise description (e.g., “Fashion photography, studio lighting, Balenciaga style”). Use negatives to suppress defects and low quality.

Step 4 – Attention Booster (optional): In the "Attention Booster" group, adjust UNetTemporalAttentionMultiply. Slightly increasing the multiplier (e.g., 1.1–1.4) can improve motion coherence; lowering it reduces over-smoothing.

Step 5 – Sampling and decode: In "Step3 - Prompt, Sampling & Decode", set KSampler steps and seed. Moderate steps (e.g., 25–50) and a balanced CFG (with CFGZeroStar + SkipLayerGuidanceDiT enabled) usually produce stable results. Run the graph; VAEDecode converts latents to frames.

Step 6 – Export: Use CreateVideo to set fps and order the frames, then SaveVideo to write the final file. Preview, then iterate on prompts, attention multiplier, steps, or seed until you’re satisfied.
suggestedUseCases: Before/after reveals that fluidly transition from an initial setup to a final look
Fashion or product shots that morph between poses or angles while keeping brand style
Concept art explorations that interpolate between two keyframes to test motion ideas
Scene cleanup: guide from a rough plate to a retouched plate to inpaint distractions
Thumbnail-to-motion teasers for social posts using a start frame and a stylized end frame

faqItems.question: Do I need both a start and an end frame?
faqItems.answer: Yes. This workflow is designed to synthesize motion between two anchors. Provide a clear, well‑lit start frame and a visually consistent end frame for best results.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or drifting details?
faqItems.answer: Increase steps slightly, nudge the UNetTemporalAttentionMultiply up (e.g., +0.1), lower CFG if details are unstable, and keep a fixed seed while iterating. Ensure both images share resolution and similar framing.

faqItems.question: What sampler settings should I change?
faqItems.answer: Leave ModelSamplingSD3 connected to KSampler to keep the correct schedule for Wan 2.1. Adjust only steps, seed, and guidance strength (with CFGZeroStar and SkipLayerGuidanceDiT enabled) unless you know you need a different sampler.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best?
faqItems.answer: Use matching resolutions for start and end frames. Moderate sizes (e.g., 512–768 on the short edge) balance detail and VRAM usage. Larger frames increase memory and render time.

4d7abcb8e25d.title: SAM3 - Video Masking via Text Prompt
4d7abcb8e25d.description: SAM 3 lets you mask objects in a video just by typing a short phrase like "red car" or "person" — no frame-by-frame rotoscoping. It finds every matching instance, tracks them across frames with stable IDs, and outputs per-frame masks ready for compositing, blurring, or replacement.
4d7abcb8e25d.metaDescription: Mask and track objects in video via text prompts using SAM3 in ComfyUI. Output overlay, raw masks, and cut-outs—no manual rotoscoping required.
4d7abcb8e25d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs automatic video object masking from a simple text phrase using the SAM3 Video Masking node (ID: 9cea40bb-b0cf-4b40-a758-8935cfe8d52f). You load a clip with VHS_LoadVideo, describe what you want to isolate (for example, "red car" or "person") in the node’s mask_prompt, and the system finds every matching instance, tracks them across frames with stable IDs, and produces three streams: a mask overlay preview, a raw per-frame binary mask, and a subject cut-out. SaveVideo nodes handle exporting the results.

Technically, VHS_LoadVideo provides a consistent frame sequence (fps, resolution) for inference. During iteration you can cap frames using frame_load_cap to preview quickly, then switch to a full pass by setting it to 0. The SAM3 Video Masking node interprets your text prompt, segments the target across frames, and maintains identity continuity so objects don’t flicker or swap. The outputs are suitable for downstream compositing, selective blurring, color grading, or background replacement. A MarkdownNote node in the graph provides inline tips and reminders while you work.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the required nodes are installed: VideoHelperSuite (VHS_LoadVideo/SaveVideo) and the SAM3 Video Masking node.
Load your clip using VHS_LoadVideo. While testing, set frame_load_cap to a small number (e.g., 12–48) for quick previews; set it to 0 for the final full run.
In the SAM3 Video Masking node, enter a clear mask_prompt like "red car", "person in blue jacket", or "soccer ball" to target the subject you want masked and tracked.
Queue and run the graph. Inspect the three outputs: the mask overlay (visual check), the raw binary mask (matte), and the cut-out subject (foreground with transparency/black bg).
Refine as needed: make the prompt more specific (color, clothing, object type) if unrelated objects are captured. Re-run a short preview until the overlay looks stable.
For final export, set frame_load_cap to 0 and run the full sequence. Configure the SaveVideo node(s) to output filenames/folders for the overlay, raw mask, and cut-out streams.
suggestedUseCases: Privacy blurring: Generate masks for faces or license plates and apply selective blur in post.
Product isolation: Cut out a product from handheld footage for clean backgrounds or motion graphics.
Sports analysis: Track and highlight a specific player or ball throughout a play.
Sky or background replacement: Create stable mattes to swap environments without greenscreen.
Selective color grading: Isolate a subject to grade independently of the scene.

faqItems.question: How do I get the most accurate masks from a text prompt?
faqItems.answer: Be specific and descriptive. Include distinguishing attributes like color, clothing, or object type (e.g., "red sedan" instead of "car"). If multiple similar objects appear, refine the prompt further ("person in blue jacket" vs. "person").

faqItems.question: Can it track multiple instances and keep IDs stable?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The SAM3 Video Masking node finds all instances that match the prompt and tracks them with stable IDs across frames. If you only need one instance, make the prompt more specific or filter by ID in post using the raw mask stream.

faqItems.question: It works on a few frames but is slow on the full video. Any tips?
faqItems.answer: Use frame_load_cap for quick iteration, then switch to 0 for final output. Reducing input resolution or trimming the clip can improve speed. Running on a GPU with sufficient VRAM is recommended for real-time responsiveness.

faqItems.question: What should I export for compositing in another editor?
faqItems.answer: Export the raw mask (as a video matte) and the cut-out subject. In your NLE or VFX app, use the mask as a luma/alpha matte, or place the cut-out directly over your background plate for precise compositing.

Commerce Hero Video is a guided image-to-video pipeline that turns a plain product photo into a premium e-commerce hero image and a short motion spot. It starts with LoadImage to bring in your product shot, then relights and polishes it with GeminiImage2Node (configured for hero-style lighting and background cleanup) to produce a crisp, on-brand hero still. That hero is saved with SaveImage and previewed via PreviewAny so you can iterate quickly on lighting, reflections, and background tone.
Next, the Prompt group uses GeminiNode to write a concise motion prompt—think short ad copy with cues for camera moves and product highlights. The Generate Product Hero group then feeds the hero still and the motion prompt into ByteDance2ReferenceNode (SEED‑2 Reference), which generates a short, reference-conditioned video that preserves the product’s geometry while adding tasteful motion. You can monitor progress with PreviewAny and export the final spot using SaveVideo. The result: a consistent, relit hero image plus a matching micro‑video, ready for storefronts, PDPs, and paid social—without hand-animating or rebuilding the scene.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and drop your product image into the LoadImage node. For best results, use a high-resolution, well-exposed PNG or JPG (transparent PNGs produce cleaner edges).

Open the Relight Product group. In GeminiImage2Node, describe the desired hero look (e.g., studio softbox lighting, seamless backdrop, subtle ground shadow, gentle rim light). Set output size and any strength/intensity controls, then run the group. Inspect the result with PreviewAny; if needed, tweak the prompt and rerun. SaveImage will store the hero still.

Open the Prompt group. Provide the product name, key features, and tone (e.g., sleek, eco-friendly, premium). Run GeminiNode to generate a concise motion prompt with camera/action cues. Review the text (via MarkdownNote or node preview) and edit for accuracy or brand voice.

Go to Generate Product Hero. Ensure the saved hero image is connected as the reference into ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Paste the motion prompt into its text field. Set clip length, frame rate, resolution, and reference strength to balance product fidelity vs. movement. Optionally set a seed for repeatable results.

Execute the video generation. Use PreviewAny to review the motion and edges (look for warping or background shimmer). If the product drifts or deforms, increase reference strength or shorten duration. If motion feels stiff, lower reference strength or extend duration slightly.
When satisfied, confirm SaveVideo’s path and container settings, then save the final clip. Re-run with alternative seeds or minor prompt variations to A/B test hero looks and motion cues.
suggestedUseCases: Shopify or WooCommerce hero banners that pair a polished hero still with a looping 3–5s product motion.
Amazon/Etsy listing upgrades: consistent main image plus a short product video highlighting key features.
Paid social cutdowns (e.g., Instagram Reels, TikTok) that showcase packaging, materials, or colorways with light camera motion.
D2C landing pages and launch teasers where the same relit hero aesthetic is carried into micro‑video.
A/B testing hero lighting and motion variants without reshooting products.

faqItems.question: Which nodes actually do the relight and the video generation?
faqItems.answer: GeminiImage2Node handles the relight and hero-style enhancement of your uploaded product image. ByteDance2ReferenceNode (SEED‑2 Reference) generates the short video, conditioning on the hero still plus your motion prompt.

faqItems.question: How can I keep the product shape stable in the video?
faqItems.answer: Increase the reference strength in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, reduce clip length slightly, and use a consistent seed. Also avoid prompts that imply heavy deformation; prefer camera moves (pan/tilt/dolly) and subtle lighting changes.

faqItems.question: What input images work best?
faqItems.answer: High-resolution, in-focus images with clean separation from the background. Transparent PNGs or shots with simple backgrounds relight more cleanly. Avoid motion blur and severe lens distortion.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the hero look and the motion prompt?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Edit the style text in GeminiImage2Node to target lighting, backdrop color, reflections, and shadows. In the Prompt group, you can accept, edit, or fully replace GeminiNode’s motion prompt to match brand voice and specific camera cues.

4ebc86e57ea6.title: Luma: Text to Video
4ebc86e57ea6.description: High-quality videos can be generated using simple prompts.
4ebc86e57ea6.metaDescription: Generate text-to-video with Luma in ComfyUI. Control camera via LumaConceptsNode and save MP4 output with SaveVideo. Fast, guided T2V iteration.
4ebc86e57ea6.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns plain text prompts into short, high-quality videos using Luma's text-to-video model. The core of the graph is the LumaVideoNode, which sends your prompt and settings to Luma's API and polls for the rendered result. The LumaConceptsNode feeds structured "concepts" into LumaVideoNode, giving you fine control over camera behavior like pans, tilts, or zooms without overloading the prompt text. A SaveVideo node writes the returned video to disk, while a MarkdownNote provides in-graph guidance and tips.

Technically, the workflow is an API-driven pipeline: LumaVideoNode packages your prompt and the optional concept object from LumaConceptsNode, submits a generation request, and waits for completion. The seed parameter in this workflow is used only to determine whether LumaVideoNode should re-run (i.e., to bypass caching) and does not control the visual randomness of the final video. This design lets you iterate quickly on camera motion, timing, and composition by changing LumaConceptsNode settings while keeping your textual description short and precise.
howToUse: Load the "Luma: Text to Video" workflow in ComfyUI and locate the key nodes: LumaVideoNode (API call), LumaConceptsNode (camera control), and SaveVideo (output).
Open LumaVideoNode and enter your text prompt. Add optional fields (e.g., negative phrases, duration/size if available). Provide your Luma API credentials if the node requires them.
Configure LumaConceptsNode to set camera behavior (e.g., pan, tilt, zoom, orbit speed). Keep these instructions here rather than in the prompt to avoid conflicts.
If you want to force a fresh render, change the seed value on LumaVideoNode. Note: seed only triggers a re-run and does not make results deterministic.
Set the output directory/filename in the SaveVideo node. Ensure the path is writable and you have enough disk space.
Run the graph. The LumaVideoNode will submit the job and wait for completion; when finished, SaveVideo will write the returned video file to your chosen location.
suggestedUseCases: Cinematic establishing shots with controlled camera moves (slow dolly, gentle pan) for concept previews.
Product hero clips for social media, emphasizing a single subject with a subtle orbit or zoom.
Environment or mood studies where camera motion enhances scale (e.g., fly-throughs or push-ins).
Storyboard animatics and previsualization, quickly iterating on camera language from text.
Educational or explainer shorts where smooth motion guides viewer attention.

faqItems.question: Why does changing the seed not make the video deterministic?
faqItems.answer: In this workflow, seed is only used to decide whether LumaVideoNode should re-run (invalidate cache). It does not control Luma’s internal randomness, so outputs can vary between runs even with the same prompt and concepts.

faqItems.question: How do I control camera movement reliably?
faqItems.answer: Use LumaConceptsNode to specify camera behavior (e.g., pan, tilt, zoom). Keep movement instructions in the concepts object and avoid duplicating or contradicting them in the text prompt. Start with a single movement at a modest intensity and iterate.

faqItems.question: Where is the video saved and in what format?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo writes the file to the path you set in its parameters. The Luma API returns a ready-to-save video (commonly MP4), and SaveVideo stores that file without additional conversion.

faqItems.question: I’m getting API or network errors. How do I fix this?
faqItems.answer: Use the API in a secure environment: allow access from 127.0.0.1/localhost, call it from HTTPS contexts when embedding in web services, and verify you can reach the Luma API from your machine. Check firewall/proxy settings, confirm your API key, and re-run.

50199f76fe74.title: Relight and Environment Merge
50199f76fe74.description: Using a combination of illustration LoRA and relight LoRA, this workflow allows you to properly light illustrated characters in a keyframe.
50199f76fe74.metaDescription: Relight illustrated characters to match a new environment and merge them in ComfyUI using a Subgraph with illustration + relight LoRAs. Includes prompt tips.
50199f76fe74.extendedDescription:
This workflow relights an illustrated character to match a new background plate and merges them into a cohesive keyframe. The heavy lifting is packaged inside a Subgraph node (type ID: 9e3c3756-d15f-4361-8e99-c35673036e68), so you only interact with a few clear inputs and controls. You provide a character image and an environment image via LoadImage nodes, drive the look with prompt text (see the in-graph Note/MarkdownNote), and export results with SaveImage.

Technically, the Subgraph stacks an illustration LoRA for style cohesion with a relight LoRA that adapts shading and color to the environment. The subgraph handles conditioning, relight guidance, and foreground/background compositing, exposing simple strength sliders and merge options so you can balance “style” versus “lighting” without touching the internals. Notes in the graph include Chinese prompt text—keep those characters intact and append your own edit instructions after them to refine light direction, mood, color temperature, or rim light accents. For local users, ensure any referenced text encoder files (e.g., qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors) are available so the subgraph can encode prompts as intended.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI. If running locally, download any referenced models (e.g., text encoders like qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors) to your models/text_encoders folder so the Subgraph can load them.
Load your inputs: connect a character image (PNG with transparency recommended) to the character LoadImage node and an environment/background plate to the environment LoadImage node.

Prompting: locate the Note/MarkdownNote node in the graph. Keep the existing Chinese characters exactly as they are, then append your additional image edit instructions after them. Example: （保留中文说明）…，补充：soft side light, warm key, subtle rim light, match environment shadows.

Adjust the Subgraph: select the node with type ID 9e3c3756-d15f-4361-8e99-c35673036e68. Tweak the exposed controls (e.g., illustration LoRA strength, relight LoRA strength, blend/merge options) to balance style versus lighting. If you need finer control, double‑click to open the Subgraph and tune internal parameters.

Queue and run: execute the workflow to preview results. Iterate by refining prompt text (append after the Chinese text), adjusting LoRA strengths, and re-running until the character lighting and environment feel cohesive.
Export: the SaveImage node writes outputs to your ComfyUI/output folder. Set a filename prefix if available to keep versions organized.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboarding and key art: relight consistent character poses across multiple background plates.
Anime/illustration composites: place stylized characters into new scenes while preserving the original art style.
Game keyframe marketing shots: match lighting to in-game environments for promo imagery.
Motion design previsualization: create on-model, properly lit character frames before moving to animation.

faqItems.question: Do I have to keep the Chinese characters in the prompt notes?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Keep the Chinese characters intact as provided in the Note/MarkdownNote. Append any additional image edit instructions after them. Removing or altering them may change conditioning and produce inconsistent results.

faqItems.question: Can I use photographed characters or only illustrations?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is tuned for illustrated characters (it uses an illustration LoRA). You can try photos, but for the best results reduce the illustration LoRA strength and rely more on relight strength to avoid over-stylization.

faqItems.question: Why do my results look over-lit or color-shifted?
faqItems.answer: Lower the relight LoRA strength, refine your appended prompt instructions (e.g., softer key, neutral color temperature), and ensure the environment plate isn’t overly saturated or clipped. Small prompt nudges and balanced LoRA weights usually fix this.

faqItems.question: Do I need a cutout with transparency for the character?
faqItems.answer: A transparent PNG (clean silhouette) gives the best composite. If your source lacks alpha, pre‑mask the character before import to avoid halos or background bleed at the edges.

527ecf1f2eb4.title: LTX-2.5 (Pro): FLF2V
527ecf1f2eb4.description: Generate a video from two reference images using LTX-2.5, blending the content of both frames into a single animated sequence. Ideal for creating transition shots, morphing between two subjects or scenes, and building multi-shot narratives from still references.
527ecf1f2eb4.metaDescription: Create smooth two-image morphs in ComfyUI with LTX-2.5: load two frames, generate an API-driven transition video, and save the result with SaveVideo.
527ecf1f2eb4.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns two still images into a single, fluid video transition using the LTX-2.5 image-to-video API. Two LoadImage nodes supply your start and end reference frames, which are passed into LtxApi25ImageToVideo. The node blends structural cues from both inputs to synthesize an in-between sequence that morphs from the first image toward the second, producing a natural-looking transition, reveal, or morph. Finally, SaveVideo encodes the generated frames to a video file you can review or drop into an edit.

Technically, the LtxApi25ImageToVideo node makes an API call to the LTX-2.5 backend, which analyzes both images, aligns major features, and interpolates motion across a specified duration and frame rate. Because the processing happens remotely, you’ll typically configure an API key/endpoint in the node and choose key parameters like output length and FPS. Keeping both input images similar in aspect ratio, framing, and subject scale helps the model establish a clean “path” between them, reducing artifacts and ensuring a smoother morph. SaveVideo then writes the result to disk at your chosen frame rate, ready for playback or further editing.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm you see the three key nodes: two LoadImage nodes feeding into LtxApi25ImageToVideo, followed by SaveVideo.
Open each LoadImage node and select your start (first) and end (second) reference images. For best results, use images with matching aspect ratios and similar subject framing.

Open LtxApi25ImageToVideo and configure required API settings (key/endpoint) if needed. Set core options such as output duration and frame rate; adjust any blend/transition controls the node exposes to tune how strongly the animation leans toward each image.
Optionally set SaveVideo parameters (output path/filename and FPS) to match your target deliverable. Ensure the FPS here matches what you chose in the LtxApi25ImageToVideo node.
Queue and execute the workflow. The node will upload the images to the LTX-2.5 service, generate intermediate frames, and pass them to SaveVideo for encoding.
Review the output video. If you see stretching or jitter, try aligning subject scale between the two images, matching aspect ratios, or adjusting duration/FPS, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Seamless scene transitions: move from one establishing shot to another without a hard cut.
Character or product morphs: transform one subject into another for reveals and comparisons.
Before/after storytelling: animate between two states (e.g., restoration, makeover, design iterations).
Narrative bridges: connect still keyframes into a short motion beat between cuts.
Mood board to motion: turn two style frames into a quick animated exploration.

faqItems.question: Do my two images need to be the same size and aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: It’s strongly recommended. The node or API may auto-resize, but mismatched sizes/aspects often cause stretching or warped motion. Align aspect ratio and approximate subject scale for the cleanest transition.

faqItems.question: How do I control speed and smoothness of the morph?
faqItems.answer: Use the duration and frame rate options in LtxApi25ImageToVideo to set total length and temporal resolution. If the node exposes blend or transition controls, adjust them to favor a gentler or more aggressive move between frames. Longer durations and consistent subject framing usually look smoother.

faqItems.question: Where is the video saved and in what format?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo writes the generated sequence to a file path you set in the node (ComfyUI’s output directory by default). Choose your target frame rate there; the exact container/codec options depend on your environment and SaveVideo configuration.

faqItems.question: Does this send my images to an external service?
faqItems.answer: Yes. LtxApi25ImageToVideo uses an API to run LTX-2.5 remotely, so your images are uploaded for processing. Ensure you’ve configured your API credentials and reviewed the provider’s privacy and data-retention policies before use.

536dc32faee1.title: ACE-Step 1.5XL Base: Text to Music
536dc32faee1.description: Generate high-quality audio from text prompts using the 4B parameter ACE-Step 1.5 XL model.
536dc32faee1.metaDescription: Text-to-music in ComfyUI with ACE-Step 1.5 XL. Prompt, set duration, sample with AuraFlow schedule, decode to audio, and export MP3.
536dc32faee1.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns text prompts into music using the ACE-Step 1.5 XL Base (4B) model inside ComfyUI. It pairs UNETLoader with the acestep_v1.5_xl_base_bf16.safetensors diffusion model and VAELoader with the ace_1.5_vae.safetensors decoder. Your prompt is encoded by TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5, an EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio node creates a blank latent audio clip at your chosen duration, and KSampler performs the denoising pass to synthesize music. VAEDecodeAudio reconstructs the waveform from latents, and SaveAudioMP3 writes the final track to disk.

Under the hood, ConditioningZeroOut provides a clean fallback when the negative prompt is empty, while ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the model’s sampler to the correct flow/schedule so KSampler can produce stable, on-style results. PrimitiveNode and PrimitiveInt nodes supply simple controls for duration, steps, guidance (CFG), and seed. The workflow is organized into clear groups (Model, Duration, Prompt) so you can quickly load the right weights, set the clip length, write a prompt, and iterate rapidly by adjusting steps, CFG, and seed.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then download/place the models: acestep_v1.5_xl_base_bf16.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models and ace_1.5_vae.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/vae.
Open the Model group: set UNETLoader to the ACE-Step 1.5 XL Base model file and VAELoader to the ACE 1.5 VAE. ModelSamplingAuraFlow should remain connected to the model output.
Open the Duration group: set your target length in EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio (and any connected PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveNode controlling seconds or frames). Longer clips use more VRAM and time.
Open the Prompt group: enter your text in TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5. Optionally add a negative prompt; if left blank, ConditioningZeroOut ensures stable behavior.
Tweak generation controls on KSampler: choose steps (e.g., 30–60), CFG (e.g., 3–6), and a seed. Use seed -1 or change the seed to explore new variations; keep denoise at 1.0 for pure text-to-music.

Run the workflow. After KSampler finishes, VAEDecodeAudio converts latents to audio, and SaveAudioMP3 writes an MP3 to your ComfyUI output folder. Listen, then iterate on prompt, steps, CFG, duration, and seed.
suggestedUseCases: Create background music cues for videos, podcasts, and livestreams.
Prototype game loops and ambient beds quickly during early development.
Generate mood-specific stingers, intros, and outros for social content.
Explore stylistic ideas for composers and sound designers before full production.
Rapidly iterate royalty-free tracks for ads, trailers, or demos.

faqItems.question: How long can I make the music?
faqItems.answer: Clip length is set in EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio (often via a PrimitiveInt for seconds). Longer durations require more VRAM and time. If you hit out-of-memory errors, reduce duration, steps, or batch size.

faqItems.question: What sampler settings should I start with?
faqItems.answer: A practical starting point is 30–60 steps with CFG 3–6 and denoise 1.0. Keep ModelSamplingAuraFlow connected so the sampler schedule matches the model. Increase steps for finer detail; moderate CFG to avoid artifacts.

faqItems.question: How do I reduce artifacts or muddiness?
faqItems.answer: Use clear, style-specific prompts (genre, instruments, mood, tempo). Keep CFG moderate, try a different seed, and raise steps slightly. A short negative prompt (e.g., "no distortion, no clipping") can help; ConditioningZeroOut handles empty negatives safely.

faqItems.question: Where is the audio saved and can I change the format?
faqItems.answer: SaveAudioMP3 writes an MP3 to your ComfyUI output directory. If you prefer WAV, replace or add a compatible WAV save node (if installed) after VAEDecodeAudio and route the decoded audio there.

558cc012978d.title: Video Restoration
558cc012978d.description: Using LTX 2.3 Video to Video you can restore old footage. This LoRA is great for getting details out of older archival film.
558cc012978d.metaDescription: ComfyUI video restoration workflow using LTX 2.3 Video-to-Video LoRA with VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine to enhance archival and anime footage.
558cc012978d.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow restores old or low-quality footage using an LTX 2.3 Video-to-Video LoRA. It splits your video into frames with VHS_LoadVideo, enhances each frame with the custom LTX 2.3 V2V processor (class_id: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3), then reassembles the result with VHS_VideoCombine. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline tips so you can adjust settings without leaving the canvas.

Technically, VHS_LoadVideo handles decoding and frame range control: use skip_first_frames to trim the head of a clip and frame_count to limit how many frames are processed. Those frames are passed to the LTX 2.3 Video-to-Video node, which applies the LoRA-driven restoration to recover texture, lines, and fine detail common in archival film and anime sources. You’ll typically balance LoRA strength and denoise to preserve motion while lifting detail. Finally, VHS_VideoCombine encodes the restored frames back into a video, where you can set the output fps and codec to match your delivery needs. The result is a repeatable, frame-accurate pipeline for bringing older footage back to life without hand-tuning every shot.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the MarkdownNote for quick reference.
Open VHS_LoadVideo and set your input video path. Adjust skip_first_frames to trim the start and frame_count to limit how many frames will be processed.

In the LTX 2.3 Video-to-Video node (class_id: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3), select the LTX 2.3 LoRA and tune key controls (e.g., LoRA strength and denoise) to balance detail recovery with temporal stability.
Configure VHS_VideoCombine: choose an output file path, set fps (match the source or your target), and select encoding parameters appropriate for your final use.
Queue and run the workflow. Monitor VRAM usage and iteration time; reduce resolution or denoise strength if you encounter memory issues.
Review the output video. If you see flicker or over-sharpening, slightly lower denoise or LoRA strength and re-run. Iterate until the balance of detail and stability looks right.
suggestedUseCases: Restoring digitized VHS or MiniDV home videos with improved clarity and reduced softness.
Cleaning and enhancing scanned archival film or newsreels while preserving historical texture.
Anime and cel-animated footage cleanup to recover line art and fine shading from older transfers.
Upscaling and refining low-bitrate web videos where compression artifacts obscure detail.
Pre-restoration pass before color grading to deliver a cleaner base for finishing.

faqItems.question: How do I process only part of a long clip?
faqItems.answer: Use skip_first_frames to trim the start and frame_count to set how many frames are processed after the skip. For example, to convert minutes 1–17 of a 600-frame clip, set skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480.

faqItems.question: What input and output formats are supported?
faqItems.answer: VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine rely on ffmpeg under the hood and work with common formats like MP4, MOV, and MKV using H.264/H.265 or ProRes. Choose an output codec in VHS_VideoCombine that matches your delivery needs.

faqItems.question: How can I minimize flicker between frames?
faqItems.answer: Lower the denoise amount and/or LoRA strength in the LTX 2.3 Video-to-Video node to preserve more of the original structure. Keep a fixed seed during testing and match the output fps to the source to avoid cadence issues.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: This graph focuses on frame restoration and recombination. If audio isn’t preserved in your encode, export the restored video and then mux the original audio back in with ffmpeg or your NLE.

560738f98e65.title: Extract Color Palette
560738f98e65.description: Extracts a cohesive color palette from any input image and renders it as a clean, full-resolution color bar. You can choose how many colors to pull and whether each color's width reflects its visual dominance in the image or all colors are shown in equal proportions.
560738f98e65.metaDescription: Extract a clean color palette from any image in ComfyUI. Choose swatch count and equal or weighted widths, and export a full-resolution color bar.
560738f98e65.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow extracts a cohesive color palette from any input image and renders it as a clean, full-resolution color bar. It lets you control how many colors to include and whether each swatch’s width is equal or proportional to its visual dominance in the source. The result is a ready-to-share palette image that’s ideal for mood boards, branding guides, UI tokens, or color study references.

Technically, the pipeline is straightforward and fast. LoadImage brings your source image into the graph, then a GLSLShader analyzes pixel colors, groups similar hues into N buckets, estimates their relative presence, and draws the final horizontal palette. A PrimitiveInt sets the target number of colors, while a ComfySwitchNode toggles between equal-width and dominance-weighted swatches. Use ResolutionSelector to set the exact output dimensions for your color bar, and SaveImageAdvanced to control file naming and destination. Everything runs inside ComfyUI, so you can iterate quickly by adjusting a couple of node values and re-queuing.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm all nodes are present: LoadImage, GLSLShader, PrimitiveInt, ComfySwitchNode, ResolutionSelector, and SaveImageAdvanced.
Load your source image with LoadImage. For best results, crop out borders/watermarks and use a representative frame or region of interest.
Set the number of colors using the PrimitiveInt node (e.g., 5–12 for branding and UI, higher for complex scenes).
Choose swatch layout: set the ComfySwitchNode to Equal for uniform widths or to Weighted to size each swatch by its visual dominance in the image.

Pick your output size in ResolutionSelector (for example, 2048x256 for web, 4096x512 for print) and run the queue. Review the result and adjust the PrimitiveInt or switch mode if needed, then SaveImageAdvanced will write the palette with your chosen filename and path.
suggestedUseCases: Brand audits and style guides: derive a primary/secondary palette from logos, packaging, or campaign imagery.
UI/UX theming: generate starting color tokens from a hero image for design systems and component libraries.
Art direction and mood boards: summarize the color mood of references or film stills into clean swatches.
Photography and grading references: compare dominant tones across scenes or locations.
Dataset and asset QA: quickly spot color biases or inconsistencies in image collections.

faqItems.question: How are the colors chosen?
faqItems.answer: The GLSLShader groups similar pixel colors into a specified number of buckets and estimates how much of the image each bucket represents. It then renders swatches for the top buckets, ordered and sized according to your selected mode (equal or dominance-weighted).

faqItems.question: Equal vs weighted widths: which should I use?
faqItems.answer: Use Equal when you want a balanced, presentation-friendly palette where each color gets the same visual weight. Use Weighted to reflect the image’s true color proportions—this is helpful for analysis, grading references, and dataset QA.

faqItems.question: How many colors should I pick?
faqItems.answer: For branding and UI, 5–8 colors usually give a clean, usable set. For complex scenes or analysis, 10–16 can capture more nuance. Too many colors may introduce near-duplicates; if that happens, lower the count or crop the image to the most relevant region.

faqItems.question: Why do I see unexpected colors or noisy results?
faqItems.answer: Highly compressed, noisy, or patterned images can introduce tiny color fragments. Try using a higher-quality source, cropping busy areas, or reducing the number of colors. Switching to Weighted mode can also minimize the impact of small, insignificant colors.

faqItems.question: Can I control the output size and file naming?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Set exact dimensions in ResolutionSelector to control the palette’s resolution, and configure SaveImageAdvanced for the output directory and filename pattern.

5652fbe7f479.title: Character + Clothing Virtual Try on Studio Photoshoot
5652fbe7f479.description: Upload an image of your character and a flat lay image of your clothing items. Generate 4 fashion editorial photographs of your character in the outfit. Select which image to upscale and add back details.
5652fbe7f479.metaDescription: Virtual try-on for characters: upload a character and flat-lay outfit, generate 4 styled poses, then upscale your favorite to 2048 with consistent details.
5652fbe7f479.extendedDescription:
This workflow builds a fast, reference-guided virtual try‑on pipeline for characters. You provide two images via LoadImage: a clear character image (face and body framing) and a flat‑lay of the clothing. A prompt entered with PrimitiveStringMultiline describes pose, studio lighting, background, and styling cues. OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 then generates a batch of four fashion‑editorial variations and arranges them into a 2×2 contact sheet for quick review. PreviewImage shows the grid, and ImageCompare can be used to examine differences side‑by‑side.

Under the hood, the same references (character and clothing) drive both the initial batch and the upscale path to preserve facial identity and outfit details. A utility node (663da6e9-8b62-4291-a9d6-e4b8fd672197) in this graph is wired to handle the 2×2 grid output and crop it back into four 1K (approx. 1024×1024) tiles. You select one tile with ImageFromBatch by setting batch_index (0–3, starting at top‑left) and feed it into the Upscale Selected Image group. The upscale pass uses OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 again at 2048×2048 while reusing your original references for consistency, then writes results with SaveImage. MarkdownNote and Note nodes in the canvas provide inline reminders and tips.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 is configured (API key/model as required in your setup).
Open the two LoadImage nodes and upload: (1) your character photo (neutral background recommended), and (2) a flat-lay image of the clothing with the garment fully visible.
Edit the PrimitiveStringMultiline prompt to describe pose, camera framing, studio lighting, background (e.g., seamless gray), and any styling notes you want reflected in the shots.

Run the 2x2 Grid Generation group. Inspect the 2×2 grid in PreviewImage and use ImageCompare if you want to A/B details. The tiles are indexed as: top-left = 0, top-right = 1, bottom-left = 2, bottom-right = 3.

In the Upscale Selected Image group, set the ImageFromBatch node’s batch_index to the tile you want to upscale. Run the upscale pass to generate a 2048×2048 refinement that reuses your character and outfit references.
Use SaveImage outputs from both groups to export the 1K tiles and the final 2K selection. If needed, adjust the prompt or references and rerun for new poses.
suggestedUseCases: Lookbook and catalog mockups for original characters or avatars wearing new outfits.
Previsualizing cosplay or wardrobe combinations before a photoshoot.
Social media content creation: quick editorial poses with consistent styling.
Character design iteration: testing silhouettes and fabrics across different studio setups.
Indie fashion previews: showcasing a garment on a consistent character model without a full shoot.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow keep the face and outfit consistent between the grid and the upscale?
faqItems.answer: Both stages use the same character and flat-lay clothing images as references in OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2. The upscale pass reuses those references, so identity and garment details are reinforced rather than regenerated from scratch.

faqItems.question: What input images work best for reliable try-on results?
faqItems.answer: For the character: a clear, well-lit image with the face unobstructed and minimal background clutter. For the garment: a flat-lay on a plain background with the full front of the item visible, not folded, and without heavy occlusions or busy patterns in the backdrop.

faqItems.question: How do I pick which of the four images to upscale?
faqItems.answer: Use the ImageFromBatch node and set batch_index to the tile you want (0=top-left, 1=top-right, 2=bottom-left, 3=bottom-right). The author note reminds that indexing starts at 0.

faqItems.question: Can I change pose, camera, or background without swapping images?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Edit the PrimitiveStringMultiline prompt to specify pose direction (e.g., three-quarter, walking stride), focal length or framing (full body, mid-shot), lighting (softbox, rim light), and background (seamless, colored paper). Re-run the 2×2 Grid Generation group to preview new variations.

58a3f7167dba.title: Minimax H3 Video Restyling
58a3f7167dba.description: Using the open-weights version of Minimax H3, restyle a video's background and lighting using a guided key art image. You can also do a full character swap and voice/language replacement as well. A super powerful workflow for your VFX toolbox!
58a3f7167dba.metaDescription: Restyle video with MiniMax H3 using key art or character swap. Control lighting, palette, and identity; prompt via LLM; preserve or replace audio.
58a3f7167dba.extendedDescription:
This workflow restyles an existing video using the open-weights MiniMax H3 model, guided by a reference “key art” image or a character image. In key art mode, it transfers background, palette, and lighting while preserving the performance; in character swap mode, it targets the subject’s appearance for a full identity change. The core is the MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo node, driven by UNETLoader (MiniMax H3), CLIPLoader (text conditioning), RandomNoise, and a sampler chain built from KSamplerSelect, BasicScheduler, SamplerCustomAdvanced, and BasicGuider. VAELoader and VAEDecode convert generated latents back to frames, and ImageFromBatch lets you QC results mid-run.

ResolutionSelector and VHS_VideoInfo handle the practicalities—frame size, fps, and clip duration (the clip length parameter expects whole seconds). SetNode/GetNode are used as convenient toggles and parameter routers, including the mode switch between key art swap and character swap. LoadImage supplies your guiding key art or character reference, while OpenRouterLLMNode (in the GENERATE PROMPT group) can help draft a shot-specific prompt that CLIPLoader uses for text conditioning. A VOICE OPTIONS branch can keep your original audio or pass it to a voice-replacement path; VAEDecodeAudio decodes the final audio stream for muxing with the new visuals.

The result is a VFX-friendly process for look development and restyling: keep the motion and timing of your source while re-lighting the scene, shifting color mood, replacing backgrounds, or swapping a character—useful for previz, mood boards, and quick creative iterations.
howToUse: Load the workflow and open the SETUP groups. Point the source video input to your clip, then use VHS_VideoInfo to verify fps and duration. Set the clip length parameter in whole seconds and pick your output resolution with ResolutionSelector.

In MODELS, load the open-weights MiniMax H3 in UNETLoader, the matching text encoder in CLIPLoader, and the appropriate VAE in VAELoader. Confirm your sampler path: choose a method in KSamplerSelect, with BasicScheduler, SamplerCustomAdvanced, and BasicGuider connected to MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo.

Import your guide with LoadImage. Use the SetNode/GetNode toggle to choose between key art swap (scene/background + lighting restyle) and character swap (subject identity). Ensure the selected image is well-framed and high quality.

Write a concise shot-aware prompt (camera, lighting, environment, style cues) in the GENERATE PROMPT group. Optionally, use OpenRouterLLMNode to expand your brief into a detailed prompt, then feed it into CLIPLoader. Add a negative prompt if needed (e.g., artifacts to avoid).

Tune strength and consistency via the MODIFY group parameters (PrimitiveFloat and ComfyMathExpression feed key weights such as style/denoise strength, reference influence, and temporal coherence into MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo and the sampler). Lower strength preserves more of the original look; higher strength pushes the restyle further.

Run a short preview range first. Inspect frames with ImageFromBatch to confirm identity, lighting, and texture stability. When satisfied, render the full clip. In VOICE OPTIONS, choose to keep original audio or route to voice/language replacement (VAEDecodeAudio handles final audio decoding).
suggestedUseCases: Look development: quickly test different lighting palettes and art directions on existing footage using a single key art image.
Background and environment restyling for previz or social content while preserving the original performance and timing.
Character swap for concept tests and pitch frames without reshooting, using a clean character reference image.
Localized content: swap style and language/voice for regional variants while keeping the same edit.
Mood boards and dailies: generate consistent restyled passes to align teams on visual targets.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between key art swap and character swap modes?
faqItems.answer: Key art swap emphasizes scene-level changes (background, lighting, color palette) using your key art as guidance while preserving the subject. Character swap targets the subject’s identity and attire to match a character reference. The mode toggle is handled via SetNode/GetNode, which routes the reference conditioning into MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo differently.

faqItems.question: How do I get stable results across frames?
faqItems.answer: Keep your source clip well-lit and steady, use a high-quality guide image, and tune the MODIFY parameters. Lowering denoise/style strength preserves more original structure; increasing temporal/consistency weights (fed by PrimitiveFloat/ComfyMathExpression into MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo and the sampler) reduces flicker. Preview a short segment and adjust before rendering the full clip.

faqItems.question: Which models do I need to load?
faqItems.answer: Load the open-weights MiniMax H3 in UNETLoader, a compatible text encoder in CLIPLoader, and a matching VAE in VAELoader. The sampler path uses KSamplerSelect, BasicScheduler, SamplerCustomAdvanced, and BasicGuider to drive diffusion steps for MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo.

faqItems.question: Do I have to replace the audio?
faqItems.answer: No. In VOICE OPTIONS you can keep the original audio or use the replacement path if configured. VAEDecodeAudio handles the final audio decoding. If you choose replacement, set the language/voice options provided in that group; otherwise, pass through the source audio.

5931e9bdf9db.title: Video Restyle
5931e9bdf9db.description: Use a base video + a stylized reference image to create the stylized video using WAN 2.1 VACE
5931e9bdf9db.metaDescription: Transform videos with style using ComfyUI's Video Restyle workflow. Leverage WAN 2.1 VACE for stunning video style transfers.
5931e9bdf9db.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, titled 'Video Restyle', is designed to transform a base video into a stylized version using a reference image. It leverages the WAN 2.1 VACE model, which excels in video style transfer. The workflow incorporates several custom nodes, such as ComfyUI-WanVideoWrapper and comfyui-depthanythingv2, to preprocess and encode video data efficiently. The process begins with loading a base video and a stylized reference image. The video is then preprocessed using edge detection techniques like CannyEdgePreprocessor or depth estimation via DepthAnything_V2. These preprocessing steps help in extracting essential features from the video frames, which are crucial for the style transfer process.

The workflow is particularly useful due to its flexibility and precision in video restyling. By combining various nodes like WanVideoModelLoader and WanVideoSampler, it allows for detailed control over the video transformation process. Users can experiment with different preprocessing techniques, such as depth versus edge detection, to achieve the desired artistic effect. The integration of the WanVideoVACEEncode node ensures that the final output is a high-quality, stylized video that maintains the original video's dynamics while incorporating the artistic elements from the reference image.
howToUse: Load the 'Video Restyle' workflow in ComfyUI.
Import your base video using the VHS_LoadVideo node.
Load a stylized reference image through the LoadImage node.
Choose a preprocessing method: either connect the CannyEdgePreprocessor or DepthAnything_V2 to the reroute node.
Configure the WanVideoModelLoader and WanVideoSampler nodes for style transfer.
Run the workflow and export the stylized video using the Save Video(Mp4) group.
suggestedUseCases: Creating artistic music videos by applying unique styles to each scene.
Enhancing marketing videos with visually appealing artistic effects.
Transforming home videos into stylized short films.
Developing creative content for social media platforms.
Producing educational videos with engaging visual styles.

faqItems.question: Can I use any video format with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The workflow supports common video formats, but it's recommended to use formats compatible with the VHS_LoadVideo node for best results.

faqItems.question: How do I choose between depth and edge preprocessing?
faqItems.answer: Experiment with both methods; depth is better for preserving 3D structure, while edge detection emphasizes outlines and contours.

faqItems.question: What is the role of the WanVideoVACEEncode node?
faqItems.answer: The WanVideoVACEEncode node encodes the processed video frames into the final stylized video output, ensuring high quality.

faqItems.question: Is it possible to adjust the intensity of the style transfer?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can tweak the settings in WanVideoSampler and other related nodes to control the style intensity.

What sets this technique apart is its ability to maintain high fidelity and coherence in the generated video, preserving the essence and details of the original image while introducing realistic motion. The Wan2.2 model, a successor in the Wan series, is specifically designed to handle complex transformations with enhanced computational efficiency, making it possible to generate high-quality videos from images with unprecedented detail and fluidity.

This workflow is particularly notable for its use of the Wan2.2 Image to Video subgraph, a specialized node that encapsulates the sophisticated processes involved in the transformation. This subgraph is a distilled version of the comprehensive Wan2.2 workflow, optimized for performance and ease of use. Users benefit from a streamlined process that requires minimal input while delivering maximum output quality. The integration of this advanced model into the ComfyUI ecosystem not only simplifies the video generation process but also expands the creative possibilities for artists, filmmakers, and content creators looking to explore new dimensions of visual storytelling.

Developing educational content where static diagrams are converted into instructional videos.
Producing animated social media posts from still graphics to increase viewer interaction.

faqItems.question: What makes the Wan2.2 model suitable for image to video transformation?
faqItems.answer: The Wan2.2 model is designed to handle complex image transformations with high fidelity, ensuring that the resulting video maintains the quality and detail of the original image.

faqItems.question: What are the system requirements for running this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for commercial projects?

faqItems.question: How does the Wan2.2 subgraph improve the workflow process?
