5ae006b13a36.title: Ideogram v4: Text to Image (API)
5ae006b13a36.description: Input a text prompt in structured JSON format. Generate a high-quality image with precise layout control, text rendering, and color palette support.
5ae006b13a36.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use Ideogram v4 with a structured JSON prompt for precise layout, crisp in-image text, and brand-safe color palettes. Save high-quality results.
5ae006b13a36.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates how to drive Ideogram v4 via a structured JSON prompt to get clean text rendering, consistent brand colors, and reliable layout control. Instead of a single free-form sentence, you build a compact JSON object that describes the scene, in-image text, a color palette, and per-object bounding boxes. That JSON is fed into the IdeogramV4 partner API node, which returns a high-quality image that adheres to your specified layout as closely as the model allows. The output flows directly to SaveImage.

To make authoring easier, the JSON Prompt Builder group (enable it by selecting the group and pressing Ctrl+B) includes a MarkdownNote with a schema/template and an optional GeminiNode that can transform a plain brief into a well-formed JSON prompt. You can preview the structured prompt with PreviewAny before sending it to IdeogramV4, iterate on bounding boxes or palette values, and then render the final image. This approach is ideal when you need reliable in-image text, brand-safe palettes, and object placement that a natural-language prompt alone struggles to achieve.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the IdeogramV4 node is configured (API access, model selection, and any required credentials per your setup).
Enable the JSON Prompt Builder group (select it and press Ctrl+B). Open the MarkdownNote to copy the provided JSON template and schema tips.
Author your structured JSON: define the scene prompt, optional palette (hex colors), and layout items (e.g., text or objects) with bounding boxes. Use PreviewAny to quickly inspect the JSON.
Optional: Use the GeminiNode to draft or refine the JSON from a plain-language brief, then review and edit the output to match the template in the MarkdownNote.
Paste the final JSON into the IdeogramV4 node’s prompt field and execute the node (or the whole graph). Watch the image preview in ComfyUI; adjust your JSON and re-run as needed.
When satisfied, SaveImage will write the rendered result to disk. Iterate on bounding boxes, text content, and palette to tighten alignment and style.
suggestedUseCases: Poster and flyer concepts with headline/subhead text locked into specific regions.
Product mockups that combine brand-safe colors, hero imagery, and on-image copy.
Social graphics or ads where logo, CTA, and legal text must appear in fixed boxes.
Infographics or UI-themed visuals that benefit from structured regions and labels.
Storyboards or pitch frames with consistent layout and readable in-frame captions.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use structured JSON, or can I just type a normal prompt?
faqItems.answer: You can enter plain natural language directly into the IdeogramV4 node. However, this workflow is optimized for a structured JSON prompt, which gives much stronger control over in-image text, color palette, and object placement via bounding boxes.

faqItems.question: What does the JSON look like?
faqItems.answer: Use the template in the MarkdownNote as your source of truth. A minimal example might include: prompt (overall description), palette (array of hex colors), and layout items with type, text/subject, and a bbox [x, y, w, h] in normalized 0–1 coordinates. Example (keys may vary by template): { "prompt": "retro poster of a mountain sunrise", "palette": ["#0F0F0F", "#FF6A00", "#FFD54D"], "layout": { "items": [ {"type": "text", "text": "SUMMER FEST", "bbox": [0.1, 0.05, 0.8, 0.2]}, {"type": "image", "subject": "mountain sunrise", "bbox": [0.1, 0.28, 0.8, 0.55]} ] } }

faqItems.question: My text is cropped or misaligned. How can I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Increase padding in the text item’s bounding box, reduce the text length, and avoid overlapping boxes. Keep bbox values within 0–1, ensure items don’t collide, and iterate—small bbox adjustments often resolve clipping and alignment issues.

faqItems.question: How do I keep brand colors consistent?
faqItems.answer: Define a concise palette array of your brand hex colors in the JSON. Limit it to a few key colors to nudge the model strongly. If results drift, simplify the palette, reduce conflicting style cues, and re-run. The model aims to respect your palette while balancing overall image quality.

5b8156052b93.title: Recraft: Style Control Image Generation
5b8156052b93.description: Control style with visual examples, align positioning, and fine-tune objects. Store and share styles for perfect brand consistency.
5b8156052b93.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate on-brand images with Recraft styles, color control, and optional SVG export using RecraftTextToImage and vectorization nodes.
5b8156052b93.extendedDescription:
This workflow demonstrates style-controlled image generation with Recraft inside ComfyUI. It centers on RecraftTextToImageNode for raster image synthesis and uses dedicated style selector nodes—RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster, RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration, and RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage—to quickly switch aesthetics without rewriting prompts. RecraftColorRGB lets you lock brand hues, while RecraftControls aggregates global parameters that the generator uses to keep outputs consistent. Results are saved via SaveImage, and MarkdownNote provides in-graph guidance.

For brand-ready deliverables, the optional Convert into SVG (need credits) group routes raster outputs through RecraftVectorizeImageNode and exports clean vectors using SaveSVGNode. This is especially useful for logos and flat graphics that need to scale. Note: in these Recraft nodes, the seed value only determines whether the node should re-run; it does not make results deterministic. To explore new variations, change the seed to trigger a fresh run or refine the style and color inputs.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm Recraft API access per the Author Notes (local/https context and connectivity). If the partner nodes show connection errors, resolve those before proceeding.
Choose a style: connect exactly one of RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster, RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration, or RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage to the style input used by RecraftTextToImageNode.
Set color constraints: edit RecraftColorRGB to your brand color (hex/RGB) and ensure it is wired into the controls path (via RecraftControls) that feeds RecraftTextToImageNode.

Enter your prompt in RecraftTextToImageNode. Run the graph to generate the first result. To request a new variation without changing your setup, change the seed value to force the node to re-run (seed does not control the visual result).

Save your raster output with SaveImage. For vectors, enable the Convert into SVG group: route the generated image into RecraftVectorizeImageNode and then into SaveSVGNode to export an .svg (this may require credits as noted).
Iterate for consistency: switch between style nodes for different looks, fine-tune RecraftControls to adjust behavior, and keep RecraftColorRGB fixed to enforce brand colors across a batch.
suggestedUseCases: Logo and icon exploration with quick style switching and optional SVG export for scalable assets.
Brand illustration systems: maintain consistent hues and aesthetics across multiple scenes.
Social and ad creatives where color and style consistency matter across formats.
Product or feature mockups rendered in a realistic style for presentations and landing pages.
Internal concept boards: rapidly compare LogoRaster vs. DigitalIllustration vs. RealisticImage looks from the same prompt.

faqItems.question: What is the difference between the Recraft style nodes?
faqItems.answer: Each style node configures the generator for a distinct aesthetic. RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster suits flat, logo-like marks; RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration targets stylized drawings and clean illustrations; RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage aims for photographic realism. Swap the node to change the overall look without rewriting your prompt.

faqItems.question: How do I enforce brand colors?
faqItems.answer: Use RecraftColorRGB to set your desired color and keep it connected in the controls path (via RecraftControls) that feeds RecraftTextToImageNode. This constrains the palette around your specified hue for better brand consistency. For multi-color palettes, iterate with different RecraftColorRGB settings or vectorize and adjust colors downstream.

faqItems.question: Why doesn’t the same seed reproduce the same image?
faqItems.answer: In this workflow the seed is only used to determine whether a node should re-run; it does not make the result deterministic. To explore new variations, change the seed to force a fresh run, or adjust your prompt, style node, and color settings to guide the output.

faqItems.question: How do I get vector (SVG) output and when do I need credits?
faqItems.answer: Enable the Convert into SVG group: send your raster result into RecraftVectorizeImageNode and then into SaveSVGNode to write an .svg file. Vectorization quality is best on simple, high-contrast graphics (e.g., logos). As noted in the workflow group, this step may require Recraft credits. For API details, see the partner-node docs: https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/partner-nodes/overview and the Recraft tutorial: https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/partner-nodes/recraft/recraft-text-to-image.

5b94a8f404fa.title: Seamless Video Transitions - LTX 2.3 FLW LoRA
5b94a8f404fa.description: Upload two input videos and generate a seamless transition between the two shots.
5b94a8f404fa.metaDescription: Create seamless transitions between two videos in ComfyUI using LTX 2.3 FLW LoRA. Load videos, set the transition window, and export a smooth merged clip.
5b94a8f404fa.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow creates a seamless, learned transition between two input clips using an LTX 2.3 FLW LoRA. You feed one video into each LoadVideo node, and a dedicated transition node (UUID: 63482e7d-23c9-4396-a7a2-cd4ca2316eac) synthesizes a smooth handoff from the end of the first shot to the start of the second. The SaveVideo node then assembles the processed frames into a single output clip. A built-in MarkdownNote provides an at-a-glance guide to recommended settings and practical tips.

Technically, the workflow performs diffusion-based video-to-video generation guided by the LTX 2.3 FLW LoRA to harmonize color, texture, and motion across the cut. For temporal consistency, inference runs over the full frame range (not just the transition window). That design keeps the look stable across the entire sequence but also means longer clips and higher resolutions will increase runtime and VRAM use. You’ll typically set the in/out ranges for each source clip, define a transition length, and adjust the LoRA influence/strength and seed in the transition node. SaveVideo controls the output frame rate and file name for export.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the LTX 2.3 FLW LoRA transition node (UUID: 63482e7d-23c9-4396-a7a2-cd4ca2316eac) loads without errors. Review the embedded MarkdownNote for quick tips.

Use the two LoadVideo nodes to import your source clips (A and B). If possible, match resolution and FPS between the clips, and trim or set frame ranges so the key visual moments you want to bridge are near the cut.

In the transition node, set the start/end frames for the handoff, choose a transition duration (in frames), and adjust the LoRA influence/strength and seed. Start with a moderate strength and a longer transition window if your shots differ a lot.
Configure the SaveVideo node (e.g., output filename and FPS). Keep resolution and FPS consistent with your inputs to minimize artifacts and speed up generation.
Run the workflow. Review the output for flicker or warping at the handoff; if needed, tweak transition length and LoRA strength, or move the cut to frames with more shared structure, then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Softening hard cuts in edits to create fluid, stylized transitions between contrasting scenes.
Bridging shots with different lighting or framing by harmonizing color and texture across the handoff.
Smoothing jump cuts in talking-head or product footage by inserting a learned transition segment.
Creating dynamic, eye-catching scene changes for reels, shorts, and social content.
Linking still or minimally moving shots with a subtle morph-like motion for montage sequences.

faqItems.question: Why does the workflow process every frame if I only need the transition?
faqItems.answer: To maintain temporal consistency. Running inference across the full frame range helps keep the look stable and reduces popping before and after the handoff. If you need faster runs, trim your inputs to just the necessary ranges, reduce resolution/FPS, or shorten the clips.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce artifacts like flicker or warping at the transition?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing the transition duration, lowering the LoRA influence/strength, and locking the seed for repeatable results. Place the cut around frames with similar composition (camera angle, subject size), and ensure both inputs share the same resolution and FPS.

faqItems.question: What GPU/VRAM do I need?
faqItems.answer: Requirements scale with resolution, clip length, and transition duration. Start with short clips at a modest resolution to gauge performance. Longer sequences or HD+ resolutions benefit from GPUs with more VRAM; if you hit limits, downscale or shorten the frame ranges.

faqItems.question: Does the output include audio?
faqItems.answer: The SaveVideo node outputs a silent video. If you need audio, export the video and reattach audio from one of the source clips (or a music track) in your video editor.

5cd417e793b8.title: LTX 2.3 Audio-Reactive LoRA
5cd417e793b8.description: Create audio-reactive videos with LTX 2.3 and the Audio-Reactive LoRA.
5cd417e793b8.metaDescription: Turn a single image into an audio‑reactive video with LTX 2.3 and an Audio‑Reactive LoRA. Load image + audio, auto‑prompt with Gemini, preview, and export.
5cd417e793b8.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into an audio‑reactive video using the LTX‑Video 2.3 model enhanced with the Audio‑Reactive LoRA. You provide one image via LoadImage and an audio track via LoadAudio; a GeminiNode in the Create Audio‑Reactive LoRA Prompt group helps craft a clean, descriptive text prompt from your idea (and optionally your image context). That prompt, together with the image and audio, flows into the LTX 2.3 video generator node (dacae91a-7342-43be-a654-227b303c33bc), where the Audio‑Reactive LoRA modulates motion and visual rhythm in response to the soundtrack. You can preview output with PreviewAny and export the final result with SaveVideo.

Technically, the workflow applies the Audio‑Reactive LoRA from https://huggingface.co/100percentrobot/LTX-2.3-Audio-Reactive-LORA at inference time on top of LTX 2.3. The LoRA strength parameter controls how strongly the audio‑driven behavior influences the video: use 1.0–2.0 overall, with 1.4+ for more pronounced reactivity. This design is practical for fast, beat‑aware animations of posters, album art, and social posts: you focus on a concise prompt and good source media, while the LTX node handles frame synthesis and timing, and SaveVideo writes a ready‑to‑share clip.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and expand the groups: Load Image, Load Audio, Create Audio‑Reactive LoRA Prompt, and LTX 2.3 Audio‑Reactive LoRA.
In Load Image, select a single, high‑quality PNG/JPG. Choose an aspect ratio that matches your target output to avoid cropping.
In Load Audio, load your soundtrack (e.g., WAV/MP3). If the track is long, plan a segment length that fits your desired video duration.

In Create Audio‑Reactive LoRA Prompt, enter a brief style/subject description in the GeminiNode to auto‑generate a clean prompt. If you prefer, bypass Gemini and feed a manual text prompt directly into the LTX 2.3 node’s prompt input.

In the LTX 2.3 Audio‑Reactive LoRA group, set the LoRA strength between 1.0 and 2.0 (start at 1.4 for stronger effects). Optionally set seed, duration/frame count, and any resolution/FPS fields to suit your output and audio length.
Queue/Run the workflow. Use PreviewAny to check motion and timing, then render the full sequence and save the final clip with SaveVideo.
suggestedUseCases: Music‑driven cover art or poster animations for social posts and reels
Album or single teasers that pulse and morph with the beat
Animated title cards for YouTube, Twitch, or podcast intros
Looping VJ backdrops that respond to ambient tracks
Motion‑enhanced slides for event screens or installations

faqItems.question: What LoRA strength should I use?
faqItems.answer: Use 1.0–2.0 overall. Start at 1.4 for a stronger, more noticeable audio‑reactive effect and lower it if the motion feels too intense or stylization overrides the source image.

faqItems.question: Do I need the GeminiNode to write prompts?
faqItems.answer: No. The GeminiNode helps auto‑format prompts, but you can disable/bypass it and connect a manual text prompt directly to the LTX 2.3 node’s prompt input if you prefer full control.

faqItems.question: How precise is the audio sync?
faqItems.answer: The Audio‑Reactive LoRA drives motion based on the audio’s energy/rhythm. It produces convincing beat‑aware visuals, but it’s not frame‑accurate editing. For tight cuts, adjust your audio segment and video duration/frame count and fine‑tune LoRA strength.

faqItems.question: Which formats are supported?
faqItems.answer: LoadImage typically accepts PNG/JPG and LoadAudio commonly supports WAV/MP3. SaveVideo outputs a standard video file (commonly MP4). If a format fails, convert your media to these common types.

5cef286d4c51.metaDescription: Transform a single image into an animated sprite sheet for games or animations using ComfyUI's advanced AI workflow.

suggestedUseCases: Creating animated character sprites for video games.

Generating prototype animations for concept art.
Designing interactive educational content with animated visuals.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the number of frames in the animation?

faqItems.question: Is it possible to remove the background from the animated sprite sheet?

faqItems.question: What formats can the final sprite sheet be saved in?

5d0cbc370579.title: AIrt MAchIne (API version)
5d0cbc370579.description: Upload an image to generate a unique, looping AI video. The workflow uses an LLM to create prompts, employs Kling3.0 for video generation, and stitches the clips into a seamless final loop.
5d0cbc370579.metaDescription: Transform images into looping AI videos using AIrt MAchIne with LLM prompts and Kling 3.0 for seamless video generation.
5d0cbc370579.extendedDescription: The AIrt MAchIne workflow is designed to transform a static image into a dynamic, looping AI-generated video. This innovative process begins with an image upload, which serves as the foundation for generating a unique video sequence. The workflow leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to create prompts that guide the video generation process, ensuring each output is distinct and creative. The Kling 3.0 model is central to video creation, providing advanced capabilities for generating high-quality, seamless video clips. These clips are then stitched together to form a continuous loop, offering a visually engaging experience. The workflow utilizes a combination of nodes, including ImageResizeKJv2 for resizing images, GeminiNode for integrating Google's Gemini model, and VHS_VideoCombine for merging video components. This setup allows users to produce professional-quality videos with minimal input, making it a valuable tool for content creators and marketers looking to enhance their visual media with AI-driven creativity.
howToUse: Load the AIrt MAchIne workflow in ComfyUI.
Upload your desired image using the LoadImage node.
Run the workflow to initiate prompt generation and video creation.
Review the preview of the generated video loop using the PreviewImage node.
Save the final video using the SaveVideo node, or bypass save groups for direct output.
suggestedUseCases: Create engaging social media content by transforming static images into dynamic video loops.
Enhance marketing campaigns with unique AI-generated videos that capture audience attention.

5fa9b44388cb.title: Hunyuan Video Text to Video
5fa9b44388cb.description: Generate videos from text prompts using Hunyuan model.
5fa9b44388cb.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate text-to-video with Tencent Hunyuan in ComfyUI using SD3-style sampling, tiled VAE decode, and FluxGuidance for clean, coherent motion.
5fa9b44388cb.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns short text prompts into coherent, multi‑frame videos using Tencent’s Hunyuan Video model. It starts by loading the model stack in Step1 - Load models: DualCLIPLoader provides the text encoders, CLIPTextEncode converts your positive and negative prompts into embeddings, and UNETLoader brings in the Hunyuan Video UNet weights. ModelSamplingSD3 configures the sampler for Hunyuan’s SD3‑style noise schedule, while FluxGuidance applies classifier‑free guidance during denoising. Step2 - Video size uses EmptyHunyuanLatentVideo to define width, height, frame count/fps, and duration, and RandomNoise seeds the initial latent video. The Custom sampler section (SamplerCustomAdvanced with KSamplerSelect and BasicScheduler) then iteratively denoises the video latents into a structured animation.

After sampling, the pipeline decodes latents back to RGB frames using VAELoader with VAEDecodeTiled (recommended by default for most GPUs) or VAEDecode, then assembles and writes the result via CreateVideo and SaveVideo. The workflow is designed for practical iteration: adjust prompt wording in Step3 - Prompt, tweak steps and guidance for fidelity and motion, and manage memory with VAEDecodeTiled and fp8 weight_dtype in UNETLoader when needed. For details and tips specific to Hunyuan Video, see the linked documentation.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open Step1 - Load models. In UNETLoader, select the Hunyuan Video checkpoint. In VAELoader, choose the matching VAE. If VRAM is tight, set UNETLoader weight_dtype to fp8 (if your hardware supports it).

Go to Step2 - Video size. In EmptyHunyuanLatentVideo, set width and height (use multiples of 16), fps, and either frames or seconds to define the clip length. Set a seed in RandomNoise for reproducibility or leave it random for variety.

Open Step3 - Prompt. Enter a clear positive prompt in CLIPTextEncode (e.g., the provided anime example) and add a concise negative prompt to avoid unwanted elements (e.g., blurry, low detail, jitter).

In Custom sampler, pick a sampler in KSamplerSelect (start with dpmpp_2m or euler) and set steps in BasicScheduler (e.g., 20–35). Use FluxGuidance to adjust guidance scale (CFG); higher values follow the prompt more strongly but can introduce artifacts.

Use VAEDecodeTiled for decoding by default. If you encounter out‑of‑memory errors, lower tile_size and increase overlap slightly to hide seams. Only switch to VAEDecode if you have ample VRAM and need maximum speed.

Queue the workflow. Inspect the frames and motion. If motion is weak, increase steps or modestly raise guidance; if flicker appears, reduce guidance or steps. When satisfied, CreateVideo and SaveVideo will export the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Concept animations for characters, products, or environments from quick text prompts
Stylized social clips (e.g., anime loops, abstract visuals) for shorts and stories
Previsualization for motion and framing before commissioning full production
Background ambience loops for streams, events, or digital signage
Education and research demos illustrating text‑conditioned motion synthesis

faqItems.question: I’m running out of VRAM. How can I make this workflow lighter?
faqItems.answer: Use VAEDecodeTiled (default) and reduce tile_size while increasing overlap slightly to hide seams. In UNETLoader, choose fp8 weight_dtype if supported by your GPU. Lower resolution, shorten duration (fewer frames), or reduce steps in BasicScheduler.

faqItems.question: What settings give stable, coherent motion?
faqItems.answer: Keep width/height as multiples of 16 and start with 20–35 steps. Set a fixed seed in RandomNoise. Use FluxGuidance with a moderate guidance scale; too high can cause flicker, too low weakens prompt adherence. Refine prompts to be specific but not overly long.

faqItems.question: When should I use VAEDecode vs. VAEDecodeTiled?
faqItems.answer: Use VAEDecodeTiled by default—it’s memory‑efficient and recommended for most GPUs. Switch to VAEDecode only if you have sufficient VRAM and want faster decoding without tiling. If you see seams with tiled decode, increase overlap or lower tile_size.

faqItems.question: Which sampler and schedule should I choose?
faqItems.answer: Keep ModelSamplingSD3 as provided for Hunyuan. Start with dpmpp_2m or euler in KSamplerSelect and 20–35 steps in BasicScheduler. If details smear, try more steps; if results are noisy, reduce steps or lower guidance in FluxGuidance.

5fd7dc1f9db5.title: SDPose-OOD: Video to Pose Map
5fd7dc1f9db5.description: Upload a video to extract pose keypoints and generate a pose map. The workflow supports multiple person detection and uses an enhanced SDPose model for accurate whole-body feature extraction.
5fd7dc1f9db5.metaDescription: Extract multi-person whole-body pose maps from video with SDPose-OOD in ComfyUI, then export a pose-map video aligned to the original timing.
5fd7dc1f9db5.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial walks you through SDPose-OOD: Video to Pose Map — a workflow that converts any input video into a clean pose map sequence. The pipeline starts with LoadVideo to decode frames, runs each frame through the SDPose-OOD pose extractor (backed by the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint) to detect whole-body keypoints, and then assembles the pose frames into a final clip with CreateVideo and SaveVideo. The SDPose-OOD node (type ID 01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604) supports multi-person detection and outputs a rendered pose map per frame, covering body, hands, and face landmarks.

Technically, the SDPose-OOD model estimates 2D keypoints for every visible person in each frame, then the node renders those landmarks as a pose map image (skeleton/lines and joints) that’s consistent across the sequence. By keeping the original frame rate and dimensions from LoadVideo, CreateVideo can produce a pose video that aligns one-to-one with the source timing, making it ideal as conditioning for downstream generation (e.g., pose-guided image/video synthesis) or for motion analysis and pre-visualization. SaveVideo finalizes the result to your chosen location and codec.
howToUse: Download the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint and place it in ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/.
Open the SDPose-OOD: Video to Pose Map workflow in ComfyUI. In LoadVideo, select your source video; confirm the frame rate and resolution detected are as expected.

In the SDPose-OOD (WholeBody) node (type 01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604), select the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors model. Optionally adjust detection settings such as enabling multi-person and setting a reasonable confidence threshold.

Preview a few frames by running the graph to ensure poses are detected cleanly for all subjects. If detection is unstable, try a lower input resolution for speed or raise the confidence threshold for fewer false positives.
Connect the SDPose-OOD output to CreateVideo, pass through the frame rate from LoadVideo, and set your desired output size (usually matching the input).
Use SaveVideo to choose an output filename and format (e.g., MP4). Execute the workflow to generate and save the pose-map video.
suggestedUseCases: Pose conditioning for image/video generation (e.g., guiding a diffusion model with pose maps for consistent motion).
Pre-visualization for animation and motion studies, capturing full body, hand, and face landmarks.
Privacy-preserving motion sharing by replacing footage with anonymized pose skeletons.
Dataset creation for action recognition or pose-based analytics, exporting synchronized pose-map clips.
Rotoscoping and motion reference extraction for VFX and choreography planning.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow support multiple people in the same frame?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The SDPose-OOD node supports multi-person detection and will render pose maps for all detected subjects per frame. For crowded scenes, consider raising the confidence threshold to reduce false positives.

faqItems.question: Which model file do I need and where should it go?
faqItems.answer: Use sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors. Place it in ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/. Then select it in the SDPose-OOD node before running the workflow.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the output aligned with the source video?
faqItems.answer: Pass the frame rate from LoadVideo into CreateVideo, and keep the output resolution consistent with the input. This preserves one-to-one timing and sizing for downstream use.

faqItems.question: What can I do if detection is jittery or misses hands/face?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing the input resolution for clearer details, raise the detection confidence to reduce noise, and ensure good lighting and contrast in the source. For performance-constrained GPUs, balance resolution and frame skip to maintain stability.

603b2d01feb0.title: Comfy for Advertising - B-Roll Creation
603b2d01feb0.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow to create ad-ready product B-roll via text prompt, reference images, or light video edits using ByteDance2 text-to-video and reference nodes.
603b2d01feb0.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds polished product B‑roll shots for ads using three practical paths: prompt-only generation, reference-guided inserts, and light video edits. At its core, ByteDance2TextToVideoNode synthesizes short clips from your text prompt, while ByteDance2ReferenceNode lets you anchor style and object identity with one or more images (for example, a product packshot and a scene still). LoadImage and LoadVideo nodes bring your assets into the graph, PrimitiveNode supplies key parameters (resolution, frame count, FPS, seed), Video Slice isolates a target segment from an input clip, and SaveVideo writes the final result. MarkdownNote inside the workflow documents the intended usage and includes example prompts.

Method 1 (Prompt Only) is the fastest way to create a fresh B‑roll shot: write a descriptive prompt (e.g., the provided smartphone-in-forest orbit example), set frames/FPS/size via PrimitiveNode, and render with ByteDance2TextToVideoNode. Method 2 (Reference Images) adds control: feed a product image and a scene still into ByteDance2ReferenceNode to match lighting, color, and composition before generation, producing an insert shot that blends into an existing edit. Method 3 (Video Edit) is for subtle replacements: use LoadVideo and Video Slice to define a segment you want to enhance, mirror its timing and dimensions with PrimitiveNode, guide generation with prompt and references, then export with SaveVideo for drop‑in replacement in your NLE.

Because the key parameters are explicit, it’s easy to keep outputs consistent: lock the seed for reproducibility, match FPS and resolution to your timeline, and keep clip lengths short (3–5 seconds) for sharper detail and steadier motion. The reference path is especially effective for maintaining product identity and scene continuity while still exploring creative camera moves or lighting within your prompt.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the MarkdownNote for an overview of the three methods.
Set global parameters via PrimitiveNode: resolution (width/height), number of frames (duration), FPS, and seed. Match these to your target edit whenever possible.

Method 1 – Prompt Only: Open ByteDance2TextToVideoNode, enter your descriptive prompt (e.g., the smartphone forest orbit), confirm frames/FPS/size from PrimitiveNode are connected, then queue and render.

Method 2 – Reference Images: Use LoadImage to bring in a product reference and, optionally, a scene still. Connect them to ByteDance2ReferenceNode, route that into ByteDance2TextToVideoNode along with your prompt, adjust reference strength if exposed, then render.

Method 3 – Video Edit: Import your source clip with LoadVideo and set an in/out range using Video Slice to identify the segment you’ll replace. Mirror the segment’s resolution/FPS/duration in PrimitiveNode, guide generation with prompt and ByteDance2ReferenceNode (using a product still and/or a frame from the clip), then render.
Preview the result and export with SaveVideo. If you’re replacing part of an existing edit, ensure FPS, duration, and aspect ratio match so the shot drops in cleanly.
suggestedUseCases: Create clean product insert shots that match an existing scene’s look and lighting.
Generate on-brand B‑roll for social ads and landing pages from a single prompt.
Replace a problematic or missing pickup shot in a commercial while preserving continuity.
Produce multiple stylistic variations of the same product shot by swapping references or seeds.
Quickly mock up creative directions (camera move, environment, mood) for client reviews.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between the three methods?
faqItems.answer: Method 1 generates a clip purely from your prompt (fastest, most flexible). Method 2 adds product/scene control by conditioning with reference images for better continuity. Method 3 times your output to a selected portion of an existing video so you can replace or enhance that segment in post.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the product consistent across variations?
faqItems.answer: Use Method 2 and feed a high-quality, front-facing product image into ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Keep resolution, FPS, and seed fixed in PrimitiveNode, and reuse the same scene still to maintain lighting and composition. Change only one variable (prompt or seed) at a time.

faqItems.question: What settings work best for ad B‑roll?
faqItems.answer: Keep clips short (3–5 seconds) at 24–30 FPS for smoother motion and better detail. Match your timeline’s resolution (e.g., 1080p or 4K) in PrimitiveNode. If motion looks jittery, reduce scene complexity in the prompt or slightly increase the frame count for the same duration.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure the generated clip fits into my existing edit?
faqItems.answer: In Method 3, use Video Slice to mark the exact segment you’ll replace. Copy its resolution, FPS, and duration into PrimitiveNode, and render your new shot with those same values. Export via SaveVideo and drop it into your NLE to replace the original segment.

60e1839cbb34.title: Branded Comfy Thumbnail
60e1839cbb34.description: Generate Thumbnails with your brand guidelines as references.
60e1839cbb34.metaDescription: A ComfyUI workflow to extract video frames and compose 2-up or 4-up branded YouTube thumbnails using your logo and brand references.
60e1839cbb34.extendedDescription:
Branded Comfy Thumbnail is a frame-selection and composition workflow that turns moments from your video into on-brand YouTube thumbnails. It centers on a simple pipeline: LoadVideo ingests your source clip, GetVideoComponents exposes frame data, and ImageFromBatch lets you pick exact frames by index. Those selected frames are grouped with BatchImagesNode and then composited in a grid by a custom Merge Images node (shown in the graph with the ID 2f633b06-929a-4f4c-afff-ffea89d93a76). Brand references such as a logo, color swatches, or a background plate are brought in with LoadImage. You can review choices at each step with PreviewImage and export the final design with SaveImage.

What makes this workflow practical is its focus on speed and control for real-world thumbnail creation—no diffusion model required. The YouTube Thumbnail Generator group provides a clean 2-up or 4-up layout toggle (per the author note: switch off for 2 images, on for 4 images), so you can quickly compare options or output a final composite. A GeminiNanoBanana2 utility node is included to assist with on-brand text ideas or file naming guidance; it does not render text onto the image in this version. MarkdownNote blocks are sprinkled in to document settings and remind you of best practices while you work.
howToUse: Open the workflow and review the groups: Brand Guidelines, Load Video, Select Frames, and YouTube Thumbnail Generator. Read any MarkdownNote hints on the canvas.
In Brand Guidelines, use LoadImage to bring in your logo, brand color board, or background plate. Keep these images in your project folder for consistent reuse.
In Load Video, point LoadVideo to your source clip. Use GetVideoComponents to inspect frame count and fps, then preview a few frames with PreviewImage to gauge content.
In Select Frames, use ImageFromBatch (or multiple instances) to pull specific frames by index. Tip: index ≈ seconds × fps. Collect your chosen 2 or 4 frames with BatchImagesNode.

In YouTube Thumbnail Generator, set the Merge Images toggle per the author note: switch off for 2 images, switch on for 4 images. Feed in your selected frames (and any brand plate/logo inputs if provided), then check the result with PreviewImage.

Once satisfied, use SaveImage to export. Iterate by adjusting frame indices or swapping brand assets until you have a strong, on-brand thumbnail at your target aspect ratio (commonly 1280×720 for YouTube).
suggestedUseCases: Create fast, on-brand YouTube thumbnails from talking-head or screencast videos.
Produce consistent cover images for podcast episodes or interview series.
Generate lesson and module thumbnails for online courses and tutorials.
Design recap/announcement graphics for webinars and live streams.
Batch-select strong frames for A/B testing thumbnail variants.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow generate images from text or a model prompt?
faqItems.answer: No. It composes thumbnails from your existing video frames and brand images. There is no diffusion or generative image model in this graph; the focus is selection and layout.

faqItems.question: How do I choose an exact moment from the video?
faqItems.answer: Use GetVideoComponents to note the fps, then set ImageFromBatch index ≈ desired_seconds × fps. Add multiple ImageFromBatch nodes (with different indices) to capture several candidate frames.

faqItems.question: How do I switch between 2-up and 4-up layouts?
faqItems.answer: Use the Merge Images node’s toggle noted by the author: switch off for 2 images, on for 4 images. Make sure you supply the correct number of inputs to match the selected layout.

faqItems.question: What is the GeminiNanoBanana2 node doing here?
faqItems.answer: It’s an auxiliary helper for generating on-brand caption ideas or keywords you can use in titles, descriptions, or filenames. It does not overlay text onto the thumbnail in this version.

615266189e02.title: LTX-2.5 (Pro): Image to Video
615266189e02.description: Generate video from a single image using LTX-2.5's fast distilled model, delivering cinematic multi-shot sequences with consistent characters, lighting, and style across cuts. The workflow outputs a video file with native multishot support and automatic duration prediction. Ideal for rapid storyboarding, social media content creation, and pre-visualization in commercial production pipelines.
615266189e02.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Turn one image into a cinematic multi-shot video with LTX-2.5. Native multishot, auto duration, and consistent style across cuts.
615266189e02.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single reference image into a cinematic, multi-shot video using the LTX-2.5 fast distilled model. It links three nodes end-to-end: LoadImage brings your source still into the graph, LtxApi25ImageToVideo sends that image to the LTX-2.5 API for motion synthesis and shot generation, and SaveVideo writes the returned clip to disk. Because LTX-2.5 supports native multishot generation and automatic duration prediction, the result feels like a short edited sequence rather than a single continuous pan or zoom.

Technically, the LtxApi25ImageToVideo node conditions all shots on the same input frame, which helps maintain character, lighting, and style consistency across cuts. The node handles request/response with the remote service, queues generation, and outputs a ready-to-save video. SaveVideo then encodes the result at your chosen filename and frame rate. This makes the workflow ideal for rapid storyboarding, social posts, and pre-visualization: drop in one clean reference image, let the API infer pacing and camera moves, and export a cohesive multi-shot clip in minutes.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the three core nodes: LoadImage -> LtxApi25ImageToVideo -> SaveVideo.
In LoadImage, select a clean, well-lit source image that clearly shows your subject and overall scene style. A 16:9 composition works well for cinematic results.

Open LtxApi25ImageToVideo and add your API credentials if required. Configure generation options as exposed by the node (e.g., enable native multishot, keep automatic duration on, or set a target duration if you prefer manual control).

Optionally refine settings that affect pacing and look if available in your template (such as number of shots, motion intensity, aspect, or repeatability controls). Keep defaults for a fast first pass.
Run the workflow. The node will upload your image and settings, generate a multi-shot sequence via the LTX-2.5 model, and return a video clip.
In SaveVideo, choose the output path, filename, and frame rate. Execute to write the final video file to disk, then review and iterate on the input image or node settings as needed.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid storyboarding: visualize coverage and pacing from a single concept frame.
Social media teasers or reels that need consistent character and style across quick cuts.
Pre-visualization for ads or product spots using one hero image to explore camera moves.
Look development: test lighting, color, and motion language before a full production.
Mood films or pitch videos generated swiftly from key art.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key and is processing local?
faqItems.answer: LtxApi25ImageToVideo calls a remote service; most deployments require an API key. Your source image and parameters are sent to the provider for generation. Check the node’s credentials field and the provider’s documentation and terms before use.

faqItems.question: Can I control duration and the number of shots?
faqItems.answer: The node supports native multishot and automatic duration prediction. If your template exposes overrides, you can set a target duration and/or shot count; otherwise, leave auto duration enabled for best pacing.

faqItems.question: What image works best as input?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, high-quality image with clear subject separation and coherent lighting. Keep faces unobstructed, avoid heavy motion blur, and compose for the aspect ratio you plan to export (16:9 is a solid default).

faqItems.question: How does the workflow keep characters and style consistent across cuts?
faqItems.answer: All shots are conditioned on the same input image inside the LTX-2.5 model via the LtxApi25ImageToVideo node. This shared conditioning helps preserve character identity, lighting, and overall style from shot to shot.

62cb2b168265.title: Nano Banana 2 Lite: Image Edit
62cb2b168265.description: Edit an image using Nano Banana 2 Lite, the fastest image generation model from Google’s Gemini series, producing a side-by-side comparison of the original and edited result.
62cb2b168265.metaDescription: Compare before/after image edits using Gemini Nano Banana 2 Lite in ComfyUI. Load, edit, view side-by-side with ImageCompare, and save results.
62cb2b168265.extendedDescription:
This comparison workflow shows a clean, side-by-side view of how Nano Banana 2 Lite (via the GeminiNanoBanana2V2 node) transforms a source image based on your edit instruction. The pipeline loads your original image, applies the edit with the model, and then places the original and result next to each other using ImageCompare so you can quickly judge what changed and what stayed consistent.

Methodologically, the comparison is controlled: both panes derive from the exact same source image (LoadImage), and only the model-driven edit differs. This makes it easy to evaluate trade-offs such as speed versus fidelity, the extent of stylistic drift, and the preservation of structure or identity. Expect Nano Banana 2 Lite to prioritize responsiveness and efficient edits; in practice, that can mean fast, coherent changes for common tasks (color tweaks, small object additions/removals), while very intricate or large, global transformations may require tighter instructions or iterative passes.
howToUse: Load your source image with the LoadImage node and verify resolution/aspect ratio are appropriate for your edit goal.

Open the GeminiNanoBanana2V2 node and enter a clear edit instruction (e.g., "brighten the sky and add warm sunset tones"). Adjust any available parameters relevant to edit scope or quality. If the node requires API credentials, ensure they’re configured.
Run the workflow to generate the edited output from GeminiNanoBanana2V2.
Use the ImageCompare node’s output to review the side-by-side result. Look for preservation of composition/identity, color consistency, edges, and any unintended artifacts.
If needed, refine the instruction (more specific guidance usually reduces drift) and re-run to produce an additional comparison.
Save the comparison and edited image with SaveImageAdvanced, setting your preferred output folder and filename pattern for versioning.
suggestedUseCases: Creative direction reviews: Present before/after boards for quick stakeholder feedback on color grading, style shifts, or minor retouching.
Product photo iterations: Compare subtle edits like background cleanup, glare reduction, or color normalization before publishing.
Marketing variants: Rapidly test small stylistic changes (e.g., warmer tones, light vignette) and choose the most brand-consistent result.
Content quality control: Verify that edits do not introduce artifacts or unwanted changes by inspecting the side-by-side output.

faqItems.question: What exactly is being compared in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The workflow compares the original image (from LoadImage) with the edited image generated by GeminiNanoBanana2V2. ImageCompare places them side-by-side for visual assessment; no numeric metrics are computed.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure a fair, readable comparison?
faqItems.answer: Keep the source image constant and change only the edit instruction or a single parameter at a time. Use consistent output size, and review the same regions (faces, edges, text) for drift or artifacts.

faqItems.question: When should I choose Nano Banana 2 Lite for edits?
faqItems.answer: Choose it when you need fast, coherent edits to an existing image—such as color tweaks, lighting adjustments, or minor object-level changes—where turnaround speed is important.

faqItems.question: Why does the edit sometimes alter areas I didn’t mention?
faqItems.answer: Under-specified instructions can lead to broader changes. Make your intent explicit (what to change and what to keep), and iterate with more targeted guidance to reduce unintended drift.

The ModelSamplingAuraFlow node is crucial for sampling and refining the image output, ensuring that the final result aligns with the user's prompt. By utilizing the CLIPTextEncode node, the workflow effectively translates text prompts into visual concepts, which are then decoded into images using the VAEDecode node. The ConditioningZeroOut node helps in managing the conditioning process, ensuring that the image generation remains consistent and aligned with the input parameters. This workflow is ideal for scenarios where speed is prioritized over high fidelity, making it a practical choice for rapid prototyping and concept visualization.
howToUse: Load the Qwen-Image 2512 Turbo workflow in ComfyUI.
Ensure all necessary models are downloaded and loaded, including VAELoader and CLIPLoader.
Set your desired image size using the provided aspect ratios.
Enter your text prompt in the designated area.
Run the workflow to generate the image.
Save the generated image using the SaveImage node.

63cbc1ad946c.title: LTX-2 Image to Video (Distilled)
63cbc1ad946c.description: Transform static images into dynamic videos with synchronized audio-video generation using LTX-2 distilled model. Optimized for faster generation while maintaining quality. Features expressive lip sync, natural motion, and improved speed.
63cbc1ad946c.metaDescription: Animate a still image into video with LTX-2 (distilled) in ComfyUI. Fast, natural motion and lip sync. Validates sizes, saves MP4, and supports audio when available.
63cbc1ad946c.extendedDescription: This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a dynamic video using the distilled LTX-2 model from Lightricks. It wraps the animation pipeline inside a Subgraph node (b7c2d337-c38d-4c04-922b-2d638449d13e) so you can focus on prompting and parameters instead of wiring low-level components. Your source is loaded with LoadImage, conformed to a video-safe size using ResizeImageMaskNode, then animated by the LTX-2 Distilled Subgraph, which generates temporally coherent frames with expressive motion and lip sync. The resulting video (and audio, when provided by the model) is written to disk with SaveVideo. A MarkdownNote in the canvas provides inline guidance and links to Subgraph docs to help you understand and customize the encapsulated graph.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then confirm the LTX-2 distilled Subgraph node (b7c2d337-c38d-4c04-922b-2d638449d13e) and SaveVideo are present. Read the MarkdownNote for quick tips and subgraph documentation.

Add or open the LoadImage node and select your source image. If needed, adjust aspect ratio and size in ResizeImageMaskNode. Set width and height to values divisible by 64 (e.g., 1280x768 or 1920x1088).

Open the LTX-2 Distilled Subgraph node and craft the prompt. Follow LTX-2 prompting tips: describe core actions over time, specify visual details, and include audio/dialogue text if you want lip-sync and audio.

Set video parameters in the Subgraph: choose frame count as 8n+1 (e.g., 9, 17, 25, 33), pick FPS, and (optionally) set a seed for reproducibility. Note: if you enter invalid values, the workflow will silently snap to the closest valid settings.
Queue and run the graph. The Subgraph will generate frames (and audio when available) and SaveVideo will write the output (e.g., MP4) to your selected folder.

Review the result. Iterate by refining the prompt (actions, visuals, dialogue), adjusting resolution (default 720p; you can try 1920x1088), and tuning frame count/FPS to balance motion fidelity and speed.
suggestedUseCases: Talking portraits and interview-style clips with expressive lip sync from a single headshot.
Product hero shots that add subtle rotations, camera moves, and environmental motion from a static render.
Music or podcast teasers that animate cover art and synchronize facial movement to spoken lyrics or dialogue prompts.
Comic panels or concept art turned into short animatics to previsualize a scene.
Social media shorts that add life to brand imagery with quick, loopable motion.

faqItems.question: What resolutions and frame counts are valid for LTX-2 in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Set width and height to values divisible by 64 (e.g., 1280x768, 1920x1088). Use a frame count of the form 8n+1 (e.g., 9, 17, 25, 33). If you enter invalid values, the Subgraph will automatically choose the closest valid parameters, so you won’t see an error but your result may not match the exact numbers you typed.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow generate audio and lip sync from text?
faqItems.answer: The LTX-2 distilled Subgraph can produce expressive lip sync when your prompt includes dialogue in the audio section. When the model returns an audio track, SaveVideo will mux it into the output. If your model build/weights do not output audio, you will get a silent video (you can add audio later in an editor).

faqItems.question: How can I improve motion quality without huge render times?
faqItems.answer: Use the distilled model’s default 720p for faster runs, keep prompts precise about actions over time, and choose a moderate frame count like 17 or 25. If you upscale to 1920x1088, expect longer times. For stability, keep the seed fixed while iterating and avoid overly aggressive motion descriptions in a single short clip.

faqItems.question: Why does my output size or frame count not match what I typed?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is designed to be forgiving: it silently snaps to the nearest valid width/height (multiples of 64) and to frame counts of 8n+1. Double-check the Subgraph’s effective settings after running, and adjust your inputs to the nearest valid target if you need a specific result.

64f4db9e3e33.title: Seedance 2.0: Reference to Video
64f4db9e3e33.description: Generate cinematic videos from reference images and text prompts. Preserve subject identity and composition while adding expressive motion with synchronized audio. Control camera movement and lighting through detailed prompts.
64f4db9e3e33.metaDescription: Create cinematic videos from a reference image in ComfyUI with Seedance 2.0. Preserve identity, direct camera and lighting via prompts, and export MP4 with SaveVideo.
64f4db9e3e33.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0: Reference to Video turns a single reference image into a short cinematic video by combining a strong identity lock with prompt-driven motion and lighting. The LoadImage node supplies a clean, high-resolution reference frame, while ByteDance2ReferenceNode runs the Seedance 2.0 model to synthesize a sequence of frames that preserve the subject’s look and composition. You guide the scene using natural language—add camera cues (dolly-in, slow pan left), lighting notes (soft rim light, golden hour), and style hints (35mm, shallow depth of field) directly in the prompt.

Technically, ByteDance2ReferenceNode conditions Seedance 2.0 on both the reference image and your text prompt, then generates a video at the duration, resolution, and frame rate you specify. Key controls typically include reference adherence versus motion intensity (to balance identity preservation with expressiveness), guidance strength, negative prompts for artifact control, seed for reproducibility, and output timing (fps, seconds). The SaveVideo node then encodes the generated frames into a compact MP4 at your chosen fps and quality. This minimalist graph—LoadImage → ByteDance2ReferenceNode → SaveVideo—makes iteration fast: tweak a prompt or slider, queue again, and compare results side by side to quickly dial in the look you need.

While the workflow is optimized for visuals, you can time your motion to external audio by setting duration and beats per section to match your soundtrack. SaveVideo produces a silent video, so plan to add or replace audio in your editor after export. The result is a reliable identity-preserving image-to-video pipeline that responds well to clear prompts and produces cinematic movement without complex node graphs.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the LoadImage node. Choose a clean, high‑resolution reference image with the subject centered and the intended aspect ratio (keep dimensions divisible by 8 or 16 for stable video encoding).

Open ByteDance2ReferenceNode and enter your prompt (camera moves, lighting, style) and optional negative prompt (e.g., deformed, flicker, warped hands). If the node exposes API settings for Seedance 2.0, add your endpoint/key.

Set output specs in ByteDance2ReferenceNode: duration (e.g., 2–6 seconds), fps (e.g., 16–24), and resolution. Adjust reference adherence vs. motion strength to balance identity lock with expressive movement. Set a seed for repeatable results.

Refine creative controls: describe camera motion explicitly (dolly-in, slow pan right, tilt up), lighting (soft rim light, cinematic contrast), and lens cues (35mm, shallow depth of field). If identity drifts, increase reference adherence or shorten the duration.
Configure SaveVideo to match the chosen fps. Set filename and quality (CRF/bitrate options, if exposed). Ensure SaveVideo’s fps matches the generation fps so playback speed is correct.
Click Queue/Execute. After the run completes, find the MP4 in ComfyUI’s output folder. Review and iterate—tweak prompt wording, motion strength, or seed to converge on your desired look.
suggestedUseCases: Portrait motion shots that preserve a subject’s face while adding subtle dolly or pan moves for reels and intros.
Product hero clips with controlled parallax, soft studio lighting, and smooth camera arcs for ads or landing pages.
Fashion and lookbook snippets using stylized lighting cues and lens language while keeping outfit details intact.
Storyboard and previsualization of scenes where quick prompt edits explore alternate camera moves and moods.
Music or teaser visuals timed to a track by matching video duration and beat emphasis, then adding audio in post.

faqItems.question: What reference images work best?
faqItems.answer: Use a clean, high‑resolution image with the subject centered, minimal motion blur, and a background that matches your intended scene. Keep the aspect ratio close to your target output and avoid heavy filters that may conflict with the prompt.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the subject’s identity stable?
faqItems.answer: Increase the reference adherence (or similar control) in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, reduce duration, and use a consistent aspect ratio. Keep prompts descriptive but not contradictory, and add a negative prompt to discourage unwanted style drift.

faqItems.question: How can I control camera movement and lighting?
faqItems.answer: Use explicit language in the prompt: “slow dolly‑in,” “subtle pan left,” “tilt up,” “soft rim light,” “cinematic contrast,” “35mm, shallow depth of field.” If motion overwhelms identity, lower motion strength or raise reference adherence.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow generate audio or sync to music?
faqItems.answer: This workflow focuses on visuals. SaveVideo exports a silent MP4. To pair with music, set duration to match your track and add audio later in an editor. If your Seedance 2.0 endpoint exposes audio‑driven options, configure them in ByteDance2ReferenceNode (if available), but audio isn’t embedded by default.

655893ad7990.title: SD3.5 Large Blur
655893ad7990.description: Generate images guided by blurred reference images using SD 3.5.
655893ad7990.metaDescription: Generate stunning images using blurred references with SD3.5 Large Blur workflow in ComfyUI. Perfect for artists and designers.
655893ad7990.extendedDescription:
The SD3.5 Large Blur workflow is designed to generate high-quality images by leveraging blurred reference images as a guide. This technique utilizes the Stable Diffusion 3.5 (SD3.5) model, which is known for its ability to create detailed and visually appealing images. The workflow incorporates several key nodes, including the KSampler, CheckpointLoaderSimple, and ControlNetLoader, to efficiently manage the image generation process. By using a blurred image as a reference, the workflow can focus on capturing the essence of the image while allowing for creative interpretation in the finer details. This approach is particularly useful for artists and designers looking to create unique and imaginative visuals based on existing images.

The workflow begins by loading the necessary models and checkpoints, such as the 'sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors' and the 'sd3.5_large_controlnet_blur.safetensors'. These models are essential for the ControlNetApplyAdvanced node, which applies advanced control techniques to the image generation process. Users are encouraged to preprocess their images using the 'comfyui_controlnet_aux' tool to ensure optimal results. The CLIPTextEncode node allows for the integration of text prompts that guide the image generation, enabling users to specify desired characteristics, such as color and style. The final output is decoded using the VAEDecode node and saved with the SaveImage node, providing users with a ready-to-use image that meets their creative needs.
howToUse: Load the SD3.5 Large Blur workflow in ComfyUI.
Ensure the necessary models, 'sd3.5_large_fp8_scaled.safetensors' and 'sd3.5_large_controlnet_blur.safetensors', are loaded using CheckpointLoaderSimple.

Save the generated image using the SaveImage node.

6645006a0cb7.title: Seedance2.0 4K: Reference to Video
6645006a0cb7.description: Generate a reference-based video from a single input image using Seedance 2.0, producing native 4K output with 10-bit color depth and clean fine detail retention. The workflow takes 1 image and outputs 1 video. Ideal for high-resolution motion graphics, cinematic VFX shots requiring downstream grading, and professional video production where 4K finishing is essential.
6645006a0cb7.metaDescription: Turn a single image into a native 4K, 10-bit video using Seedance 2.0 in ComfyUI. Reference-preserving motion with ByteDance2ReferenceNode and SaveVideo.
6645006a0cb7.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows how to turn a single still image into a native 4K video using Seedance 2.0’s reference-to-video method. The workflow is intentionally minimal: LoadImage brings in your reference frame, ByteDance2ReferenceNode (the Seedance 2.0 reference model) synthesizes temporally consistent motion while preserving the look of the source, and SaveVideo encodes the generated frames into a 4K file. The result is a reference-faithful clip with clean, fine detail that’s suitable for editorial finishing and downstream color work.

Technically, the ByteDance2ReferenceNode conditions its generative video on the appearance of the input image and drives motion from learned priors, with user-adjustable parameters like output resolution, frame count, frame rate, seed, and motion/strength controls (names may vary by build). Set the node to 3840x2160 to produce true UHD frames, choose a frame count and FPS for duration, and keep a fixed seed for repeatability. SaveVideo then assembles the frames; when configured with a 10‑bit-capable encoder and pixel format, it exports in 10‑bit color, which helps maintain subtle gradients and grading latitude. If a 10‑bit encoder or pixel format isn’t available, the node will export in standard 8‑bit.
howToUse: Load the Seedance2.0 4K: Reference to Video workflow in ComfyUI. Ensure ByteDance2ReferenceNode is installed and its Seedance 2.0 model files are available. Confirm FFmpeg is set up for video export.
Open the LoadImage node and select your reference image. For best results, start with a sharp, high-resolution image composed for 16:9 framing to match 3840x2160 output.

Configure ByteDance2ReferenceNode: set resolution to 3840x2160, pick an FPS (e.g., 24 or 30), and set the frame count (e.g., 96 frames ≈ 4 seconds at 24 fps). Adjust seed for reproducibility and tune motion/strength controls to balance movement with detail retention.

Set up SaveVideo for your deliverable. To target 10-bit, choose a 10‑bit‑capable codec/pixel format (e.g., HEVC Main10 with yuv420p10le or ProRes via prores_ks) if available in your build. Specify output path and filename.

Run the graph. Review the render for motion quality and fine detail. If you see over-smearing or loss of texture, lower motion strength or try a different seed; if motion is too subtle, increase strength or frames.
Iterate: adjust FPS/frame count for different durations, tweak motion parameters to emphasize camera or subject movement, and re‑export. Keep a log of seed and settings to reproduce favored looks.
suggestedUseCases: Cinematic VFX shots: create graded, reference-faithful 4K plates from concept art for previs or background elements.
Product hero clips: generate smooth parallax or reveal motions from a single packshot while retaining branding details.
Title and logo motion: add subtle, high-fidelity motion to static designs for 4K broadcast packages.
Environment fly‑throughs: turn keyframe paintings into short exploratory camera moves for pitch decks or animatics.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure the output is truly 4K and 10-bit?
faqItems.answer: In ByteDance2ReferenceNode, set resolution to 3840x2160. In SaveVideo, select a 10‑bit-capable encoder and pixel format (e.g., HEVC Main10 with yuv420p10le or ProRes via prores_ks) and verify your FFmpeg build supports them. If 10‑bit isn’t available, the node will export 8‑bit.

faqItems.question: How can I preserve more fine detail from the reference image?
faqItems.answer: Use a sharp, high-resolution source image, keep motion/strength settings moderate, and reduce any aggressive denoising if exposed. Lock a seed for consistency and try a few nearby seeds to find a motion field that keeps textures stable.

faqItems.question: How do I change the video duration and frame rate?
faqItems.answer: Duration is frame_count ÷ FPS. Increase frame_count for longer clips, adjust FPS for smoother or more cinematic motion (e.g., 24 or 30). Make sure SaveVideo matches your intended FPS.

faqItems.question: What if I run out of GPU memory at 4K?
faqItems.answer: Try lowering the frame batch size (if exposed by your build), reducing motion complexity, or temporarily testing at a lower resolution. Once settings are dialed in, switch back to 3840x2160 for the final pass.

67981edb9ad4.title: AI on the Lot 2026 - LTX-2.3 - i2v
67981edb9ad4.description: The fifth workflow released for AI on the Lot 2026, made available for ComfyUI 101 workshop attendees to open and follow along if they choose. An image-to-video workflow built on the LTX 2.3 model, turning a still image into a generated video clip.
67981edb9ad4.metaDescription: Animate a still image into a video in ComfyUI with LTX‑2.3. Load an image, prompt motion, tune frames/FPS, and export your clip with SaveVideo.
67981edb9ad4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, animated video using Lightricks’ LTX‑2.3 image‑to‑video model. The pipeline is straightforward: LoadImage brings your source frame into the graph, a custom LTX‑2.3 node (2454ad83-157c-40dd-9f19-5daaf4041ce0) synthesizes motion conditioned on that image and a text prompt, and SaveVideo assembles the generated frames into a playable clip. MarkdownNote nodes inside the graph provide in‑context guidance and prompt tips so you can follow along during the AI on the Lot 2026 ComfyUI 101 workshop.

Technically, the LTX‑2.3 node encodes your input image into the model’s latent space and generates a temporally coherent sequence guided by your prompt. You control the character and pace of motion by describing events over time ("Core Actions") and specifying concrete "Visual Details" you want to preserve, as recommended in the LTX‑2.3 prompting tips. Typical controls exposed by the node include the text prompt, seed for reproducibility, and clip characteristics such as number of frames and/or FPS (exact parameters depend on the node build). SaveVideo then writes the frames to disk at your chosen frame rate. For model weights, use Lightricks/LTX‑2.3 from Hugging Face (see the links provided), and follow the node’s loader field to point to the correct files.
howToUse: Load the workflow file (AI on the Lot 2026 - LTX-2.3 - i2v) in ComfyUI. Ensure the LTX‑2.3 model weights are available (Hugging Face: Lightricks/LTX-2.3) and that the LTX node points to them.
Open the LoadImage node and select your source image. Keep a clean, reasonably high‑resolution image and maintain the aspect ratio you intend to output.

Configure the LTX‑2.3 node (2454ad83-157c-40dd-9f19-5daaf4041ce0): write a prompt that describes the Core Actions over time and the Visual Details to preserve. If available, set seed, number of frames, motion strength, and/or guidance as needed. Refer to the MarkdownNote tips in the graph.
Set the SaveVideo node’s output path and FPS. The video’s resolution follows the generated frames; FPS controls playback smoothness and duration when combined with the frame count.
Run the graph once with conservative settings (shorter clip or lower FPS) to validate everything works. Inspect the preview/output and note how the prompt affected motion and fidelity.
Iterate: refine the prompt, adjust motion strength or frame count (if exposed), and re‑run. Use a fixed seed for repeatable results or change it to explore variations.
suggestedUseCases: Cinemagraph‑style animations from product or lifestyle photos for social posts and ads
Animating key art or storyboards for fast previz and mood exploration in film/video
Subtle portrait or environmental motion for profile headers, hero banners, or teasers
Turning static marketing stills into short looping video assets
Creating dynamic B‑roll from brand images when live footage is unavailable

faqItems.question: How should I prompt LTX‑2.3 for the best motion?
faqItems.answer: Describe Core Actions as they unfold over time (e.g., “the camera slowly dolly‑zooms in as leaves drift across the foreground”) and list concrete Visual Details you want to preserve (composition, lighting, color, subject attributes). Keep directives concise and unambiguous.

faqItems.question: What image inputs work best?
faqItems.answer: Clean, well‑lit images with clear subject separation tend to animate more coherently. Use a resolution that matches your VRAM and the workflow’s defaults, and keep the aspect ratio consistent across input and output to avoid stretching.

faqItems.question: How do I control clip length and smoothness?
faqItems.answer: Clip length is a function of the number of generated frames and the SaveVideo FPS. Increase frames for longer clips and adjust FPS for playback feel. If the LTX‑2.3 node exposes frame count or duration, change it there; then set the desired FPS in SaveVideo.

faqItems.question: My results change between runs. How can I make them repeatable?
faqItems.answer: Set and reuse a fixed seed in the LTX‑2.3 node (if available), keep the prompt identical, and avoid changing other generation parameters. Changing the seed is useful when you want controlled variations.

67a816af8a73.title: Wan 2.2 14B Fun Control
67a816af8a73.description: Generate videos guided by pose, depth, and edge controls using Wan 2.2 Fun Control.
67a816af8a73.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate controllable videos with Wan2.2 Fun Control using pose, depth, and edges. Learn setup, prompts, sampling, and export in ComfyUI.
67a816af8a73.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow demonstrates how to generate controllable videos with Wan2.2 Fun Control (14B), guided by pose, depth, and edge inputs. At its core, the Wan22FunControlToVideo node fuses your text prompt from CLIPTextEncode with one or more control streams derived from a reference video. The model stack loads via UNETLoader and VAELoader, while CLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode provide multilingual text conditioning. Sampling runs through ModelSamplingSD3 with KSamplerAdvanced to balance quality, speed, and control strength. Finally, VAEDecode reconstructs frames and SaveVideo exports the result.

You can preprocess control videos directly in the graph: LoadVideo and GetVideoComponents ingest your footage, Canny extracts edges, and optional custom nodes (comfyui_controlnet_aux and ComfyUI-DepthAnythingV2) add pose/depth maps. CreateVideo sets resolution, frame count, and FPS to match Wan2.2’s training regime (multi-resolution 512/768/1024, 81 frames at 16 FPS). The Start_image group lets you anchor the first frame with LoadImage for a consistent subject/look. An optional LoraLoaderModelOnly applies the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA for faster renders at the cost of reduced motion dynamics. This gives you a flexible, reproducible pipeline for video-to-video generation with reliable structure preservation and style control.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and install required models and custom nodes. Download wan2.2_fun_control_high_noise_14B_fp8_scaled.safetensors for UNETLoader and your VAE. For depth/pose controls, add comfyui_controlnet_aux and ComfyUI-DepthAnythingV2.

Step 1 – Load models: Set CLIPLoader and VAELoader, then point UNETLoader to the Wan2.2 Fun Control checkpoint. If you want speed over motion fidelity, enable the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA via LoraLoaderModelOnly (or switch to the fp8+4-steps LoRA group).

Step 3 – Control video and preprocessing: Load your reference video with LoadVideo. Use GetVideoComponents to read fps and frame count. Connect Canny to extract edge maps. Optionally add depth (DepthAnythingV2) and pose (OpenPose from controlnet_aux) nodes to generate additional control streams.
Step 2 – Start_image (optional): If you need a consistent subject or style anchor, load an initial image with LoadImage and wire it into the Start_image inputs provided by the workflow.

Step 4 – Prompt and sampling: Enter your positive/negative prompts in CLIPTextEncode. In ModelSamplingSD3 + KSamplerAdvanced, start with 8 steps for the base model (CFG 3–6), or 4 steps if using the Lighting LoRA. Keep seed locked for reproducible results.

Step 5 – Video size & length: In CreateVideo, pick 512, 768, or 1024 resolution and set FPS to 16 with up to 81 frames for best alignment with Wan2.2. Run the graph. Inspect frames in PreviewImage, then decode with VAEDecode and export using SaveVideo (e.g., MP4).
suggestedUseCases: Edge-accurate stylization: Preserve scene geometry with Canny while reimagining the look via prompts (e.g., cinematic, anime, or painterly styles).
Pose-driven character motion: Use pose controls to transfer choreography or gestures to a new character while keeping consistent identity via Start_image.
Depth-aware relighting and parallax: Combine depth maps with prompts to emphasize 3D structure, depth-of-field, or subtle camera movement cues.
Design and product demos: Maintain object contours and motion while generating polished, on-brand video variations from rough captures.
Previsualization and animatics: Lock in motion beats with pose/trajectory guidance and iterate on style quickly before full production.

faqItems.question: Do I need all three controls (edge, depth, pose) to get good results?
faqItems.answer: No. Wan2.2 Fun Control works with any single control stream (e.g., just Canny) or combinations. More controls generally increase structural faithfulness but can limit stylistic freedom. Start with edges, then add depth or pose if you need stronger guidance.

faqItems.question: How should I match video length and FPS?
faqItems.answer: Use GetVideoComponents to read your source video’s FPS and frame count, then set CreateVideo to 16 FPS and up to 81 frames for best alignment with Wan2.2’s training. If your source differs, you can still run it—just expect slightly different motion timing.

faqItems.question: What does the Wan2.2 Lighting LoRA do?
faqItems.answer: The Lighting LoRA reduces generation time and can improve lighting consistency, but it tends to reduce video dynamics. The workflow includes a dedicated fp8 + 4 steps LoRA group for speed. If you prioritize richer motion, disable the LoRA and increase steps modestly.

faqItems.question: How can I improve temporal coherence and reduce flicker?
faqItems.answer: Use stronger controls (edges + depth), keep CFG moderate (around 3–6), fix the seed, and match resolution/FPS to 512/768/1024 at 16 FPS. Ensure prompts are stable across the whole run and avoid overly aggressive negative prompts that can destabilize details.
