68c39b4c6a6f.title: Seedance 2.0 Cinematic Prompt Studio
68c39b4c6a6f.description: Create production-ready cinematic shots with concise, director-style Seedance 2.0 prompts built around intentional camera motion, visual storytelling, and strong final frames.
68c39b4c6a6f.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate cinematic Seedance 2.0 videos in ComfyUI using concise, director-style prompts with optional image references and Gemini-assisted prompt crafting.
68c39b4c6a6f.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Cinematic Prompt Studio is a ComfyUI workflow for turning concise, director-style prompts into production-ready cinematic shots. It pairs optional image references with a structured Seedance 2.0 prompt that emphasizes intentional camera motion, visual storytelling beats, and a strong final frame. The workflow is organized into three groups: Load Images, Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt, and Generate Video.

Technically, LoadImage supplies one or more visual references, while GeminiNode converts a short shot brief into a Seedance 2.0–formatted prompt (camera verbs, lens/composition cues, lighting, pacing, and a closing frame directive). These are fed into ByteDance2ReferenceNode, which performs image-conditioned or text-only video generation via the Seedance 2.0 backend. PreviewAny lets you inspect intermediate outputs and play back results in-canvas, and SaveVideo writes the final render to disk. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides on-canvas guidance and a prompt template so you can iterate quickly and keep prompts concise and cinematic.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and review the three groups: Load Images, Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt, and Generate Video. Check the MarkdownNote for on-canvas tips.
Add optional references in the Load Images group using the LoadImage node (e.g., a character sheet, product packshot, or location still). Leave it empty for text-only shots.

In the Generate Seedance 2.0 Prompt group, enter a brief shot description (subject, setting, mood) and desired camera motion. Run the GeminiNode to transform this into a Seedance 2.0–style prompt. Inspect the output and edit if needed to keep it concise and directive.

Route the generated prompt and any reference image outputs into the ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Configure its exposed parameters (e.g., aspect ratio, duration, guidance) as available in your installation. Ensure your API credentials are set for any external services used by GeminiNode and ByteDance2ReferenceNode.

Execute the Generate Video group. Use PreviewAny to review the result. If the motion feels vague or the ending is weak, refine the prompt with explicit camera verbs (e.g., steady dolly-in, slow tilt-up, lock-off ending) and a clear final-frame instruction, then re-run.
When satisfied, save the output using SaveVideo. Name your file and choose the desired container/codec based on what the node exposes.
suggestedUseCases: Previsualization for narrative or commercial shoots: block camera moves and tone before production.
Character or product hero shots with controlled reveals and strong end frames.
Establishing shots and mood pieces to define location, lighting, and pacing.
Social media motion posters and short teasers with clear, readable camera motion.
Look development for brand style guides: consistent framing, motion, and lighting across variants.

faqItems.question: Do I need a reference image, or can I generate from text only?
faqItems.answer: References are optional. LoadImage provides identity and style cues (faces, products, environments) for image-conditioned results. If you omit references, ByteDance2ReferenceNode will generate from the prompt alone.

faqItems.question: How do I make the camera motion feel intentional instead of random?
faqItems.answer: Write concise, directive prompts. Use specific camera verbs (dolly-in, push, crane down, handheld sway, static lock-off), define beats (start, middle, end), and explicitly instruct the final frame (e.g., end on a locked close-up). GeminiNode helps structure this into Seedance 2.0 format, but clarity in your brief matters most.

faqItems.question: What settings control duration, resolution, or aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: These are configured on ByteDance2ReferenceNode, subject to what your node version exposes and what the backend supports. Set aspect ratio and duration there if available. Keep durations short for crisper motion and stronger final frames.

faqItems.question: How do I get consistent subjects across multiple shots?
faqItems.answer: Reuse the same reference images and keep your key identity cues and framing language consistent across prompts. Avoid over-describing style changes between shots, and maintain similar camera and composition cues for continuity.

68dcfc02a679.title: ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT： Text to Music
68dcfc02a679.description: Generate high-quality music from text prompts using a 4B parameter SFT model. Control output with CFG for precise prompt adherence.
68dcfc02a679.metaDescription: Generate music from text with ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT in ComfyUI. Control duration, CFG, and sampling for precise, high-quality audio. Exports directly to MP3.
68dcfc02a679.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns text prompts into finished music using the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT (4B) model. It follows a familiar diffusion pipeline adapted for audio: DualCLIPLoader and TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 convert your prompt (and optional negative prompt) into conditioning; EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio creates a latent audio canvas for your chosen duration; UNETLoader brings in the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT model; and KSampler performs iterative denoising guided by CFG. ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the sampler strategy tuned for ACE-Step audio, while VAELoader + VAEDecodeAudio convert the final latent back into a waveform that SaveAudioMP3 writes to disk.

Technically, CFG (classifier-free guidance) lets you balance creativity and prompt adherence: lower CFG values explore broadly, higher values follow your text more strictly. ConditioningZeroOut provides a clean unconditional branch if you don’t specify a negative prompt, ensuring stable guidance. Workflow groups (Model, Duration, Prompt) make it easy to swap checkpoints, set seconds, and iterate on prompts. The result is a practical, reproducible text-to-music pipeline that can quickly iterate across genres, moods, instruments, and structure—ideal for ideation, temp scoring, and background tracks.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure required nodes are installed. Place the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT UNet, the matching audio VAE, and ACE-Step text encoders where your ComfyUI installation expects model files.

Open the Model group: set UNETLoader to the ACE-Step 1.5XL SFT checkpoint, VAELoader to the corresponding audio VAE, and DualCLIPLoader to the ACE-Step text encoder weights. Leave ModelSamplingAuraFlow at its defaults unless you need a different sampler configuration.

Open the Duration group: use EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio (and the connected PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveNode controls) to choose the length of the clip. Adjust duration or frame count as exposed by the node. Longer durations increase VRAM/time.

Open the Prompt group: write a descriptive text prompt in TextEncodeAceStepAudio1.5 (e.g., "uplifting orchestral score, strings and brass, cinematic, fast tempo, no vocals"). Optionally provide a negative prompt or use ConditioningZeroOut for a clean unconditional branch.

Configure KSampler: set steps, CFG, and seed via the attached Primitive nodes. As a starting point, try 30–60 steps and CFG 2.5–5.0. Keep the seed fixed for reproducibility or randomize to explore variations.

Run the workflow. Inspect the output after VAEDecodeAudio, then SaveAudioMP3 will export your clip. If results drift from your intent, refine the prompt, tweak CFG, adjust steps, or change the seed and run again.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid background music generation for social videos, reels, or shorts.
Ideation of genre, mood, and instrumentation for temp scores or briefs.
Ambient and lo-fi loops for streams, focus sessions, or prototypes.
Exploring multiple stylistic variations quickly by seeding and CFG sweeps.
Game jams and prototyping level themes without a full composing pass.

faqItems.question: What do KSampler and ModelSamplingAuraFlow each control?
faqItems.answer: KSampler performs the denoising process using your steps, CFG, and seed. ModelSamplingAuraFlow configures the sampler strategy/schedule tailored for ACE-Step audio, so you get stable, high-quality convergence without manual scheduler tuning.

faqItems.question: How do I change the length of the generated music?
faqItems.answer: Use EmptyAceStep1.5LatentAudio in the Duration group. Adjust its duration or frame parameters (often driven by connected PrimitiveInt/PrimitiveNode controls). Longer clips require more compute and memory.

faqItems.question: My output sounds off-topic or noisy. How can I improve it?
faqItems.answer: Refine the prompt with clearer descriptors (genre, instruments, mood, tempo, mix notes) and add a negative prompt (e.g., "distortion, artifacts, vocals"). Try lowering CFG slightly if the audio is harsh, or increasing steps moderately if it lacks detail. Changing the seed can also help.

faqItems.question: Can I export WAV instead of MP3?
faqItems.answer: This workflow saves with SaveAudioMP3. If you prefer WAV, add or swap in a SaveAudioWAV node (if available in your setup) after VAEDecodeAudio and select the desired format and path.

68f726502f5a.title: Nano Banana Pro: AI Image Enhancement

68f726502f5a.extendedDescription: The 'Nano Banana Pro: AI Image Enhancement' workflow is designed to upscale and enhance AI-generated images, transforming them into high-resolution 4K outputs with improved sharpness and coherence. This workflow leverages the power of the Nano Banana Pro model, known for its exceptional ability to refine image details and enhance visual quality. The process begins with the LoadImage node, which allows users to upload their AI-generated images into the system. The core of the enhancement process is handled by the GeminiImage2Node, which applies sophisticated algorithms to upscale and enhance the image. Finally, the SaveImage node ensures that the enhanced image is saved in the desired format and location.

Upload your AI-generated image using the LoadImage node.
Ensure the GeminiImage2Node is correctly configured to use the Nano Banana Pro model.
Run the workflow to process the image through the enhancement pipeline.
Locate the SaveImage node to specify the output format and destination for the enhanced image.
Review the 4K enhanced image output for quality and detail improvements.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing digital artwork for high-resolution prints.
Improving the quality of AI-generated images for professional portfolios.
Upscaling images for use in marketing materials and presentations.
Refining details in images for use in high-definition displays.
Preparing AI-generated images for use in multimedia projects.

faqItems.question: What types of images can be enhanced using this workflow?
faqItems.answer: This workflow is designed for AI-generated images, but it can also enhance other digital images with similar characteristics.

faqItems.question: Is there a limit to the size of the image I can upload?
faqItems.answer: The size limit depends on your system's capabilities, but the workflow is optimized for handling standard AI-generated image sizes efficiently.

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the level of enhancement applied to the image?
faqItems.answer: The Nano Banana Pro model automatically optimizes enhancement, but you can tweak settings in the GeminiImage2Node for specific adjustments.

faqItems.question: What output formats are supported by the SaveImage node?

69850664cf89.title: Restore Old Photos
69850664cf89.description: This app enhances your old photos. You can simply upload your image to fix faded or damaged photos in seconds.
69850664cf89.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow to restore old photos with a custom restoration node, A/B comparison, and easy export using LoadImage, ImageCompare, and SaveImage.
69850664cf89.extendedDescription:
Restore Old Photos is a focused ComfyUI workflow for bringing faded, scratched, or low-contrast images back to life without guesswork. It combines essential utility nodes with a dedicated restoration stage to let you preview, compare, and export confidently. The flow begins with LoadImage, passes through a custom restoration operator (node ID 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6), and gives you non-destructive control via ComfySwitchNode so you can instantly flip between the untouched input and the restored result.

Technically, the original and processed images are routed into ImageCompare for side-by-side evaluation, while PreviewAny provides quick on-canvas checks as you iterate. PrimitiveStringMultiline is included to keep multi-line notes (e.g., session settings or change logs) directly in the graph, and SaveImage writes your final selection to disk. This layout emphasizes A/B validation and repeatability: adjust the restoration node’s settings (as exposed by the custom node), use the switch to judge impact, verify with ImageCompare, and export only when the result meets your standards.
howToUse: Open the Restore Old Photos workflow in ComfyUI. If you see a missing-node warning for 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6, install the corresponding custom node/extension and restart ComfyUI.
Select LoadImage and choose your old or damaged photo. The image will feed both the restoration branch and the baseline (original) branch for comparison.

Open the custom restoration node (ID 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6) and adjust its available controls (e.g., overall repair/enhancement strength, color/contrast options if provided). Click Queue Prompt to process.
Use ComfySwitchNode to toggle between Original and Restored outputs. Watch updates in PreviewAny for quick checks.
Open ImageCompare to view the original and restored images side by side. Zoom in to inspect faces, edges, and textures. Tweak the restoration node settings and re-queue until you are satisfied.
Before exporting, ensure ComfySwitchNode is routed to the restored branch that you prefer. Then use SaveImage to write the final image to disk (set your filename/prefix and output folder as needed).
suggestedUseCases: Digitizing and refreshing family photo albums with minimal manual retouching.
Preparing heritage or archival images for exhibits, newsletters, or websites.
Improving scans of old newspapers, yearbooks, or magazines for readability and presentation.
Reviving vintage portraits for genealogy projects or memorial books.
Quick cleanups of auction or catalog photos where clarity and contrast matter.

faqItems.question: What does the custom node 4c000cf8-4ec4-49a6-853c-e78dd316edc6 do exactly?
faqItems.answer: It’s the dedicated restoration stage in this workflow. Depending on its implementation and exposed parameters, it typically performs operations like denoising, contrast and color restoration, and artifact reduction. Open the node to see which controls are available in your install.

faqItems.question: Do I need a GPU to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: A GPU is recommended for speed and smoother iteration. Some setups can run on CPU, but processing will be significantly slower. If you experience slow previews, lower image resolution during testing and switch back to full size for the final pass.

faqItems.question: Can I export both the original and the restored image?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Run once with ComfySwitchNode set to the restored branch and SaveImage enabled, then toggle the switch to the original branch and run again to save that version as well. ImageCompare is for evaluation; SaveImage handles the actual file export.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow include upscaling?
faqItems.answer: No. It focuses on restoration at the input’s native resolution. If you need upscaling, you can add an upscaler node after the restoration stage in a separate workflow or a modified version of this graph.

6991493996fd.title: HappyHorse 1.1: Image to Video
6991493996fd.description: Animate a static first frame into a short video with synchronized audio using HappyHorse 1.1, taking 1 input image and producing 1 video output. Ideal for e-commerce product demos, brand marketing content, and short episodic series.
6991493996fd.metaDescription: Animate a single image into a short video with synced audio using HappyHorse 1.1 in ComfyUI. Simple LoadImage → API → SaveVideo pipeline.
6991493996fd.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a short, shareable video with synchronized audio using the HappyHorse 1.1 service. The pipeline is intentionally simple: LoadImage feeds your first frame, HappyHorseImageToVideoApi sends it to the HappyHorse 1.1 API for motion synthesis and audio alignment, and SaveVideo writes the returned clip to disk as a single video file. Because generation happens through the API node, you don’t need local GPU compute for the heavy lifting.

Technically, the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node packages your image and the node’s settings (such as duration, resolution, and other options exposed by the node) into a request. The HappyHorse 1.1 backend generates a sequence of coherent frames from the static first frame and returns a video container that includes both the visual track and synchronized audio. SaveVideo then preserves the container and filename you specify. This setup is ideal for rapid creation of product demos, branded motion posters, or short episodic content where you want quick iteration and consistent, audio-backed motion from a single frame.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node is installed and visible. If it’s missing, install the required custom node/extension and restart ComfyUI.
Load your source still using the LoadImage node. Choose a clear, well-lit image with your subject centered for best motion inference.

Open the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi node and enter any required credentials or endpoint settings. Configure the available options (e.g., duration, resolution/aspect ratio, and audio handling) as exposed by the node.
Verify the connections: LoadImage output should feed the HappyHorseImageToVideoApi image input. Set a filename and output directory on the SaveVideo node.

69a3789c4840.title: Wan 2.1 FLF2V 720p F16
69a3789c4840.description: Generate videos by controlling first and last frames using Wan 2.1 FLF2V.
69a3789c4840.metaDescription: ComfyUI Wan 2.1 FLF2V: create 720p, 16‑frame videos guided by start and end images plus text prompts. Precise transitions with CLIPVision and KSampler.
69a3789c4840.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows you how to generate smooth, guided video clips by explicitly controlling the first and last frames using Wan 2.1 FLF2V. The core of the workflow is the WanFirstLastFrameToVideo node, which fuses three condition sources: your prompt embeddings from CLIPTextEncode, visual guidance from CLIPVisionEncode of the start/end images, and the Wan 2.1 UNet loaded by UNETLoader. The workflow is configured for 720p output and 16 frames (F16), giving you a compact, visually coherent clip that cleanly transitions from the first frame to the last.

Under the hood, the model components are loaded in the "Load Models Here" group: VAELoader and VAEDecode handle latent-to-RGB decoding of frames; CLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode create text and (optionally) negative prompt embeddings; CLIPVisionLoader with CLIPVisionEncode extract visual features from your start and end images. ModelSamplingSD3 defines the timestep/schedule used by KSampler to drive diffusion steps for the Wan 2.1 UNet. Finally, CreateVideo assembles the decoded frames and SaveVideo writes the MP4 to disk. This setup is ideal when you want precise control over motion and composition—e.g., matching storyboard keyframes—while still benefiting from text-driven styling.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. In the "Load Models Here" group, point UNETLoader to the Wan 2.1 FLF2V diffusion weights, CLIPLoader to the Wan text encoder, CLIPVisionLoader to the vision encoder, and VAELoader to the Wan VAE. If using the Wan_2.1_ComfyUI_repackaged split files, place them in ComfyUI/models (clip → models/clip, clip_vision → models/clip_vision, vae → models/vae, diffusion/unet → models/checkpoints or models/unet as instructed in the repo).

In the "Start & End frames" group, use two LoadImage nodes to import your first and last frame images. Feed each image to its own CLIPVisionEncode so the WanFirstLastFrameToVideo node receives both vision embeddings. Match your images to 1280×720 (or the workflow’s resolution) to avoid unwanted cropping or padding.

Open the "Prompt" group. Enter your positive prompt in a CLIPTextEncode node (e.g., "glass flower blossom"). If you use a negative prompt, add it to a second CLIPTextEncode (the provided Chinese string is a strong artifact-suppression example). Ensure both text encodes are connected to WanFirstLastFrameToVideo.

In "Sampling & Video Generation", set KSampler parameters: steps (e.g., 20–30), CFG scale (e.g., 3–6), and seed for reproducibility. Leave ModelSamplingSD3 on its default preset unless you know the schedule you want to use for Wan 2.1.

Verify the frame count and resolution are set as intended (this preset is 720p, F16). Run the graph. VAEDecode will convert latents to frames, then CreateVideo will assemble the sequence. Adjust fps and quality settings in CreateVideo to control playback speed and bitrate.

Use SaveVideo to write the final MP4 to disk. If the transition feels too abrupt or too loose, iterate: refine your start/end images, tighten the prompt and negative prompt, tweak CFG/steps, or adjust the motion-related controls inside WanFirstLastFrameToVideo if exposed.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard-to-shot: lock in a first and last composition to visualize a planned camera move or subject motion between two keyframes.
Product spins and reveals: start with a clean hero angle and end on a detail close-up, while prompting for specific lighting or material style.
Logo and brand stingers: guide the animation between two layout frames while enforcing style via prompt and negative prompt.
Environment transitions: morph from daytime to dusk or from empty to populated scenes using paired keyframes and descriptive prompts.
Before/after concept previews: demonstrate a designed change (e.g., interior remodel) by transitioning between two reference frames.

faqItems.question: Do I have to provide both a start and an end frame?
faqItems.answer: Yes—this FLF2V workflow is designed to use both. If you only have one image, duplicate it into both inputs to produce subtle motion without a large scene change.

faqItems.question: How can I change the duration or resolution?
faqItems.answer: Increase the frame count parameter (e.g., F24 or F32) to lengthen the clip, and adjust the resolution fields to your target size. Keep aspect ratios consistent with your start/end images to avoid padding or distortions. Higher frame counts and resolutions require more VRAM.

faqItems.question: Which settings most affect motion smoothness?
faqItems.answer: Your start/end images and prompt coherence matter most. Technically, KSampler steps and CFG scale influence stability: slightly higher steps and moderate CFG (3–6) often improve consistency. If exposed, motion or guidance weights in WanFirstLastFrameToVideo can also tighten the match to the keyframes.

faqItems.question: I see artifacts or flicker—how do I reduce them?
faqItems.answer: Use a strong negative prompt (the provided Chinese example helps), lower CFG slightly, ensure both images share exposure/composition, and raise steps moderately. Also verify models (UNet/CLIP/CLIPVision/VAE) match the Wan 2.1 repackaged set and that resolution aligns with your inputs.

6a2b37d44146.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds a fast, repeatable contact sheet for fashion editorial concepts by compositing three inputs—your character, a scene/background, and a product—into cohesive images. Three LoadImage nodes bring in your assets, a PrimitiveStringMultiline node holds your creative brief, and a GeminiImage2Node uses the "Nano Banana Pro" model to integrate the images according to your instructions (lighting, mood, styling, composition). Because the model conditions on all three sources plus text, it can harmonize color and lighting while preserving key identity and product details.

Once the GeminiImage2Node produces one or more variations, a BatchImagesNode assembles them into a multi-tile contact sheet for quick side-by-side review. Finally, SaveImage writes the resulting grid (and/or individual frames, depending on how the graph is wired) to your output folder. The result is a practical, iteration-friendly tool: feed it new characters, scenes, or products and quickly compare editorial directions without rebuilding the pipeline.
howToUse: Load the "Step 1: Contact Sheet Workflow" JSON into ComfyUI and confirm all nodes are green. If GeminiImage2Node or BatchImagesNode are missing, install their custom-node packages and reload.

Open each LoadImage node and select your assets: a clean character image, a suitable scene/background, and a product cutout (PNG with transparency is ideal when available). Prefer high-quality, well-exposed sources.

In the PrimitiveStringMultiline node, write your creative brief: e.g., "fashion editorial, studio key light with soft rim, glossy magazine color grade, 3/4 camera angle, product prominently featured, refined shadows."

In GeminiImage2Node, select the "Nano Banana Pro" model. If the node exposes controls like output size or variation count, set them to your needs (e.g., square or portrait frames, multiple variations). Keep defaults for other parameters on your first run.
Optionally adjust BatchImagesNode to define your contact sheet layout (columns/rows, padding, order) so multiple variations are tiled in a single grid for review.
Set a filename prefix in SaveImage, then run/queue the workflow. Review the tiled contact sheet in the ComfyUI viewer and find the saved files in your ComfyUI output directory.
suggestedUseCases: Fashion lookbook exploration: quickly compare lighting and styling directions across multiple compositions.
E-commerce hero and lifestyle testing: place a product with consistent character presence across different scenes to evaluate visual impact.
Social campaign planning: generate a grid of on-brand editorial variations to shortlist the strongest creatives.
Client pitch decks: produce polished contact sheets that communicate multiple concepts in one deliverable.
Moodboard development: harmonize disparate references (character, set, product) into unified editorial frames.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best for the character, scene, and product?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, high-resolution sources (e.g., 1024–2048 px on the long side). Keep similar scales across inputs so the model can align them more naturally. Transparent PNGs for products help with clean placement.

faqItems.question: How do I keep brand details (logos, patterns) accurate in the composite?
faqItems.answer: Start with a clear, front-facing product image and call out constraints in the brief (e.g., “preserve logo and pattern”). If the GeminiImage2Node exposes style/strength controls, reduce the style strength to favor fidelity.

faqItems.question: How can I generate multiple looks on the same setup?
faqItems.answer: Create several brief variants in PrimitiveStringMultiline or, if available, increase the variation/batch setting in GeminiImage2Node. BatchImagesNode will tile the resulting frames into a single contact sheet for fast comparison.

faqItems.question: Where are the outputs saved and in what format?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage controls filename prefix and format (PNG/JPG). Files are written to your ComfyUI output directory. Set a unique prefix per run to keep iterations organized.

6afbca6e9d22.title: Sora 2: Text & Image to Video
6afbca6e9d22.description: OpenAI's Sora-2 and Sora-2 Pro video generation with synchronized audio.
6afbca6e9d22.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate Sora-2/Sora-2 Pro text- or image-to-video in ComfyUI with proper pad/crop sizing, preview, and SaveVideo output (audio supported).
6afbca6e9d22.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow demonstrates end-to-end text- and image-to-video generation using the OpenAIVideoSora2 node, with optional synchronized audio. You can start from a text prompt alone or condition the video with a reference image loaded via LoadImage. Because Sora-2 and Sora-2 Pro expect fixed input sizes, the workflow offers two branches to make your image fit: Option 1 uses ResizeAndPadImage to letterbox without cropping, and Option 2 crops to fill the frame. PreviewImage lets you confirm framing before you trigger the API call, and SaveVideo writes the returned video to disk.

Technically, the OpenAIVideoSora2 node is the core of the graph, exposing model selection (Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro), resolution, and prompt fields. The supported sizes are: Sora-2 (720x1280, 1280x720) and Sora-2 Pro (720x1280, 1280x720, 1024x1792, 1792x1024). The workflow groups keep things organized: Upload image, Option1 - Pad image, and Option 2 - Crop image. MarkdownNote and Note nodes include usage and pricing links for the partner API. ImageScale and ResizeAndPadImage align your image to the chosen video size so the API accepts it, while SaveVideo captures the API’s output, including audio when available. This design helps you iterate quickly—preview the conditioned frame, adjust your prompt, then render.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the MarkdownNote/Note nodes for API details and pricing. Ensure you’re running in a secure environment (localhost/127.0.0.1) per the partner node requirements.

Open the OpenAIVideoSora2 node: choose the model (Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro), set one of the supported resolutions, and enter your text prompt. Configure credentials/endpoint as required by the partner docs.

If conditioning with an image, add it via the LoadImage node in the Upload image group. Then choose either Option1 - Pad image (ResizeAndPadImage to fit without cropping) or Option 2 - Crop image (configure the resize/crop path to fill the frame). Use PreviewImage to verify composition.
Important: the input image must exactly match the selected video size. If it doesn’t, adjust with the pad or crop branch until PreviewImage shows the correct resolution and framing.
For text-to-video only, bypass the image branch (select those nodes and press Ctrl-B in ComfyUI) so OpenAIVideoSora2 runs from the text prompt alone.
Set an output path in SaveVideo, then queue and run. When the job completes, check the saved file. If the API returned audio, it will be included in the video; otherwise you’ll get a silent clip.
suggestedUseCases: Prompt-to-video concept sketches for storyboards using 1280x720 for fast iteration.
Image-anchored product spins or hero shots by padding a brand image to 720x1280 portrait.
Social content (Reels/Shorts) with portrait 1024x1792 via Sora-2 Pro to keep subjects large in frame.
Cinematic openings or camera moves guided by a style reference image to lock look and palette.
Education or explainer clips where a diagram image is preserved with letterboxing to avoid cropping labels.

faqItems.question: Which model and resolution should I choose: Sora-2 or Sora-2 Pro?
faqItems.answer: Use Sora-2 for 720x1280 or 1280x720 when you want faster, standard aspect results. Choose Sora-2 Pro if you need the additional sizes (1024x1792, 1792x1024) or higher fidelity. Always match your input image to the exact resolution you select.

faqItems.question: How do I make my image match the required video size?
faqItems.answer: Use Option1 - Pad image (ResizeAndPadImage) to letterbox and preserve the entire image, or use Option 2 - Crop image to fill the frame edge-to-edge. Check the result with PreviewImage before running the API. The API will reject mismatched sizes.

faqItems.question: Can I run text-to-video without providing an image?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Bypass the image branch (select those nodes and press Ctrl-B) so OpenAIVideoSora2 receives only your text prompt. You can re-enable the image path later to switch back to image-to-video.

faqItems.question: How is audio handled?
faqItems.answer: When available, the OpenAIVideoSora2 API returns a video that includes synchronized audio. SaveVideo writes the received video file to disk. If the API response is silent, your output will not contain audio.

faqItems.question: I’m getting network or authorization errors. What should I check?
faqItems.answer: Confirm you’re running in a secure environment that allows localhost/127.0.0.1, your API credentials are set in the OpenAIVideoSora2 node, and your firewall/proxy isn’t blocking the request. See the partner node overview and pricing links in the MarkdownNote.

howToUse: Load the "Wan2.7: Text to Video" workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the Wan2TextToVideoApi and SaveVideo nodes are present and connected.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use Wan2TextToVideoApi?

faqItems.question: How long can the generated videos be?

faqItems.question: How can I improve lip sync quality?

faqItems.question: Can I reproduce the same result reliably?

This ComfyUI workflow uses GrokImageNode to generate images from text prompts via the Grok Imagine API, then saves the results with SaveImage. It’s designed for cases where you want clean, readable text inside images (signage, posters, UI mockups) alongside strong visual detail. The pipeline is intentionally minimal—prompt in, image out—so you can focus on prompt craft and rapid iteration.

Technically, GrokImageNode sends your prompt and any parameters exposed by the node (such as aspect ratio/dimensions, seed or image count, depending on your build) to the remote Grok Imagine model, returning a generated image tensor to ComfyUI. The SaveImage node then writes that image to ComfyUI’s output directory using your chosen filename prefix. The result is a straightforward, reliable text-to-image flow that leverages an external API for quality and better text rendering, while keeping all the convenience of ComfyUI’s node-based workspace.
howToUse: Open ComfyUI and load the workflow JSON for “Grok Imagine Image Quality: Generation.” Ensure the GrokImageNode custom node is installed and available.
Open GrokImageNode and add your API key (either directly in the node or via the method documented for the node on your system). Confirm you have network access.

Enter a clear prompt in GrokImageNode. If your build exposes options like aspect ratio/dimensions, seed, or image count, set them to match your target layout (e.g., 16:9 for thumbnails, 1:1 for square social posts).
Open the SaveImage node and set a filename prefix and output format if available. Leave defaults if you’re fine saving into ComfyUI’s standard output folder.
Click Queue/Execute to run the workflow. The GrokImageNode will request an image from the Grok Imagine API and pass it to SaveImage for writing to disk.

Review the output. If you need sharper or more accurate embedded text, refine your prompt (keep embedded text short and in quotes) and adjust parameters (like aspect ratio or seed, if available), then re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Poster, flyer, or social graphic concepts with prominent, readable headlines
UI mockups and app screens that require legible interface text in context
Product packaging and label explorations where typography matters
YouTube thumbnails or blog headers needing bold, crisp text overlays
Signage and billboard ideation with clear, high-contrast type

faqItems.question: Does this run locally or require an internet connection?
faqItems.answer: GrokImageNode calls the Grok Imagine API, so it requires an active internet connection and a valid API key. The generation happens remotely; saving occurs locally via SaveImage.

faqItems.question: How can I improve text accuracy inside the image?
faqItems.answer: Keep embedded text concise, place it in quotes in your prompt, and specify context (e.g., “street sign,” “poster,” or “UI screen”). Choose an aspect ratio that matches the intended layout and avoid overly long or complex sentences.

faqItems.question: Where are my images saved?
faqItems.answer: SaveImage writes files to ComfyUI’s output directory, using the filename prefix and format you set in the node. Open the node to adjust the prefix, format, or subfolder if those options are available in your build.

faqItems.question: Can I get consistent results across runs?
faqItems.answer: If your GrokImageNode build exposes a seed parameter, set and reuse the same seed to help with reproducibility. Also keep prompts and other parameters identical between runs.

6c3fa01b5d73.title: 3x3 Contact Sheet
6c3fa01b5d73.description:
Generate a 3x3 grid of image variations from a simple prompt and reference image using Nano Banana. 

Pick your favorite frame from the grid, then recreate it as a standalone high-quality image while maintaining character and outfit consistency.

Great for concept exploration, pose variations, camera angles, outfit ideas, and fast visual inspiration without generating each image individually.
6c3fa01b5d73.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow to generate a 3x3 contact sheet of prompt-based image variations, then recreate any cell as a consistent, high-quality standalone image.
6c3fa01b5d73.extendedDescription:
This workflow builds a fast 3x3 contact sheet of image ideas from a single prompt and a subject reference image, then lets you turn your favorite cell into a standalone image with consistent character and outfit details. The 3x3 Contact Sheet group fans out nine variations through the GeminiNanoBanana2V2 generator (wrapped in a CustomCombo), then assembles them into a grid and saves the result. StringReplace is used to keep text inputs flexible and to label or organize outputs, while LoadImage and SaveImage handle your references and final files. Helpful notes inside the graph are provided via MarkdownNote nodes.

After reviewing the grid, the Select Image group makes it easy to target one frame for re-generation at higher fidelity while reusing the same subject/reference inputs and prompt. This preserves the identity and outfit cues you established up front, so the single image matches what you saw in the grid. It’s a quick, reliable way to explore pose, angle, and styling options without iterating each image manually.
howToUse: Load the workflow and locate the two groups: 3x3 Contact Sheet and Select Image. In the Contact Sheet group, open the LoadImage node(s) and add your subject reference (and any optional outfit/style references).

Enter a concise prompt describing the concept, pose, or scene in the GeminiNanoBanana2V2/CustomCombo section. Leave the Select Image group bypassed and run only the 3x3 Contact Sheet group to generate the grid.
Review the saved 3x3 grid output (saved via the SaveImage node). Pick the cell you want to turn into a standalone image.
Enable the Select Image group: select all nodes in the Select Image group and remove bypass (Ctrl+B). Bypass the 3x3 Contact Sheet group so it doesn’t run again.

Use the Select Image group’s controls to choose the target frame (by index or position, as provided in the group). Keep your prompt and reference images the same to maintain character/outfit consistency.

Run the Select Image group. The workflow recreates the chosen frame as a separate image and saves it with SaveImage. Iterate by adjusting the prompt or StringReplace inputs if you want quick variants (e.g., different outfits or camera angles) and rerun.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid character exploration: test poses, camera angles, and expressions from a single subject reference.
Outfit and styling boards: compare different looks or accessories in one grid before committing to a final render.
Storyboarding and thumbnails: block out nine composition ideas to guide a final shot.
Product or prop ideation: explore alternative materials, finishes, or backdrops quickly.
Client reviews and moodboards: present multiple options at once, then finalize the selected frame.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow keep character and outfit consistency when I recreate a single image?
faqItems.answer: The Select Image group reuses the same subject/reference image(s) and prompt you used for the grid. By feeding those back into the GeminiNanoBanana2V2 generator, the standalone image aligns closely with the chosen cell’s look and outfit.

faqItems.question: Where are my images saved?
faqItems.answer: By default, SaveImage writes to ComfyUI/output (or the folder set in the SaveImage node). The contact sheet and the final single image will be saved according to that configuration.

faqItems.question: My 3x3 results look too similar (or too random). How can I adjust variation?
faqItems.answer: Use the controls inside the 3x3 Contact Sheet group (e.g., seed or randomness parameters inside the CustomCombo/GeminiNanoBanana2V2 node) to increase or decrease variation. Keep the core prompt stable for consistency, and use StringReplace to quickly test small prompt tweaks across the grid.

faqItems.question: Can I swap models or references?
faqItems.answer: Yes. You can replace the subject/reference images in LoadImage to change identity/outfit cues. GeminiNanoBanana2V2 is the model used here; if you have compatible alternatives, you can substitute them in the CustomCombo section, then test a new grid.

6d0042d2f554.title: Krea 2 LoRAs Showcase

6d0042d2f554.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow is a hands-on showcase for six Krea 2 LoRAs, organized into clear groups: Nose Invisibles LoRA, VHS Analog LoRA, RetroAnime LoRA, Commodore 64 Style LoRA, NeonDrip LoRA, and PSX Low Poly LoRA. Technically, each group encapsulates a LoRA application path that adapts your base checkpoint at inference time, with controls for LoRA strength and prompt inputs. The workflow wires shared inputs to each branch so you can keep prompts consistent while varying LoRA weights. Custom nodes (IDs: 33681612-45f1-4901-b3fd-b83f0b48c9c0, 376d014e-b4fd-430e-8201-70629e00857f, 68a3ded7-ee8c-4dc0-8c96-128fdcdd4ef8, 307cc882-db9e-4f8c-93c5-130e09e2c305, fd7b28a7-8ec8-44ef-ad93-dff7afc6086b, 91c1ae42-2e94-4f8e-b10f-25415ac0b64e) bundle the LoRA logic per style group, while SaveImageAdvanced handles filenames, folders, and embedding ComfyUI metadata for reproducibility. This structure is ideal for quick A/B testing of style intensity, prompt phrasing, and seed changes without re-wiring your graph.
howToUse: Load the Krea 2 LoRAs Showcase workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the base model and VAE paths are valid. Ensure the Krea 2 LoRA files referenced in each group are available on your system.

Enter your positive prompt and (optionally) a negative prompt. Include any trigger words relevant to the selected style (e.g., retro, VHS, scanlines, low poly, neon, anime) to help the LoRA steer results.

Pick one or more style groups to run (Nose Invisibles, VHS Analog, RetroAnime, Commodore 64 Style, NeonDrip, PSX Low Poly). Adjust the LoRA strength in each branch: start around 0.6–1.0 for strong style LoRAs and 0.2–0.5 for corrective LoRAs like Nose Invisibles.
Set your seed and sampler-related parameters where exposed in the workflow. Keeping the same seed and steps across branches makes comparisons more meaningful.
Queue and run the workflow. Each branch will render its variant and SaveImageAdvanced will write images to the configured output directory with metadata for easy tracking.
Review the outputs side-by-side, then iterate: nudge LoRA strength, refine prompts, or change the seed. Use SaveImageAdvanced’s filename pattern to keep versions organized.
suggestedUseCases: Creative direction: audition multiple aesthetics quickly to choose a style direction for a project.
Styleboards and client reviews: generate consistent, labeled variants for clear side-by-side comparisons.
Character/portrait cleanup: apply Nose Invisibles at low strength to subtly refine facial features while preserving style.
Retro game and low-poly concepting: explore PSX Low Poly and Commodore 64 looks for mockups, covers, or UI elements.
Prompt testing: keep style constant while adjusting prompts to learn which phrasing yields the best results.

faqItems.question: Which base model should I use with these Krea 2 LoRAs?
faqItems.answer: Match the LoRA’s intended base (e.g., SD 1.5 vs. SDXL). Check the LoRA’s card or filename and load a compatible base checkpoint in the workflow. Mixing SDXL LoRAs with SD 1.5 (or vice versa) will produce poor results.

faqItems.question: How do I add my own Krea 2 LoRA to this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Duplicate one of the existing style groups, swap the LoRA file path in that group’s loader, and keep the wiring to SaveImageAdvanced. Reuse the same prompt and seed to compare it fairly with the existing branches.

faqItems.question: My images look over-stylized or washed out. What should I tweak?
faqItems.answer: Lower the LoRA strength, add targeted negatives (e.g., oversaturated, heavy artifacts, extra noise), and moderate CFG/steps. For subtle looks, keep style LoRAs below 0.8 and corrective LoRAs (like Nose Invisibles) around 0.2–0.4.

faqItems.question: Where do my images go and what metadata is saved?
faqItems.answer: SaveImageAdvanced writes to the output folder you configured and embeds ComfyUI metadata (prompt, seed, and node parameters) into the file. This lets you reproduce or adjust settings later with confidence.

6fec31e40f4a.title: LTX 2.3 - Anime2Real
6fec31e40f4a.description: This experimental workflow will take Anime characters and try to make them realistic using an LTX 2.3 IC LoRA trained by Alisson Pereira.
6fec31e40f4a.metaDescription: Turn anime video into realistic footage in ComfyUI using LTX 2.3 IC LoRA. Load, trim frames, process per-frame, and recombine with Video Helper Suite.
6fec31e40f4a.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow, LTX 2.3 - Anime2Real, demonstrates how to convert anime footage into realistic-looking video using a frame-by-frame image-to-image process. It relies on Video Helper Suite nodes to handle video I/O: VHS_LoadVideo extracts frames from your source clip, and VHS_VideoCombine stitches the processed frames back into a video file. The core transformation happens in a custom processing block (shown in the workflow as node 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3), which applies the LTX 2.3 IC LoRA (trained by Alisson Pereira) to push each frame toward photorealism.

Technically, the pipeline loads your clip, trims or limits the frame range with controls like skip_first_frames and frame_count, then feeds each frame through the LoRA-powered image-to-image pass before recombining the output frames. Because this is an experimental anime-to-realism mapping, results will vary with source quality, lighting, and character design. The design keeps the flow simple—no manual frame extraction or external editors—so you can iterate quickly on parameters and see how they affect temporal consistency and realism.
howToUse: Open the LTX 2.3 - Anime2Real workflow in ComfyUI and ensure the LTX 2.3 IC LoRA is installed and referenced by the custom processing node (2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3).
In VHS_LoadVideo, set your source video path. Use skip_first_frames to trim the start of the clip and frame_count to limit how many frames are processed after the skip.
Optionally adjust other VHS_LoadVideo controls (e.g., force_rate to normalize FPS) so the clip duration and frame pacing match your target output.
Review the custom processing node’s parameters (if exposed), such as LoRA strength or denoise-level. Lower intensity tends to preserve anime identity; higher intensity pushes stronger realism.
In VHS_VideoCombine, set the target frame rate and output path. If your workflow includes audio handling, provide the extracted audio path to remux sound into the final video.

Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the output for flicker or over-processing; iterate by adjusting frame_count, LoRA strength/denoise (if available), or FPS to balance realism and temporal stability.
suggestedUseCases: Converting short anime clips into realistic references for concept art or previsualization.
Creating photoreal style tests for character design or cosplay planning.
Generating realistic b-roll variations of stylized footage for music videos or edits.
Building study material to compare stylized and realistic interpretations of the same scene.

faqItems.question: What models or files do I need before running this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You need the LTX 2.3 IC LoRA (trained by Alisson Pereira) installed in your ComfyUI models/loras directory (or wherever your LoRA loader expects it). The workflow’s custom processing node (2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3) should point to that LoRA. Ensure any base model or sampler settings required by that node are properly configured.

faqItems.question: How do skip_first_frames and frame_count affect processing?
faqItems.answer: skip_first_frames tells VHS_LoadVideo to ignore a set number of frames at the start. frame_count defines how many frames to process after the skip. Together, they let you target a precise segment of your clip for conversion, which speeds iteration and testing.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or instability between frames?
faqItems.answer: Keep settings consistent across frames, avoid overly high denoise or LoRA strength (if those controls are available), and test shorter segments first. Stable input (clear faces, steady camera) helps. If the node exposes a fixed seed or temporal options, use them for more consistent per-frame outputs.

faqItems.question: Can I keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: Yes, if your workflow extracts audio in VHS_LoadVideo and your VHS_VideoCombine node is set up to accept an audio path, you can remux the original audio into the final video. If audio inputs aren’t present in your version, export audio separately and remux with a video editor or ffmpeg.

7016f027bcf1.title: Wan 2.2 14B First-Last Frame to Video
7016f027bcf1.description: Generate smooth video transitions by defining start and end frames.
7016f027bcf1.metaDescription: Breakthrough FLF2V for Wan 2.2: generate smooth, prompt-guided videos that exactly match your first and last frames in ComfyUI.
7016f027bcf1.extendedDescription:
This workflow introduces First–Last Frame to Video (FLF2V) for Wan 2.2 (14B), a conditioning method that lets you specify both the opening and closing frames and have the model synthesize a smooth, prompt-guided journey between them. Instead of expanding from a single keyframe or relying on optical-flow interpolation, the WanFirstLastFrameToVideo node enforces boundary conditions at t=0 and t=1 inside the diffusion process. That means the start and end images are respected as ground truths while the model generates new, coherent in-betweens that follow your text prompt.

Under the hood, the workflow loads Wan 2.2 with UNETLoader, a compatible text encoder via CLIPLoader (UMT5 XXL FP8 scaled), and VAE components, then runs KSamplerAdvanced with an SD3-style schedule (ModelSamplingSD3). An optional “lightning” 4-step LoRA can dramatically speed up renders at a modest quality trade-off. The result is a practical, reproducible pipeline in ComfyUI that improves on prior image-to-video approaches by jointly conditioning on both endpoints, reducing identity drift, preserving scene intent, and producing transitions that feel authored rather than warped.
howToUse: Load models (Step 1 - Load models): Ensure Wan 2.2 weights are available for UNETLoader and VAE/CLIP components are set. If using the provided UMT5 XXL FP8 scaled text encoder, point CLIPLoader to umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors.

Choose a performance preset: Box-select the fp8_scaled group and press Ctrl + B to enable it. Optionally enable the fp8_scaled + 4steps LoRA group (via LoraLoaderModelOnly) for much faster sampling, but expect some quality loss. If enabling one, disable the other to avoid double-loading.
Upload first and last frames: In Step 2.1 and Step 2.2, use LoadImage to set the start_image and end_image. Use matched aspect ratios for best spatial consistency.

Configure size and length: In Step 3 - Video size & length, set resolution, total frames, and FPS according to your VRAM. Defaults are conservative for low-VRAM GPUs; on a 24GB card (e.g., RTX 4090D), 640×640 is typical for fp8.

Author the prompt (Step 4 - Prompt): Use CLIPTextEncode to enter your positive prompt (and optional negatives). Keep prompt intent consistent with both endpoint images to minimize identity or style jumps.

Sampling and run: ModelSamplingSD3 sets the expected schedule for Wan 2.2. Adjust KSamplerAdvanced settings (steps/CFG/seed) as needed. Then run the graph: VAEDecode reconstructs frames, CreateVideo assembles them, and SaveVideo writes the final file.
suggestedUseCases: Creative morphs and title or logo reveals where the end state must precisely match a designed frame.
Storyboard-to-animatic transitions: lock first/last beat frames and let the model generate convincing in-betweens.
Style-evolving shots (e.g., painting-to-real, day-to-night) that preserve identity constraints at both ends.
Before/after product or character transformations without relying on brittle optical flow.
Data-driven demonstrations where known boundary conditions are required (e.g., prototype A to prototype B).

faqItems.question: How is FLF2V different from frame interpolation or single-frame image-to-video?
faqItems.answer: FLF2V is generative. It conditions the diffusion process on both the start and end images concurrently, so the model synthesizes new, coherent midframes rather than warping pixels between frames. Compared with single-frame I2V, it reduces identity drift and guarantees the final frame matches your target image.

faqItems.question: What are the hardware and speed considerations?
faqItems.answer: The fp8_scaled configuration significantly lowers VRAM use. As a reference from the author’s notes, 640×640 uses about 84% VRAM on an RTX 4090D 24GB. Enabling the 4-steps lightning LoRA can speed up renders further, but expect some quality and temporal consistency trade-offs.

faqItems.question: Do I need a specific text encoder or sampler setup?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The workflow uses CLIPLoader with a compatible text encoder (e.g., UMT5 XXL FP8 scaled) and sets ModelSamplingSD3 to match Wan 2.2’s expected schedule. KSamplerAdvanced then handles steps, CFG, and seed. Using the provided components as wired ensures stable, reproducible results.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the motion consistent with my prompt and endpoints?
faqItems.answer: Use start/end images with matching aspect ratios and related content, keep the prompt intent aligned with both frames, and avoid conflicting style cues. Increase steps or CFG for sharper adherence, and reduce resolution or total frames if you encounter VRAM pressure.

70dea50257fa.title: LTXV Text to Video
70dea50257fa.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate text-to-video with the LTX-0.9.5 model. Set size, frames, and sampler, then render and save high-quality clips from detailed prompts.
70dea50257fa.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a written prompt into a short video using the LTX-0.9.5 text-to-video checkpoint. It starts by loading the model and text encoder with CheckpointLoaderSimple and CLIPLoader, then converts your prompt and optional negative prompt into embeddings via CLIPTextEncode. Those embeddings are adapted for video with LTXVConditioning so the model can synthesize temporally coherent motion from your text description.

Next, EmptyLTXVLatentVideo defines the canvas of your clip—frame count, width/height, FPS, and seed—while LTXVScheduler and the Custom sampler block (SamplerCustom + KSamplerSelect) drive the denoising process across all frames. After sampling, VAEDecode turns latent frames into RGB images. CreateVideo stitches the frame sequence into a playable file, and SaveVideo writes it to disk. The workflow is organized into clear groups (Step1 - Load models, Step2 - Video size, Step3 - Prompt, Custom sampler) so you always know where to adjust models, resolution, timing, and sampling.

What makes this useful is the control you get at each stage: descriptive prompting (via CLIPTextEncode) for content and motion; precise duration and aspect (via EmptyLTXVLatentVideo); and predictable results with seeds and sampler choices (KSamplerSelect). The author notes that LTX-0.9.5 benefits from long, detailed prompts—concise prompts often produce weaker results—so plan to describe subjects, actions, scene context, and camera motion for best quality.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then in Step1 - Load models select your LTX-0.9.5 checkpoint with CheckpointLoaderSimple and load the matching CLIP with CLIPLoader. If a model path is missing, download the checkpoint and point the node to it.
Open Step2 - Video size and set EmptyLTXVLatentVideo: choose width/height (use multiples of 16), FPS, number of frames, and a seed. Start small (e.g., 512×288, 16–32 frames) to iterate quickly.

In Step3 - Prompt, enter a long, descriptive positive prompt in CLIPTextEncode and, optionally, a negative prompt to suppress artifacts (e.g., the provided example with "low quality" and "motion smear"). Include subject, setting, motion, and camera cues.

In Custom sampler, keep the default LTXVScheduler and choose a sampler in KSamplerSelect. Set steps and CFG in SamplerCustom. As a starting point, try moderate steps and CFG, and lock a seed for reproducibility.

Queue the workflow. Inspect the preview frames and the generated video. If results are bland or unstable, lengthen and refine your prompt, adjust negatives, tweak steps/CFG, or try a different sampler.
When satisfied, configure CreateVideo (FPS/quality) and SaveVideo (filename/path) to export the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Concept animation for storyboards and previsualization
Short product or feature teaser loops for social posts
Atmospheric B‑roll backgrounds for motion design
Character motion exploration and style tests
Quick visual ideation for pitches and mood boards

faqItems.question: Why does the model prefer long prompts?
faqItems.answer: LTX-0.9.5 relies on rich textual conditioning to drive both appearance and motion. Brief prompts often lack detail about subject, setting, and dynamics, leading to generic or unstable video. Describe who/what, where, lighting, motion, and camera behavior.

faqItems.question: What do CLIPLoader and CheckpointLoaderSimple each load?
faqItems.answer: CheckpointLoaderSimple loads the LTX-0.9.5 text-to-video checkpoint. CLIPLoader loads the CLIP text encoder used by CLIPTextEncode to turn your text and negative text into embeddings for LTXVConditioning.

faqItems.question: How do I change video length and smoothness?
faqItems.answer: Length is frames divided by FPS (set in EmptyLTXVLatentVideo and CreateVideo). Increase frames for longer clips. Smoother motion often benefits from more frames and careful prompting; you can also test different samplers in KSamplerSelect and adjust steps in SamplerCustom.

faqItems.question: I get artifacts or motion smear—how can I reduce them?
faqItems.answer: Add targeted negatives (e.g., "motion smear, motion artifacts"), try a different sampler, and tune steps/CFG in SamplerCustom. Reducing resolution can help stability; once the motion looks good, scale up cautiously. Ensure width/height are multiples of 16.

70e6b211c5ff.title: Seedance 2.0 Reference to Video - Concept Art + Stop Motion Style
70e6b211c5ff.description: A useful prompt and example images for generating stop motion style shorts with concept art.
70e6b211c5ff.metaDescription: Turn concept art into a stop‑motion‑style short with LoadImage, ByteDance2ReferenceNode, and SaveVideo in ComfyUI. Fast reference‑to‑video with consistent style.
70e6b211c5ff.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single piece of concept art into a short, stop‑motion‑style video. It uses LoadImage to bring your reference artwork into the graph, feeds it into ByteDance2ReferenceNode to synthesize motion while preserving the look of the original design, and then encodes the result with SaveVideo. The ByteDance2ReferenceNode is the engine of the pipeline: it performs reference‑to‑video generation by conditioning on your image so the character, style, and palette remain consistent across frames while introducing controlled movement.

Technically, the workflow keeps things simple and focused on iteration. You supply a clean, well‑framed reference image; ByteDance2ReferenceNode generates a sequence of frames guided by the reference, and SaveVideo writes those frames to an MP4 at a frame rate you choose. To emphasize a stop‑motion aesthetic, you typically use a lower FPS (for example, 8–12) and modest motion magnitude so changes appear stepwise and tactile. Because the setup is lightweight (LoadImage → ByteDance2ReferenceNode → SaveVideo), it’s easy to re‑run with different reference images or parameter tweaks to dial in timing, motion intensity, and framing.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the LoadImage node and select your concept art (PNG/JPG). Prefer a clean, centered subject with a clear silhouette.
Verify resolution and aspect ratio. If needed, crop your image externally so the subject fills the frame; this helps the reference keep details stable.

Open ByteDance2ReferenceNode and adjust its exposed parameters. Typical controls include how long the clip runs (frames/duration), motion amount, and how strongly the result adheres to the reference image. Start with modest motion so the stop‑motion look feels deliberate.
Open SaveVideo and set a filename/prefix and frames per second. For a stop‑motion vibe, try 8–12 FPS; for smoother motion, raise FPS. Ensure the node is connected to the generated frames.
Queue and run the workflow. Review the output video, then iterate: nudge the motion amount, tweak duration, or swap the reference image until you get the desired style.
Optionally export multiple takes: keep the same reference but vary FPS (e.g., 8, 10, 12) and motion intensity to compare which combination best sells the stop‑motion effect.
suggestedUseCases: Pitch and previs: turn static character or prop concept art into quick motion tests for direction alignment.
Stop‑motion‑style idents and bumpers for social media or title cards.
Stylized animatics: add subtle motion to a single illustration to convey mood without full animation.
Character turntables with slight, jittery movement to audition materials, patterns, or silhouettes.
Mood loops for backgrounds or scene elements where a handcrafted, tactile feel is preferred.

faqItems.question: What kind of reference image works best?
faqItems.answer: Use a high‑quality image with a clear subject, strong silhouette, and minimal background clutter. Center the subject, avoid heavy motion blur, and keep lighting consistent—these factors help the node preserve appearance across frames.

faqItems.question: How do I enhance the stop‑motion look?
faqItems.answer: Lower the FPS in SaveVideo (around 8–12), keep motion amount modest, and avoid excessive smoothing. Shorter clips with small, discrete movements feel more like physical stop‑motion than long, fluid camera moves.

faqItems.question: How do I control video length and size?
faqItems.answer: Set clip length via the duration/frames controls in ByteDance2ReferenceNode and set playback speed with FPS in SaveVideo. Use an image resolution that fits your GPU memory; larger frames cost more VRAM and time.

faqItems.question: Why does the subject drift or deform between frames?
faqItems.answer: This often happens when motion is set too high or the image has weak structure. Reduce motion amount, use a cleaner/higher‑res reference, and increase how strongly the node adheres to the reference if that control is available.

723870e886d7.title: Product Placement
723870e886d7.description: Swap products into a reference scene while preserving composition and lighting. Generates a final product image and an automatic video prompt for creating polished product videos.
723870e886d7.metaDescription: Swap products into a scene and auto-generate a Kling 3.0 video prompt. Create consistent product stills and motion clips with Nano Banana 2 and Gemini 3.1 Pro.
723870e886d7.extendedDescription:
This Product Placement workflow swaps your product into a reference scene while keeping the shot’s original composition and lighting cues. It centers on the GeminiNanoBanana2 node running the Nano Banana 2 checkpoint, which takes the scene image as conditioning and blends in your product input to produce a coherent, scene-aware still. With BatchImagesNode you can run the same scene across multiple SKUs, and PreviewImage lets you quickly QC placement, scale, and seed variations. The workflow is organized under the Products group for easy reuse in product photography pipelines.

Beyond the hero still, the workflow automatically drafts a video prompt for motion. The GeminiNode (Gemini-3.1-Pro) analyzes the final image and generates a concise, Kling-ready description and shot guidance. That text—visible in PreviewAny—feeds into KlingVideoNode (Kling 3.0) to render a short product clip that follows the look established by the still. SaveVideo finalizes the output so you leave with both a polished product image and an on-brand motion teaser.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm models/services are available: Nano Banana 2 checkpoint for GeminiNanoBanana2, Gemini-3.1-Pro access for GeminiNode, and Kling 3.0 for KlingVideoNode.
Import your reference scene with LoadImage. Import your product as a transparent PNG or pre-cut image with LoadImage. For multiple SKUs, connect a folder to BatchImagesNode to iterate products.

Open GeminiNanoBanana2: connect the scene and product inputs, then set seed and strength parameters appropriate for your look. Adjust product scale/offset/rotation controls in this node to align the item naturally in the scene. Run and inspect the result via PreviewImage.
Iterate placement: nudge product transform and try a few seeds to land perspective and size. Keep strength moderate to preserve scene composition while allowing the product to blend with context.

Auto-generate motion prompt: route the final still into GeminiNode (Gemini-3.1-Pro) and run it to produce a Kling-friendly prompt and shot suggestion. View and optionally tweak the text in PreviewAny before proceeding.

Create the clip: pass the finalized prompt (and optionally the still as an init/reference input if exposed) to KlingVideoNode. Set duration and resolution, render, preview, then use SaveVideo to export the final video.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce A/B testing: drop multiple product variants into the same lifestyle scene and pick the best-performing hero still and teaser clip.
Rapid localization: reuse a single scene while swapping region-specific packaging or labels across a batch.
Social promos: turn a product still into a short motion teaser with consistent framing and brand look.
Catalog refresh: update older scenes with new product versions without re-shooting.
Marketplace compliance: standardize angles and backgrounds while showcasing different SKUs.

faqItems.question: Do I need a cutout or mask for the product?
faqItems.answer: A transparent PNG or pre-cut product image works best for clean placement. This workflow assumes you supply an already isolated product via LoadImage or BatchImagesNode.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow preserve composition and lighting cues?
faqItems.answer: GeminiNanoBanana2 conditions on the reference scene (using the Nano Banana 2 checkpoint), which helps the placement respect the scene’s framing and visual context. You can fine-tune blending via the node’s strength and seed to balance fidelity and integration.

faqItems.question: Can I edit the automatically generated video prompt?
faqItems.answer: Yes. GeminiNode (Gemini-3.1-Pro) drafts the Kling prompt, which you can review in PreviewAny. Adjust the text before sending it to KlingVideoNode to better match brand tone, pacing, or camera directions.

faqItems.question: What if I don’t have access to Kling 3.0?
faqItems.answer: You can still use the workflow for high-quality stills. The image path (LoadImage → GeminiNanoBanana2 → PreviewImage) runs independently. Add Kling later to extend the still into motion.

72448fe4e4b5.extendedDescription:

736ab92b893a.title: Wan 2.2 5B Fun Control
736ab92b893a.description: Multi-condition video control with pose, depth, and edge guidance. Compact 5B size for experimental development.
736ab92b893a.metaDescription: Tutorial: Use Wan 2.2 5B Fun Control in ComfyUI for edge-guided text-to-video and image/video-to-video with KSampler, ModelSamplingSD3, and Canny control.
736ab92b893a.extendedDescription:
Wan 2.2 5B Fun Control is a compact, multi-condition video diffusion workflow that demonstrates how to steer motion and composition using control signals—most notably edges via the Canny node—while generating short clips from text, images, or reference video. The core of the graph is the Wan22FunControlToVideo node, which fuses your prompt (from CLIPTextEncode), optional start image or video (LoadImage, LoadVideo + GetVideoComponents), and control maps (Canny) into a temporally coherent latent sequence. A UNETLoader loads the wan2.2_fun_control_5B_bf16.safetensors diffusion model and pairs it with VAELoader (wan2.2_vae) and CLIPLoader; sampling is driven by KSampler using ModelSamplingSD3 to match Wan 2.2’s scheduler. VAEDecode converts latents to frames, CreateVideo packs frames to a clip, and SaveVideo writes the final file.

Technically, the workflow is organized into clear groups: Step1 - Load models, Step 2 - Start_image, Step3 - Prompt, and Step 3 - Control video and video preprocessing. Edge guidance is prepared by the Canny node (low/high thresholds) and passed to Wan22FunControlToVideo to anchor structure and motion. You can preview intermediate frames with PreviewImage, then finalize your result with CreateVideo and SaveVideo. While Wan 2.2 Fun Control supports multiple conditions (e.g., depth and pose), this template wires up edge control by default; you can extend it by adding depth/pose nodes and routing their outputs to Wan22FunControlToVideo. Note: at only 5B parameters, Wan 2.2 Fun Control trades fidelity for speed and accessibility—expect softer details and lean on strong control signals, simpler scenes, and shorter clips for best results.
howToUse: Load the workflow and models: In Step1 - Load models, point UNETLoader to wan2.2_fun_control_5B_bf16.safetensors, VAELoader to wan2.2_vae.safetensors, and initialize CLIPLoader. Ensure ModelSamplingSD3 is connected to KSampler.

Choose your input mode: For text-to-video, leave Start_image and LoadVideo disconnected. For image-to-video, add a source frame via LoadImage (Step 2 - Start_image). For video-controlled generation, import a clip with LoadVideo and split fps/frames using GetVideoComponents.

Set control guidance: In Step 3 - Control video and video preprocessing, tune the Canny node thresholds (low/high) to get clean edges, then feed its output to Wan22FunControlToVideo. If you want no edge guidance, bypass/disconnect the Canny input.

Author your prompts: In Step3 - Prompt, enter a descriptive positive prompt with motion cues and style, and a robust negative prompt to suppress artifacts (e.g., low quality, jpeg artifacts, extra fingers). CLIPTextEncode outputs drive Wan22FunControlToVideo.

Configure sampling and timing: In KSampler, set steps and CFG (start with 20–30 steps, CFG 3–6) and fix a seed for repeatability. In CreateVideo (or within Wan22FunControlToVideo if exposed), set fps (24 is typical) and the desired frame count/duration.

Run and export: Execute the graph. Inspect PreviewImage for a few frames; if edges are too rigid or too loose, adjust Canny thresholds or control strength in Wan22FunControlToVideo. When satisfied, CreateVideo and SaveVideo will write your final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard previsualization: Quickly block out camera and character motion from text with edge guidance to hold composition.
Logo or product motion sketches: Use a clean silhouette (Canny from a start image) to generate short animated reveals.
Pose/motion studies from reference video: Load a clip, extract edges, and reimagine the scene in a new style while preserving movement.
Concept teasers for environments: Simple pans or parallax-style shots steered by edge maps for consistent geometry.
Educational demos: Teach control conditioning by toggling Canny on/off and comparing results with the same prompt.

faqItems.question: Why do my results look soft or low-detail?
faqItems.answer: Wan 2.2 Fun Control uses a 5B-parameter model prioritized for compactness and experimentation. Improve perceived quality by keeping scenes simple, using strong and clean Canny edges, reducing clip length, increasing sampling steps moderately (e.g., 20–30), and lowering CFG (3–6) to reduce oversaturation and noise.

faqItems.question: Can I use depth or pose instead of edges?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the model supports multiple conditions. This template wires Canny by default; to use depth or pose, add appropriate nodes (e.g., a depth estimator or a pose detector) and feed their outputs into the corresponding inputs of Wan22FunControlToVideo.

faqItems.question: What frame rate and duration should I use?
faqItems.answer: The model was trained with clips at 24 FPS and up to around 121 frames. Matching 24 FPS and keeping clips short (2–5 seconds) generally yields more stable motion and fewer artifacts with this 5B model.

faqItems.question: How do I get more consistent motion from a reference video?
faqItems.answer: Load your source via LoadVideo, route it through GetVideoComponents to preserve fps and frame order, and generate a clean edge map with Canny. Increase control strength in Wan22FunControlToVideo if available, and lower CFG to reduce hallucinations. Using a fixed seed helps with reproducibility.

Technically, the workflow routes your image through a small set of custom utility nodes (IDs: d33c1791-dfd2-4102-8540-aa63e4434cd2, f2228dc9-64e8-43b1-a4ca-b8a57eed8f64, e3dd2fcb-0e5e-47a8-963b-adea96749eb0, 601fd020-3eba-4b24-b15f-a2a9c0307d3a, eaabb89a-2cd6-4960-ad44-1b152bff77c1, 86a340d1-ba23-44b6-8470-6b3d64167d65) that handle layout and final compositing to a 16:9 frame, with Reroute nodes keeping the graph clean. GeminiNode is used to synthesize or refine brief shot notes from your text prompt (and, if supported by your Gemini node variant, the loaded image). Notes are displayed in PreviewAny so you can copy them into production docs; some layouts may also render text onto the frame if that branch is enabled. Because it uses no diffusion sampler, iteration is fast and predictable—ideal for blocking sequences or creating polished hero frames from your own art.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and verify that GeminiNode is installed and configured (API key and model selection as required by your Gemini node).
Open the LoadImage node and select your sketch, thumbnail, or keyframe. For best results, use art that roughly fits a 16:9 crop.
Set the target canvas size in the PrimitiveNode (e.g., width 1920 and height 1080) to enforce a 16:9 output. Adjust any other exposed primitives such as margins or label strings if present.
In GeminiNode, enter a short description of the shot (e.g., camera, action, tone). If your Gemini node supports image input, connect the image to it for context; otherwise provide only text.
Queue the workflow. Review both the composed frame and the generated notes in PreviewAny. Tweak the prompt, crop, or canvas settings and re-queue until it looks right.
When satisfied, set your output path/file pattern in SaveImage and run the graph to export the final 16:9 board image. Repeat with new images to build your sequence.
suggestedUseCases: Blocking story beats for an animatic with consistent 16:9 frames and concise shot notes.
Creating hero keyframes for pitch decks or styleframes sourced from your own concept art.
Pre-visualizing camera moves and composition on top of existing thumbnails.
Team reviews: quickly standardize and share frames with accompanying written notes.

faqItems.question: Do I need a diffusion model or checkpoint for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No. This workflow does not generate new imagery. It standardizes your existing art to a 16:9 frame and uses GeminiNode to produce optional shot notes, so iteration is fast and consistent.

faqItems.question: How do I change the output resolution or aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Update the width and height values in the PrimitiveNode. For 16:9, use sizes like 1920x1080 or 1280x720. If you switch to another aspect ratio, ensure any layout or crop nodes downstream are adjusted accordingly.

faqItems.question: Which Gemini model should I use in GeminiNode?
faqItems.answer: Use the model your Gemini node supports that balances speed and quality for note generation (for example, a ‘Pro’ model for richer notes or a ‘Lite’ model for faster iterations). Configure this inside GeminiNode along with your API key.

faqItems.question: Can I batch multiple images?
faqItems.answer: This template focuses on single frames for rapid iteration. To batch, run the workflow repeatedly with different images, or extend it by adding a batch image loader and connecting it to the same layout and save path.
