9cc2917611e9.title: Flux.1 Schnell Full: Text to Image
9cc2917611e9.description: Generate images quickly with Flux.1 Schnell full version. Uses Apache2.0 license, requires only 4 steps to generate images while maintaining good image quality.
9cc2917611e9.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Ultra-fast 4-step text-to-image with Flux.1 Schnell. Load models, set size, prompt, sample, and save—quality results with minimal steps.
9cc2917611e9.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow generates images from text using Flux.1 Schnell (full) with a minimal, fast sampling setup. It combines DualCLIPLoader to load both CLIP-L and T5XXL text encoders, CLIPTextEncodeFlux to turn your prompts into Flux-ready conditioning, and UNETLoader to load the flux1-schnell.safetensors diffusion model. EmptySD3LatentImage defines the latent canvas size and batch, KSampler performs denoising in as few as four steps, and VAELoader + VAEDecode reconstruct the final image for SaveImage to write to disk. A ConditioningZeroOut node provides an unconditional branch for classifier-free guidance when you’re not using a negative prompt. MarkdownNote nodes in the canvas clarify what to do at each stage.

Technically, the workflow follows a standard latent diffusion path adapted for Flux/SD3-style latents: initialize an EmptySD3LatentImage, encode text with CLIPTextEncodeFlux, run the UNet through KSampler with a low step-count tuned for the Schnell variant, then decode with the selected VAE. The “Step 1 - Load Models Here” group centralizes model selection: flux1-schnell in UNETLoader, CLIP-L + T5XXL in DualCLIPLoader, and a compatible VAE in VAELoader. “Step 2 - Image Size” sets your width/height and batch, and “Step 3 - Prompt” handles positive/negative prompts. The result is a fast, 4-step text-to-image pipeline that balances speed and quality under the permissive Apache-2.0 license for the Flux.1 Schnell weights.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. Locate the grouped sections: Step 1 - Load Models Here, Step 2 - Image Size, Step 3 - Prompt.

Step 1 - Load Models Here: In UNETLoader, select flux1-schnell.safetensors (place it in ComfyUI/models/unet). In DualCLIPLoader, select CLIP-L and T5XXL encoders (e.g., clip_l.safetensors and t5xxl_fp16.safetensors, commonly stored in models/clip). In VAELoader, choose a compatible VAE file (placed in models/vae).
Step 2 - Image Size: Open EmptySD3LatentImage and set width, height, and batch size. Start with a square frame (e.g., 1024 × 1024) and batch size 1 for lower VRAM use.

Step 3 - Prompt: Enter your positive prompt in CLIPTextEncodeFlux. If you want a negative prompt, enter it there as well; otherwise, leave negative empty and let ConditioningZeroOut provide the unconditional branch.

Sampling: In KSampler, keep steps at 4 for maximum speed. Adjust guidance (CFG) moderately if needed and use the default sampler/scheduler provided by the workflow. If you need more fidelity, try 6–8 steps.

Run and save: Execute the workflow. VAEDecode reconstructs the image, and SaveImage writes it to disk (configure filename prefix/subfolder in SaveImage). Inspect results, refine your prompt or size, and rerun.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept art and mood boards where speed matters more than ultra-fine detail.
Thumbnail and social media asset ideation with quick prompt iterations.
Storyboarding and previsualization for scenes, products, or UI layouts.
Creative writing prompts to visualize characters, settings, or props.
Design exploration: testing styles, color palettes, and compositions fast.

faqItems.question: Which model files do I need and where do they go?
faqItems.answer: You need flux1-schnell.safetensors for the UNet (place in models/unet), CLIP-L and T5XXL encoders for text (e.g., clip_l.safetensors and t5xxl_fp16.safetensors in models/clip), and a compatible VAE (models/vae). Select each in UNETLoader, DualCLIPLoader, and VAELoader respectively.

faqItems.question: Why only 4 steps, and can I increase them?
faqItems.answer: Flux.1 Schnell is tuned for very low step counts, making 4 steps a great speed/quality trade-off. For extra detail or difficult prompts, try 6–8 steps; expect longer render times.

faqItems.question: Do I need a negative prompt?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow includes ConditioningZeroOut to provide an unconditional branch for classifier-free guidance if you leave the negative prompt empty. Use a negative prompt only if you need to steer away from specific artifacts or styles.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best?
faqItems.answer: Start around 1024 × 1024 or similar pixel counts. Larger resolutions increase VRAM and time. Keep batch size at 1 on lower-memory GPUs and scale up cautiously.

9cca5e2b3dde.title: Video to Normal Map
9cca5e2b3dde.description: Convert a Video to a temporally stable Normal Map
9cca5e2b3dde.metaDescription: Convert video to a stable normal map using ComfyUI for enhanced 3D modeling and animation. Achieve seamless transitions with this workflow.
9cca5e2b3dde.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow is designed to convert video footage into a temporally stable normal map, which is particularly useful for enhancing 3D modeling and animation projects. By leveraging nodes such as the NormalCrafterNode and VHS_LoadVideo, the workflow processes each frame of the video to extract and generate a normal map that maintains consistency across frames. This temporal stability is crucial for applications where seamless transitions between frames are necessary, such as in video games or cinematic visual effects.

The workflow begins by loading the video using the VHS_LoadVideo node, which extracts individual frames and prepares them for processing. The NormalCrafterNode then takes these frames and computes the normal maps, ensuring that the lighting and shading information is accurately represented. The VHS_VideoCombine node is used to reassemble the processed frames back into a video format, while the VHS_VideoInfo node provides metadata about the video, such as frame rate and resolution. This combination of nodes makes the workflow highly effective for creating high-quality normal maps from video content, which can be used to add depth and realism to 3D environments.
howToUse: Load the workflow into ComfyUI and ensure all necessary custom nodes are installed.
Use the VHS_LoadVideo node to import your video file into the workflow.
Configure the NormalCrafterNode to process each video frame and generate normal maps.
Utilize the VHS_VideoCombine node to compile the processed frames back into a video format.
Check the output using the VHS_VideoInfo node to verify frame rate and resolution consistency.
Export the final video with the newly created normal maps for use in your projects.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing realism in video game environments by applying normal maps to textures.
Creating detailed visual effects for films and animations.
Developing training datasets for machine learning models focused on 3D object recognition.
Improving the visual quality of virtual reality experiences.
Augmenting architectural visualization projects with realistic lighting effects.

faqItems.question: What is a normal map and why is it important?
faqItems.answer: A normal map is a texture that stores information about the surface normals of a 3D object. It is used to simulate lighting and shading effects, adding depth and detail without increasing polygon count.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow ensure temporal stability across frames?
faqItems.answer: The workflow processes each frame individually but maintains consistent lighting and shading parameters, ensuring that the normal maps align seamlessly across frames.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow with any video format?
faqItems.answer: The VHS_LoadVideo node supports various common video formats, but it's recommended to use standard formats like MP4 or AVI for best compatibility.

faqItems.question: Do I need any special hardware to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: While no special hardware is required, having a GPU can significantly speed up the processing time, especially for high-resolution videos.

9d588c37e728.title: Dynamic Motion Design
9d588c37e728.description: Create polished motion design videos with Seedance-ready prompts.
9d588c37e728.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Turn UI screenshots into motion design videos using Gemini for Seedance prompts and ByteDance2ReferenceNode for image-to-video animation.
9d588c37e728.extendedDescription: Dynamic Motion Design is an image-to-video ComfyUI workflow that turns static UI screenshots and brand assets into polished motion design clips. It uses GeminiNode or GeminiNanoBanana2 to convert your brief and references into a single Seedance-ready motion prompt, then feeds that prompt—along with your uploaded images—into ByteDance2ReferenceNode to generate the actual animation. You can monitor progress with PreviewImage and PreviewAny, and export the result with SaveVideo. The workflow is organized into three groups for clarity: Generate Seedance Motion Designer Prompt (LLM-driven prompt crafting), Generate UI Frames (quick previews and frame checks), and Generate Video (final render and export).
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and review the MarkdownNote for any in-graph tips.

In the Generate UI Frames section, use LoadImage to import your base image (e.g., a landing page or app screen). Optional: Load additional brand/style references and connect them to ByteDance2ReferenceNode as visual guidance.

In the Generate Seedance Motion Designer Prompt section, write a short creative brief (motion goals, tone, brand cues). Choose GeminiNode (cloud) or GeminiNanoBanana2 (local) to synthesize a concise Seedance-ready prompt. Preview and copy the generated prompt from PreviewAny or MarkdownNote if needed.

Adjust prompt details for motion design specifics: camera moves (pan, zoom, parallax), element emphasis (CTA, logo), pacing, transitions, and timing. Keep it concise and declarative—Seedance prompts work best when unambiguous.

Switch to the Generate Video section. Ensure ByteDance2ReferenceNode receives the Seedance prompt and your image/reference inputs. Set key parameters (resolution, motion strength, duration/frame count, seed) as available on the node. Use PreviewImage/PreviewAny to spot-check initial frames.
When satisfied, render the full sequence and export with SaveVideo. You can also reuse the same Seedance prompt in the external Seedance Motion Designer if you want to iterate outside ComfyUI.
suggestedUseCases: Animating product landing pages for pitch decks or portfolio reels (subtle pans, CTA emphasis, logo animations).
Brand reveal stingers using product shots and style boards as references.
Mobile app UI micro-animation prototypes to showcase flows and transitions.
Social-ready motion snippets that highlight key features or promotions.
Design explorations to establish motion language and pacing for a new brand.

faqItems.question: What is a Seedance-ready prompt, and why use GeminiNode here?
faqItems.answer: A Seedance-ready prompt is a concise, structured text description tailored for the Seedance Motion Designer. The workflow uses GeminiNode or GeminiNanoBanana2 to turn your brief and visual references into a clear, unambiguous prompt that emphasizes motion intent (camera moves, pacing, focal elements). This improves consistency and reduces trial-and-error when driving ByteDance2ReferenceNode or exporting the prompt for Seedance.

faqItems.question: What does ByteDance2ReferenceNode do in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: ByteDance2ReferenceNode is the image-to-video engine that interprets your Seedance prompt alongside the uploaded base image and any style/brand references. It generates the animated sequence based on those inputs and its parameters (e.g., resolution, motion strength, duration/frame count, and seed).

faqItems.question: When should I use GeminiNode vs. GeminiNanoBanana2?
faqItems.answer: Use GeminiNode if you have network access and want the full cloud LLM for richer prompt synthesis. Use GeminiNanoBanana2 if you prefer a local, lightweight option or need to work offline. Both produce Seedance-ready prompts; choose based on connectivity and resource constraints.

faqItems.question: How can I improve results and control the motion?
faqItems.answer: Start with a clean, high-resolution base image. Add clear brand/style references that match your desired look. Keep the Seedance prompt brief and directive—specify camera moves, focal elements, pacing, and transitions. In ByteDance2ReferenceNode, iterate on motion strength, duration/frame count, and seed. Use the Generate UI Frames previews to validate composition before rendering the final video.

9dac2dae8bfc.title: Wan 2.2 14B Fun Camera Control
9dac2dae8bfc.description: Generate videos with camera motion controls including pan, zoom, and rotation using Wan 2.2 Fun Camera Control.
9dac2dae8bfc.metaDescription: Image-to-video with precise pan, zoom, and rotation using Wan 2.2 in ComfyUI. Two-pass denoise for stable, cinematic motion. Optional fast LoRA mode.
9dac2dae8bfc.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single still image into a smooth, camera-driven video using Wan 2.2 14B Fun Camera Control. It loads the Wan 2.2 model with UNETLoader and ModelSamplingSD3, encodes your text prompt with CLIPLoader + CLIPTextEncode, and builds a camera path with WanCameraEmbedding. The WanCameraImageToVideo node fuses your prompt, start image, and camera embeddings to generate temporally consistent frames that follow pan, zoom, and rotation cues. Frames are decoded with VAELoader + VAEDecode, assembled with CreateVideo, and written out via SaveVideo.

Under the hood, the workflow runs a two-pass denoise with KSamplerAdvanced: a High noise phase to establish motion, structure, and parallax, followed by a Low noise phase to refine details and reduce flicker. This separation helps keep subjects stable while letting the virtual camera move dynamically. The template includes an optional LightX2V 4 Steps LoRA (via LoraLoaderModelOnly) to accelerate generation at the cost of motion richness and fine detail; use the Default (Without Lightning LoRA) path for the best dynamics. The provided fp8_scaled Wan 2.2 checkpoint is optimized for 640×640 and, on an RTX 4090D 24GB, typically uses ~84% VRAM and takes about 536s for the first run and ~513s for subsequent runs at that resolution.
howToUse: Step 1 – Load models: Open the workflow and, in the Step 1 - Load models group, set UNETLoader to the Wan2.2 fun camera 14B fp8_scaled model, load the matching VAE in VAELoader, and load CLIP in CLIPLoader. Leave ModelSamplingSD3 as provided.

Step 2 – Provide a start image: In Step 2 - Upload start_image, use LoadImage to select a clean, well-lit source image at or near 640×640. Center your subject and avoid heavy compression artifacts for best stability.

Step 3 – Write your prompt: In Step 3 - Prompt, enter your descriptive prompt in CLIPTextEncode (and adjust any negative text field if present). Keep prompts concise and consistent with the content of the start image.

Step 4 – Define camera motion: In Step 4 - Camera Conditions, set WanCameraEmbedding parameters for pan, zoom, and rotation across the timeline. Use modest ranges (e.g., gentle pans and 5–15% zoom) for stable parallax. These embeddings feed WanCameraImageToVideo to drive motion.

Step 5 – Choose quality vs. speed: Use the Default (Without Lightning LoRA) path for maximum motion fidelity, or enable the LightX2V 4 Steps LoRA via LoraLoaderModelOnly to reduce steps and render time (expect some loss of dynamics/detail).

Step 6 – Generate and export: Run the graph. The High noise pass establishes motion; the Low noise pass refines details. In CreateVideo and SaveVideo, set FPS and output quality, then save your final video.
suggestedUseCases: Product hero shots from a still: slow dolly-in with a subtle orbit to add depth and polish.
Character portraits: gentle arc or roll around a face while preserving identity and texture.
Environment concept art: slow pan-and-zoom to reveal scenery with light parallax.
UI/mockup reels: controlled zooms and pans to highlight interface sections without reanimating in a DCC.
Social posts and teaser loops: quick motion from static key art to increase engagement.

faqItems.question: Do I need a start image, or can this start from noise?
faqItems.answer: This template is designed for image-to-video. Load a start image with LoadImage to anchor content and identity, then use WanCameraEmbedding to add motion.

faqItems.question: How do I keep the subject stable while the camera moves?
faqItems.answer: Use moderate camera ranges (small pans/zooms/rotations), keep the subject centered in the start image, and favor the Default (Without Lightning LoRA) path. If you see drift, reduce the High noise sampler strength/steps slightly and lock the seed.

faqItems.question: How can I speed up generation?
faqItems.answer: Enable the LightX2V 4 Steps LoRA (via LoraLoaderModelOnly), lower the resolution (e.g., stay at 640×640), reduce KSamplerAdvanced steps, and shorten duration/FPS. Note the Lightning/LightX2V path trades speed for motion richness and detail.

faqItems.question: What resolution and VRAM should I expect?
faqItems.answer: The fp8_scaled Wan 2.2 model is set up for 640×640. On an RTX 4090D 24GB, VRAM usage is ~84% with first-run times around 536s and subsequent runs ~513s. Higher resolutions require more VRAM and may reduce stability.

9e033fb4e06a.title: Portrait Relight
9e033fb4e06a.description: Upload your target image and a reference lighting image. Relights your target image.
9e033fb4e06a.metaDescription: Transform your images with the Portrait Relight workflow, using reference lighting to enhance and unify your visuals.
9e033fb4e06a.extendedDescription: The 'Portrait Relight' workflow in ComfyUI is designed to enhance your images by altering their lighting based on a reference image. This workflow utilizes the Qwen-Image-Edit model to intelligently adjust the lighting of a target image, making it appear as if it was lit under the conditions of the reference image. The process involves several key nodes, including the LoadImage node for importing images, and the SaveImage node for exporting the final result. The workflow is particularly useful for photographers and digital artists looking to achieve consistent lighting across different images or to experiment with creative lighting effects without the need for physical lighting equipment.
howToUse: Start by loading your target image using the LoadImage node in ComfyUI.
Upload a reference image with the desired lighting using the same LoadImage node.
Ensure the Qwen-Image-Edit model is selected to process the images for relighting.
Adjust any additional settings or prompts as needed, such as maintaining canny edge details.
Run the workflow to generate the relighted image.
Save the output using the SaveImage node to store your newly relighted portrait.
suggestedUseCases: Enhancing portrait photography by applying studio-like lighting effects.
Creating a unified lighting style across a series of images for a cohesive photo album.
Experimenting with different lighting scenarios for digital art projects.
Improving the visual appeal of product photos by adjusting lighting to highlight features.
Testing lighting effects for film or animation pre-production.

faqItems.question: What type of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Portrait images with clear lighting and shadow details tend to work best, as the model can effectively adjust these elements to match the reference lighting.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for non-portrait images?
faqItems.answer: Yes, while optimized for portraits, the workflow can be applied to any image where lighting adjustments are desired.

faqItems.question: Do I need any special hardware to run this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No special hardware is required, but a GPU will significantly speed up the processing time, especially for high-resolution images.

faqItems.question: How do I maintain specific details in the image?
faqItems.answer: You can append additional image edit prompt instructions in the workflow to maintain specific details, such as edges, during the relighting process.

9e910f3b95c2.title: Kling 3.0: Video Generation
9e910f3b95c2.description: Input text or image prompts to generate 15-second video sequences with multi-shot compositions, complex camera movements, and consistent subjects.
9e910f3b95c2.metaDescription: Generate 15-second videos from text or image prompts using Kling 3.0 with multi-shot compositions and complex camera movements.
9e910f3b95c2.extendedDescription: The Kling 3.0: Video Generation workflow is designed to transform text or image prompts into captivating 15-second video sequences. This workflow leverages the Kling 3.0 model, renowned for its ability to create multi-shot compositions and complex camera movements while maintaining subject consistency throughout the video. The workflow integrates several key nodes, including LoadImage for initial prompt input, KlingVideoNode for generating the video content, and SaveVideo for exporting the final product. By utilizing these nodes, users can create dynamic videos that are not only visually appealing but also coherent in their narrative structure. This makes the workflow particularly useful for content creators looking to produce engaging video content with minimal input.
howToUse: Load the ComfyUI interface and import the Kling 3.0: Video Generation workflow.
Use the LoadImage node to input your initial text or image prompt.
Configure the KlingVideoNode to set parameters for video length, camera movement, and subject consistency.
Run the workflow to process the input through the Kling 3.0 model, generating the video sequence.
Use the SaveVideo node to export the final 15-second video to your desired location.
suggestedUseCases: Creating promotional videos with dynamic visuals for marketing campaigns.
Generating short video content for social media platforms.
Producing educational videos with consistent subject focus and engaging visuals.
Developing creative video art projects with complex camera movements.

faqItems.question: What types of prompts can I use with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: You can use both text and image prompts to initiate the video generation process. The Kling 3.0 model will interpret these prompts to create the video content.

faqItems.question: How long are the videos generated by this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The videos generated are 15 seconds long, making them ideal for quick, engaging content suitable for various platforms.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the camera movements in the generated video?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the KlingVideoNode allows you to configure parameters for camera movement, enabling you to tailor the video dynamics to your needs.

faqItems.question: Is there a way to ensure subject consistency throughout the video?
faqItems.answer: The Kling 3.0 model is designed to maintain subject consistency across the video, ensuring that the main elements remain coherent and recognizable.

9ed4f6b88b6a.title: Seedance 2.5: Text to Video
9ed4f6b88b6a.description: Generate 30-second cinematic videos from text prompts with Seedance 2.5, producing synchronized sound and music alongside the footage. Input a single text prompt to create one video with precise camera control and multi-shot storytelling. Ideal for brand films, episodic series, and e-commerce content where quality matters more than budget.
9ed4f6b88b6a.metaDescription: Create 30-second cinematic videos from a single prompt using Seedance 2.5 in ComfyUI. Camera-aware prompts, multi-shot sequences, and optional synced audio.
9ed4f6b88b6a.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.5: Text to Video is a compact ComfyUI workflow that turns a single, well-structured prompt into a cinematic video. At its core is the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode, which connects to the Seedance 2.5 text-to-video service to render up to 30 seconds of footage from natural language. The node accepts your prompt, duration, resolution, and seed, then returns a ready-to-save video (and, when enabled, an audio track with synchronized music and effects). The SaveVideo node captures the result and writes an MP4 to your output directory for easy preview and sharing.

Technically, the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode handles all model-side sampling, motion synthesis, and timing based on your input prompt and parameters. You can embed camera instructions (for example: dolly in, slow pan left, low-angle, 35mm lens) and multi-shot storytelling cues directly in the text (for example: Shot 1 … CUT TO: Shot 2 …). This gives you precise control over pacing and composition without hand-directing keyframes. SaveVideo finalizes the render with your chosen filename pattern and frame rate, making the workflow ideal for brand films, episodic beats, product hero shots, and any scenario where quality and control matter more than budget.
howToUse: Load the Seedance 2.5: Text to Video workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then locate the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and SaveVideo nodes.

Open ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and configure access: paste your API key (or set the environment variable specified by the node’s docs), then set duration (up to ~30s), resolution/aspect, FPS, and seed.

Write a detailed prompt. For camera and story control, include cues like: Shot 1: wide establishing, dawn fog, slow dolly in. CUT TO: Shot 2: medium close-up, pan left, dramatic rim light. You can also add a negative prompt if the node supports it.
If the node exposes an audio option, enable it to request synchronized sound/music. Otherwise, the workflow will produce a silent MP4.
Review SaveVideo settings (output filename pattern, container/codec if available) and ensure the node is connected to the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode output.
Queue the workflow. When it completes, find the rendered MP4 in your ComfyUI output directory, review the result, then iterate by tweaking the prompt, seed, and shot timings.
suggestedUseCases: Brand and product hero videos where consistent look, camera language, and pacing are important.
Episodic teasers or story beats blocked out as multi-shot sequences from a single prompt.
E-commerce detail reels: sweeping product close-ups, material highlights, and dramatic moves.
Mood films and animatics to previsualize campaigns before full production.
Social promos that benefit from synchronized music and cinematic camera moves.

faqItems.question: How do I control multiple shots and camera moves in one prompt?
faqItems.answer: Include clear structure in the prompt. Use markers like "Shot 1:", "CUT TO:", or time cues (e.g., "0–5s:") and add camera directives (dolly in, crane up, pan left, 35mm lens, low-angle). Seedance 2.5 parses these cues to inform pacing and composition.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow generate audio?
faqItems.answer: When the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode’s audio option is available and enabled, the API can return a video with synchronized music/effects. If disabled or unsupported in your region/plan, the output will be a silent MP4.

faqItems.question: What parameters most affect quality and coherence?
faqItems.answer: Strong, specific prompts with clear shot structure, a fixed seed for iteration, and a supported resolution/aspect ratio generally yield the most consistent results. If the node offers guidance or strength controls, moderate values often balance detail against motion stability.

faqItems.question: Why can’t I render longer than ~30 seconds?
faqItems.answer: Duration limits are enforced by the Seedance 2.5 API. Set the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode duration within the allowed range. For longer edits, generate multiple clips (e.g., per scene) and stitch them in an editor.

9f0b568bf8a1.title: Anime Generator
9f0b568bf8a1.description: Creating your own generated anime characters and anime-style art with this app.
9f0b568bf8a1.metaDescription: ComfyUI Anime Generator tutorial: load anime SD models, set 1MP resolution, craft prompts, and render clean anime art with KSampler, CLIP, and VAE.
9f0b568bf8a1.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow generates anime characters and anime-style scenes from text prompts using a classic Stable Diffusion pipeline. In Step 1 (Load Models), UNETLoader, CLIPLoader, and VAELoader load your chosen anime-tuned checkpoint, text encoder, and VAE. Step 2 (Image Size (1MP)) uses ResolutionSelector to set an efficient, 1‑megapixel canvas, which then feeds EmptyLatentImage to create a latent noise tensor at the selected dimensions. Step 3 (Prompt) processes your positive and negative prompts through CLIPTextEncode, and KSampler iteratively denoises the latent with the UNet, guided by your prompts and sampler settings. Finally, VAEDecode turns the denoised latent into a full-resolution image and SaveImage writes the output to disk.

Technically, the core of the generation happens in KSampler, which accepts the UNet weights (UNETLoader), text embeddings (CLIPTextEncode), and an initial noise latent (EmptyLatentImage). The ResolutionSelector ensures the latent size stays near 1 MP for speed and quality balance—ideal for anime linework and clean shading. The VAE you load matters: it defines how colors and fine details are encoded/decoded. CLIPTextEncode supports positive and negative prompts, so you can include quality tags and style hints (e.g., "masterpiece, anime, dramatic lighting") while excluding defects (e.g., "worst quality, blurry, jpeg artifacts"). This combination delivers crisp, stylized anime art with consistent control over composition, detail, and style.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and locate the three groups: Step 1 – Load Models, Step 2 – Image Size (1MP), Step 3 – Prompt.

In Step 1, choose your models: UNETLoader → select an anime-tuned SD 1.5 checkpoint; CLIPLoader → matching CLIP for that checkpoint; VAELoader → a compatible VAE. Keep UNet/CLIP/VAE from the same model family to avoid mismatches.

Set your target size in ResolutionSelector (Step 2). Pick a ~1 MP resolution such as 1024×1024, 1152×896, or 1216×832. The node will pass width/height to EmptyLatentImage to build the correctly sized noise latent.

Enter prompts in Step 3. CLIPTextEncode (positive) for what you want (e.g., "masterpiece, best quality, anime, cyborg in profile, high-contrast cyan/violet glow"). CLIPTextEncode (negative) for what to avoid (e.g., "worst quality, low quality, blurry, jpeg artifacts, sepia").
Configure KSampler: choose a sampler (e.g., Euler a, DPM++ SDE Karras), set steps (20–30 is a good start), CFG scale (5–8), and a seed (fixed for reproducibility, -1/random for variety).
Run the graph. Inspect the VAEDecode output and adjust prompts, steps, CFG, or ResolutionSelector as needed. SaveImage will write final images to your output folder.
suggestedUseCases: Designing original anime character portraits and profile avatars.
Exploring outfit, hairstyle, and color variations for character concepts.
Creating mood pieces or keyframes with specific lighting and composition.
Generating quick style studies (cel shading, high-contrast neon, soft pastel) via prompt tweaks.

faqItems.question: Which models are compatible with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: This setup is designed for SD 1.5-style checkpoints that use a single CLIP and VAE (e.g., anime-tuned models). Load a matching trio: UNet checkpoint in UNETLoader, its corresponding CLIP in CLIPLoader, and a compatible VAE in VAELoader. Mixing families can produce washed colors or artifacts.

faqItems.question: Why do my images look blurry or washed out?
faqItems.answer: Common causes are a mismatched or low-quality VAE, too few sampling steps, or overly low CFG. Try a VAE known to match your checkpoint, raise steps to 25–35, set CFG around 6–8, and add a strong negative prompt (e.g., “blurry, jpeg artifacts, low contrast”).

faqItems.question: How do I change aspect ratio without harming quality?
faqItems.answer: Use ResolutionSelector to pick dimensions near 1 MP that fit your aspect ratio (e.g., 1216×704 for wide, 896×1152 for tall). Staying near 1 MP balances detail and speed. Then adjust prompts with composition hints like “portrait, headshot” or “full body” to guide framing.

faqItems.question: How can I get consistent or varied results?
faqItems.answer: Set a fixed seed in KSampler for reproducible outputs with small, controlled prompt edits. For variety, randomize the seed, slightly alter wording, or try a different sampler (e.g., DPM++ vs. Euler a). Keep CFG and steps stable when comparing results.

9f1bb8c2f14f.title: Color Curves to Video
9f1bb8c2f14f.description: Build cinematic color-curve grades and generate a video from a single reference image with native Curve Editors, histogram-guided RGB curves, and a GLSL shader in Color Curves to Video.
9f1bb8c2f14f.metaDescription: Grade an image with histogram-guided RGB curves and a GLSL shader, then generate a Seedance 2.0 video from the graded still—all inside ComfyUI.
9f1bb8c2f14f.extendedDescription:
This workflow builds cinematic color grades with precision and then animates your graded still into a short video. It starts with LoadImage and ImageHistogram in the Input And Histogram group to help you read the tonal distribution of your reference image. You then shape the look using multiple CurveEditor nodes in the Native Curve Editors group (master plus red, green, and blue) and send those curves to a GLSLShader in the GLSL Curve/LUT Grade group. The shader applies your per-channel remaps in real time, so you can iterate quickly while checking before/after with ImageCompare and live previews with PreviewAny. SaveImage lets you export the graded still if that’s all you need.

To create motion from the look you’ve crafted, the Motion Prompt And Seedance group uses a ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Seedance 2.0) that generates a video conditioned on your graded reference image and a motion prompt. A GeminiNode can optionally draft or refine motion prompts for you, while PrimitiveFloat nodes drive key parameters such as curve blend or shader strength for fine control. Finally, SaveVideo assembles the generated frames into a video file. The result is a streamlined grade-to-video pipeline that’s easy to tune and iterate.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure required custom nodes are installed: GLSLShader and ByteDance2ReferenceNode (for Seedance 2.0). GeminiNode is optional for prompt drafting. Open the Input And Histogram group and load your reference image with LoadImage.
Open ImageHistogram to inspect shadows, midtones, and highlights. Use this as a guide while you adjust the master and RGB CurveEditor nodes in the Native Curve Editors group.

Tweak the CurveEditor nodes (master, red, green, blue) to set your contrast curve and color balance. The curves feed the GLSLShader in GLSL Curve/LUT Grade, which applies the remap per pixel. Use PreviewAny to see live updates and ImageCompare to A/B before vs. after.

Fine-tune the grade using the PrimitiveFloat nodes wired into the GLSLShader (for example, overall curve blend or strength) until the look feels right. If you want a still output, run SaveImage to export the graded image.

To animate, go to Motion Prompt And Seedance. Enter a motion prompt and seed. If GeminiNode is configured, use it to propose or refine a motion prompt and connect its output to the ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Ensure the graded image is connected as the reference.

Set your desired length and frame rate in SaveVideo (and any duration/frames settings in ByteDance2ReferenceNode). Execute the video branch to render, preview with PreviewAny, and then SaveVideo to export the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Turn a product photo into a cinematic color-graded promo with gentle parallax or camera drift.
Create mood-driven social media loops from a still poster or key art while preserving the grade.
Previsualize motion concepts (e.g., slow dolly, tilt, or wind ripple) on a graded hero image.
Batch-match looks across a series by reusing the same curve settings, then generate motion variants.
Produce short graded B-roll clips for editing timelines starting from a single well-lit photograph.

faqItems.question: Do I need a diffusion model or checkpoint for this workflow?
faqItems.answer: No checkpoint is required for grading—the GLSLShader applies your CurveEditor settings directly. For video, you do need the ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Seedance 2.0) and its dependencies. Without it, you can still grade and export the still image.

faqItems.question: Is the GeminiNode required?
faqItems.answer: No. GeminiNode is optional and only helps draft or refine a motion prompt. You can type a prompt manually and send it to ByteDance2ReferenceNode. If you do use Gemini, make sure your API credentials are configured per the node’s instructions.

faqItems.question: How can I avoid banding or color clipping when using curves?
faqItems.answer: Keep curves smooth with as few anchor points as needed, avoid extreme S-curves, and blend the grade with the PrimitiveFloat controls feeding the GLSLShader. Use ImageHistogram to keep blacks and whites within range, and export with a high bitrate in SaveVideo to minimize compression artifacts.

faqItems.question: My video colors drift from the graded still. How do I keep the look consistent?
faqItems.answer: Confirm that the ByteDance2ReferenceNode uses the graded image output as its reference input. Reduce motion strength or stylization settings if available, keep a fixed seed for repeatability, and ensure no additional color transforms are applied downstream before SaveVideo.

9f9f595534d8.title: Moonvalley: Image to Video
9f9f595534d8.description: Generate cinematic, 1080p videos with an image through a model trained exclusively on licensed data.
9f9f595534d8.metaDescription: ComfyUI template: convert a single image into a cinematic 1080p video using the Moonvalley image-to-video API. Simple LoadImage → Moonvalley → SaveVideo pipeline.
9f9f595534d8.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single image into a cinematic 1080p video using the Moonvalley image-to-video model. The graph is intentionally simple: LoadImage feeds your source frame, MoonvalleyImg2VideoNode sends it to the Moonvalley API for motion synthesis, and SaveVideo encodes the returned frames as an MP4. A MarkdownNote is included with direct links to the Moonvalley video generation docs and the Partner API overview so you can quickly reference parameters and setup tips.

Technically, LoadImage provides an RGB tensor to MoonvalleyImg2VideoNode, which handles authentication and the remote generation request. The node receives a sequence of frames from the Moonvalley service—trained exclusively on licensed data—at 1920x1080 and passes them downstream. SaveVideo assembles those frames into a playable file with your chosen filename and frame rate. Because the heavy lifting runs on Moonvalley’s servers via API, this pipeline produces smooth, high-resolution clips without relying on local GPU horsepower.

This template is useful when you need fast, consistent, and legally sound image-to-video results. You can drop in any reference image (e.g., product packshot, character portrait, landscape keyframe) and generate a short, polished motion clip suitable for previews, social posts, or story beats. It’s also easy to extend—swap LoadImage for an upstream text-to-image generator to build an end-to-end concept-to-motion workflow.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the MarkdownNote for links to the Moonvalley video generation and Partner API docs.

Open MoonvalleyImg2VideoNode and add your Moonvalley API key (either directly in the node or via ComfyUI’s Partner API settings, as described in the docs). Ensure your network allows outgoing API requests.
Use LoadImage to select a clear, high-quality source image. For best results, start with a 16:9 image (ideally 1920×1080) so the output doesn’t need aggressive resizing.
In MoonvalleyImg2VideoNode, review the available parameters (e.g., clip length and motion strength if exposed by your version). Keep defaults for a quick test, then adjust to taste.
Open SaveVideo and set a filename (and FPS if the node exposes it). Confirm the output format is MP4.
Click Queue/Execute. When finished, find the saved MP4 in ComfyUI’s output folder and review. Iterate on the input image and Moonvalley parameters to refine motion and pacing.
suggestedUseCases: Turn product photos into subtle hero shots for ads, landing pages, or app store previews.
Add life to character portraits or concept art for pitch decks, animatics, and social teasers.
Create establishing-shot motion from environment stills for mood boards and story beats.
Generate looping background motion for event screens, presentations, or video intros.
Prototype motion directions from static keyframes before committing to full production.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use this?
faqItems.answer: Yes. MoonvalleyImg2VideoNode calls the Moonvalley service. Add your API key in the node or via ComfyUI’s Partner API settings (see the linked docs). Make sure your network allows the request to reach the Moonvalley API.

faqItems.question: What input and output formats are supported?
faqItems.answer: LoadImage accepts common image formats like PNG and JPG. The pipeline outputs a video via SaveVideo, typically as an MP4 in the ComfyUI output folder.

faqItems.question: How do I get the best 1080p results?
faqItems.answer: Start with a clean, high-resolution 16:9 image (ideally 1920×1080), keep the subject well-framed with good contrast, and avoid heavy compression artifacts. If the node exposes motion-related parameters, begin with moderate motion and increase gradually.

faqItems.question: Why won’t the node authenticate or generate?
faqItems.answer: Double-check that your API key is valid, entered in the correct place, and that your system can reach the Moonvalley API (no strict firewall/proxy blocks). Refer to the Partner API/FAQ links in the MarkdownNote for common login and connectivity issues.

9fbb34bb59b3.title: QR Code Image Generator
9fbb34bb59b3.description:
Turn an ordinary QR code into artwork. Instead of a plain black-and-white square, this blends your code directly into an image — the pattern becomes part of the composition, hidden in the textures, shadows, and shapes of the scene rather than stamped on top of it. The result still scans reliably with any phone camera, but it looks like something you'd actually want to put on a poster, album cover, business card, or product label.

Just supply your link and a prompt or reference image describing the look you want, and you'll get back a piece that works as both a picture and a working code.
9fbb34bb59b3.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow to blend a QR code into artwork using a prompt or reference image, balancing style and scan reliability for print and digital uses.
9fbb34bb59b3.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a plain QR code into a stylized image where the code pattern is blended into textures, shadows, and shapes rather than overlaid on top. You provide a link (or any QR payload) and either a text prompt or a reference image to describe the look you want. The system produces an artwork that still scans reliably with a phone camera while looking polished enough for posters, album covers, business cards, or product labels.

Technically, the heavy lifting happens in a single custom node (UUID: 323b0c6a-e2f0-42c3-93b4-36b7878136fd). This node encodes your URL into a QR matrix, then synthesizes or stylizes an image so local contrast and edges align with the QR modules, preserving a readable pattern inside the composition. You can balance aesthetics and readability by adjusting style strength and QR visibility. The final image is written to disk by the SaveImage node as a PNG in ComfyUI's output folder.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI and locate the custom QR node (UUID: 323b0c6a-e2f0-42c3-93b4-36b7878136fd) and the SaveImage node.
In the QR node, paste your URL or text payload. Add either a text prompt to describe the style or provide a reference image for guidance.
Set image size (a square frame is recommended) and adjust controls for style strength and QR visibility to balance aesthetics and readability. Optionally fix a seed for reproducible results.
Run the workflow. Preview the generated image and confirm that the QR code area remains unclipped with a clear margin around the edges.

Test with your phone’s camera. If it doesn’t scan easily, re-run with higher QR visibility, slightly lower style strength, simpler textures near the code, or increased overall contrast. The SaveImage node will write each result to the ComfyUI/output folder.
suggestedUseCases: Event posters and flyers where the QR code should be scannable but visually integrated into the design.
Album or podcast artwork that includes a QR linking to streaming or social profiles without a visible black-and-white block.
Business cards and product labels that keep brand aesthetics intact while embedding a working QR code.
Social posts or landing page hero images that double as scannable calls-to-action.

faqItems.question: How do I improve scan reliability if the result looks good but won’t scan?
faqItems.answer: Increase the QR visibility setting, reduce the overall style strength near the code, keep a clear quiet zone (blank margin) around the QR area, and avoid extreme blur or heavy texture over modules. Also test under normal indoor lighting and ensure the final crop doesn’t cut into the code edges.

faqItems.question: Can I guide the look with a reference image instead of a text prompt?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Provide a reference image to the custom QR node. The node will align textures and edges to the QR matrix while borrowing colors and structure from your reference. If the code becomes hard to scan, reduce style strength or simplify the reference.

faqItems.question: What image size works best?
faqItems.answer: Start with a square canvas to keep the QR proportions consistent. Higher resolution improves detail, but ensure the QR modules remain crisp with good contrast. For print, generate at the final print size or plan to upscale with care and re-test scanning afterward.

faqItems.question: Where do the images save?
faqItems.answer: The SaveImage node writes the outputs as PNG files in your ComfyUI/output folder. Each run will create a new file; use the seed or naming options to keep versions organized.

9ff401a65647.title: Qwen-Image-Layered Decomposition
9ff401a65647.description: Decompose an image into editable RGBA layers for high-fidelity recolor, replace, resize, and reposition workflows using Qwen-Image-Layered.
9ff401a65647.metaDescription: Decompose images into RGBA layers for precise editing with Qwen-Image-Layered. Ideal for recoloring, resizing, and repositioning elements.
9ff401a65647.extendedDescription: The Qwen-Image-Layered Decomposition workflow is designed to decompose an image into editable RGBA layers, enabling high-fidelity image manipulation. This workflow leverages the Qwen-Image-Layered model to break down images into separate layers, each containing a Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha channel. This decomposition allows for precise control over each layer, making it possible to recolor, replace, resize, or reposition elements within an image without affecting the entire composition. Technically, the workflow utilizes nodes such as SaveImage and LoadImage to manage image file operations, while ImageScaleToMaxDimension ensures images are processed at optimal resolutions. The integration of nodes like f754a936-daaf-4b6e-9658-41fdc54d301d and 1ea4fa01-a81b-4420-a03c-f60019e69a92 facilitates the decomposition process by handling complex image data transformations.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI by selecting 'Qwen-Image-Layered Decomposition' from the workflow library.
Prepare your image by ensuring it is within the recommended input size of 640px or 1024px for high-resolution processing.
Use the LoadImage node to import your image into the workflow.
Execute the workflow to decompose the image into RGBA layers using the Qwen-Image-Layered model.
Edit the layers as needed, using tools to recolor, resize, or reposition elements.
Save the edited image using the SaveImage node to export your final composition.
suggestedUseCases: Graphic design projects requiring precise color adjustments and element repositioning.
Creating multi-layered compositions for digital art and illustrations.
Developing assets for video games where individual elements need to be manipulated independently.
Enhancing product images for e-commerce by adjusting colors and positions without affecting the entire image.
Restoring and retouching photographs by isolating and editing specific areas.

faqItems.question: What is the recommended input size for images?
faqItems.answer: The recommended input size is 640px for standard processing, and 1024px for high-resolution images.

faqItems.question: Can I edit the layers individually after decomposition?
faqItems.answer: Yes, each layer can be edited individually, allowing for changes in color, size, and position without affecting other layers.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow handle large images?
faqItems.answer: The ImageScaleToMaxDimension node ensures that images are resized to optimal dimensions for processing, maintaining quality while managing performance.

faqItems.question: Is this workflow suitable for beginners?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the workflow is designed to be user-friendly, with step-by-step instructions and intuitive node operations, making it accessible to users of all skill levels.

a013e57e6d51.title: Seedance1.0 Pro: Text to Video
a013e57e6d51.description: Generate high-quality videos directly from text prompts using ByteDance's Seedance model. Supports multiple resolutions and aspect ratios with natural motion and cinematic quality.
a013e57e6d51.metaDescription: Generate cinematic-quality videos from text prompts using the Seedance1.0 Pro workflow, powered by ByteDance's Seedance model.
a013e57e6d51.extendedDescription: The Seedance1.0 Pro: Text to Video workflow leverages the advanced capabilities of ByteDance's Seedance model to transform text prompts into high-quality videos. This workflow is designed to support multiple resolutions and aspect ratios, ensuring that the generated videos maintain natural motion and cinematic quality. At the core of this process is the ByteDanceTextToVideoNode, which interprets the text prompts and orchestrates the video generation process. The SaveVideo node then captures and stores the output, making it easily accessible for further use. This workflow is particularly useful for creators looking to produce engaging video content quickly and efficiently without the need for extensive video editing skills.
howToUse: Load the Seedance1.0 Pro: Text to Video workflow in ComfyUI.
Enter your desired text prompt into the ByteDanceTextToVideoNode.
Configure the resolution and aspect ratio settings to suit your needs.
Run the workflow to generate the video using the Seedance model.
Use the SaveVideo node to save the generated video to your desired location.
suggestedUseCases: Creating promotional videos for products or services using simple text prompts.
Generating educational content with dynamic visuals to enhance learning.
Producing social media content quickly with engaging video formats.
Developing video prototypes for film or animation projects.
Creating personalized video messages for marketing or personal use.

faqItems.question: What text prompts work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Descriptive and detailed text prompts yield the best results, as they provide the model with more context to generate accurate and engaging videos.

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the video resolution and aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the workflow supports multiple resolutions and aspect ratios, allowing you to tailor the output to your specific needs.

faqItems.question: Is an internet connection required to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes, an internet connection is necessary as the workflow utilizes ByteDance's API, which requires network access from a secure environment.

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate a video?
faqItems.answer: The time to generate a video depends on the complexity of the text prompt and the chosen resolution, but it typically takes a few minutes.

a084de008c94.title: Wan2.6: Image to Video
a084de008c94.description: Transform images into high-quality videos with enhanced image quality, smoother motion, 1080P resolution support, and natural movement generation for professional results.
a084de008c94.metaDescription: Convert images to high-quality videos with the Wan2.6 workflow, featuring enhanced image quality and smooth motion at 1080P resolution.
a084de008c94.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, titled 'Wan2.6: Image to Video,' is designed to transform static images into high-quality videos. It leverages the Wan2.6 model, known for its ability to enhance image quality and generate smooth motion, to produce videos with a resolution of up to 1080P. The workflow begins with the 'LoadImage' node, which imports the image you wish to convert. This image is then processed by the 'WanImageToVideoApi' node, which applies sophisticated algorithms to ensure natural movement and enhanced visual fidelity. Finally, the 'SaveVideo' node saves the output as a video file, ready for professional use.

Technically, this workflow excels due to the integration of the Wan2.6 model, which is specifically tuned for video generation from images. It uses advanced interpolation techniques to create fluid motion between frames, ensuring that the resulting video is not only high in quality but also visually coherent. The workflow is particularly useful for content creators and professionals who need to convert images into engaging video content quickly and efficiently, without compromising on quality.
howToUse: Load your image into the workflow using the 'LoadImage' node.
Configure the 'WanImageToVideoApi' node with your desired settings for motion and resolution.
Run the workflow to process the image and generate the video.
Use the 'SaveVideo' node to save the output video to your desired location.
Review the video for quality and make any necessary adjustments by reconfiguring the nodes.
suggestedUseCases: Creating promotional videos from static product images.
Generating dynamic video content for social media from still photographs.
Developing educational content that requires visual transformation from images to videos.
Producing artistic video projects that start from photographic sources.
Enhancing presentations with video content derived from images.

faqItems.question: What types of images work best with this workflow?
faqItems.answer: High-resolution images with clear details work best, as they provide more data for the Wan2.6 model to generate smooth and high-quality videos.

faqItems.question: Can I adjust the motion smoothness in the video?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the 'WanImageToVideoApi' node allows you to configure settings related to motion smoothness and other video characteristics.

faqItems.question: What is the maximum resolution supported by this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The workflow supports video outputs up to 1080P resolution, ensuring high-quality results suitable for professional use.

faqItems.question: Is it possible to batch process multiple images into videos?
faqItems.answer: Currently, the workflow is designed for single image processing. For batch processing, you would need to run the workflow separately for each image.

a09d65985659.title: Image Enhancer
a09d65985659.description: Upload your image and add some subtle details and sharpness.
a09d65985659.metaDescription: ComfyUI Image Enhancer: sharpen subtle details and optionally upscale images. Load, compare before/after, and save clean, crisp results in minutes.
a09d65985659.extendedDescription: Image Enhancer is a lightweight ComfyUI workflow that sharpens fine details and optionally upscales your images with minimal fuss. It starts with LoadImage to bring your source image into the graph, then passes it through a single enhancement/upscale node (ID: 33e8ca06-a6ea-4ed7-967d-e8f18733f2ba). That node applies subtle edge-aware sharpening and detail boosting, and—if enabled—scales the image to a higher resolution. Because it’s model-agnostic, the exact method depends on what the node exposes on your setup (for example, a built-in sharpen filter or a third‑party upscaler model).
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI, then click the LoadImage node and select the image you want to enhance.

Select the enhancement node (33e8ca06-a6ea-4ed7-967d-e8f18733f2ba). Set its enhancement strength and, if available, choose an upscale factor or model. Start conservatively (e.g., low/medium strength).
Make sure the original image (from LoadImage) and the enhanced output (from the 33e8… node) are both connected to ImageCompare so you can preview before/after.
Click Queue/Execute. Inspect the result in ImageCompare and watch for halos or over-sharpening. If needed, lower strength or scale and re-run.
When satisfied, open the SaveImage node, set your output folder and filename prefix, ensure it’s wired to the enhanced output, and run the node to export.
Repeat with additional images by changing the file in LoadImage and reusing the same settings, or fine-tune per image for best quality.
suggestedUseCases: Product shots: add clarity to textures, logos, and stitching while keeping a natural look.
Portraits: gently refine hair and eye details without introducing harsh artifacts.
Social media and web images: make compressed images crisper before reposting.
Texture sources for 3D or game assets: upscale and sharpen diffuse maps or scanned materials.
Archival scans: subtly enhance old photos while preserving their original character.

faqItems.question: What model or algorithm does the enhancement node use?
faqItems.answer: The enhancement/upscale behavior comes from the custom node (ID: 33e8ca06-a6ea-4ed7-967d-e8f18733f2ba). Its exact model or method depends on your installation. Check the node’s parameters—some builds expose a selectable upscaler (e.g., ESRGAN/Real-ESRGAN or similar) and a sharpening/detail slider.

faqItems.question: How do I avoid halos or over-sharpened edges?
faqItems.answer: Lower the enhancement strength and avoid very high upscale factors in a single pass. Use ImageCompare to inspect edges at 100% zoom. If the node provides separate ‘sharpen’ and ‘detail’ controls, reduce sharpen first. You can also try a two-pass approach: modest enhancement at native size, then a gentle upscale.

faqItems.question: Will this fix very low-resolution or heavily compressed images?
faqItems.answer: It can improve perceived sharpness, but there are limits. For tiny or blocky sources, use a modest upscale (e.g., 1.5–2× if available) and conservative sharpening. Overshooting scale or strength often amplifies compression artifacts.

faqItems.question: Why do colors or contrast look slightly different after enhancement?
faqItems.answer: Some enhancement pipelines alter micro-contrast. Compare in ImageCompare and adjust the node’s strength or any tone-related settings if available. Also ensure your input is standard sRGB and avoid re-saving as low‑quality JPEG, which can shift tones.

a0d7f0c8aa8c.title: SDPose: Image Multi-Person Detection
a0d7f0c8aa8c.description: Upload an image to detect human poses. Supports detection for both single individuals and multiple people within the same scene.
a0d7f0c8aa8c.metaDescription: Detect and preview multi-person human poses from any image using SDPose-OOD in ComfyUI. Adjustable max detections, clean overlays, and easy export.
a0d7f0c8aa8c.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow runs SDPose-OOD to detect people and their whole‑body pose in a still image, with built‑in support for multi‑person scenes. The core detector is packaged inside a subgraph (node type id 01b6a731-fb78-4070-9a38-c87146da9604) so the top-level canvas stays clean while you still get fast, accurate detections. The pipeline starts with LoadImage, optionally normalizes dimensions via ResizeImageMaskNode, then forwards the image into the SDPose subgraph. Detected persons are visualized using DrawBBoxes and overlaid on the original image with ImageBlend for a readable, non-destructive preview. You can inspect results live with PreviewImage and export them using SaveImage.

What makes this preset useful is how quickly you can go from a raw photo to clear, multi-person pose detections with minimal setup. A PrimitiveInt node exposes max_detections so you can control how many people are returned—handy for crowded scenes. Under the hood, the workflow expects the sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors checkpoint (see Model Links) and can pair with the RT-DETR variant noted in the workflow for robust person localization. If you need deeper access—like raw keypoints, confidence scores, or custom thresholding—right‑click the subgraph to Unpack Subgraph and wire out the internal outputs you need.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm the MarkdownNote for quick tips and model requirements.
Prepare models locally: download sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors to ComfyUI/models/checkpoints (and the RT-DETR file noted in the workflow to the folder indicated). Restart ComfyUI if newly added.
Use LoadImage to select your input image. Optionally adjust ResizeImageMaskNode if you want to standardize dimensions for speed or memory.
Set PrimitiveInt → max_detections to control how many people the SDPose subgraph should return (try values like 1, 5, or 10 for crowded images).
Run the workflow. Inspect detections with PreviewImage; DrawBBoxes and ImageBlend overlay results on the original for clarity.
If you want raw keypoints or custom thresholds, right‑click the SDPose subgraph and choose Unpack Subgraph to expose internal outputs/controls, then SaveImage to export your overlays.
suggestedUseCases: Batch auditing group photos to quickly locate and count people before further editing.
Pre-processing reference images for downstream pose-guided generation or retargeting workflows.
Sports or dance analysis where you need fast multi-person detection as a first pass.
Safety/compliance checks to verify presence of people in frames before automated publishing.
Creating datasets with person-localized overlays (bounding boxes) for manual review.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow support multiple people in one image?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Use the PrimitiveInt node to set max_detections. Increase it for crowded scenes to allow the detector to return more people.

faqItems.question: What models do I need and where do I put them?
faqItems.answer: Download sdpose_wholebody_fp16.safetensors to ComfyUI/models/checkpoints. The workflow also references an RT‑DETR variant; follow the workflow’s Model Links and place it in the folder indicated. Restart ComfyUI after adding models.

faqItems.question: Can I export pose keypoints or just the overlay?
faqItems.answer: The preset focuses on image overlays via DrawBBoxes and ImageBlend. To export raw keypoints or scores, right‑click the SDPose subgraph, select Unpack Subgraph, expose the relevant outputs, and route them to a suitable save node.

faqItems.question: How can I improve detection quality on large or crowded images?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing max_detections, provide a higher-resolution input (use ResizeImageMaskNode thoughtfully), and ensure the correct model files are loaded. A GPU is recommended for faster, more stable results.

a0e9a3b16f63.title: Gemini Omni Flash
a0e9a3b16f63.description: Precisely edit your input video with a simple prompt.
a0e9a3b16f63.metaDescription: Prompt-based video editing with Gemini Omni Video in ComfyUI. Load a clip, add duration and aspect ratio, preview, and export clean edits fast.
a0e9a3b16f63.extendedDescription:
This workflow lets you precisely edit an input video with a single, well-structured prompt using Google’s Gemini Omni Video through the GeminiVideoOmni node. It starts by loading your source clip via LoadVideo, then routes the frames and your instructions to GeminiVideoOmni, which performs the video-to-video transformation. A small, focused subgraph called Prompt Constructor (subgraph id: 331103d2-d660-4a88-abf0-1117dc46b2df) helps you assemble a clean, model-friendly prompt that includes the two required parameters for Gemini Omni Video: duration and aspect ratio. The output can be reviewed instantly in PreviewAny and finalized with SaveVideo.

Technically, the workflow reduces ambiguity by embedding temporal (duration: e.g., 5s) and spatial (aspect ratio: e.g., 16:9) constraints directly into the prompt, which is important for stable, temporally consistent edits. The MarkdownNote node embedded in the graph provides guidance and examples so you can iterate quickly. Together, these nodes create a tight loop for prompt-driven visual effects, color/style changes, or localized alterations, without manual keyframing or complex compositing.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the graph. Locate the core nodes: LoadVideo, Prompt Constructor (subgraph id 331103d2-d660-4a88-abf0-1117dc46b2df), GeminiVideoOmni, PreviewAny, and SaveVideo.
Load your source clip with LoadVideo. Note the clip’s duration and aspect ratio (or resolution) so you can match them in the prompt to avoid cropping, letterboxing, or time mismatch.

Open the Prompt Constructor subgraph. Enter your edit instructions and include the required fields in plain text, for example: "duration: 4.0s; aspect ratio: 16:9; Make the sky a dramatic sunset while keeping the camera motion and timing unchanged." Keep the request specific and concise.

Ensure the Prompt Constructor’s output is connected to GeminiVideoOmni along with the video from LoadVideo. In GeminiVideoOmni, confirm any required configuration (such as API credentials or model selection) is set according to the node’s UI.

Run the workflow. Use PreviewAny to review the generated result. If framing looks off, adjust the aspect ratio in your prompt to match the source. If timing drifts, align the duration to the exact clip length.
When you’re satisfied, finalize the export with SaveVideo. Set your output path and desired settings (e.g., fps or quality if available in your node version) and run to write the edited video.
suggestedUseCases: Look development and color restyling: apply a consistent color grade or film look across a short clip with explicit duration and AR control.
Targeted visual modifications: change sky/weather, adjust lighting, or recolor an object while preserving the original camera motion.
Concept previews for clients: quickly iterate on VFX ideas with prompt-only edits before committing to manual compositing.
Style transfer and mood shifts: give footage a painterly, comic, or cinematic vibe that stays stable over the full duration.
Background cleanup: subtle de-emphasis or smoothing of backgrounds to draw attention to the subject.

faqItems.question: Why do I need to include duration and aspect ratio in the prompt?
faqItems.answer: The Gemini Omni Video model expects both fields to resolve temporal and spatial constraints. Providing them helps prevent timing drift, cropping, or letterboxing and improves overall consistency. Use the Prompt Constructor subgraph to add them correctly.

faqItems.question: What happens if my prompt’s duration doesn’t match the source clip?
faqItems.answer: You may see truncation, repetition, or timing artifacts. For best results, set the prompt duration to the exact clip length (in seconds) from LoadVideo so the edit aligns frame-for-frame.

faqItems.question: How do I avoid stretching or cropped outputs?
faqItems.answer: Match the prompt’s aspect ratio to the source video’s aspect ratio. If the input is 1920x1080, use aspect ratio: 16:9. Mismatches can introduce letterboxing or unintended crops.

faqItems.question: Does this workflow handle audio?
faqItems.answer: This workflow focuses on visual edits. If you need audio, export the edited video and remux it with the original audio track in a video editor or command-line tool.

a1bb55d904c9.title: Wan2.1 VACE Inpainting
a1bb55d904c9.description: Edit specific regions in videos while preserving surrounding content. Great for object removal or replacement.
a1bb55d904c9.metaDescription: Edit video regions with Wan2.1 VACE Inpainting for seamless object removal or replacement while preserving surrounding content.
a1bb55d904c9.extendedDescription:
The Wan2.1 VACE Inpainting workflow is designed to seamlessly edit specific regions in video content while preserving the integrity of the surrounding areas. This is particularly useful for tasks such as object removal or replacement in video sequences. Utilizing the Wan2.1 model, this workflow leverages a combination of nodes including KSampler for sampling, CLIPTextEncode for text encoding, and VAEDecode for decoding video frames. The workflow is structured into several steps, starting from loading models and video files, to creating masks and compositing the final video output.

Technically, the workflow employs the WanVaceToVideo node to convert inpainted frames back into video format, while the TrimVideoLatent and CreateVideo nodes manage the video length and format. The ImageCompositeMasked node is crucial for blending the inpainted regions with the original video, ensuring a natural look. By using core nodes, the workflow avoids the need for additional custom installations, making it accessible and easy to implement. This workflow is particularly valuable for content creators and video editors who need to make precise edits without affecting the overall quality of the video.
howToUse: Load the Wan2.1 VACE Inpainting workflow in ComfyUI.
Import the video you wish to edit using the LoadVideo node.
Create a mask for the region you want to inpaint using the ImageToMask node.
Configure the KSampler and CLIPTextEncode nodes with your desired settings and prompts.
Run the workflow to process the video and generate the inpainted output.
Save the final video using the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Removing unwanted objects from a video scene.
Replacing objects in a video with alternative content.
Enhancing video quality by correcting specific regions.
Creating special effects by altering video elements.
Preserving video continuity while making targeted edits.

faqItems.question: What models are used in this workflow?

faqItems.question: Can this workflow handle high-resolution videos?

faqItems.question: Do I need custom nodes for this workflow?

The core of the transformation occurs through the WanImageToVideoApi node, which processes the image and audio to produce a cohesive video output. howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and ensure you have the Wan2.5 and Wan models installed.
Upload your image using the LoadImage node in the 'Step1 - Upload image' group.
Optionally, add audio by using the LoadAudio or RecordAudio nodes. Ensure the audio is between 3-30 seconds and under 15MB.
Connect the audio output to the Wan Text to Video input if using audio.
Run the workflow to process the image and audio through the WanImageToVideoApi node.
Save the resulting video using the SaveVideo node.
suggestedUseCases: Creating engaging social media content by animating still images.

faqItems.question: What are the requirements for the audio file?

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow without an internet connection?

faqItems.question: How do I enable the RecordAudio node?

The VAEDecode node then decodes this latent representation into a visible image, which can be saved using the SaveImage node. This workflow is particularly useful for artists and designers who wish to incorporate specific styles or elements from reference images into new creations, offering a seamless blend of textual and visual inspiration.
howToUse: Load the SDXL Revision Text Prompts workflow into ComfyUI.
Import your desired reference images using the LoadImage node.
Enter your text prompts in the CLIPTextEncode node, such as 'car, city, anime style'.
Configure the KSampler node to adjust sampling parameters for desired output quality.
Run the workflow to generate the image, which will be decoded and saved using the VAEDecode and SaveImage nodes.
Review the generated image and make adjustments to prompts or reference images as needed for refinement.
suggestedUseCases: Creating concept art by blending elements from various reference images.
Designing marketing visuals that incorporate specific brand elements.
Generating unique artistic styles by combining textual prompts with visual references.
Developing storyboards for animations or films using thematic prompts and images.

faqItems.question: What types of images work best as reference images?
faqItems.answer: High-quality images with clear elements work best, as they provide more detailed information for the CLIPVisionEncode node to process.

faqItems.question: Can I use multiple reference images at once?

faqItems.question: How do I adjust the style of the generated image?
