dc1311a65bc4.title: Seedance2.0: First-Last-Frame to Video
dc1311a65bc4.description: Upload the first and last frames of your video. Generate a high-quality video sequence using the Seedance2.0 model.
dc1311a65bc4.metaDescription: Seedance 2.0 FLF2V in ComfyUI: generate stable, identity-consistent videos from first and last frames using boundary-conditioned diffusion.
dc1311a65bc4.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 brings a boundary‑conditioned approach to video generation: supply the first and last frames, and the model synthesizes the in‑between motion with striking temporal stability. Instead of guessing a trajectory from a single image or relying on text prompts, the pipeline conditions on both endpoints to infer a coherent path for objects, lighting, and camera movement. In ComfyUI, this is encapsulated by the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, which takes two images and produces a full sequence that faithfully lands on your final frame.

This first‑last‑frame to video (FLF2V) method reduces identity drift, flicker, and composition shifts that commonly plague single‑frame or text‑to‑video methods. Unlike basic frame interpolation—which can only warp what already exists—Seedance 2.0 synthesizes novel content between your keyframes while preserving structure and intent. The result is cleaner motion planning, stronger subject consistency, and more predictable outcomes for real productions.
howToUse: Prepare two images: the exact first and last frames you want. Use the same resolution and aspect ratio for both to ensure clean conditioning.
Add two LoadImage nodes in ComfyUI and load your first and last frames. Connect their outputs to the corresponding inputs on ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode.
Ensure the Seedance 2.0 model is available and selected by the ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode (follow your installation’s model placement conventions).
Configure the generation timeline in ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode (e.g., desired frame count and FPS). For reproducible results, fix the seed in your ComfyUI session or node settings.
Execute the graph to preview the generated sequence. If motion is too aggressive or not reaching the desired composition, refine your end frame or adjust duration.
Connect the node’s video output to SaveVideo, set your target FPS and encoding, and run to export the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: Storyboard-to-shot: animate between two keyframes to quickly validate motion and timing before full production.
Product demos: rotate or reposition a product from A to B with stable identity and controlled end composition.
UI/UX motion design: craft polished transitions between interface states using precise start and end visuals.
Cinematic blocking: previsualize camera or subject repositioning with reliable landings on the final frame.
Before-after visualizations: show transformations (e.g., environment, space planning) with a coherent narrative arc.

faqItems.question: How is this different from frame interpolation between two images?
faqItems.answer: Interpolation warps existing pixels from the endpoints. Seedance 2.0 synthesizes new in-between frames using two-endpoint conditioning, enabling plausible motion and detail that aren’t present in either input while still honoring both boundaries.

faqItems.question: Do my first and last frames need to match in size or aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode expects matching resolutions for stable results. Prepare both frames at the same size before loading them with LoadImage to avoid unintended rescaling or artifacts.

faqItems.question: Can it handle large viewpoint or subject changes between the first and last frames?
faqItems.answer: It can infer substantial motion, but extreme jumps may increase artifacts or ambiguity. For best results, keep the endpoints visually related and adjust duration (more frames) to give the model room to plan a coherent path.

faqItems.question: How do I ensure consistent, repeatable outputs?

dc4b3f6dab6e.title: Step 2: Contact Sheet Workflow
dc4b3f6dab6e.description: Upload the fashion editorial and product image. Generate 8 distinct angle variations with product consistency from only 2 Nano Banana generations.
dc4b3f6dab6e.metaDescription: ComfyUI contact sheet workflow: turn 2 Nano Banana Pro generations into 8 consistent product angles, compiled into a 9:16 4K contact sheet.
dc4b3f6dab6e.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow builds a fast, repeatable contact-sheet generator for fashion products. You provide two inputs—a fashion editorial reference and a clean product image—and the graph produces eight distinct angle variations while preserving product identity. The pipeline pivots on Nano Banana Pro for image generation and uses a small, consistent set of prompts to drive variety without drifting from the product look. Outputs are compiled into a vertical 9:16 contact sheet at 4K resolution (2160x3840) for quick review or social/merchandising handoff.

Technically, the graph uses LoadImage to bring in your editorial reference and product packshot. A PrimitiveStringMultiline node holds the eight angle directives (you can edit these to change viewpoints), while a PrimitiveNode stores simple numeric settings (such as the number of angles or seeds). GeminiImage2Node (configured for gemini-3-pro-image-preview) can be used as a helper to analyze the editorial reference or produce caption text that feeds into your prompt block. Two essentials nodes (UUIDs 68c58c16-e698-45a4-97f9-54ae8eb9dee9 and 487baed2-dc27-49c3-a6b2-0bf45a53e64d from comfyui_essentials) handle image collation and layout with BatchImagesNode assembling the eight results, RegexReplace cleaning file names, and SaveImage writing a single 8-up contact sheet plus optional individual frames. The result is a compact, reliable step that expands only two Nano Banana generations into eight consistent angles.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the nodes panel. Confirm custom nodes from comfyui_essentials are installed so UUIDs 68c58c16-e698-45a4-97f9-54ae8eb9dee9 and 487baed2-dc27-49c3-a6b2-0bf45a53e64d resolve correctly.
Use the LoadImage nodes to import your fashion editorial reference and your product image (ideally a clean packshot or masked image). Verify both preview correctly.

Open the PrimitiveStringMultiline node and review the angle directives (e.g., front, three-quarter, profile, low-angle, over-shoulder, back, etc.). Edit or replace this list to match the eight angles you want.

Select Nano Banana Pro as the model in the generation nodes in the graph (where applicable) and confirm the output resolution is set for vertical 9:16 at 4K (2160x3840). Use the PrimitiveNode to set any numeric parameters (e.g., seed or count = 8).

Optionally enable or wire GeminiImage2Node (gemini-3-pro-image-preview) to extract captions or angle hints from the editorial image, then feed those into your prompt block. If you prefer manual control, leave the multiline prompt as your sole driver.

Run the workflow. BatchImagesNode will collect the eight results, the essentials layout nodes will assemble the 8-up grid, RegexReplace will sanitize file names, and SaveImage will write the final contact sheet (plus optional individual frames) to your chosen output folder.
suggestedUseCases: E‑commerce PDP build-outs: generate a consistent set of eight product angles to complement editorial imagery.
Art direction alignment: quickly validate camera angles and styling against an editorial reference before a full render pass.
Social and campaign planning: produce a vertical 9:16 4K contact sheet for decks, storyboards, or Instagram/TikTok story previews.
Marketplace listing standardization: enforce a repeatable set of angles across SKUs to improve visual consistency.
Client review rounds: share a single consolidated sheet of eight angles for faster approvals.

faqItems.question: How do I change which eight angles are generated?
faqItems.answer: Edit the PrimitiveStringMultiline node. Replace or reorder the angle directives to match the views you need. The workflow will generate one image per line, then assemble all eight into the contact sheet.

faqItems.question: Do I have to use GeminiImage2Node?
faqItems.answer: No. GeminiImage2Node (gemini-3-pro-image-preview) is an optional helper for deriving captions or angle hints from the editorial reference. You can rely entirely on the manual directives in PrimitiveStringMultiline if you prefer full control.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow maintain product consistency?
faqItems.answer: Consistency comes from using the same product image input and a tightly scoped set of prompts with Nano Banana Pro. Keep the product image clean and well-lit, avoid overly creative modifiers, and reuse a fixed seed if you want stricter repeatability.

faqItems.question: Can I export individual images instead of only a contact sheet?
faqItems.answer: Yes. BatchImagesNode passes each frame to SaveImage. You can keep both the 8-up grid and the individual frames, or disable the grid output path if you only want separate images.

This ComfyUI workflow turns any sentence into a Vox-style archival newspaper match-cut montage. An OpenAIChatNode (driven by OpenAIChatConfig) takes your sentence and splits it into a clean list of words. FL_PromptMulti then expands those words into per-word image prompts, and OpenAIGPTImage1 calls OpenAI’s gpt-image-1 model to render each word as a bold editorial headline on an aged newsprint page. SaveImage can optionally write out the individual frames for inspection and iteration.

Once the frames are generated, ImageRemoveAlpha+ ensures each image has an opaque background for video encoding. ImageListToImageBatch organizes the frames, and ImageBatchRepeatInterleaving duplicates each frame a set number of times to create the snappy, stop‑motion pacing typical of match cuts. CreateVideo assembles the batch into an MP4 at your chosen frame rate, and SaveVideo writes the final clip. You can quickly change the visual direction by editing the base prompt in OpenAIChatConfig—switch from monochrome broadsheet to magazine color, tabloid grit, ransom-note collage, or comic-book halftone—while FPS and repeat count let you fine‑tune timing and readability.
howToUse: Load the Text Match Cut workflow in ComfyUI and add your OpenAI API key to OpenAIChatNode/OpenAIGPTImage1 (or set it via environment variables if supported).

Open the OpenAIChatConfig node and set the base prompt. Describe the visual style (e.g., “aged editorial page, off‑white newsprint, halftone, bold serif headline”) and instruct it to output a clean list of words from your sentence.

In OpenAIChatNode, enter your sentence. The node will return a list of words to feed downstream. Optionally, refine the system/user prompts in OpenAIChatConfig to filter out stop-words or punctuation.
Review FL_PromptMulti’s template. Ensure it places each {item} (word) into a clear image prompt (e.g., “A single editorial page photographed on newsprint. Centered headline text: ‘{item}’ …”).
Adjust OpenAIGPTImage1 settings (model: gpt-image-1). Set the desired image size/aspect for your video. Use SaveImage to preview a few frames and confirm typography and paper texture look right.

Tune pacing: set the per-frame Repeat Count in ImageBatchRepeatInterleaving and the FPS in CreateVideo. Higher repeats or lower FPS increase hold time per word. Then run the queue and export via SaveVideo.
suggestedUseCases: Explainer video intros where keywords pop in quick succession for emphasis.
Documentary title cards or chapter markers styled like archival press clippings.
Social teasers that rhythmically match-cut brand pillars or product features.
Educational shorts that reveal vocabulary or historical dates as bold headlines.
Editorial motion graphics for news segments or investigative pieces.

faqItems.question: Which model generates the images, and can I change the style?
faqItems.answer: The OpenAIGPTImage1 node uses OpenAI’s gpt-image-1. Style is controlled by the base prompt in OpenAIChatConfig and the FL_PromptMulti template. Edit those to switch from aged newspaper to magazine color, tabloid, ransom-note collage, or comic-book aesthetics.

faqItems.question: How do I control pacing and readability of each word on screen?
faqItems.answer: Use ImageBatchRepeatInterleaving to set how many times each frame is repeated, and adjust FPS in CreateVideo. More repeats or lower FPS increases on-screen time per word. For fast, punchy cuts, use fewer repeats and higher FPS.

faqItems.question: My sentence includes punctuation or filler words. Can I filter them out?
faqItems.answer: Yes. In OpenAIChatConfig, instruct the chat node to return an array of meaningful words only (e.g., remove articles like “a,” “an,” “the,” and strip punctuation). You can also instruct it to uppercase or normalize each word for consistent typography.

faqItems.question: How can I get cleaner, more legible headline typography?
faqItems.answer: Refine the image prompt in FL_PromptMulti to be explicit: specify a bold serif or sans-serif headline, centered layout, high-contrast ink on off-white newsprint, and minimal background clutter. Keeping each word short and using uppercase often improves results.

faqItems.question: What about cost and performance with longer sentences?
faqItems.answer: Each word triggers an image generation call to gpt-image-1, so long sentences increase time and API cost. Consider capping the word count in OpenAIChatConfig, batching test runs at smaller image sizes, and previewing via SaveImage before exporting the final video.

e173ace9bf90.title: 2.1 Creator - Diffusion Basics
e173ace9bf90.description: Learn the diffusion basics using Z-Image-Turbo.
e173ace9bf90.metaDescription: Learn diffusion basics with ComfyUI's 2.1 Creator workflow using Z-Image-Turbo for text-to-image generation.
e173ace9bf90.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow, titled '2.1 Creator - Diffusion Basics,' is designed to introduce users to the foundational concepts of image generation using diffusion models. At its core, the workflow leverages the Z-Image-Turbo model to transform random noise into coherent images based on textual prompts. The process begins with the 'EmptyLatentImage' node, which generates a noisy canvas at a specified resolution. This noise is then iteratively refined through the 'KSampler' node, which utilizes the 'ModelSamplingAuraFlow' to guide the denoising process, informed by the textual input encoded by the 'CLIPTextEncode' node.

The workflow is structured to load essential components like the UNET model ('UNETLoader'), a text encoder ('CLIPLoader'), and a variational autoencoder ('VAELoader') to facilitate the conversion of text to image. The 'VAEDecode' node plays a crucial role in converting the final latent representation back into a viewable image format. Finally, the 'SaveImage' node ensures that the generated image is saved with a specified prefix. This workflow is particularly useful for those new to diffusion models, providing a hands-on approach to understanding how text-based image generation works technically and practically.
howToUse: Load the '2.1 Creator - Diffusion Basics' workflow in ComfyUI.
Ensure the Z-Image-Turbo model, CLIP text encoder, and VAE are loaded using the respective nodes.
Set your desired image resolution and generate an initial noise canvas using the 'EmptyLatentImage' node.
Input your text prompt into the 'CLIPTextEncode' node to guide the image generation process.
Run the workflow to iteratively refine the noise into a coherent image using the 'KSampler' node.
Save the generated image using the 'SaveImage' node with your chosen file prefix.
suggestedUseCases: Creating editorial-style images for fashion shoots.
Generating conceptual art from descriptive text prompts.
Prototyping visual ideas quickly for creative projects.
Enhancing storytelling with custom visuals for narratives.
Exploring artistic interpretations of abstract concepts.

faqItems.question: What is the purpose of the 'EmptyLatentImage' node?
faqItems.answer: The 'EmptyLatentImage' node initializes the process by creating a canvas of random noise, which serves as the starting point for the diffusion process.

faqItems.question: How does the 'CLIPTextEncode' node work?
faqItems.answer: The 'CLIPTextEncode' node converts your text prompt into guidance vectors, which help steer the image generation process in alignment with the described content.

faqItems.question: Why is the VAE important in this workflow?
faqItems.answer: The VAE compresses images into a latent space for efficient processing and then decodes the final latent representation back into a viewable image.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for high-resolution images?
faqItems.answer: Yes, you can specify different resolutions in the 'EmptyLatentImage' node, but keep in mind that higher resolutions may require more computational resources.

e1e03cafda18.title: Style Transfer Vid2Vid - GPT Image 2 + Seedance 2.0
e1e03cafda18.description: Create up to 4 style transfer video to video generations using state of the art models. This workflow creates a depth map from your input video to guide the Seedance 2.0 generation. The first frame of the video is extracted and used as reference with your style prompts using GPT-Image-2.
e1e03cafda18.metaDescription: Depth-guided vid2vid style transfer in ComfyUI using Seedance 2.0 and GPT-Image-2. Batch up to 4 styles with first-frame reference for motion-stable results.
e1e03cafda18.extendedDescription:
This depth-aware, reference-guided video-to-video workflow applies consistent style transfer to your footage while preserving motion and scene geometry. It starts by ingesting your clip with LoadVideo, then computes a per-frame depth map to anchor structure and camera movement (handled by the custom processing node c3b10638-32f0-4101-9b21-21fcda8712d8). The very first frame is extracted and saved (via SaveImage and helper utilities like 8dbec705-cae4-4197-9594-85b48cc18483), then passed to OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 together with your text prompt from PrimitiveStringMultiline. GPT-Image-2 generates a style-matched reference image from that initial frame, which the workflow uses to steer the overall look.

The core stylization is driven by Seedance 2.0 through ByteDance2ReferenceNode, which fuses three signals: the depth map (structure), the first-frame style reference (appearance), and your prompt (semantic guidance). You can queue up to four style variations in one run using the batch fan-out/collector nodes (a3edb32a-4533-45e3-8eb2-84399225da2e), then reassemble the generated frames into final videos with CreateVideo and SaveVideo. The result is a set of stable, on-style clips that maintain the original timing and motion while reflecting your chosen aesthetic.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and verify required models and APIs: Seedance 2.0 (for ByteDance2ReferenceNode) and an API key for OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2.
In LoadVideo, select your source video and set basic options (resolution/fps as needed). The workflow will extract frames and compute a depth map automatically.
Open PrimitiveStringMultiline and enter up to 4 style prompts (one per line) to enable batch generation. Set seeds if you want repeatable outputs.
In OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2, add your API key and adjust generation settings if exposed (e.g., strength or guidance). This node will style the first frame into a reference image.

In ByteDance2ReferenceNode, review style/depth/consistency controls (if available). Higher depth influence generally preserves motion and structure better; stronger style influence increases stylization.

Queue Prompt to run. When processing finishes, the workflow assembles each variation with CreateVideo and saves them via SaveVideo. Check the output folder for both the styled clips and any saved reference frames.
suggestedUseCases: Music videos or dance clips where motion should stay true to the original but the look needs a bold artistic style.
Product b-roll recolored and restyled for different campaigns while keeping the same camera moves.
Turning live-action footage into anime, comic, or painterly versions without losing scene depth.
Brand-consistent social edits that apply a house style across multiple takes in one batch.
Previsualization: quickly explore several visual directions on the same shot for client review.

faqItems.question: How does this workflow keep motion stable while changing the style?
faqItems.answer: It computes a per-frame depth map from your input video to preserve scene structure, then uses ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Seedance 2.0) to blend that structure with a style reference created from the first frame by GPT-Image-2. Increasing depth/consistency settings (if exposed) typically reduces flicker and warping.

faqItems.question: Do I need an OpenAI API key for GPT-Image-2?
faqItems.answer: Yes. OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 calls GPT-Image-2 to create a style-matched reference from the first frame. Add your API key in that node’s settings and adjust any available parameters to control the reference output.

faqItems.question: Can I generate multiple styled versions at once?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Enter up to four prompts (one per line) in PrimitiveStringMultiline. The batch nodes (a3edb32a-4533-45e3-8eb2-84399225da2e) fan out the inputs so the pipeline produces up to four videos in one run.

faqItems.question: Why is my result flickering or drifting from the source motion?
faqItems.answer: Try increasing the depth influence or temporal consistency in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, lowering the style strength, and using a fixed seed. Also ensure the input fps and resolution are sensible for your GPU; excessively high settings can cause instability.

faqItems.question: Does the output video include audio?
faqItems.answer: No. SaveVideo writes silent video files. If you need audio, export it from the original clip and remux it onto the styled output in your video editor.

e2716c39cb46.metaDescription: Edit images by region with Seedream 5.0 Pro in ComfyUI. Use two images and a prompt to make precise, lighting‑preserving edits for products, portraits, and layouts.
e2716c39cb46.extendedDescription:
Seedream 5.0 Pro is an instruction‑guided image editing workflow built around the ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 model. It takes two images—a base image to be edited and a guide/reference image—plus a clear text prompt, then applies targeted changes while preserving the original lighting, depth, and surface texture. In ComfyUI, the images are brought in with LoadImage nodes, passed to ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 for editing, and written out using SaveImageAdvanced for organized, reproducible results.

Technically, ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 performs diffusion‑based edits conditioned on both the base image and your instruction prompt, with the second image acting as a guide for regions, layout, or stylistic cues. This dual‑conditioning lets you localize changes (e.g., background swaps, product color updates, layouted text) without destroying the scene’s geometry or material qualities. SaveImageAdvanced helps you version outputs with consistent filenames and metadata, making iteration straightforward.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the two LoadImage nodes, the ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 node, and the SaveImageAdvanced node.

In the first LoadImage, select your base image (the photo you want to edit). In the second LoadImage, select a guide/reference image (e.g., a mask, layout mockup, or style/layout reference). For best results, keep aspect ratios consistent.

Open ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 and enter a clear, instructional prompt describing the change, e.g., “Replace the background with clean studio white; keep product color and reflections intact.” If your node exposes seed or guidance controls, set them for reproducibility and to balance prompt vs. guide influence.
Configure SaveImageAdvanced with an output folder and filename pattern (include tokens like prompt snippets or seeds if available) so each iteration is saved and easy to compare.
Run the graph. Inspect the output. If the change is too broad or too subtle, refine your prompt or adjust the guide image (e.g., a tighter mask or a clearer layout), then re‑run.

Iterate: swap in alternative guide images for different regions or layouts, or adjust phrasing in your prompt to increase or decrease the aggressiveness of the edit while monitoring texture and lighting retention.
suggestedUseCases: Product photography cleanup: replace or unify backgrounds, refine shadows, or adjust brand colors while preserving material finishes.
Portrait consistency: subtle wardrobe, makeup, or backdrop adjustments that keep identity, skin texture, and lighting intact.
Structured layouts with multilingual text: guide placements using a layout/reference image and prompt the final look for social posts or ads.
Packaging and label iterations: swap labels or patterns on the same object while keeping highlights, depth, and reflections.
Catalog standardization: harmonize framing and backgrounds across a series without re‑shooting.

faqItems.question: What are the two images used for?
faqItems.answer: The first (base) image is the photo you want to edit. The second (guide) image provides spatial or stylistic guidance—such as a mask, a layout mockup, or a reference that indicates where and how changes should happen. The ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 node conditions on both inputs along with your prompt.

faqItems.question: How can I control which areas change while keeping the rest untouched?
faqItems.answer: Use a deliberate guide image. For precise localization, provide a clean mask‑style guide or a clear layout reference. Then use a focused prompt that describes only the intended change (e.g., “Change background to white; do not alter the subject”). Iterating with tighter guides generally increases control.

faqItems.question: What image sizes work best?
faqItems.answer: Use reasonably high‑quality inputs and keep the base and guide images aligned in aspect ratio. If the node resizes automatically, feeding matched dimensions reduces warping and improves edge fidelity. For web use, a longest side around 1024–1536 px is a practical starting point.

faqItems.question: Can I batch process multiple images with this setup?
faqItems.answer: This graph is configured for one base/guide pair at a time. ComfyUI can batch with additional nodes (e.g., directory loaders and iterators), but those are not included here. To batch, extend the workflow with batch‑friendly loaders and route them through the same ByteDanceSeedreamNodeV2 and SaveImageAdvanced pattern.

e2ceec4fc610.title: Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash: Video Extend
e2ceec4fc610.description: Extend an existing video by up to 10 seconds per step, building stories up to 40 seconds total with Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash. The model analyzes the last 10 seconds of context, keeping characters, motion, and audio coherent as the scene continues from where it left off. Optionally attach reference images to introduce new characters mid-story. Works on uploaded clips and previously generated videos; describe how the scene should continue in plain language. Ideal for longer narratives, scene branching, and iterative storytelling.
e2ceec4fc610.metaDescription: Extend videos up to 10s per step (max ~40s) with Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash in ComfyUI. Keep visual continuity and branch stories using prompts and image refs.
e2ceec4fc610.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows how to extend an existing video in coherent, story-aware chunks using the GeminiVideoOmniV2 node (Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash). It loads your clip with LoadVideo, extracts the final moments as context via Video Slice, and asks Gemini to continue the scene for up to 10 seconds per run. The model reads the last 10 seconds of visual context so characters, motion, camera framing, and scene layout carry forward naturally instead of restarting from scratch. SaveVideo then exports the extended result as a new clip.

Technically, the pipeline is a loop-friendly chain: LoadVideo → Video Slice (tail window) → GeminiVideoOmniV2 (prompted continuation) → SaveVideo. You can iterate this up to four times to build a 40-second story, or branch at any step by changing the prompt. The GeminiVideoOmniV2 node also supports optional image references, which you can attach mid-story to introduce new characters or props while maintaining continuity with the previous scene. The included MarkdownNote explains the required input asset path and tips for best results.
howToUse: Open the workflow in ComfyUI and review the MarkdownNote for input instructions and tips. Place your source clip at input/rooster_duel_western.mp4 (or update the LoadVideo path to your file).
Select the LoadVideo node and confirm your clip loads correctly (resolution, FPS). If you’re replacing the example, keep consistent dimensions for smoother extensions.

Configure the Video Slice node to use the last 10 seconds as the context window. This tail slice is what Gemini reads to continue the scene. If your clip is shorter, it will use whatever duration is available.

Open GeminiVideoOmniV2: enter your Gemini API key (if required), write a plain-language continuation prompt (what should happen next), and set the extension duration to 5–10 seconds. Optionally attach one or more image references to introduce new characters/props mid-story.
Set SaveVideo output filename and codec settings as needed. Click Queue Prompt to run. When complete, preview the result to ensure the continuation matches your intent.

Iterate or branch: feed the newly saved clip back into LoadVideo and repeat to build up to ~40 seconds total, or duplicate the node chain and vary the prompt to explore alternate story paths from the same context.
suggestedUseCases: Narrative continuation for short films or storyboards, extending scenes in small, controllable beats.
A/B branching to explore multiple plot directions from the same ending context frame.
Previsualization for directors, quickly testing camera moves or blocking beyond the current cut.
Social media teasers or cliffhangers that extend viral clips while keeping subjects and motion consistent.

faqItems.question: How long can I extend a video with this template?
faqItems.answer: The workflow is tuned for up to 10 seconds per step and about 40 seconds total across iterations. You can run more steps, but visual quality and continuity may degrade as context drifts.

faqItems.question: How do I keep characters and style consistent across steps?
faqItems.answer: Keep prompts consistent, describe key subjects and camera behavior clearly, and reuse the last 10 seconds as context via the Video Slice node. For stronger identity anchoring, attach one or more reference images to the GeminiVideoOmniV2 node.

faqItems.question: Does the output include audio?
faqItems.answer: This template focuses on visual continuation. LoadVideo/SaveVideo in many ComfyUI setups export silent MP4s. If you need audio, keep your original track and re-sync or design new audio in post after export.

faqItems.question: Can I branch the story and try alternative continuations?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Duplicate the GeminiVideoOmniV2 + SaveVideo segment, keep the same Video Slice tail input, and vary the prompt (and optional image refs). You’ll get multiple alternate continuations from the same context.

e41b80eb587d.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate illustrated images with Qwen-Image and the Alvdansen Illustration LoRA. Learn setup, prompts, LoRA strength, and saving outputs.
e41b80eb587d.extendedDescription:

The core of the graph is a custom Qwen‑Image generator node (id: e5cfe5ba-2ae0-4bc4-869f-ab2228cb44d3) that accepts your prompt and applies the style LoRA at inference. Technically, the workflow loads the Qwen-Image checkpoint and blends in the Alvdansen Illustration LoRA weights at a user-defined strength. Your prompt determines subject and composition; the LoRA biases line work, texture, and palette toward the trained style family. You control the look by adjusting LoRA strength (subtle to strong stylization), resolution/aspect ratio, and seed for reproducibility or variation. This setup is useful when you want consistent art direction without retraining—iterate quickly, compare outputs with different seeds, and fine‑tune style intensity before exporting via the SaveImage node.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. Make sure the Qwen-Image extension/node is installed as described in the Qwen‑Image docs (see link in the MarkdownNote).

Download the Alvdansen Illustration v1.0 LoRA (https://huggingface.co/alvdansen/illustration-1.0-qwen-image). Place the LoRA file in a folder your Qwen‑Image node can access (commonly ComfyUI/models/loras) and ensure the base Qwen‑Image model is available to the generator node.

Open the Qwen‑Image generator node (id: e5cfe5ba-2ae0-4bc4-869f-ab2228cb44d3). Enter your text prompt describing subject and desired look (e.g., character pose, setting, lighting, medium). Select the Alvdansen Illustration LoRA and set its strength (start around 0.6–0.9 for a clear style; lower values like 0.3–0.5 for subtle influence).

Set image size and seed in the same node to control composition and reproducibility. Use a fixed seed to refine a concept; change the seed for new variations. If the node supports batching, set a small batch size (e.g., 2–4) to explore multiple options at once.
Click Queue Prompt to generate. The SaveImage node will automatically write results to your ComfyUI/output folder (check filename prefix/path in the SaveImage node).

Iterate: adjust LoRA strength for more/less stylization, refine prompt language with art terms (line weight, ink wash, watercolor, halftone, screentone), and try different aspect ratios suited to your target (squares for avatars, vertical for covers, wide for panels).
suggestedUseCases: Character design sheets with consistent line work and palette across iterations.
Graphic novel or bande dessinée panel explorations to test composition and mood.
Indie risograph poster and zine mockups with bold shapes and limited-color looks.
Children’s book and storybook watercolor-style concept pages.
Retro shoujo manga spot illustrations with expressive line and screentone-like texture.

faqItems.question: How do I control how strong the illustration style appears?
faqItems.answer: Use the LoRA strength in the Qwen‑Image generator node. Higher values push the image closer to the Alvdansen Illustration look; lower values keep more of the base model’s default style. Start around 0.7–0.9 for strong stylization and 0.3–0.6 for subtle influence.

faqItems.question: Where do the images save, and how can I change the filename?
faqItems.answer: The SaveImage node writes outputs to ComfyUI/output by default. Open the SaveImage node to set the output path and filename prefix so you can organize different runs and styles.

faqItems.question: Can I combine this with other LoRAs or conditioning?
faqItems.answer: You can stack additional LoRAs only if the Qwen‑Image node you’re using supports multiple adapters. This minimal workflow focuses on a single style LoRA. If you need edge or pose control, use a Qwen‑Image workflow that includes the appropriate conditioning nodes and routes.

faqItems.question: How do I get consistent characters across multiple images?
faqItems.answer: Keep the character descriptors in your prompt consistent (hair, outfit, colors, era) and fix the seed while you iterate. When you’re happy with the look, vary the seed slightly for new poses while maintaining the same core description and LoRA strength.

e4a4339afda4.title: Image to 3D
e4a4339afda4.description: Upload an image and generate an orbit video and 3d file (.obj) of your asset.
e4a4339afda4.metaDescription: Convert a single image into a 3D Gaussian Splat, render an orbit video, and export OBJ/GLB using ComfyUI nodes like RenderSplat, CreateVideo, and SplatToMesh.
e4a4339afda4.extendedDescription:
This Image to 3D workflow turns a single reference image into a lightweight 3D Gaussian Splat scene, then renders an orbiting turntable video and exports a 3D file you can use downstream. It starts with LoadImage to ingest your source, then passes it to a single-image 3D estimator node (b64333d5-4e6f-4e99-9506-2ec4f63259fe), which predicts a 3D point/splat representation from the photo. CreateCameraInfo builds an orbit camera path (radius, elevation, and frame count), and RenderSplat renders the sequence along that path. CreateVideo assembles the frames and SaveVideo writes the final orbit clip to disk.

For 3D export, the splat scene can go two ways: SplatToFile3D saves a direct 3D file (commonly .obj), while SplatToMesh converts the splats into a triangle mesh suitable for SaveGLB (for .glb). The splat path is fast and faithful to the reconstruction, while the mesh path increases compatibility with DCC tools and game engines. Because this is an experimental single-image reconstruction, it works best on object-centered photos with clean backgrounds—occluded or unseen regions are plausibly inferred and may need cleanup in your 3D tool of choice.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the node graph. In LoadImage, choose a clear, object-centered photo (square or near-square works well).
Select the 3D estimator node (b64333d5-4e6f-4e99-9506-2ec4f63259fe). If it exposes quality or resolution settings, start with a moderate input size (e.g., ~512–768 px) to manage VRAM.
Configure CreateCameraInfo to define your orbit: set the number of frames, orbit radius, and elevation range. A full 360° orbit with 120–240 frames gives smooth results.
In RenderSplat, set output resolution, background (transparent or solid), and any splat rendering options (size, exposure). Do a quick test render with fewer frames to verify framing.
To produce a video, connect RenderSplat to CreateVideo, set FPS (e.g., 24–30), then SaveVideo to write the turntable clip. Check the ComfyUI/output folder for the saved file.

To export 3D, either: (a) use SplatToFile3D to write a direct 3D file (e.g., OBJ), or (b) feed the splat into SplatToMesh, adjust target face count/smoothing, then SaveGLB for a GLB. Inspect results in your 3D app and refine if needed.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce and product turntables from a single packshot to quickly preview a 3D-like rotation.
Concept art and prop ideation where a fast 3D reference helps explore form and silhouette.
Previsualization and storyboards that benefit from orbiting views without full modeling time.
AR/VR placeholders and blocking assets when you need quick, approximate geometry.
Education and demos showcasing single-view 3D reconstruction and Gaussian splatting.

faqItems.question: What outputs does this workflow create?
faqItems.answer: It renders an orbit video via CreateVideo + SaveVideo, and exports 3D via two routes: SplatToFile3D (commonly OBJ) for a direct splat-based file, or SplatToMesh + SaveGLB for a triangle mesh saved as GLB.

faqItems.question: How can I get the best results from a single photo?
faqItems.answer: Use an object-centered shot with minimal background clutter, good lighting, and as few occlusions as possible. Start with moderate input resolution to avoid VRAM issues, verify framing with a short test orbit, then increase frames or resolution once you’re happy.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between the splat export and the mesh export?
faqItems.answer: The splat export preserves the Gaussian Splat representation for fast, view-consistent rendering. The mesh export converts splats to triangles for broader compatibility with DCC tools and engines. Mesh conversion is an approximation and may need cleanup or retopology.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the orbit path and video settings?
faqItems.answer: Yes. CreateCameraInfo controls orbit radius, elevation, and frame count. RenderSplat sets resolution and background. CreateVideo lets you choose frame rate; SaveVideo writes the final clip. Adjust these to match your desired look and performance budget.

e4ab88456b9b.title: LTX 2.3 - Lipdub LoRA + Voice Clone
e4ab88456b9b.description: Upload a driving video and prompt the desired dialogue to generate a lipdub of your video using LTX 2.3. The workflow then clones your dubbed audio back to the original character's voice using Chatterbox. It is a fully open source workflow for changing the speech of your character from a driving video.
e4ab88456b9b.metaDescription: Lip-sync and voice-clone a talking video in ComfyUI using LTX 2.3 Lipdub LoRA and Chatterbox VC. Upload a clip, type dialogue, and export a natural lipdub.
e4ab88456b9b.extendedDescription:
This workflow builds a full, open‑source lip‑dub pipeline around LTX 2.3 and Chatterbox voice conversion. You provide a "driving" video of a person speaking, plus the dialogue you want them to say. LoadVideo ingests your clip, and GetVideoComponents extracts frames, FPS, and the original audio. Your typed dialogue flows from a PrimitiveStringMultiline prompt through RegexReplace to clean punctuation and spacing, then into the LTX 2.3 Lipdub node (the custom node with ID 1e1eaad5-a949-4d3e-9a68-694e64a936a0). That node applies a Lipdub LoRA finetune to LTX 2.3 to retime mouth shapes to your script while preserving the subject’s identity, head motion, and scene context.

For audio, the same dialogue drives a temporary dub track that’s then passed to FL_ChatterboxVC. Using the original video’s audio (from GetVideoComponents) as a voice reference, Chatterbox VC re-voices the dub so it matches the speaker’s timbre and vocal traits. Finally, CreateVideo assembles the edited frames and cloned audio at the source FPS, and SaveVideo writes the final lip‑synced render. Note the dimension rule from the MarkdownNote: set input width × height to half your intended final size (for example, 960×544 in gives ~1920×1088 out).
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the MarkdownNote to review the dimension rule. Set your input width × height to half your target output (e.g., 960×544 for ~1920×1088).
Use LoadVideo to import your driving video (a clear, front-facing shot with visible lips works best). GetVideoComponents will provide frames, FPS, and the original audio for reference.
Enter your desired dialogue in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node. The RegexReplace node is pre-wired to clean up punctuation/spacing; adjust its pattern if your text needs special handling.

Configure the LTX 2.3 Lipdub node (ID 1e1eaad5-a949-4d3e-9a68-694e64a936a0). Ensure it receives the video frames and cleaned text. The Lipdub LoRA will drive the mouth shapes while keeping identity and motion intact.

Route audio into FL_ChatterboxVC: use the generated dub/guide audio as the source and the original video’s audio (from GetVideoComponents) as the voice reference. Adjust conversion options (e.g., pitch retention/f0) to taste.

CreateVideo to mux the edited frames with the cloned audio using the source FPS. Finally, SaveVideo to export your lipdub. Review the result; if alignment is off, tweak text timing or punctuation and re-run.
suggestedUseCases: Dubbing social clips into new languages while keeping the original on-camera identity and voice timbre.
Fixing flubbed lines in talking-head content without a reshoot.
Localizing product explainers or training modules with consistent on-screen presenters.
Creating clean, meme-style overdubs where mouth movements match custom punchlines.
Rapid voice tests: audition several scripts while retaining the speaker’s voice and performance.

faqItems.question: Why is my output resolution double what I set?
faqItems.answer: This workflow expects input width × height to be half of your desired output, as noted in the MarkdownNote. For example, 960×544 in will render about 1920×1088 out. Halve your target resolution when setting inputs.

faqItems.question: How does the voice cloning keep the same speaker’s timbre?
faqItems.answer: FL_ChatterboxVC uses the original video’s audio (from GetVideoComponents) as a voice reference. It converts the generated dub audio to match the target speaker’s timbre and style, so the lips match your script while the voice still sounds like the on-screen person.

faqItems.question: My lip-sync is close but not perfect. What should I adjust?
faqItems.answer: Start with the text: add or remove brief pauses via punctuation (commas/periods), keep sentences concise, and avoid long, run-on phrases. Ensure the CreateVideo FPS matches the source FPS. Clear, front-facing footage with unobstructed lips also improves alignment.

faqItems.question: What video and audio quality work best?
faqItems.answer: Use short to medium clips with stable lighting and a sharp view of the mouth. For the Chatterbox reference, cleaner speech (minimal music/noise) helps the conversion. If the original track is noisy, trim a clean segment for reference or apply light noise reduction upstream.

e6f74ca84e32.title: FLUX 3 Video: Text to Video
e6f74ca84e32.description: Generate full videos from a single text prompt with Flux.3, which expands natural language into complete scenes with synchronized audio, no reference images or complex settings needed. Outputs 1 video in 720p at 24fps, 5 to 20 seconds long, supporting any aspect ratio from 9:16 to 21:9 with built-in sound design. Ideal for quick social media clips, ad mockups, and concept films requiring realistic motion and cinematic style.
e6f74ca84e32.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate 720p, 24fps text-to-video clips (5–20s) with Flux 3, including synchronized audio. Simple two-node workflow: Flux3TextToVideoNode + SaveVideo.
e6f74ca84e32.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a single text prompt into a finished video clip using the Flux 3 model. The Flux3TextToVideoNode interprets natural language into a complete moving scene with coherent action, camera motion, and synchronized sound. It’s designed for quick turnarounds: you set the prompt, pick a duration between 5–20 seconds, choose an aspect ratio from 9:16 to 21:9, and the node generates a 720p, 24 fps result with built-in audio.

Technically, the pipeline is minimal and focused. Flux3TextToVideoNode handles end-to-end generation from text, returning the video content (and its audio track) at the requested length, frame rate, and aspect ratio. The SaveVideo node then writes the output to disk as a single playable file. With only two nodes, it’s easy to understand, fast to set up, and reliable for creating social-ready clips, ad mockups, and cinematic concept shots without extra reference images or complex settings.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the two nodes: Flux3TextToVideoNode and SaveVideo.

Open Flux3TextToVideoNode and enter your text prompt. Set duration (5–20 seconds), choose an aspect ratio (e.g., 9:16, 16:9, 21:9), and confirm 24 fps/720p defaults as needed. If this node uses a hosted API, add your API key/endpoint.
Refine the prompt for motion and sound: specify subject, environment, camera movement, lighting, pacing, and audio vibe (e.g., "soft ambient hum," "busy city ambience").
Open SaveVideo and set the output filename/path where your final video will be written.
Queue and run the workflow. Monitor the progress on Flux3TextToVideoNode; generation time varies with duration and network/API speed.
When complete, open the saved file from the path in SaveVideo to review the 720p, 24 fps video with synchronized audio.
suggestedUseCases: Vertical social clips (9:16) for TikTok, Reels, or Shorts with built-in ambience.
Quick ad mockups and product teasers where motion, framing, and sound need to feel cinematic.
Previsualization for film/storyboards to test camera moves and scene tone before production.
B-roll style inserts (16:9 or 21:9) for editorial timelines or pitch decks.
Concept films or mood pieces exploring lighting, environment, and motion from a single prompt.

faqItems.question: How do I control video length and aspect ratio?
faqItems.answer: Open Flux3TextToVideoNode and set the duration (any value between 5 and 20 seconds) and choose an aspect ratio (e.g., 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 21:9). The node will render 720p at 24 fps to match those settings.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow require a GPU or local model download?
faqItems.answer: Flux3TextToVideoNode is designed to run via an API in many setups. If your version uses a hosted endpoint, you’ll need a valid API key and internet access, not a local GPU. Check the node’s parameters for authentication requirements.

faqItems.question: Can I remove or replace the audio?
faqItems.answer: Flux3TextToVideoNode generates synchronized audio with the clip. This workflow saves that track as-is. For a silent version or custom music, export the clip, then mute/replace the audio in your video editor or adapt the workflow with nodes that strip or swap audio.

faqItems.question: How can I get more consistent or cinematic results from prompts?
faqItems.answer: Be explicit about subject, motion, and tone. Include camera directives (e.g., "slow dolly-in," "handheld, slight shake"), lighting ("golden hour rim light"), environment cues, and audio mood ("subtle city ambience"). Keep within the 5–20s range for stable timing.

The process begins with generating a cinematic image using a specialized model, Z-Image-Turbo, which captures the unique aesthetics associated with Wes Anderson films. This image is then enhanced using the Nano Banana Pro model, which focuses on improving textures and details to achieve a polished look. Finally, the enhanced image is converted into a video using the Kling 3.0 model, known for its superior video generation capabilities. The workflow leverages key nodes such as SaveImage for storing intermediate results and KlingImageToVideoWithAudio for the final video output, ensuring a seamless transition from image to video.

Technically, the workflow is built on a series of interconnected nodes that automate the process of image generation, enhancement, and video creation. The GeminiImage2Node plays a crucial role in translating the textual prompt into an initial image, while the f2fdebf6-dfaf-43b6-9eb2-7f70613cfdc1 node is responsible for applying the Nano Banana Pro model's enhancements. The KlingImageToVideoWithAudio node integrates audio into the video, adding an additional layer of depth and engagement. This workflow is particularly useful for content creators looking to produce high-quality, stylistically unique videos with minimal manual intervention.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for other visual styles?

e8099b642c9f.title: MiniMax H3: Text to Video
e8099b642c9f.description: Generate video with native stereo audio directly from a text prompt using MiniMax H3, an omni-modal model that synthesizes voice, sound effects, and music in a single pass. Output is up to 2K resolution, 24fps, and roughly 15 seconds long, with no file inputs required — just a prompt to one video output. Ideal for rapid concept visualization, social media content creation, and audio-synced storytelling.
e8099b642c9f.metaDescription: Prompt-only MiniMax H3 ComfyUI: generate ~15s, 24fps video with native stereo audio up to 2K. Uses ResolutionSelector and SaveVideo for a one-pass result.
e8099b642c9f.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single text prompt into a finished video with native stereo audio using MiniMax H3, an omni‑modal model that synthesizes visuals, voice, sound effects, and music in one pass. There are no file inputs to manage—just describe what you want, and the graph returns a roughly 15‑second clip at 24 fps, up to 2K resolution, with stereo sound baked in.

Under the hood, a MiniMax H3 subgraph (node 79dd8a95-ce9d-4c14-b264-2162e8bec5ce) handles generation and decoding. It uses the MiniMax H3 video and audio VAEs (minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors and minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors) to reconstruct frames and stereo audio from the model’s latents. ResolutionSelector maps convenient presets to valid dimensions in multiples of 32 (e.g., 960×544, 1152×640, 1216×672), and SaveVideo multiplexes the frames and stereo audio stream into a single MP4. A MarkdownNote in the canvas provides quick tips and prompt examples. The result is a compact, prompt‑only pipeline ideal for rapid concept visualization, social posts, and audio‑synced storytelling.
howToUse: Load the MiniMax H3: Text to Video workflow in ComfyUI. Open the MarkdownNote for a quick overview. If prompted for missing models, download minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors and minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors from the provided links and place them with your VAEs.

Open the MiniMax H3 subgraph node (79dd8a95-ce9d-4c14-b264-2162e8bec5ce) and enter your prompt. Describe both visuals and audio cues (e.g., camera motion, pacing, voice style, sound effects, and music mood).

Choose an output size with ResolutionSelector. Start with a mid‑range 16:9 preset (e.g., 960×544 or 1152×640) for fast iteration; increase toward the 2K limit once you like the result. All presets are multiples of 32 for model compatibility.
Leave timing at the defaults (the model is tuned for ~15 seconds at 24 fps) unless the subgraph exposes controls you wish to adjust. Then queue the workflow.
Monitor progress. The subgraph runs generation and the VAEs reconstruct video frames and stereo audio. When complete, the SaveVideo node writes a single MP4 containing both streams.
Review the output video. Iterate by refining visual details and audio direction in your prompt (e.g., "warm narrators voice, gentle ocean ambience, light acoustic music") and re‑run.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid concept visualization with sound: storyboard beats, tone, and motion plus temp voice/music in one render.
Social media shorts: prompt concise scenes with built‑in soundtrack and effects for quick posting.
Product teasers and motion logos: short branded clips with synchronized whooshes, risers, and VO cues.
Education and explainers: simple narrated visuals with ambient beds or light music for intros/outros.
Atmospheric loops: mood pieces (e.g., "rainy neon alley with distant traffic and soft synth pads") for backgrounds.

faqItems.question: How do I steer the audio (voice, SFX, music) in the result?
faqItems.answer: Include explicit audio guidance in your prompt. Specify narration style (voice gender/tone/accent), music genre and mood (e.g., "lo‑fi, soft piano, no drums"), and key sound effects ("gentle wind, distant traffic, minimal footsteps"). Placing audio cues near the relevant visual beats often improves alignment.

faqItems.question: What resolutions, frame rate, and duration does this workflow support?
faqItems.answer: The graph targets ~15 seconds at 24 fps and supports up to ~2K resolution. Use ResolutionSelector to choose valid 16:9 sizes in multiples of 32 (e.g., 608×352, 736×416, 864×480, 960×544, 1056×608, 1152×640, 1216×672, 1280×736). Larger sizes increase generation and decode time.

faqItems.question: Can I use my own audio or voiceover instead of the generated audio?
faqItems.answer: This tutorial workflow is prompt‑only and outputs the model’s native stereo audio. To replace audio with your own track, extend the graph: disable or ignore the generated audio stream and mux your external WAV/MP3 before SaveVideo (or post‑replace audio in your NLE).

faqItems.question: Do I need to install additional models or files?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the subgraph expects the MiniMax H3 VAEs: minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors and minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors. If ComfyUI reports missing files on first run, download them from the provided links and place them in your models directory so the node can decode video and stereo audio correctly.

e8182e8f88c4.title: Meshy 6: Image to Model
e8182e8f88c4.description: Upload an image and generate a 3D model with Meshy 6. Create characters, objects, or mechanical parts with production-quality geometry and clean topology.
e8182e8f88c4.metaDescription: Convert a single image into a textured, riggable 3D model in ComfyUI using Meshy 6. Preview in 3D and export GLB with optional refine, texture, and animation.
e8182e8f88c4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow shows you how to turn a single 2D image into a production-ready 3D asset using the Meshy 6 API. Starting with LoadImage, your reference is sent to MeshyImageToModelNode, which generates a clean, watertight mesh with UVs directly from the image. You can then iterate on quality and detail using MeshyRefineNode, add PBR textures with MeshyTextureNode, and view results in real time through the Preview3D node.

For character and creature work, MeshyRigModelNode can auto-rig the mesh and MeshyAnimateModelNode can apply motion for quick previews or turntables. The final result is exported via SaveGLB (or directly from the Preview3D export control) as a GLB file. The workflow is organized under the Meshy Toolset group for easy enabling, and all generated models are auto-saved to ComfyUI/output/ for a frictionless handoff to DCC tools or game engines.
howToUse: Open the Meshy 6: Image to Model workflow in ComfyUI. Select the Meshy Toolset group and press Ctrl+B to enable it. Read the MarkdownNote for any setup reminders.
Add your Meshy API key where required by the Meshy nodes (e.g., MeshyImageToModelNode and related nodes). Ensure you’re logged in or configured so API calls can run.
Load your reference image via the LoadImage node. Use a clear, well-lit image with a clean background and a strong silhouette for best results.

Configure MeshyImageToModelNode: describe the object (e.g., “red sci‑fi helmet” or “stylized biped character”) and choose generation options appropriate to your subject. Then execute the workflow to create the initial 3D model.

Optionally chain refinement steps: use MeshyRefineNode to improve geometry/topology, MeshyTextureNode to generate PBR textures, and MeshyRigModelNode + MeshyAnimateModelNode if you need a rigged or animated preview. Inspect the output in Preview3D as you iterate.
Export your result: use SaveGLB to write the model to ComfyUI/output/ automatically, or use the export control in the Preview3D node to download a GLB file.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid prototyping of game props and environment assets from concept art or product photos.
Blocking and previsualization for characters and creatures with quick rig-and-animate previews.
E‑commerce and marketing turntables from a single packshot (e.g., shoes, gadgets, collectibles).
Educational and research visuals where fast 3D from reference is needed for demonstrations.
Indie pipelines needing clean topology and UVs for immediate texturing or engine import.

faqItems.question: Do I need a Meshy account or API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The MeshyImageToModelNode (and related Meshy nodes) call the Meshy 6 API. Provide a valid API key in the node(s) or your environment so jobs can run and return results.

faqItems.question: Where are my models saved?
faqItems.answer: By default, models are auto-saved to ComfyUI/output/ via the SaveGLB node. You can also export directly from the Preview3D node’s export button to download the GLB.

faqItems.question: How can I improve model fidelity and topology?
faqItems.answer: Start with a high-quality image showing a clear silhouette of a single subject. After the initial MeshyImageToModelNode pass, run MeshyRefineNode to improve geometry, then MeshyTextureNode for PBR textures. Iterate while checking results in Preview3D.

faqItems.question: Can I rig and animate any model?
faqItems.answer: MeshyRigModelNode works best with humanoids and simple bipeds. Props and mechanical parts typically don’t need rigging; skip rigging for those. Use MeshyAnimateModelNode to preview motion where appropriate.

eb53769b541b.title: Seedance 2.0 Mini: Text to Video

eb53769b541b.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Generate cinematic text-to-video with Dreamina’s Seedance 2.0 Mini using ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and SaveVideo, with seeds and AI camera control.
eb53769b541b.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 Mini: Text to Video is a minimal, focused ComfyUI workflow that turns a plain-language prompt into a finished video in one pass. It centers on a single generation node—ByteDance2TextToVideoNode—to call Dreamina’s Seedance 2.0 Mini API, and a SaveVideo node to write the result to disk. Because generation happens via API, your local machine mainly handles orchestration and saving, not heavy rendering. The node accepts your text prompt and key generation settings (such as duration, aspect ratio/resolution, FPS, and seed) and returns a ready-to-save clip.

Technically, the ByteDance2TextToVideoNode encapsulates model inference: it submits your prompt and parameters to Seedance 2.0 Mini, which handles motion, subject fidelity, and scene composition. The model supports AI camera behavior (e.g., dolly, pan, orbit-like motion) through prompt cues and/or any dedicated camera fields exposed by the node. For character continuity across multiple shots, keep a stable character description and reuse the same seed between runs. The downstream SaveVideo node then encodes the returned video stream to a file format supported by your ComfyUI/FFmpeg setup, typically MP4 or WebM.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. Confirm the graph contains ByteDance2TextToVideoNode feeding into SaveVideo.
Open ByteDance2TextToVideoNode and enter your API credentials if required by your setup (key/token or environment config).
Write a clear text prompt describing subject, setting, mood, and motion. Add camera cues (e.g., “slow dolly in,” “orbiting shot”) in the prompt or any camera-specific fields provided by the node.
Set core parameters: duration (seconds), FPS, resolution/aspect ratio, and a seed. Use the same seed and consistent character description to maintain identity across multiple runs.
Optionally refine with negative cues (if the node exposes a negative prompt or quality controls) to avoid unwanted artifacts. Keep wording concise and specific.
In SaveVideo, choose the output filename/path and desired container if available. Queue the workflow. Review the result; iterate by adjusting the prompt, camera cues, or seed for refinements.
suggestedUseCases: AI filmmaking previsualization: block shots, test camera moves, and establish tone before full production.
Branded content drafts: quickly generate product hero shots with controlled camera motion and consistent brand characters.
Storyboarding and animatics: produce short animated beats from text to communicate pacing and scene transitions.

faqItems.question: How do I keep a character consistent across multiple shots?
faqItems.answer: Use a stable, detailed character description (e.g., clothing, age, style) and reuse the same seed value in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode across runs. Keep your wording and aspect ratio consistent between shots to reduce drift.

faqItems.question: Where do I control the camera movement?
faqItems.answer: Add camera directions to your prompt (e.g., “handheld close-up,” “slow dolly-in,” “360° orbit”) and use any camera-related fields exposed by ByteDance2TextToVideoNode if available. Seedance 2.0 Mini interprets these cues to drive AI camera behavior.

faqItems.question: What video formats can I save?

ed1c4eade3a3.title: Seedance 2.0 - Viral Cinemagraph Effect
ed1c4eade3a3.description: A one click workflow to generate a viral cinemagraph frame effect using Seedance 2.0. Upload an image of your character, optionally describe the motion of the scene and click generate. This workflow bypasses the realistic human input ban/limitation. A cinemagraph is a hybrid of a still photo and video, where a static image features a subtle, repeating, and seamless motion.
ed1c4eade3a3.metaDescription: Create a seamless cinemagraph from a single image with Seedance 2.0. Mask the motion area, describe movement, and export a looping video in one click.
ed1c4eade3a3.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.0 - Viral Cinemagraph Effect turns a single character image into a short, looping cinemagraph with subtle motion. The workflow starts by loading your still using LoadImage (or BatchImagesNode for multiples), then uses a lightweight text pipeline (PrimitiveStringMultiline → RegexReplace → GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2) to interpret your motion description into concise, model-friendly motion hints. A mask-driven pass defines where movement should happen: MaskPreview helps you visualize the region, and MaskToImage converts that mask for downstream use so the subject or selected area animates while the rest of the frame stays perfectly still.

At the core, ByteDance2ReferenceNode applies Seedance 2.0’s reference-based image-to-video motion on just the masked region, preserving identity and composition from your source photo. Frames are assembled with GetVideoComponents and CreateVideo, then you can inspect results with PreviewAny and export via SaveVideo (and SaveImage for any keyframe/mask snapshots). Two custom utility nodes (f4cfd806-6db2-425e-9f50-3eb8fe546a77 and e42b05e2-13fc-4ad5-822d-b89a8a297d35) are included in the graph to support the pre/post steps the workflow needs; they’re prewired and require no manual changes for a one‑click run. The result is a clean, seamless loop ideal for socials, hero headers, and character reveals—precise, controlled motion without rebuilding the entire scene.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and drop your source image into the LoadImage node (use BatchImagesNode if you want to process multiple images).

Describe the motion you want (e.g., "hair gently sways and eyes blink") in the PrimitiveStringMultiline node. The RegexReplace and GeminiNode/GeminiNanoBanana2 will auto-simplify this into concise motion hints.
Define the moving region: use MaskPreview to check the region to animate and adjust as needed, then let MaskToImage convert it for the motion pass so the background stays static.
Open ByteDance2ReferenceNode to review key controls such as motion intensity and loop length (if exposed in your build). Set fps/duration in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo to match your platform.
Click Queue Prompt/Generate. Monitor intermediate frames with PreviewAny; tweak mask softness or motion intensity if you see edge artifacts or jitter.
Export your result with SaveVideo (MP4) and optionally SaveImage for masks or key frames you want to keep for iteration.
suggestedUseCases: Character portraits with subtle breathing, blinking, or hair movement for social posts and profile headers.
Product hero shots with gentle highlights or background elements looping to draw attention without distraction.
Album/cover art and thumbnails that stand out with minimal, classy motion.
Cinematic mood posts where only water, smoke, or fabric moves to create depth.
Marketing teasers and reveal loops that preserve brand imagery while adding motion.

faqItems.question: How do I control which part of the image moves?
faqItems.answer: Use the mask stage. Preview the animated region with MaskPreview and refine the mask before it’s converted by MaskToImage. Keep edges soft for cleaner blends and ensure the moving region doesn’t intersect high-contrast edges unless that’s intentional.

faqItems.question: My loop has visible pops at the seam—how can I fix it?
faqItems.answer: Reduce motion intensity in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, shorten the duration slightly, and soften the mask edges. Also check fps/duration in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo so the start and end frames align more naturally. Subtle motion yields smoother loops.

faqItems.question: What image types and resolutions work best?
faqItems.answer: High-quality, well-lit portraits or product shots with a relatively clean background produce the best cinemagraphs. Square and vertical formats are social-friendly; set your desired output size/fps in GetVideoComponents/CreateVideo to match your target platform.

faqItems.question: Do I need to change the custom utility nodes with ID-like names?
faqItems.answer: No. The nodes f4cfd806-6db2-425e-9f50-3eb8fe546a77 and e42b05e2-13fc-4ad5-822d-b89a8a297d35 are preconfigured for this workflow. Leave them as-is unless you know their specific role in your local build.

eda6aeddc2ec.title: ElevenLabs: Speech to Speech
eda6aeddc2ec.description: Upload a source audio file to apply a new voice tone or clone a different voice, generating a modified audio output.
eda6aeddc2ec.metaDescription: ComfyUI Speech-to-Speech with ElevenLabs: convert any audio into a new voice using preset voices or instant voice cloning, and export MP3/Opus easily.
eda6aeddc2ec.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs voice conversion using the ElevenLabs Speech-to-Speech API. You provide a source audio clip (via LoadAudio or RecordAudio), choose a target voice (via ElevenLabsVoiceSelector for a preset voice or ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone to create a new clone), and the ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech node generates a new recording that preserves the timing and content of the original while changing the vocal timbre to match the selected voice. The output can be saved with SaveAudioMP3 or SaveAudioOpus.

Technically, the pipeline routes your source waveform into ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech along with a target voice ID. In Option 1, ElevenLabsVoiceSelector queries your ElevenLabs account and outputs a selected voice for direct use. In Option 2, ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone uploads a clean reference sample and returns a new voice resource that is then fed into the Speech-to-Speech node. The Note node contains guidance, and several nodes are initially bypassed so you can enable only what you need. This design makes it easy to A/B between preset voices and instant clones while keeping file management simple with explicit save nodes.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and read the Note node. Add your ElevenLabs API key where required by the ElevenLabs nodes (node fields or your ComfyUI env/config).
Provide source audio: either import a file with LoadAudio (place your WAV/MP3/OGG file) or record a take with RecordAudio in the Source Audio group.

Choose a target voice: Option 1 (Use Preset Voice) – select a voice in ElevenLabsVoiceSelector. Option 2 (Create a Voice Clone) – supply a clean reference clip to ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone. Important: some nodes start bypassed; select them and press Ctrl-B to enable.

Wire the chosen voice output (from VoiceSelector or InstantVoiceClone) and the source audio into ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech. Adjust available voice settings (e.g., stability, similarity boost) in the node to balance timbre accuracy vs. expressiveness.
Queue and run the workflow. Inspect the ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech output. If the conversion sounds breathy or noisy, try a cleaner/louder source, trim silence, or lower similarity to reduce artifacts.
Save your result using SaveAudioMP3 or SaveAudioOpus. Pick the format based on your delivery needs (MP3 for broad compatibility, Opus for efficient streaming) and set the output path.
suggestedUseCases: Voice anonymization for interviews, user testing, or internal reviews while preserving natural pacing.
Character voice creation for podcasts, machinima, or indie games using a consistent, cloned persona.
Rapid ADR or pickup lines for video projects when the original voice is unavailable.
Multivoice demos for creatives: try the same read with multiple preset voices to pick a direction.
Brand voice prototyping: convert team recordings into a consistent house voice before booking sessions.

faqItems.question: Do I need an ElevenLabs account and API key?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The ElevenLabsVoiceSelector, ElevenLabsInstantVoiceClone, and ElevenLabsSpeechToSpeech nodes call the ElevenLabs API. Add your API key to the nodes or ComfyUI’s configuration as instructed in the Note node.

faqItems.question: What audio works best for cloning and conversion?
faqItems.answer: Use clean, single-speaker recordings with minimal background noise and reverb. Aim for steady levels without clipping, and avoid music. A clear 30–60 second sample is typically enough for Instant Voice Clone.

faqItems.question: What’s the difference between MP3 and Opus outputs?
faqItems.answer: SaveAudioMP3 produces a widely compatible file ideal for general distribution. SaveAudioOpus yields smaller files at similar perceptual quality—useful for web or app playback—though some workflows may require MP3.

faqItems.question: Is the source audio sent to external servers?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Audio for voice selection, cloning, and speech-to-speech is processed by ElevenLabs’ servers via their API. Review ElevenLabs’ terms, privacy policy, and your usage limits on their dashboard.

ef10fc1fe4d3.title: Moonvalley: Motion Transfer
ef10fc1fe4d3.description: Apply motion from one video to another.
ef10fc1fe4d3.metaDescription: Transfer motion from one video to another with the Moonvalley: Motion Transfer workflow using ComfyUI. Ideal for animators and video editors.
ef10fc1fe4d3.extendedDescription:
The 'Moonvalley: Motion Transfer' workflow is designed to seamlessly transfer motion from one video to another using ComfyUI. This workflow leverages the Moonvalley video generation model, which specializes in capturing and replicating intricate motion details. The core of the process involves the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode', which applies the motion dynamics from a reference video onto a target video. This is particularly useful for animators and video editors who want to imbue static scenes with dynamic motion without the need for extensive manual animation.

Technically, the workflow begins by loading a reference video using the 'LoadVideo' node. This video should be at least 5 seconds long to ensure sufficient motion data is captured. The 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' then analyzes the motion patterns and applies them to the target video. Finally, the 'SaveVideo' node is used to export the newly animated video. The inclusion of 'MarkdownNote' nodes provides in-line documentation and notes, making the workflow easy to follow and modify. This process is efficient and produces high-quality results, making it a valuable tool for creative professionals.
howToUse: Load your reference video using the 'LoadVideo' node. Ensure the video is at least 5 seconds long for optimal motion capture.
Configure the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to analyze the motion from your reference video.
Connect your target video to the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to apply the captured motion.
Use the 'SaveVideo' node to export the newly animated video.
Review the 'MarkdownNote' nodes for additional tips and documentation within the workflow.
Adjust parameters as needed to refine the motion transfer and achieve the desired effect.
suggestedUseCases: Animating static scenes in films or video projects.
Creating dynamic promotional videos by adding motion to still footage.
Enhancing video game cutscenes with realistic character movements.
Developing educational content with engaging, animated visuals.
Producing artistic video installations that combine static and dynamic elements.

faqItems.question: What types of videos work best for motion transfer?
faqItems.answer: Videos with clear, distinct motion patterns work best. Ensure the reference video is at least 5 seconds long for optimal results.

faqItems.question: Can I use this workflow for live-action videos?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the workflow is suitable for both animated and live-action videos, as long as the motion is clear and distinct.

faqItems.question: How do I adjust the intensity of the motion transfer?
faqItems.answer: You can tweak the parameters within the 'MoonvalleyVideo2VideoNode' to adjust the intensity and style of the motion transfer.

faqItems.question: Is there a way to preview the results before saving the video?
faqItems.answer: Currently, you need to complete the workflow and save the video to review the results. Consider using short video clips for faster iterations.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow handle audio generation?
