ef37c26c9bbf.title: MiniMax H3: FLF2V
ef37c26c9bbf.description: Generate a video from a first and last frame using MiniMax H3, producing a smooth animation between the two images. You provide 2 images, and the workflow outputs a single video clip. Ideal for creating seamless transitions in animation, visualizing before-and-after transformations, and generating consistent motion for character or scene sequences.
ef37c26c9bbf.metaDescription: Generate a smooth video between two images in ComfyUI using MiniMax H3. Load first/last frames, run the node, and export an MP4 with SaveVideo.
ef37c26c9bbf.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns two still images—a defined first frame and last frame—into a single, smoothly animated video using the MiniMax H3 (Hailuo-03) first–last frame API. Two LoadImage nodes feed your start and end images into the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode, which sends them to the MiniMax service to predict the in-between frames. The node returns the generated sequence back to ComfyUI, and SaveVideo encodes it as a video file at your chosen frame rate.

Technically, the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode performs an API call to MiniMax H3’s First–Last Frame to Video endpoint, conditioning motion on the content of both input images to synthesize temporally consistent intermediate frames. Because the motion is guided by your exact start and end frames, you get a coherent transition without training or manual keyframing. This makes the setup ideal for before/after reveals, scene transitions, and quick animatics where you want subject consistency and controlled start/end states.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI, then open the two LoadImage nodes and select your First Frame and Last Frame images (use the same aspect ratio and resolution for both).
Open the MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode and enter your MiniMax API credentials. Review any generation options the node exposes (e.g., clip length or frame count) and set them to your needs.
Open the SaveVideo node and set your filename pattern and FPS. Confirm the output directory shown in the node matches where you want the file saved.
Queue and run the workflow. The node will upload your two images to MiniMax H3, generate the in-between frames, and pass the result to SaveVideo.
Preview the output video from the path shown in the SaveVideo node. If needed, adjust your start/end frames or the node settings and re-run for a smoother transition.
suggestedUseCases: Before–after reveals for product mockups, design makeovers, or restoration showcases.
Seamless scene or logo transitions for title cards and motion graphics.
Character or pose interpolation between two keyframes for animatics and storyboards.
Environment shifts (e.g., day-to-night or season changes) using two photographs.
UI/UX state transitions that animate between two static screens.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key to use this workflow?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The MinimaxHailuo03FirstLastFrameNode calls the MiniMax H3 (Hailuo-03) API. Enter your API key in the node’s credential field and ensure your account has access to the First–Last Frame to Video feature.

faqItems.question: How can I get the smoothest results between two frames?
faqItems.answer: Use images with matching resolution and aspect ratio, similar framing and scale of the subject, and consistent lighting and camera angle. Large viewpoint or style jumps are harder to bridge, so pick start and end frames that are visually related.

faqItems.question: What formats and resolutions are supported?
faqItems.answer: LoadImage supports common image formats like PNG and JPG. For best results, use the same dimensions for both inputs. Note that the MiniMax API may impose size limits; if the node or API errors at high resolutions, downscale both inputs equally and try again.

faqItems.question: Where is the video saved and how do I change FPS?
faqItems.answer: The SaveVideo node writes the final clip to the output folder shown in its settings. You can change the playback speed by adjusting the FPS field in SaveVideo before running the workflow.

ef543bd4a773.title: Seedance Playblast2Render
ef543bd4a773.description:
This workflow turns a raw CG playblast into a final rendered shot using Seedance 2.0.

It preserves your animation and camera from the playblast, while Nano Banana Pro generates reference images and multi-angle grids to define asset look and improve consistency. A custom Gemini node builds structured prompts, allowing Seedance to reinterpret the shot with a controlled, production-ready style.

The result is a fast, repeatable pipeline that replaces traditional rendering with AI-driven output while keeping full control over motion and intent.
ef543bd4a773.metaDescription: Turn a CG playblast into a styled, production-ready render with Seedance 2.0. Preserve motion and camera, add references, and export final video in ComfyUI.
ef543bd4a773.extendedDescription:
Seedance Playblast2Render is a ComfyUI workflow that turns a raw CG playblast into a styled, production-ready render using Seedance 2.0. The pipeline preserves your original motion and framing by conditioning the renderer on the playblast video, then layers in controlled art direction through curated references and a structured prompt. VHS_LoadVideo (with VHS_VideoInfo) ingests the playblast and extracts frame rate and duration, while ImageFromBatch+ helps you pick hero frames for style exploration. Nano Banana Pro (via the GeminiNanoBanana2 node) generates multi-angle look boards and reference grids you can assemble with ImageBatchMulti and LoadImage. PreviewImage/PreviewAny nodes are sprinkled throughout so you can confirm each stage before committing to a render.

A custom GeminiNode builds a clean, shot-aware prompt from your notes, guided by included system instructions for Seedance. Those references and the playblast are fed to ByteDance2ReferenceNode to lock in motion, silhouette, and camera, and then rendered in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode. SetNode/GetNode keep shared parameters (like shot names or FPS) synchronized across groups. When you’re happy, SaveVideo writes out the final clip. The result is a repeatable, fast path that replaces a traditional offline render pass with AI-driven output—while keeping full control over timing, camera, and intent.

The workflow is organized into clear groups: LOAD PLAYBLAST, (OPTIONAL) GENERATE STYLE FRAMES, GENERATE INDIVIDUAL ASSETS, GENERATE SHOT AND STYLE DESCRIPTION FOR SEEDANCE, and DIFFUSION RENDERER BASED ON REFERENCE IMAGES AND PLAYBLAST ANIMATION. There’s also a GENERATE FAUX-PLAYBLAST group if you want to test the pipeline without a real playblast. Because it leverages structured prompting (GeminiNode), reference conditioning (ByteDance2ReferenceNode), and reference grids (GeminiNanoBanana2 + ImageBatchMulti), it’s especially strong at keeping character/prop continuity and delivering a consistent look across shots.
howToUse: Load your playblast: In LOAD PLAYBLAST, use VHS_LoadVideo (or LoadVideo) to import the clip. Inspect FPS, frame count, and duration with VHS_VideoInfo. If needed, use CM_FloatToInt/Int to match integer frame counts downstream.

Optionally create style frames: In (OPTIONAL) GENERATE STYLE FRAMES, pick a hero frame with ImageFromBatch+ and assemble look references using ImageBatchMulti and LoadImage. If you’re using Nano Banana Pro, run GeminiNanoBanana2 to produce multi-angle boards; verify results with PreviewImage/PreviewAny.

Author the prompt: In GENERATE SHOT AND STYLE DESCRIPTION FOR SEEDANCE, add your shot notes and asset callouts (MarkdownNote). Run GeminiNode to generate a structured Seedance prompt; if the workflow exposes SetNode/GetNode, store shared parameters (shot name, FPS) for reuse.

Attach references and motion: In the DIFFUSION RENDERER group, connect the playblast output to ByteDance2ReferenceNode to preserve animation and camera. Feed in any Nano Banana Pro grids or loaded reference images (ImageBatchMulti). Tune the reference strength/conditioning parameters as needed in the node UI.

Render with Seedance: Connect ByteDance2ReferenceNode into ByteDance2TextToVideoNode. Ensure frame range, FPS, and seed are set for reproducibility. Use PreviewAny/PreviewImage to review test passes and make adjustments to the prompt, reference strength, or style boards.
Export the result: When satisfied, connect the renderer output to SaveVideo, set your codec/filename, and write out the final shot. Rinse and repeat for the next sequence to maintain consistency.
suggestedUseCases: Look development passes: lock style and continuity across sequences while preserving timing from editorial.
Stylized previs or animatics: upgrade blockouts into presentable, art-directed clips without a full offline render.
Character and prop continuity: use multi-angle grids to keep hero assets on-model from shot to shot.
Pitch, teasers, and indie cinematics: quickly generate compelling visuals from rough animation.
Product or automotive turntables: retain accurate motion paths while applying consistent brand styling.

faqItems.question: How does the workflow preserve my animation and camera?
faqItems.answer: Your playblast video is fed into ByteDance2ReferenceNode as a conditioning source. That node guides ByteDance2TextToVideoNode so timing, motion, and framing from the playblast are respected while Seedance 2.0 reinterprets the appearance with your prompt and references.

faqItems.question: Do I need Nano Banana Pro style grids, or can I use my own references?
faqItems.answer: Both work. GeminiNanoBanana2 can generate multi-angle boards to establish a consistent look, but you can also load your own refs with LoadImage and assemble them with ImageBatchMulti. The key is to provide clear, angle-diverse references for stable asset identity.

faqItems.question: How do I keep shot duration and FPS identical to the playblast?
faqItems.answer: Use VHS_VideoInfo to read the source FPS and frame count, then propagate those values to the renderer. If you encounter fractional values, CM_FloatToInt and Int help align integer frame counts so the output matches the playblast length.

faqItems.question: What should I tweak first if the style is drifting or inconsistent?
faqItems.answer: Increase reference influence in ByteDance2ReferenceNode, simplify or clarify the structured prompt from GeminiNode, and ensure your ImageBatchMulti contains clean, multi-angle references. Also fix the random seed in ByteDance2TextToVideoNode for repeatable results when iterating.

ef5d632ed2c5.title: Video Outpainting
ef5d632ed2c5.description: Video Outpainting using the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA. Expand your video in any direction!
ef5d632ed2c5.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Use LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA to expand videos in any direction. Load, trim frames, outpaint, and export with VHS nodes.
ef5d632ed2c5.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow performs video outpainting: it expands the canvas of each frame in your clip and synthesizes believable new content around the original footage. It loads your source video with VHS_LoadVideo, processes the frames with a custom outpainting processor configured to use the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA, and reassembles the frames into a finished video with VHS_VideoCombine. A MarkdownNote in the graph provides inline guidance.

Technically, the core outpainting step (custom node ID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3) pads the frame in your chosen direction(s) and inpaints the newly added regions while preserving the original content. The LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA conditions the diffusion process so the generated edges stay stylistically and semantically consistent from frame to frame. The workflow exposes two key timeline controls: skip_first_frames (trim frames from the start) and frame_count (how many frames to process after the skip). For example, on a 600‑frame clip you can set skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 to process frames 60–539. This makes it easy to test short segments before rendering the entire video.

Because it’s built on VHS nodes, you get reliable frame extraction and recombination, plus straightforward control over frame rate and output location. Use this when you need to convert vertical footage to widescreen, add headroom/side padding for reframing, or extend a background to fit new aspect ratios without obvious cropping.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm required components are present: VHS (Video Helper Suite) for VHS_LoadVideo and VHS_VideoCombine, and the custom outpainting node (ID: 2e37ecc9-770a-4ac2-972c-e953901f49d3) configured with the LTX 2.3 Video Outpainting IC LoRA. If the LoRA/model path is unresolved, point the node to the correct file.
Open VHS_LoadVideo and select your source video. Verify the frame rate and resolution are appropriate for your GPU. Large resolutions and very wide expansions increase VRAM usage and render time.
Set skip_first_frames and frame_count to target the exact segment you want to process. Example: For a 600‑frame clip, skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 processes frames 60–539.

In the Outpainting Processor (custom node), choose the expansion direction(s) and amount (e.g., left/right/top/bottom padding or target aspect ratio). Adjust generation strength/denoise as needed—smaller padding and moderate strength generally reduce artifacts and flicker.

Open VHS_VideoCombine, set the output fps to match your source (unless you intentionally want a different frame rate), choose an output path/codec, and ensure it’s writing to a location with enough disk space.

Queue the workflow. Review the result. If edges wobble or textures drift, try reducing the padding amount, lowering denoise/strength, or processing in shorter segments (tuning settings per segment) and then stitch the results.
suggestedUseCases: Reframe vertical (9:16) smartphone videos to widescreen (16:9) by outpainting side margins instead of cropping.
Add headroom or side padding to dialogue or interview shots to accommodate captions, lower thirds, or safe framing.
Extend backgrounds and set pieces for VFX comps or motion graphics overlays without losing original subject framing.
Widen establishing shots from narrow or handheld footage to better match a project’s aspect ratio.
Repurpose social content across platforms with different aspect ratio requirements while preserving the main action.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: No. VHS_VideoCombine outputs a silent video from the processed frames. To restore audio, mux it from the original clip in your video editor or with ffmpeg, e.g., ffmpeg -i processed.mp4 -i source.mp4 -map 0:v -map 1:a -c copy out_with_audio.mp4.

faqItems.question: How do skip_first_frames and frame_count work together?
faqItems.answer: skip_first_frames trims frames from the start, and frame_count limits how many frames are processed after the skip. For a 600‑frame video: skip_first_frames: 60 and frame_count: 480 processes 480 frames starting at frame 60. Use smaller values to test quickly before rendering the entire clip.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce flicker or edge artifacts across frames?
faqItems.answer: Use conservative padding amounts, keep denoise/strength moderate, and ensure fps in VHS_VideoCombine matches the source. If issues persist, process the video in shorter segments with settings tuned to each section, then stitch the segments in your editor.

faqItems.question: What if I run out of GPU memory?
faqItems.answer: VRAM usage scales with resolution, padding size, and frame batch size. Reduce the input resolution, outpaint a smaller margin, or process fewer frames at a time. Close other GPU‑intensive apps and ensure the LoRA/model paths are correctly set to avoid reloading overhead.

ef8586090398.title: 1 Image to Car Product Shots
ef8586090398.description: Upload a photo of your vehicle and generate a studio quality video of the vehicle from multiple angles.
ef8586090398.metaDescription: Transform a single car image into a studio-quality video with ComfyUI's workflow for professional automotive product shots.
ef8586090398.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow is designed to transform a single image of a vehicle into a high-quality video showcasing the car from various angles. howToUse: Load the ComfyUI workflow and import your vehicle image using the LoadImage node.
Process the image with the ByteDanceSeedreamNode to generate multiple angles.
Use the CreateVideo node to compile these frames into a cohesive video.
Save individual frames with the SaveImage node if needed.

suggestedUseCases: Create dynamic product videos for automotive e-commerce listings.
Enhance marketing materials with professional-grade car videos.
Generate engaging social media content showcasing vehicle features.
Develop virtual showrooms with rotating car displays.
Produce training materials for automotive sales teams.

faqItems.question: What image format should I use for the best results?
faqItems.answer: For optimal processing, use high-resolution images in JPEG or PNG format.

faqItems.question: Can this workflow handle images of vehicles other than cars?
faqItems.answer: While optimized for cars, the workflow can be adapted for other vehicle types with adjustments to the processing nodes.

faqItems.question: How long does it take to generate a video?
faqItems.answer: The time varies based on image resolution and system capabilities, but typically it takes a few minutes to process and compile the video.

faqItems.question: Is there a limit to the number of angles the video can include?
faqItems.answer: The workflow can generate multiple angles, but the number is limited by the processing power and memory available on your system.

f0257c86b3a0.title: LTX 2.3_ID_lora_CelebVHQ
f0257c86b3a0.description: Bring voice consistency to your open source video generation pipeline with Qwen 3 TTS and LTX 2.3 with the CelebHVQ ID-LoRA.
f0257c86b3a0.metaDescription: Create identity-consistent talking videos from a photo using LTX 2.3, CelebVHQ ID-LoRA, and Qwen 3 TTS. Auto-generate prompts, synthesize voice, and render.
f0257c86b3a0.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial workflow turns a single image into a short, voice-driven video with strong visual identity and perceived lip alignment. It combines Lightricks LTX 2.3 for video generation with an ID-LoRA (CelebVHQ) to keep the subject’s face and styling consistent across frames, while Qwen 3 TTS produces a matching voice track. The pipeline is organized into clear groups: Load Image, Create Prompts, Prompt Extraction, Create Voice, and Create Video.

Under the hood, GeminiNode analyzes your uploaded image (via LoadImage) and drafts two complementary texts: a speech line with expressive cues and a scene/appearance description. RegexExtract then parses these into an ID-LoRA-ready format with three tagged sections: [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS]. FB_Qwen3TTSCustomVoice uses the [SPEECH] and style hints from [SOUNDS] to synthesize a voice track, saved with SaveAudioMP3. The LTX 2.3 video node (the custom node in this graph) consumes the structured prompt plus your reference image to render a talking video, with the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA improving identity retention in dynamic, in-the-wild scenarios. PreviewAny lets you iterate quickly, and SaveVideo writes the final clip. Local users can optionally load the LTX spatial upscaler (ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors) for cleaner details at higher resolution.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and place required models locally: LTX 2.3 checkpoint(s), the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA, and optionally the ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors in latent_upscale_models.
Open the Load Image group and drop in a well-lit, forward-facing photo of your subject (crop to head-and-shoulders for best identity retention).
In Create Prompts, set your GeminiNode credentials/model if needed, then run it. It will propose a scene/appearance description and a speech line with expression tags.

Check Prompt Extraction. RegexExtract splits content into [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS]. Edit these fields if necessary so the exact words in [SPEECH] match what you want the subject to say, and the style cues in [SOUNDS] reflect the intended voice and ambience.

In Create Voice, open FB_Qwen3TTSCustomVoice. Choose or configure a voice profile or reference, feed it the [SPEECH] text (and style hints), then generate and SaveAudioMP3. Use PreviewAny to confirm pacing and tone.

In Create Video, enable the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA and ensure the structured prompt is passed to the LTX 2.3 node. Adjust duration/resolution to fit your GPU. Run the video render, preview with PreviewAny, and export with SaveVideo. If you enabled the LTX x2 upscaler locally, the workflow will produce a sharper output.
suggestedUseCases: Talking-head explainers or announcements from a single portrait with consistent identity across multiple clips.
Character-driven shorts where the same subject appears in different scenes but maintains facial features and styling.
Voice-driven social posts: generate the speech with Qwen 3 TTS and pair it with an expressive, on-brand visual.
Podcast or newsletter teasers that turn a static host photo into a quick video bite.
Template-based content where a team updates only the [SPEECH] text each week while keeping the same look and voice.

faqItems.question: What does the CelebVHQ ID-LoRA do here?
faqItems.answer: It helps LTX 2.3 preserve the subject’s identity and facial features across frames, especially in dynamic, in-the-wild shots. It works best with a clear, frontal image and a well-structured prompt that separates [VISUAL], [SPEECH], and [SOUNDS].

faqItems.question: How is lip-sync achieved without a separate lip-sync model?
faqItems.answer: The workflow aligns perceived mouth movements by making the [SPEECH] text explicit and pairing it with matching TTS audio. While not frame-perfect lip-sync, using concise lines, clear punctuation, and expression cues improves alignment. You can retime in post if you need exact phoneme matching.

faqItems.question: Can I use a different ID-LoRA (e.g., TalkVid) or my own?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Swap the LoRA in the LTX 2.3 node. CelebVHQ is tuned for in-the-wild motion; TalkVid is typically stronger for close-up, studio-like talking head shots. For custom LoRAs, keep the same structured prompt format and test different strengths.

faqItems.question: Do I need the LTX x2 upscaler model?
faqItems.answer: It’s optional. If you place ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors in latent_upscale_models, the workflow can render crisper outputs at higher resolution. If VRAM is limited, disable upscaling or render at a lower base resolution.

f052abfce10e.title: LTX-2 Canny to Video
f052abfce10e.description: Generate high-quality videos from edge detection (Canny) guidance with synchronized audio-video generation using LTX-2. Features precise edge control, structural consistency, and efficient performance.
f052abfce10e.metaDescription: Transform edge-detected images into high-quality videos with LTX-2, ensuring precise edge control and structural consistency.
f052abfce10e.extendedDescription:
The 'LTX-2 Canny to Video' workflow is designed to transform edge-detected images into high-quality videos with synchronized audio. Utilizing the LTX-2 model, this workflow leverages the Canny edge detection technique to ensure precise edge control and structural consistency throughout the video. The process begins with the 'LoadVideo' node to import your source video, which is then decomposed into its components using the 'GetVideoComponents' node. The 'Canny' node plays a crucial role by detecting edges in the images, providing a guide for the video generation process.

This workflow is particularly useful for creators who need to maintain the structural integrity of the original footage while enhancing it with AI-generated elements. The LTX-2 model, developed by Lightricks, ensures that the generated video maintains high quality and coherence. The workflow also includes nodes like 'ImageScaleBy' and 'ResizeImageMaskNode' for adjusting image dimensions, and 'SaveVideo' to compile and save the final video. By following the recommended settings and parameters, users can achieve optimal results with minimal manual intervention.
howToUse: Load the workflow and import your source video using the 'LoadVideo' node.
Decompose the video into components with the 'GetVideoComponents' node.
Apply the 'Canny' node to detect edges in the video frames.

suggestedUseCases: Creating artistic videos with enhanced edge definition.

f1dc525f26dd.title: HappyHorse 1.1: Text to Video
f1dc525f26dd.description: Generate a video with synchronized audio from a text prompt using HappyHorse 1.1, producing a single video output with dialogue, sound effects, and music baked in. Ideal for short episodic series, e-commerce commercials, and game cutscenes.
f1dc525f26dd.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow for HappyHorse 1.1: generate text-to-video with synchronized dialogue, SFX, and music, saved as a single ready-to-share video.
f1dc525f26dd.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow turns a plain-text prompt into a fully produced video with synchronized dialogue, sound effects, and music using the HappyHorse 1.1 model. The HappyHorseTextToVideoApi node sends your prompt and settings to the HappyHorse service, which generates a single video file with the audio track baked in. The SaveVideo node then writes that returned video to disk at your chosen path, so you end up with one ready-to-share file.

Technically, the workflow is lean and focused: HappyHorseTextToVideoApi handles all generation remotely (visuals and audio together) and outputs a unified video object. There is no intermediate frame assembly or separate audio pipeline to manage in ComfyUI. This makes it ideal for rapid iteration on short episodic content, product spots, and cutscenes where timing between visuals and sound is critical but you want to avoid multi-node complexity. By structuring your prompt with clear scene descriptions, quoted dialogue, and simple sound/music cues, you can guide HappyHorse 1.1 to produce coherent, timed sequences that SaveVideo preserves as a single file.
howToUse: Load the "HappyHorse 1.1: Text to Video" workflow in ComfyUI and locate the HappyHorseTextToVideoApi and SaveVideo nodes.

Open the HappyHorseTextToVideoApi node and enter your API credentials/endpoint if required. Write your prompt with scene description, dialogue in quotes (e.g., "Hello there"), and simple sound/music cues.
Adjust any exposed parameters in the HappyHorseTextToVideoApi node (such as duration, aspect ratio, or seed if available) to match your target format.
Configure the SaveVideo node with your desired output directory and filename (use a container that supports audio, e.g., .mp4).
Queue and run the workflow. The API node will generate a single video with audio baked in; SaveVideo will write it to disk.
Review the output, refine your prompt for pacing and clarity (short lines of dialogue, concise SFX/music cues), and re-run to iterate.
suggestedUseCases: Short episodic series or micro-shorts with dialogue-driven scenes.
E-commerce product spots that mix narration, on-screen action, and light music.
Game cutscenes or animatics where visuals must align with character lines and SFX.
Social media explainers with voice, ambient SFX, and background music.
Rapid previz for storyboards that need audio timing without manual editing.

faqItems.question: Do I need an API key and where do I put it?
faqItems.answer: Yes. The HappyHorseTextToVideoApi node typically requires valid credentials and an endpoint. Enter them in the node’s fields if provided, or configure as documented for the node (e.g., ComfyUI settings or environment variables).

faqItems.question: Can I control voices, SFX, or music style?
faqItems.answer: You can guide outcomes through prompt design (speaker names with quoted lines, short SFX cues like [door slams], and music descriptors like "soft lo-fi"). If the node version exposes specific controls (e.g., voice/mix options), set them there. Exact controls depend on the API features available to your account.

faqItems.question: What are the limits for duration, resolution, or fps?
faqItems.answer: Those limits are determined by the HappyHorse 1.1 API and your plan. Check the node/API documentation for supported durations and formats. If the node exposes parameters like duration or aspect ratio, set them within the advertised bounds.

faqItems.question: Can I get separate audio stems for dialogue, SFX, and music?
faqItems.answer: Not with this workflow. HappyHorseTextToVideoApi returns a single video with audio baked in, and SaveVideo writes that to disk. If you need stems, you’ll need an alternative API mode or a different workflow that supports multi-track output.

f3096e2ffb64.title: Seedance 2.5: Video Extend
f3096e2ffb64.description: Extend an existing video forward or backward by generating new segments that seamlessly preserve the original characters, scenes, and aspect ratio. The source video must be 1.9–30 seconds long, and you specify the duration of the new clip (4–30 seconds, default 5), with output delivered as MP4 or MOV. Ideal for continuing unfinished footage, creating extended narrative sequences, and building longer edit chains.
f3096e2ffb64.metaDescription: Extend a video forward or backward 4–30s with Seedance 2.5 in ComfyUI. Preserves characters, scene, and aspect ratio. Outputs MP4 or MOV.
f3096e2ffb64.extendedDescription:
Seedance 2.5: Video Extend is a ComfyUI workflow for continuing an existing video either forward (adding new moments after the last frame) or backward (adding pre-roll before the first frame). It is designed to preserve the original characters, setting, and aspect ratio while generating a new segment 4–30 seconds long (default 5). The pipeline loads your source clip with LoadVideo, extracts a short context range with Video Slice, conditions a reference-aware model via ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2, and synthesizes the new frames using the workflow’s Seedance 2.5 generation node (d9aa59a4-3784-4796-9f1b-5b467fb41fa1). The final sequence is encoded with SaveVideo as MP4 or MOV.

Technically, the Video Slice node selects the most informative frames at the head or tail of your source (depending on whether you extend backward or forward). Those frames feed ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2, which anchors appearance, layout, and motion cues so the generator can extrapolate in-time while maintaining character identity and scene consistency. The generation node (d9aa59a4-3784-4796-9f1b-5b467fb41fa1) then produces the new segment at the original aspect ratio, and SaveVideo assembles the output clip. A MarkdownNote inside the graph documents limits and defaults: the input video must be 1.9–30 seconds; the requested extension can be 4–30 seconds (default 5).
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and open the MarkdownNote to review the input and duration limits (source: 1.9–30s, extension: 4–30s, default 5s).
In LoadVideo, select your source clip (e.g., sloth_bullfight.mp4). Confirm the clip plays end-to-end without corruption and note its aspect ratio.

In Video Slice, choose the direction and context: for forward extension, slice the last portion of the clip; for backward extension, slice the first portion. Keep enough context (e.g., 1–2 seconds) for stable appearance and motion cues.
Open ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2 and verify it is wired to the sliced frames. If available, adjust reference strength to balance strict appearance matching versus freer motion extrapolation.
In the Seedance 2.5 generation node (d9aa59a4-3784-4796-9f1b-5b467fb41fa1), set the target extension duration (4–30s). Keep the aspect ratio consistent with the source.

In SaveVideo, pick the output container (MP4 or MOV) and frame rate settings if exposed. Run the graph, preview the result, and iterate by tweaking slice range or reference strength if you see identity drift or composition shifts.
suggestedUseCases: Continue an unfinished shot by adding a natural outro after the final frame.
Create lead-in pre-roll to establish scene context before the original first frame.
Bridge two clips by generating a short connective sequence that preserves character and layout.
Extend a hero moment in a trailer while maintaining subject identity and camera feel.
Lengthen B-roll segments to fit a target edit timeline without jarring cuts.

faqItems.question: How do I extend the video backward instead of forward?
faqItems.answer: Use Video Slice to select context from the start of the source clip (first 1–2 seconds) and route that to ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2. The generation node will then synthesize new frames that precede your original first frame.

faqItems.question: What clip lengths are supported?
faqItems.answer: The input video must be between 1.9 and 30 seconds. You can request an extension between 4 and 30 seconds (default is 5 seconds). Staying near 4–8 seconds often yields the most consistent identity and motion.

faqItems.question: How can I reduce identity drift or scene changes?
faqItems.answer: Provide a clean, stable context in Video Slice (faces unobstructed, consistent lighting), and keep enough context duration. If exposed, increase reference strength in ByteDance2ReferenceNodeV2. Avoid abrupt camera cuts right at the slice point.

faqItems.question: Does the workflow change the aspect ratio or add audio?
faqItems.answer: No. It preserves the source aspect ratio. The SaveVideo node outputs a silent MP4 or MOV unless you later merge audio in your editor.

f3aa8cbf5c11.title: Apply Glitch And Distortion Effects

f3aa8cbf5c11.metaDescription: Create stunning glitch effects on images using ComfyUI. Customize distortion, chromatic aberration, and randomness for unique visual styles.
f3aa8cbf5c11.extendedDescription: This ComfyUI workflow is designed to apply glitch and distortion effects to images, offering a creative way to transform visuals with a unique style. The workflow begins with the LoadImage node, which imports the image you wish to modify. After the glitch effects are applied, the SaveImage node allows you to export the final result. The inclusion of a MarkdownNote node provides documentation and guidance directly within the workflow.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and locate the LoadImage node.
Click on the LoadImage node to import your desired image file.
Adjust the parameters in the FL_Glitch node, such as distortion intensity and chromatic aberration, to achieve the desired effect.
Preview the changes in real-time to fine-tune the glitch effects.
Once satisfied, use the SaveImage node to export the distorted image.
Review the MarkdownNote node for additional tips and documentation on using the workflow.
suggestedUseCases: Create album artwork with a modern, digital aesthetic.
Design promotional materials with eye-catching visual effects.
Enhance social media graphics with unique glitch styles.
Develop concept art for video games or films that require a cyberpunk theme.
Experiment with artistic photography by adding digital distortion.

faqItems.question: What types of images work best with this glitch effect?
faqItems.answer: Images with high contrast and bold colors tend to produce the most striking glitch effects, but the workflow can be applied to any image type.

faqItems.question: Can I control the intensity of the glitch effects?
faqItems.answer: Yes, the FL_Glitch node includes parameters for adjusting the distortion intensity, allowing you to customize the effect to your liking.

faqItems.question: Is it possible to revert the changes if I'm not satisfied with the result?
faqItems.answer: You can easily reload the original image using the LoadImage node and adjust the parameters again until you achieve the desired effect.

f4a0425aa8e9.title: Comfy for Advertising - Product Photography
f4a0425aa8e9.metaDescription: ComfyUI workflow for product photos and short promo videos using OpenAI gpt-image-1 edits and ByteDance first/last-frame interpolation.
f4a0425aa8e9.extendedDescription:
This three-step ComfyUI workflow streamlines product advertising assets from stills to motion. Step 1 uses OpenAIGPTImage1 to generate polished product photography from a reference product image and an optional background, guided by a concise prompt. LoadImage brings in your product and backdrop, ImageBatchMulti can feed multiple variations, and SaveImage captures your best takes. Step 2 focuses on precise edits: open the mask editor to paint where changes should apply (e.g., background cleanup, reflections, label tweaks), then re-run OpenAIGPTImage1 for targeted inpainting. ImageCompare gives a side-by-side before/after for quick QC before saving finals.

Step 3 turns your chosen stills into a short, smooth product video. Feed a start and end frame into ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode to synthesize the in-betweens, then SaveVideo encodes the sequence to a shareable clip. Keeping consistent resolution and aspect ratio across nodes improves temporal consistency. MarkdownNote blocks inside the graph annotate each stage so you can adjust prompts, masks, and frame settings with confidence.
howToUse: Load the workflow and verify prerequisites: ensure your OpenAI API key is configured for the OpenAIGPTImage1 node (node or environment settings) and that SaveVideo can access ffmpeg if required.

STEP 1 – Product Photography: Use LoadImage to import your product reference and an optional background. In OpenAIGPTImage1, write a clear prompt (e.g., lighting, angle, surface). Connect the product image (and background if used), set the target size/aspect, then run. Review outputs and SaveImage the best results.

STEP 2 – Edits with Masking: Right-click the image feeding the mask input on OpenAIGPTImage1 and choose Open Mask Editor. Paint only the regions you want to change (e.g., remove stand, refine shadows, swap backdrop), refine the prompt, and re-run. Use ImageCompare to evaluate before/after and SaveImage the approved version.

Optional – Batch Variations: To test multiple backdrops or crops, assemble them with ImageBatchMulti and route the batch into OpenAIGPTImage1. Lock the seed if you want product geometry to stay consistent across backgrounds.

STEP 3 – Product Video: Pick two stills as your start and end keyframes (for example, the raw product shot and the refined hero). Feed them into ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode, set frame count/duration and resolution to match your stills, preview frames, then pass the sequence to SaveVideo to export the final clip.
suggestedUseCases: E-commerce hero images and gallery shots with consistent lighting and clean backgrounds.
Rapid background swaps for marketplace compliance (plain white/neutral) without reshooting.
Packaging refresh mockups to preview new labels, colorways, or finishes.
Short social promo clips that smoothly transition between two product looks.
A/B testing multiple art direction variations (surface, lighting, angle) at scale.

faqItems.question: Do I need an OpenAI account to run this?
faqItems.answer: Yes. OpenAIGPTImage1 calls OpenAI’s gpt-image-1 for generation and inpainting. Add your API key in the node or environment so the requests can authenticate.

faqItems.question: How do I limit edits to specific areas of the product image?
faqItems.answer: Use the mask editor on the OpenAIGPTImage1 mask input. Paint only where changes should happen. The node respects the mask and leaves unmasked regions intact.

faqItems.question: How is the video clip generated from stills?
faqItems.answer: ByteDance2FirstLastFrameNode takes a first and last frame and synthesizes in-between frames to create a smooth transition. Then SaveVideo encodes the sequence to a video file. Keep both keyframes at the same size and aspect ratio for best results.

faqItems.question: Any tips to keep logos and product geometry consistent?
faqItems.answer: Be explicit in your prompt (brand, model, material), keep masks tight to the areas you’re changing, and lock the seed when batching variations. Avoid extreme prompts that could alter core product shape.

f4e29143100c.title: Storyboard To Video - Seedance 2.0
f4e29143100c.description: Generate an 8-panel storyboard from a simple text prompt, then use that storyboard as the foundation for Seedance 2.0. The storyboard provides a visual blueprint for the sequence, allowing you to guide the video with more control over the action, camera angles, composition, and overall storytelling.
f4e29143100c.metaDescription: Generate an 8-panel storyboard from text and animate it with Seedance 2.0. Plan shots, control camera moves, and export guided videos in ComfyUI.
f4e29143100c.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a plain-language scene description into an 8‑panel storyboard and then animates that plan with Seedance 2.0. Inside the Previs Storyboard Generator group, your text is processed through LLM/image nodes (GeminiNode and OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2), with StringConcatenate assembling structured per‑panel prompts. The generated frames are arranged into a single contact sheet with ImageStitch, previewed via PreviewAny, and saved by SaveImage. This gives you a fast visual blueprint—shot order, camera angles, and composition—before you ever render a video.

When you’re happy with the board, switch to the Seedance Video group. There, ByteDance2ReferenceNode uses the storyboard image (selected through the Image input) as a visual guide to drive motion and style while generating the clip. You can monitor progress with PreviewAny and export the final result with SaveVideo. The workflow relies on ComfyUI’s group bypass toggles so you can iterate on the storyboard first, then hand it off cleanly to Seedance 2.0 for animation—keeping creative control through every step.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI. Ensure required nodes are installed and configured: GeminiNode, OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2, and ByteDance2ReferenceNode (Seedance 2.0). Add any needed API keys for Gemini/OpenAI per their node docs.

Bypass the Seedance 2.0 group (right‑click the group > Bypass Group Nodes). In the Previs Storyboard Generator group, enter a clear scene description covering subject, action, setting, and camera intent (e.g., wide, dolly‑in, close‑up). Run the graph to generate the 8‑panel storyboard.

Review the storyboard in PreviewAny. If needed, refine your description (or any text fields feeding StringConcatenate) and re‑run until the panels match your narrative and framing. The stitched board is saved via SaveImage.

Switch to animation: bypass the Previs Storyboard Generator group and remove bypass on the Seedance 2.0 group. In the Seedance group’s Image selector, pick the stitched 8‑panel storyboard you just saved.

Adjust any exposed controls in ByteDance2ReferenceNode as needed (e.g., motion characteristics or how strongly the reference guides the look), then run the graph to generate video. Monitor progress with PreviewAny.
Export the final clip with SaveVideo. If motion or framing needs adjustment, iterate: tweak your storyboard prompt for clearer composition cues, regenerate panels, and re‑run Seedance 2.0.
suggestedUseCases: Previsualization for short films, ads, or social posts where quick shot planning and coherent motion are critical.
Animatics and motion tests for story beats: lock composition in a board, then preview timing and movement with Seedance 2.0.
Explainer or tutorial videos: outline a multi‑step process in the storyboard, then animate for clarity and engagement.
Game or UX concept pitches: show camera flow and key interactions via a guided, storyboard‑driven clip.
Music video ideation: block out beats and transitions across eight panels, then animate to evaluate visual rhythm.

faqItems.question: Do I need API keys or extra models to run this?
faqItems.answer: Yes. OpenAIGPTImageNodeV2 and GeminiNode require valid API keys configured per their node instructions. The Seedance 2.0 step runs through ByteDance2ReferenceNode, which must be installed and properly set up. Verify all nodes load without errors before running.

faqItems.question: Can I use my own storyboard instead of generating one?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Use LoadImage to bring in a custom storyboard (e.g., a contact sheet) and feed that into the Seedance 2.0 group’s Image input. You can bypass the Previs Storyboard Generator group when doing this.

faqItems.question: How can I get better control over camera angles and pacing?
faqItems.answer: Be explicit in your scene description and any prompt text feeding StringConcatenate: include per‑panel cues like “Panel 1: wide establishing shot,” “Panel 2: medium tracking right,” etc. High‑contrast, well‑framed panels improve guidance. If exposed, increase the reference influence in ByteDance2ReferenceNode for closer adherence to the board.

faqItems.question: The video doesn’t match my storyboard closely. What should I try?
faqItems.answer: Check that the Seedance group’s Image input points to the stitched 8‑panel board you generated. Strengthen visual cues in the storyboard (clean silhouettes, consistent style), refine prompt text for composition clarity, and, if available, raise the reference guidance in ByteDance2ReferenceNode. Iterate until framing and motion align.

f4e6a39713e4.title: Recraft: Color Control Image Generation
f4e6a39713e4.description: Generate images with custom color palettes and brand-specific visuals using Recraft.
f4e6a39713e4.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate brand-consistent images in ComfyUI with Recraft using custom RGB palettes, switchable styles, and optional SVG vectorization.
f4e6a39713e4.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow uses Recraft partner nodes to generate images from text prompts while enforcing a custom color palette. At its core, RecraftTextToImageNode handles image synthesis, with style presets provided by RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration, RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage, and RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster. You define brand or project colors with one or more RecraftColorRGB nodes, then route them through RecraftControls to guide how strictly the model adheres to your palette. The final raster output is written with SaveImage. Note: in this integration the seed only controls whether a node re-runs; it does not make results deterministic.

For vector-ready deliverables, the optional "Convert into SVG (need credits)" group passes the generated image to RecraftVectorizeImageNode and saves scalable output via SaveSVGNode—ideal for logos and flat illustrations. MarkdownNote nodes in the graph provide in-workflow guidance and links to the Recraft API tutorial and partner node overview. Because these are API-backed nodes, you must run in a secure environment (localhost or 127.0.0.1 for local testing, or https for web contexts) with working connectivity to the Recraft service.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and confirm your environment meets the API requirements: run locally on 127.0.0.1/localhost or use an https site, and ensure outbound access to the Recraft API.
Open RecraftTextToImageNode and enter your prompt (and any negative prompt, if available). If your node requires credentials, add your Recraft API key or config per your setup.

Choose a visual style by activating one of the style nodes: RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration (stylized), RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage (photo-like), or RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster (flat logos/icons). Make sure the selected style feeds into RecraftTextToImageNode.

Define your color palette: set RGB values in one or more RecraftColorRGB nodes (use multiple nodes for multiple brand colors), then connect them to RecraftControls. Adjust the control weights/parameters in RecraftControls to strengthen or relax color adherence.
Queue and run the graph. The generated raster image is saved via SaveImage to your ComfyUI output folder. Iterate on prompt, style, and palette strength until you’re satisfied.
Optional: For scalable output, enable the "Convert into SVG (need credits)" group to send the raster image into RecraftVectorizeImageNode and save the vector result with SaveSVGNode.
suggestedUseCases: Brand kit visuals: create hero images, spot illustrations, or iconography locked to exact brand colors.
Logo ideation: generate logo raster concepts with RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster, then vectorize to SVG for refinement.
Marketing and social graphics: produce consistent campaign artwork in set palettes for ads, banners, and posts.
UI/UX illustrations: craft flat or semi-realistic product scenes that match product or app color systems.
Product mockups: realistic renders with RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage while constraining key accent colors.

faqItems.question: How do I enforce exact brand colors?
faqItems.answer: Create one RecraftColorRGB node per color and input precise RGB values (convert hex to RGB if needed). Connect them to RecraftControls and increase the control strength/weights to tighten palette adherence. Keep your prompt consistent with the intended palette (e.g., mention "using our cobalt blue and warm gray").

faqItems.question: Why doesn’t the seed make the result repeatable?
faqItems.answer: In this Recraft API integration, the seed is used only to determine whether a node should re-run; it does not deterministically fix the output. For more consistency, keep your prompt, selected style, and color controls unchanged and re-use the same workflow settings.

faqItems.question: Which Recraft style should I pick?
faqItems.answer: Use RecraftStyleV3LogoRaster for flat, bold logo/icon work and strong palette control; RecraftStyleV3DigitalIllustration for stylized, clean illustrations; and RecraftStyleV3RealisticImage for photo-like results. Match the style to your subject matter and desired finish.

faqItems.question: Vectorization fails or incurs charges—what should I check?
faqItems.answer: The "Convert into SVG" group uses RecraftVectorizeImageNode and may require credits on your Recraft account. Vectorization works best on clean, high-contrast images (logos, flat art). Reduce textures/noise in your prompt or switch to the logo/illustration style before vectorizing.

f5199b5121f3.title: Equirectangular HDR Skybox Generator
f5199b5121f3.description: Prompt an environment and generate a equirectangular hdr image to use as skybox or lookdev in game development.
f5199b5121f3.metaDescription: Create stunning HDR equirectangular skyboxes for game development with this ComfyUI workflow using Qwen-Image and SeedVR2 models.
f5199b5121f3.extendedDescription: The Equirectangular HDR Skybox Generator workflow is designed to create high-dynamic-range (HDR) equirectangular images, ideal for use as skyboxes or in look development for game environments. This workflow leverages advanced AI models such as Qwen-Image and SeedVR2, alongside custom nodes like comfyui_essentials and seedvr2_videoupscaler, to produce high-quality, realistic textures. The process begins with the CLIPTextEncode node, which interprets the input prompt to guide the image generation process. The workflow then utilizes the ModelSamplingAuraFlow node to sample the image data, which is further refined by the KSampler and UNETLoader nodes. The VAELoader and VAEDecode nodes play a crucial role in encoding and decoding the image data, ensuring the final output is both high-resolution and visually accurate. Finally, the workflow includes nodes like SaveImage and StringConcatenate to manage output and file naming, ensuring seamless integration into game development pipelines.
howToUse: Load the Equirectangular HDR Skybox Generator workflow into ComfyUI.
Enter your desired environment description into the CLIPTextEncode node as a prompt.
Ensure the Qwen-Image and SeedVR2 models are loaded using the appropriate nodes.
Run the workflow to generate the initial equirectangular image.
Use the seedvr2_videoupscaler node to upscale the image to 4K resolution.
Save the final HDR image using the SaveImage node for use in your game development project.
suggestedUseCases: Creating realistic skyboxes for open-world games.
Developing immersive environments for virtual reality experiences.
Enhancing look development in game design with high-quality textures.
Generating HDR environments for architectural visualization.
Producing custom skyboxes for simulation software.

faqItems.question: What is an equirectangular image?
faqItems.answer: An equirectangular image is a panoramic image format that represents a 360-degree view, often used in VR and game development for creating immersive environments.

faqItems.question: How does the Qwen-Image model contribute to this workflow?

Apply the FILM VFI node to interpolate frames and increase the frame rate.

Preview and export the enhanced video for use in your projects.

f83ee3caa04e.title: Wan 2.2 5B Video Generation
f83ee3caa04e.description: Fast text-to-video and image-to-video generation with 5B parameters. Optimized for rapid prototyping and creative exploration.
f83ee3caa04e.metaDescription: Tutorial: Generate text-to-video and image-to-video in ComfyUI with Wan 2.2 5B. Load models, set prompts, choose frames, and render fast prototype clips.
f83ee3caa04e.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI workflow demonstrates fast, high-quality text-to-video and image-to-video generation using the Wan 2.2 5B model. It wires together the essential building blocks: UNETLoader loads the Wan2.2 diffusion backbone, CLIPLoader and CLIPTextEncode turn your positive and negative prompts into conditioning, and ModelSamplingSD3 configures the sampler so KSampler can produce temporally consistent latents. For pure text-to-video, the diffusion model starts from noise; for image-to-video, Wan22ImageToVideoLatent injects structure and motion cues from a source image to initialize or steer the sequence.

Once frames are synthesized in latent space, VAELoader brings in the Wan 2.2 VAE and VAEDecode turns latents into RGB frames. CreateVideo assembles those frames at your chosen FPS and length, and SaveVideo writes the final clip to disk. The workflow is organized into helpful groups: Step1 - Load models to point at wan2.2_ti2v_5B_fp16.safetensors and wan2.2_vae.safetensors, Step3 - Prompt to edit text conditioning, a Video Size & length group to set resolution and frame count, and a For i2v, use Ctrl + B to enable branch that converts a still image into a moving shot. It’s optimized for rapid prototyping—tweak prompts, steps, and sizes, then iterate quickly to explore ideas.
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI, then open the group Step1 - Load models. Point UNETLoader to wan2.2_ti2v_5B_fp16.safetensors (models/diffusion_models) and VAELoader to wan2.2_vae.safetensors (models/vae). The CLIPLoader node will load automatically if bundled with the model.
Open Video Size & length. Choose width/height (use multiples of 16 for speed/compatibility), set the number of frames and your target FPS. Lower resolutions and fewer frames render faster.

In Step3 - Prompt, enter your positive prompt and negative prompt (via CLIPTextEncode). Use clear subject, environment, and motion cues (e.g., 'handheld, gentle camera drift'). Include quality filters in the negative prompt to avoid artifacts.

Choose generation mode: For text-to-video, leave the i2v branch bypassed. For image-to-video, drop a reference image into LoadImage, then select the For i2v, use Ctrl + B to enable group and press Ctrl+B to un-bypass that path. Adjust Wan22ImageToVideoLatent strength to control how strongly the source image guides motion and appearance.
Fine-tune synthesis in KSampler: set steps, guidance (CFG), and seed. ModelSamplingSD3 is pre-wired to ensure compatible sampling for Wan 2.2—keep it connected as provided.
Queue the workflow. Preview decoded frames from VAEDecode if desired, then let CreateVideo assemble the sequence and SaveVideo write the final file. Check SaveVideo for the output path and filename.
suggestedUseCases: Concept previz and mood films: quickly iterate on look, setting, and motion from simple text descriptions.
Motion posters and social loops: generate short, looping visuals with stylized prompts.
Image-to-video treatments: add subtle camera or subject motion to static key art or storyboards.
Product or character showcases: turn a still into a short reveal or turntable-style clip.
Animation blocking: explore timing, framing, and motion beats before full production.

faqItems.question: Where do I put the model files, and which files are required?
faqItems.answer: Place wan2.2_ti2v_5B_fp16.safetensors in ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models and wan2.2_vae.safetensors in ComfyUI/models/vae. In Step1 - Load models, point UNETLoader to the diffusion model and VAELoader to the VAE. CLIPLoader will load the paired text encoder.

faqItems.question: How do I switch between text-to-video and image-to-video?
faqItems.answer: For text-to-video, keep the i2v branch bypassed. For image-to-video, load your image into LoadImage, then go to the group labeled For i2v, use Ctrl + B to enable and press Ctrl+B to un-bypass that branch. Use Wan22ImageToVideoLatent’s strength to set how much the source image influences the motion and look.

faqItems.question: My video looks too static or too jittery. How can I improve motion?
faqItems.answer: Increase frames or adjust prompts to include motion cues (e.g., slow pan, gentle breeze). For i2v, raise or lower Wan22ImageToVideoLatent strength to balance faithfulness vs. motion. Try more sampling steps or tweak guidance (CFG) for better temporal coherence, and refine your negative prompt to suppress unwanted artifacts.

faqItems.question: What performance or VRAM tips should I follow?
faqItems.answer: Start small and scale up: use lower resolution (e.g., 640×360), fewer frames, and moderate steps for quick drafts. Keep batch size at 1. Use the fp16 model provided. If you hit memory limits, further reduce width/height or frame count. Higher resolutions and longer clips increase VRAM and render time.

faqItems.question: Where are videos saved, and is audio supported?
faqItems.answer: SaveVideo controls the output path and filename; open that node to see or change where the MP4 is written. The workflow outputs silent video—audio is not generated.

f889bba5102a.title: Qwen Image: Gummy Animals LoRA
f889bba5102a.description: Apply a Qwen Image LoRA to transform any subject into a sour gummy candy-style character. Enter an animal name in the prompt to generate a stylized, edible-looking creature.
f889bba5102a.metaDescription: ComfyUI tutorial: Apply a Qwen-Image LoRA to turn any animal prompt into a translucent, sugar-coated sour gummy character with controllable style strength.
f889bba5102a.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns any animal prompt into a translucent, sugar-coated "sour gummy" character using the Qwen-Image model with a style LoRA. The core of the graph is a single Qwen-Image generation node (id: e5cfe5ba-2ae0-4bc4-869f-ab2228cb44d3) that handles text conditioning, sampling, and LoRA application, followed by a SaveImage node to write results to disk. Two annotations (Note and MarkdownNote) provide usage tips and a link to ComfyUI’s Subgraph guide so you can encapsulate and reuse the gummy-style block in your own projects.

Under the hood, the Qwen-Image node loads its VAE (qwen_image_vae.safetensors) and text encoder (Qwen 2.5 VL 7B), then injects the Gummy Animals LoRA into the model’s attention layers. This low‑rank adaptation steers the base model toward a consistent sour-candy aesthetic without retraining the full network. You control the look through the prompt (e.g., "a chubby corgi, translucent sour gummy, sugar crystals") and standard generation parameters like steps, guidance, resolution, seed, and the LoRA strength, allowing you to balance style intensity against subject fidelity. The SaveImage node captures final frames to your ComfyUI/output folder for quick iteration.
howToUse: Load the workflow JSON in ComfyUI. If you run locally, download the required Qwen-Image assets first: place qwen_image_vae.safetensors in your models/vae directory and install the Qwen-Image extension as documented for your setup. Ensure the Gummy Animals LoRA is available in your LoRA/models folder.

Open the Qwen-Image generator node (id: e5cfe5ba-2ae0-4bc4-869f-ab2228cb44d3). Enter an animal subject in the prompt (e.g., "red panda, translucent sour gummy, sugar crystals, soft backlight, studio photo on white background"). Optionally add a brief negative prompt (e.g., "fur, realistic skin, text watermark, logo").

Set the LoRA strength to control style intensity. Start around 0.7–1.0 for a strong candy look; lower values preserve more of the base model’s realism, higher values push a very stylized, fully gummy appearance.

Adjust generation parameters: resolution (e.g., 768×768 for a clean single subject), steps (e.g., 20–30), guidance scale (moderate values keep colors vibrant without oversaturation), and seed (fixed for reproducibility, -1/random for exploration).

Click Queue Prompt. Inspect the output in the ComfyUI viewer and in your ComfyUI/output directory (written by the SaveImage node). Iterate: tweak wording (add "translucent," "sugar-coated," "granulated surface"), adjust LoRA strength, and refine guidance until the texture and translucency read clearly.
Optional: Wrap the Qwen-Image + LoRA block as a Subgraph (see the included Markdown note’s Subgraph guide) to reuse this gummy-style module in other workflows or batch pipelines.
suggestedUseCases: Toy and candy concept mockups: generate mascot-like gummy animals for packaging studies.
Stickers and emojis: bright, stylized gummy creatures with clean backgrounds for easy cutouts.
Children’s content and classroom visuals: friendly, edible-looking animals for posters and slides.
Social posts and thumbnails: eye-catching, colorful gummy pets to boost engagement.
Printables and merch previews: quick exploration of colorways and poses before vector cleanup.

faqItems.question: Do I need specific model files to run this locally?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Install the Qwen-Image ComfyUI extension and download its assets. Place qwen_image_vae.safetensors in models/vae and ensure the Qwen text encoder (Qwen 2.5 VL 7B) is installed per the extension’s instructions. Put the Gummy Animals LoRA in your LoRA/models directory so the generator node can load it.

faqItems.question: How do I control how “gummy” the result looks?
faqItems.answer: Use the LoRA strength and prompt wording. Higher LoRA strength yields a stronger translucent, sugar-coated look. In the prompt, include descriptors like "translucent," "sour gummy," "sugar crystals," and "backlit." Reduce strength or remove candy-specific terms if the style overpowers the subject.

faqItems.question: Can I use non-animal subjects?
faqItems.answer: The LoRA is tuned for animals and works best when the subject is an animal (e.g., dog, cat, horse). It may produce interesting results with other nouns, but consistency and anatomy are most reliable with animal prompts.

faqItems.question: My images look muddy or not translucent. How can I fix that?
faqItems.answer: Try a brighter, high-key setup: add "on white background," "studio lighting," and "soft backlight" to the prompt. Increase LoRA strength slightly, raise steps for more detail, and keep guidance moderate to prevent oversaturation. Also try simpler compositions (single subject, centered) at 512–768px for crisper material cues.

f8cf4feac2e9.title: Expand Image
f8cf4feac2e9.description: Extend your image by filling in the surrounding scene.
f8cf4feac2e9.metaDescription: Outpaint a single photo to any aspect ratio without cropping. Auto- or hand-written captions guide Qwen Image Edit 2511 to extend the scene realistically.
f8cf4feac2e9.extendedDescription:
Expand Image is a guided outpainting workflow that grows a single photo to any target aspect ratio without cropping or distorting the original pixels. It wraps your image in a flat green matte to reach the new canvas size, then uses Qwen Image Edit 2511 to replace only the green area with believable scene continuation. Core utility nodes—GetImageSize, ImageResizeKJv2, CustomCombo, and ComfyNumberConvert—calculate the new dimensions and margins so the source stays centered and untouched while the surrounding frame becomes the editable region.

To keep the new content on-style and on-topic, the workflow can automatically write a scene-continuation caption for the missing region using TextGenerateLTX2Prompt and a local VLM backend (configured by you), then JsonExtractString parses the result. A ComfySwitchNode lets you flip between that auto caption and a manual description you type in PrimitiveStringMultiline. The final instruction is assembled with StringConcatenate and, together with CLIPLoader (for text conditioning when required), guides Qwen Image Edit 2511 to synthesize lighting, materials, and perspective that match the visible photo. PreviewAny and ImageCompare help you evaluate changes, and SaveImageAdvanced stores the outpainted result and metadata for reproducibility.
howToUse: Load the workflow and drop your image into the LoadImage node. Use PreviewAny to confirm the source looks correct.

Set your target canvas in the size controls (PrimitiveNode numbers feeding ImageResizeKJv2 or related inputs). The workflow will add a flat green border to reach this aspect ratio while keeping the original pixels intact.

Choose how to describe the missing region: set the ComfySwitchNode to Auto (TextGenerateLTX2Prompt + JsonExtractString) or Manual (type your description in PrimitiveStringMultiline). If using Auto, make sure your local VLM backend is configured in TextGenerateLTX2Prompt.
Refine the guidance: adjust any base style/context string (PrimitiveStringMultiline). The workflow uses StringConcatenate to build the final instruction sent to the edit model.

Run the graph. Qwen Image Edit 2511 will replace only the green area with a plausible continuation that matches lighting, materials, and perspective. Watch intermediate results with PreviewAny and compare before/after with ImageCompare.
When satisfied, save the output with SaveImageAdvanced. If you want a different framing, tweak the target aspect or your region description and run again.
suggestedUseCases: Extend portrait photos to landscape (or vice versa) for web banners and social headers without cropping subjects.
Turn vertical phone shots into print-friendly sizes by outpainting extra background that matches the scene.
Remove letterboxing by filling blank sides with continued environment for video stills or thumbnails.
Create wider product hero images by expanding the set/background while preserving the original item.
Reformat artwork or photography for posters and slides, keeping composition intact while adding margin.

faqItems.question: Does this change my original pixels?
faqItems.answer: No. The workflow keeps your source image intact and adds a flat green border to reach the new canvas size. Only that green area is replaced during outpainting.

faqItems.question: What if I don't have a local VLM set up for auto captions?
faqItems.answer: Set the ComfySwitchNode to Manual and type your continuation description in PrimitiveStringMultiline. You can still get excellent results by describing surfaces, lighting, perspective, and what should extend into the green area.

faqItems.question: How do I get more controlled results?

f9cffe716495.title: Wan2.1 VACE Text to Video
f9cffe716495.description: Transform text descriptions into high-quality videos. Supports both 480p and 720p with VACE-14B model.
f9cffe716495.metaDescription: ComfyUI Wan2.1 VACE text-to-video tutorial: generate 480p/720p clips, tune LoRA for speed, and export MP4/WEBP with clear, step-by-step guidance.
f9cffe716495.extendedDescription:
This workflow turns a short text prompt into a coherent video using Wan 2.1 VACE. It encodes your prompt with CLIPLoader + CLIPTextEncode, then drives the Wan VACE UNet (UNETLoader) through a diffusion loop (KSampler) configured for the model’s sampling behavior via ModelSamplingSD3. The WanVaceToVideo node handles time-aware latent generation, and TrimVideoLatent lets you shorten or crop the sequence to an exact frame count. After sampling, VAELoader + VAEDecode convert latents into RGB frames. Finally, CreateVideo compiles frames and SaveVideo writes MP4 output; SaveAnimatedWEBP is provided for lightweight previews.

Two model sizes are supported: VACE-14B (higher quality, slower; 480p and 720p) and VACE-1.3B (faster; 480p only). The graph is organized into clear groups: Load models here, Prompt, Sampling & Decoding, Save Video (Mp4), and Save Video (WebP), plus separate 14B and 1.3B sections for quick switching. A CausVid LoRA is included via LoraLoader to speed up generation; use it at moderate strength (0.3–0.7) and reduced steps (2–4, cfg ~1.0) for drafts. For best final quality, disable or lower the LoRA and use the default 14B settings (around 20 steps, cfg ~6.0).
howToUse: Load the workflow in ComfyUI and download the models: choose either Wan2.1 VACE-14B (480p/720p) or VACE-1.3B (480p). Point UNETLoader, VAELoader, and CLIPLoader to the matching checkpoints in the Load models here group.

Open the Prompt group and enter your positive prompt in CLIPTextEncode. Optionally add a negative prompt (e.g., the provided Chinese quality filters) in a second CLIPTextEncode wired as the negative conditioning.

Choose resolution and duration: in WanVaceToVideo set your target size (480p or 720p for 14B; 480p for 1.3B) and frame rate. Use TrimVideoLatent to fix the exact number of frames if you need a specific clip length.

Decide on speed vs. quality: to accelerate drafts, enable LoraLoader with the CausVid LoRA at 0.3–0.7 strength and set KSampler to ~2–4 steps with cfg ≈ 1.0. For final quality, bypass the LoRA, and use ~20 steps with cfg ≈ 6.0 on the 14B model.
Run the graph. If motion looks shaky or soft, lower the LoRA strength, add a few steps, or slightly reduce cfg. If content deviates from your intent, adjust the prompt and try a new seed in KSampler.
Export your result: use CreateVideo + SaveVideo to write an MP4 (set fps/bitrate as needed), or SaveAnimatedWEBP for a quick preview loop.
suggestedUseCases: Rapid previsualization for storyboards and animatics from text-only briefs.
Social media teasers or looping b‑roll at 480p for quick iteration, then 720p for final share-outs.
Stylized automotive or product shots using cinematic prompts and film looks.
Mood films and concept reels where negative prompts help suppress artifacts.
Explainer snippets or title sequences where concise motion is more important than long duration.

faqItems.question: Should I use VACE-14B or VACE-1.3B?
faqItems.answer: Use 14B for the best detail and temporal consistency (supports 480p and 720p), but it’s slower and more VRAM‑hungry. Use 1.3B when you need faster drafts at 480p or have limited hardware.

faqItems.question: Why does my video look shaky or blurry with the LoRA?
faqItems.answer: The CausVid LoRA trades some fidelity for speed. Try lowering LoRA strength to 0.3–0.5, increasing steps slightly, or bypassing the LoRA for the final render. Also keep cfg conservative (around 1.0 with LoRA) to reduce instability.

faqItems.question: How do I control length and frame rate?
faqItems.answer: Set fps in WanVaceToVideo, and pick a target number of frames there or finalize it with TrimVideoLatent. For example, 48 frames at 24 fps yields a 2‑second clip. CreateVideo and SaveVideo will honor the fps passed from the pipeline.

faqItems.question: What hardware do I need?
faqItems.answer: Requirements vary by resolution and model size. The 14B model at 720p typically needs a high‑VRAM GPU; 480p on 1.3B is more forgiving. If you hit OOM errors, switch to 1.3B, reduce resolution or frames, and avoid high LoRA strengths.

fa1f01a51d17.title: VOID: Video Inpainting
fa1f01a51d17.description: Upload a video and mask the object you want to remove. Generate a clean video with the object and its physical interactions deleted.
fa1f01a51d17.metaDescription: Remove objects from video in ComfyUI with VOID video inpainting. SAM3 text-guided masks and two-pass temporal fill for clean, consistent results.
fa1f01a51d17.extendedDescription:
This ComfyUI tutorial shows how to remove objects from a video using the VOID: Video Inpainting workflow. The graph is simple and fast to learn: LoadVideo reads your clip, a single VOID inpainting node (c3157b75-484a-459e-b8de-57823bef5130) performs segmentation and temporal inpainting, and SaveVideo writes the cleaned result. A MarkdownNote in the canvas provides inline guidance. Under the hood, segmentation is powered by SAM3 (using the sam3.1_multiplex_fp16.safetensors checkpoint). You can guide what to erase with a text cue encoded by a T5-XXL text encoder, a hand-drawn mask, or both for maximum precision.

Technically, the core VOID node runs a two-pass, temporally-aware inpainting model from the Netflix/void-model project. Pass one removes the masked content per frame and estimates plausible backgrounds; pass two propagates structure over time to reduce flicker and preserve motion parallax. This makes it well-suited for real object removal rather than single-frame patching: reflections, shadows, and brief occlusions are handled more coherently across frames. Because it operates in fp16, it balances quality and speed on modern GPUs while keeping memory use manageable.
howToUse: Open ComfyUI, load the provided VOID: Video Inpainting workflow JSON, and confirm the nodes: LoadVideo → VOID inpainting (c3157b75-484a-459e-b8de-57823bef5130) → SaveVideo.
Download the required models for local use: sam3.1_multiplex_fp16.safetensors to your checkpoints folder and the t5xxl_fp16 text encoder to text_encoders. Restart ComfyUI so the node can find them.
In the LoadVideo node, select your source clip. Keep the original frame rate and resolution if possible; lower resolutions render faster but may lose fine detail.

In the VOID inpainting node, define what to remove: enter a clear text cue (e.g., "red umbrella" or "boom mic"), provide a binary mask if you have one, or combine both (text for detection, mask for refinement). Adjust mask softness/feather and temporal consistency/window settings to reduce edge artifacts and flicker.
Execute the workflow. Inspect intermediate previews from the VOID node if available; if remnants persist, expand the mask, increase temporal consistency, or refine the text cue to be more specific.
When satisfied, set output path and encoding options in SaveVideo and run the final render. If you need audio, remux the original track onto the rendered video in your NLE or with ffmpeg.
suggestedUseCases: Remove a boom mic or crew gear from moving shots without per-frame painting.
Clean distracting passersby or vehicles from travel or documentary footage.
Logo or brand anonymization on moving subjects (e.g., shirts, cars) across entire clips.
Erase small props or signage for continuity fixes in narrative edits.
Restore archival footage by removing scratches or tape markers that persist across frames.

faqItems.question: Do I need to paint a mask, or can I work from text only?
faqItems.answer: You can do either. The VOID node supports text-guided segmentation via T5-XXL + SAM3 for quick selection, a hand-painted binary mask for precision, or both together (use text to localize and a mask to refine edges).

faqItems.question: How does this keep results stable across frames?
faqItems.answer: VOID uses a two-pass, temporally-aware inpainting process. The first pass removes the target per frame; the second propagates structure over time to reduce flicker and preserve motion cues. If you still see jitter, increase temporal consistency/window and soften mask edges.

faqItems.question: What if the result leaves faint shadows or reflections?
faqItems.answer: Expand the mask slightly (dilation) and add a small feather to cover halos. If using text-only selection, make the cue more specific (color, size, location) or add a manual mask where reflections persist.

faqItems.question: What hardware and performance considerations should I expect?
faqItems.answer: The model runs in fp16 but remains GPU-intensive. Higher resolutions, longer clips, and larger temporal windows increase VRAM and render time. For faster runs, downscale the input, shorten the clip, or reduce the temporal window. Consider chunking by hard cuts; process each shot separately.

faqItems.question: Does SaveVideo keep the original audio?
faqItems.answer: No. SaveVideo outputs a silent render. To keep audio, remux the original track in your editor or with a tool like ffmpeg after export.
